## Preface.

For four years, the final years of his life, I had the good fortune of being able to work alongside **Wilhelm Bousset** <note>1865–1920, a prominent German theologian and scholar of the History of Religions School</note> within the same faculty. Our active interaction provided me with a deep insight into the workshop of his thoughts, and I was filled anew with admiration for the almost inexhaustible abundance of problems that occupied his rich mind. The direction of my own studies brought us together for a mutual exchange in a particular field: the investigation into the history of the earliest monasticism. Although I was thus better prepared than anyone else, I was nevertheless astonished to find in his literary estate such a sum of deep-probing work—not merely disordered building blocks, but firmly joined pieces of craftsmanship that required only a light polishing. The following smaller treatises from this estate have already been released for publication: 1. *The Textual Tradition of the Apophthegmata Patrum* <note>original: "Die Textüberlieferung der Apophthegmata Patrum"; these are the "Sayings of the Desert Fathers"</note>: Commemorative Volume for Harnack, Tübingen, Mohr, 1921, pp. 102–116; 2. *On the Composition of the Historia Lausiaca* <note>A 5th-century work on the early Egyptian monks</note>, the concluding part of an essay published in the *Göttingen News* 1917: *Journal for New Testament Science* 21 (1922) pp. 81–98; 3. *The Hidden Saint*: *Archive for Religious Science* 21 (1922) pp. 1–17; 4. *The Monasticism of the Scetic Desert*: *Journal for Church History* 42, New Series 5 (1923), pp. 1–41.

Already during the printing of these essays, I enjoyed the kind support of Pastor Lic. **Theodor Hermann** in Hirschberg near Diez on the Lahn, whom Bousset had encouraged toward independent work in this field. To an even greater extent, I enjoyed his expert assistance in the publication of the extensive studies, titled *a potiori* <note>Latin: "by preference" or "primarily"</note> "**Apophthegmata**," which I may now present to colleagues in this volume, in the certain expectation of finding a strong resonance among all researchers versed in the history of the earliest monasticism. There is no doubt that Bousset regarded his "Studies" as completed, and the careful verification by Pastor Hermann has shown that he was justified in doing so. With regard to the **Apophthegmata Studies**, Hermann has examined all the works used by Bousset and verified the citations taken from them, except for what the Armenian tradition contains and the **Paulos Euergetinos** <note>An 11th-century monk who compiled a massive anthology of ascetic texts</note>. The latter's work was allegedly not available even in Göttingen, although Bousset (cf. p. 15 note 5) had used it there or borrowed it from there. However, the damage is slight: for, since the citations have proven with few exceptions to be carefully stated, and a mutual check could easily be carried out with the help of the tables, the unverified citations may also be assumed to be reliable. By an unfortunate coincidence, the two other treatises (Pachomios, Evagrius) <note>Pachomius was the founder of Christian cenobitic (communal) monasticism; Evagrius Ponticus was a highly influential ascetic theologian</note> only came into Hermann's hands shortly before printing, so that it was not

# Preface.

it was no longer possible to compare all passages; however, this was done wherever doubts could arise.

I need only briefly point to the massive amount of work accumulated in these "Studies." Yet I would like to make special mention of at least the detailed tables and indexes for the *Apophthegmata* <note>original: "Apophthegmata" — Sayings of the Desert Fathers, a collection of spiritual wisdom from early Christian monks</note> (pp. 93–208), because I know with what love and care Bousset sat over them, and what joy it would have given him to see these laborious references—the value of which only an equally qualified expert can fully appreciate—in print. It is important to me, however, to emphasize that the study of the *Apophthegmata* is by no means addressed only to a narrow circle of experts. Rather, the chapter on the time of origin, growth, and value of the *Apophthegmata* literature, and even more so the chapter on its literary and religious-historical significance, brings so much that is new and generally interesting that everyone who cares about the study of Hellenistic minor literature should feel obligated to take note of it. This applies in particular to researchers of the Gospels. It was a pleasure for me to be able to provide these sections for review to my colleague Karl Ludwig Schmidt for his treatise "The Position of the Gospels in General Literary History" in the Festschrift <note>A celebratory volume of essays by various authors to honor a scholar</note> for Hermann Gunkel's 60th birthday ¹). One may read in his treatise what fruitful conclusions he has drawn from them.

In his investigations into the **Life of Pachomius** <note>original: "Vita Pachomii" — a biography of the 4th-century founder of Christian cenobitic (communal) monasticism</note>, Bousset unfortunately overlooked the *Anecdota Oxoniensia* by W. E. Crum ²). The Coptic fragments published there can, of course, only supplement and confirm his explanations. Moreover, we will soon receive a critical edition of the Coptic *Pachomica* by Th. Lefort (Louvain) in the *Corpus of Oriental Christian Writers* ³). The same scholar has recently provided the final proof that the Rule of Pachomius was originally composed in Coptic ³). Regarding the *Life*, he writes: "We do not wish to claim that the Greek recensions of the lives of Pachomius and his first successors are simple adaptations or even translations of Coptic versions; we <note>The quote ends abruptly here as it continues on the next page</note>

2) *Anecdota Oxoniensia* — Semitic Series. Part. XII: Theological Texts from Coptic Papyri, edited with an appendix upon the Arabic and Coptic versions of the Life of Pachomius, by W. E. Crum, M. A., Hon. Ph. D. Berlin. VIII, 205 pp. Oxford 1913. Cf. the content-rich review by Th. Lefort, *Le Muséon*, Ser. 4, vol. 1 (1919). I owe this reference to Mr. Crum.
3) Cf. Th. Lefort, *An original text of the Rule of Saint Pachomius*. Reports of the sessions of the Academy of Inscriptions and Belles-Lettres, 1919, pp. 341–348 and *The Rule of St. Pachomius (Preliminary Study)*. *Le Muséon*, Ser. 4 vol. 1 (1919), pp. 61–70. Three Coptic leaves from the White Monastery (National Library Coptic Codex 129 ¹³ fol. 4–6) contain numbers 87–128 (130? Lefort gives varying information) of the translation by Jerome <note>original: "Hieronymus"</note>, whose reliability is thereby tested. Lefort refers to H. Munier, *Coptic Manuscripts*, Cairo 1916, No. 9250: two leaves, presumably from the 10th century, the text of which corresponds to what Migne, Latin Series 23 Col. 81–84, printed as *precepts and judgments of our Holy Father Pachomius* <note>original: "praecepta atque iudicia S. P. N. Pachomii"</note>. I owe the knowledge of Lefort's treatises to Mr. Crum, who allowed me to inspect them. — He also referred me to the treatise by André Wilmart, *The Latin collection of apophthegms*, *Benedictine Review* 34, 1922, 185 to 198; unfortunately, I have not yet been able to consult it. The book by A. H. Salonius, *Lives of the Fathers* <note>original: "Vitae Patrum"</note>, Lund 1922, has been used in the notes. — Recently, Paulus Bruno Albers has compiled the texts of the Rule and related matters in the 16th volume of the *Patristic Florilegium* <note>original: "Florilegium patristicum" — a collection of excerpts from the writings of the Church Fathers</note> now edited by him (Bonn, Hanstein, 1923). Unfortunately, numerous careless errors and printing mistakes mar this otherwise welcome edition.

# Preface.

...we think that if there exist one or several original Coptic redactions, there was also composed in Greek—based on generally Coptic sources—at least one Greek recension, which was in turn translated and often reworked into Coptic, and is represented in this language primarily by **B** (the Bohairic <note>A dialect of the Coptic language originating in the Nile Delta</note> text of the Vatican Codex 69 edited by Amélineau in the *Annals of the Guimet Museum* XVII [<term>Bousset M</term>; see p. 210]) and in Sahidic <note>The dialect of Coptic used in Upper Egypt</note> by the manuscripts S⁵ and S⁶ (numbers 1, 5, and 4 in the list by <term>M. Crum</term> in *Theological Texts from Coptic Papyri*, Oxford 1913, pp. 183–188)⁴. Mr. Crum, during a kind review, took issue with two minor points in Bousset’s text: first, that it is impossible to date the manuscript of the Theban fragments to the 6th century (p. 221 note 5), since the note cited by Bousset at the end mentions the Saracen era <note>original: "Sarazenenära"—referring to the Islamic era beginning in 622 AD, which proves the manuscript must be later than the 6th century</note>; likewise, the equating of <term>Tsi</term> and <term>Tismini</term> (p. 229 note 1) is inadmissible.

Regarding the <term>Evagrius Studies</term> <note>Investigations into the works of Evagrius Ponticus, a 4th-century Christian mystic</note>, I note that the proof regarding the attribution of the 8th <term>Letter of Basil</term> <note>original: "Basileiosbriefs"—traditionally attributed to Basil the Great, but here argued to be by Evagrius</note> to Evagrius has recently also been successfully carried out by a young Catholic scholar ¹). It is not without interest to compare the work of the beginner with that of the mature researcher; Bousset’s master hand reveals itself clearly in the few powerful strokes with which he has sketched the problem and led it toward its solution ²).

In closing, I would not like to omit expressing my heartfelt thanks to the American, English, Dutch, and Scandinavian scholars for the kind gifts through which they helped initiate the printing of this book. Unfortunately, their support—which was considerable at the time (1921)—very quickly proved insufficient in the face of the collapse of our currency <note>A reference to the hyperinflation in the Weimar Republic during 1923</note>, as the printing could not begin immediately. One must therefore be all the more grateful to the publisher, who selflessly took it upon himself to publish this significant work at his own risk. He has thereby performed a great service to scholarship.

Gießen, October 1923.
->Gustav Krüger.<-

# BOOK I.

## Investigations into the Textual Tradition and Character of the *Apophthegmata Patrum*. <note>The "Sayings of the Desert Fathers," a collection of wisdom and anecdotes from early Christian monks in the Egyptian desert.</note>

### Chapter 1.

### The Various Traditions: Relationship and Value.

### § 1. Cotelier’s Text (G) and the Berlin Manuscript Phillippicus 1624.

The tradition of the *Apophthegmata* literature is astonishingly complex, and the relevant source material is immensely vast. The task here will be to proceed step by step and attempt to first establish some solid points for orientation.

I begin with the most important witnesses of this literature known thus far: the Greek text published by Cotelier in his *Monuments of the Greek Church* <note>Original Latin title: *Ecclesiae Graecae monumenta*</note>, Volume I, pages 338–712 (reprinted in Migne, *Greek Patrology* <note>Original: *Patrologia Graeca*</note>, Volume 65, columns 71–440)¹.

The compiler of this collection states in his preface that he already had many predecessors in his undertaking: "Many people at various times have set forth these sayings and achievements of the holy elders in the form of a narrative, in a simple and unadorned style." <note>Original Greek: πλεῖστοι οὖν κατὰ διαφόρους καιροὺς ταῦτα τὰ τῶν ἁγίων γερόντων ῥήματά τε καὶ κατορθώματα ἐν διηγήματος εἴδει ἐξέθεντο ἁπλῷ τινὶ καὶ ἀκατασκευάστῳ λόγῳ.</note> Since the tradition had thus fallen into total disorder and presented particular difficulties for the memory, he had arranged the material alphabetically by the names of the holy men. Those sayings handed down anonymously were placed "after the completion of the alphabetical sections in chapters" <note>Original Greek: μετὰ τὴν συμπλήρωσιν τῶν κατὰ στοιχεῖον ἐν κεφαλαίοις</note> (probably like

---

1) Cotelier’s manuscript authority was the *Codex Regius 2466* (see Preface). In the margins, it seems, are variant readings from *Regius 2615*. Some deviations are noted from a *Codex Colbertinus* <note>A manuscript from the collection of Jean-Baptiste Colbert.</note>, which became known to the editor only upon the completion of the work (cf. Cotelier 794). — In addition to the Berlin manuscript Phillippicus 1624, which will be discussed in detail immediately, I list the following manuscripts that may come into consideration. No. 351 in Vladimir’s 1894 catalog of the Moscow Synodal Library contains on pages 130–293 clearly the same collection: "A book containing the sayings, that is, the deeds of the holy elders, arranged alphabetically, beginning with the letter Alpha. Concerning Saint Anthony," <note>Original Greek: Βίβλος περιέχουσα ἀποφθέγματα, ἤτοι πράξεις ἁγίων γερόντων, κατὰ ἀλφάβητον, στοιχεῖον ἄλφα. Περὶ τοῦ ἁγίου Ἀντωνίου</note> beginning with Cotelier’s Anthony 1. — Also, *Codex Coislinianus 126*, which will also be discussed in detail below, contains on pages 1–158 an alphabetically arranged collection of the *Apophthegmata* (cf. Nau, *Review of the Christian Orient* 1907, p. 45), and, since *Coislinianus 126* is almost identical to the Berlin Phillippicus 1624, it is certainly the collection published by Cotelier. The *Codex 342* listed in Vladimir contains on pages 1–185 an Alphabeticon with the same prologue that begins Cotelier’s collection ("In this book is recorded the virtuous asceticism..." <note>Original Greek: ἐν τῇ δὲ τῇ βίβλῳ ἀναγέγραπται ἐνάρετος ἄσκησις</note>; cf. *Lausiac History* <note>A 5th-century work on desert monks.</note> edited by Butler, p. 1), but then begins under Anthony 1 with a different saying <note>Original: *logion*</note>: "The ancient fathers went out into the desert and were healed" <note>Original Greek: οἱ ἀρχαῖοι πατέρες ἐξῆλθον εἰς τὴν ἔρημον, καὶ ἰάθησαν</note> (= *Lives of the Fathers* <note>Original: *Vitae Patrum*</note> edited by Rosweyde, Book VII, 35, 2) and concludes with a saying of Ors that is not found in Cotelier. Likewise, Vladimir’s *Codex 343*, pages 1–105, contains a collection that ends with the note "End of the alphabetical book of the elders." <note>Original Greek: τέλος τοῦ κατὰ στοιχεῖον γεροντικοῦ βιβλίου.</note> But the opening saying under Anthony 1 is again different: "The holy Pambo asked the holy Anthony, saying, 'What shall I do that I may be saved?'" <note>Original Greek: ἠρώτησεν ὁ Ἅ. Παμβὰ τὸν Ἅ. Ἀντώνιον, λέγων τί ποιήσω ἵνα σωθῶ</note> (Cotelier, Anthony 6). See also the collection: *Codex 346*, pages 1–103.

# Book I. Investigations into the Textual Tradition and Character of the *Apophthegmata Patrum*.

...[arranged, as] the further investigation will show, according to the principle of topical grouping) we have set forth. Having searched through many books and sought as many as we were able to find, we have inserted them at the end of the chapters. <note>Original Greek: ἐξεθέμεθα. πολλὰ δὲ ἐρευνήσαντες βιβλία καὶ ζητήσαντες ὅσα εὑρεῖν ἠδυνήθημεν, ἐνετάξαμεν εἰς τὰ τέλη τῶν κεφαλαίων.</note> We should note here for our further investigation that the collector expressly claims the newly created alphabetical order of the material as his own original work, but he does not speak as definitively regarding the "chapters" <note>thematic headings or sections</note> of the second part. Whether he already found these chapters in existence or created them himself must remain undecided for the time being.

Unfortunately, this second part is currently lost to us. In the text published by Cotelier, only the *Alphabeticon* <note>the collection arranged alphabetically by the names of the monks</note> is found.

I designate this *Alphabeticon* published by Cotelier as **G** and cite the individual pieces by the name of the respective monastic father and the number assigned by Cotelier (for example, Anthony 8, Arsenius 12, etc.). For names that are more difficult to locate, I have added the page number from Migne’s edition, which is the more easily accessible reprint of Cotelier's work.

First, however, I will discuss another manuscript of the *Alphabeticon* here, to which my attention was drawn by a remark from Nau, and which was the only one I was personally able to examine at this moment. It is located in the State Library in Berlin under the shelfmark Phillipp. 1624, Folios 1–106. The first eight leaves are missing. Consequently, the manuscript only begins with Cotelier’s entry for Isaiah 5. Since the old pagination is partly difficult to read, I cite according to the modern numbering for more convenient reference (thus 1 = 9 through 98 = 106), and I designate the four columns of each double-page leaf with a, b, c, and d. Regarding the content following the *Alphabeticon*—folios 99–114, tales of Daniel of Scetis; 115–240, the *Analphabeticon* <note>a collection not arranged alphabetically</note>; 241 to the end (fragmentary), the *Leimonarion* <note>The "Spiritual Meadow," a collection of edifying stories</note> of John Moschos—these shall be dealt with further below.

The Berlin *Alphabeticon* shows many peculiarities compared to Cotelier's text. First, it offers 38 more pieces than the latter. The Table I B, appended at the conclusion, shows that 36 of these reappear in the parallel witnesses to be discussed below, while only two have not yet been identified by me in any of the parallel traditions. Also preserved for us in B 72 d is the complete text of Pambo 11, which appears only in a mutilated form in Cotelier. The opening here reads: "They said concerning the fathers, Saint Pambo and Saint Bessarion and Saint Isaiah and Saint Paesius, that they were very powerful when they met together with Saint Athre. The presbyter of Nitria asked them..." <note>Original Greek: ἔλεγον περὶ τῶν πατέρων τοῦ Ἁ. Παμβὼ καὶ τοῦ Ἁ. Βεσσαρίωνος κ. τ. Ἁ. Ἡσαΐου κ. τ. Ἁ. Παησίου, ὅτι δυνατοὶ ἦσαν σφόδρα συντυχόντες ἅμα τῷ Ἁ. Ἀθρέ. τούτους ἠρώτησεν ὁ πρεσβύτερος τῆς Νιτρείας κ. τ. ἁ.</note> ¹

Equally interesting are several omissions in B. For instance, Elias 8 is missing here. This *Logion* <note>a short, inspired saying</note> does not originate from the authority Elias of Scetis, but—as is expressly noted in Cotelier’s text—from Elias the Hesychast <note>a "hesychast" is a monk practicing a tradition of inner silence and contemplative prayer</note>, a later authority; it was therefore certainly inserted at a later date. Likewise missing (21 c) are the four sayings of John Kilex, which in the printed text (Migne 233) are inserted after John the Eunuch from John Moschos, chapter 115. ²

1) I place the text here also because it is interesting for its enumeration of the oldest contemporary authorities from Scetis (p. 61). The Presbyter of Nitria <note>Nitria was one of the earliest Christian monastic centers in Egypt</note> is likely Isidore. The wording of the Berlin Codex is confirmed by the Armenian translation, Recension A 1, 19.

2) Probably omitted by chance are: John the Persian 1 (22 d), Karion 1 (28 a), Kopri 2 (28 d), Nilus 10 (50 a), Nisteroos 1 (50 a), Xoios 1 (52 a), Xanthias 2 (52 b), Olympios 2 (52 d), furthermore Poimen 66, 75, 77, (81), 85, 88, 89, (95), 105, 106, 119, 121, 122, 132, 133, 135, 140, 143, 155, 163–166, 172, 178, 179, 187, Sisoes 29, (84 c d), Syncletica 14, Or 9–15. # Chapter 1. The Various Traditions, Their Relationship and Value.

Numerous rearrangements must also be noted. The 187 entries under <term>Poimen</term> <note>Abba Poimen was one of the most frequently quoted Desert Fathers; his name means "Shepherd"</note> are found in the following order (for entries not listed, see page 2, note 2): 1—26. 72. 27—35. 73 (replacing 36). 37—65. 76. 67—70. 74. 80 (81 appears in the later collection 171 a.) 82. 84. 86. 77. 87. 90—94. (95. = 171 a) 96—107. 104—117. 131. 134. 118. 120. 123. 136. 124—130. 145—151. 137. 152—154. 138. 156—162. 167. 168. 139. 169. 170. 142. 171. 173. 141. 174—177. 71 a. 144. 180. 186. In addition (see Table I B below), there are nine new entries¹).

At the conclusion of the collection, following <term>Orsesios</term> 8 (9—15 are missing; see page 2, note 2), stands Orsesios 2 with the introduction: "Abba Hor said to Abba Sisoes" <note>original Greek: εἶπεν ὁ Α. Ὡρ τῷ Α. Σισώη</note> (evidently a corruption of the name <term>Orsesios</term>). Manuscript B shows a trace of an alphabetical arrangement here, according to which Orsesios stood at the end of the series, while the printed text and B itself read "Orsesios" and arranged it accordingly. The arrangement based on the spelling "Orsesios" is followed by the Latin text in the *Lives of the Fathers* <note>original Latin: *Vitae Patrum*</note> V, XI 37 and XV 51.

Finally, I should note that in 42 d regarding Moses 14—18, we find a heading based on a sound tradition: "Seven chapters which Abba Moses sent to Abba Poimen," <note>original Greek: κεφάλαια ζ', ἃ ἀπέστειλεν ὁ Α. Μωυσῆς τῷ Α. Ποιμένι</note> and that in 50 c, the piece regarding <term>Nisteroos</term> "in the community" <note>original Greek: ἐν κοινοβίῳ; referring to a cenobitic monastery</note>²) follows the significantly divergent text of the *Colbertinus Manuscript* <note>original Latin: Cod. Colbertinus</note>.

One can see from this example how confused and multifaceted the textual tradition of the *Alphabeticon* is. I suspect that almost every new manuscript will bring new surprises.

## § 2. The Collection *Lives of the Fathers* V. VI (PJ). (Coptic and Aramaic Translations.)

Closely connected with G <note>the standard Greek Alphabetical collection</note> is a second collection which has hitherto only been available in print in a Latin translation. It is found in Rosweyde’s great collection *Lives of the Fathers* <note>original Latin: *Vitae Patrum*</note> under V and VI³) under the double title: *Words of the Elders by an uncertain Greek author, translated by Pelagius*⁴) *deacon of the Holy Roman Church*—and *translated by John, subdeacon of the Holy Roman Church*. The two translators divided their task in such a way that one began in the middle of a chapter where the other had left off, so that Pelagius Chapter XVIII and John Chapter I can actually only be counted as one; thus, the entire work possessed only 21 chapters rather than 22 (18 and 4).

The corresponding Greek work was still known to <term>Photios</term> <note>a 9th-century Patriarch of Constantinople and renowned scholar</note>. In his detailed description of the work (text in Migne, *Latin Patrology* 73, 851 ff.), he gives its title as: "Book of Holy Men" <note>original Greek: ἀνδρῶν ἁγίων βίβλος</note> and describes it as a summary <note>original Greek: συγκεφαλαίωσις</note> of the so-called "Great Meadow" <note>original Greek: *Leimonarion*</note>⁵).

1) Furthermore, the following are rearranged: (17 b c) Isidor 8. 9 (Migne 221), Jerax 2 is found (21 c) under John the Eunuch 1. (Migne 232). Isidor 3. 4 are rearranged (Migne 236). Macarius of the City 1 (Migne 304) is found (37 c) after Macarius the Egyptian 32 and is accordingly missing from 49 a. After Paul (Migne 380) follows (76 d) Paul the Great 2, then Paul the Cosmite, etc. 84 c d follow one another: Sisoes 31. 28. 30. 89 d missing Serapion 3. 4; 90 c Saio, these pieces are found at 93 d; Saio, Serapion 3 + under Serapion's name John of the Cells (Migne 233, a duplicate); Serapion 4—91 a, Sarah 7. 8 are rearranged. Under Syncletica, the following follow each other: 11. 10. 12. 13. 15. (14 is missing. See page 2, note 2).
2) Compare the note in Migne 287 ³⁴.
3) Printed in Migne, *Latin Patrology* 73. 74. See A. H. Salonius, *Vitae Patrum: Critical investigations into the text, syntax, and vocabulary of the Late Latin Vitae Patrum* (B III, V, VI, VII), Lund 1920, p. 31 ff.
4) That Pelagius was the Pope who ascended the Roman throne in 555 is, after all, only a probable conjecture by Rosweyde (Migne 73, 49). After him, John III reigned from 560—573. He could thus be identical with the subdeacon named here.
5) <note>Original Greek: τοῦ μεγάλου καλουμένου Λειμοναρίου ὃ ἀπαγγέλλει τοὺς βίους καὶ τὰ ἔργα τῶν περὶ Ἀντώνιον τὸν μέγαν καὶ τῶν ἑξῆς ἀκμασάντων.</note> "of the great so-called Meadow, which recounts the lives and deeds of those around Antony the Great and those who flourished thereafter."

<meta>This page continues the technical analysis of the manuscript tradition of the Apophthegmata Patrum. While the previous page focused on the alphabetical collection (Alphabeticon) and the sequence of sayings attributed to Abba Poimen, this page examines the systematic collection (divided by chapters/topics) as described by the 9th-century scholar Photius and preserved in Greek and Latin manuscripts.</meta>

# Book I. Investigations into the Manuscript Tradition and Character of the *Apophthegmata Patrum*.

According to Photius <note>a 9th-century Patriarch of Constantinople whose "Library" provides summaries of many lost ancient works</note>, the work was divided into 22 chapters. The first 19 chapters correspond to the 21 chapters of the Latin translation. Likely due to an oversight, Pelagius III (on compunction <note>original Greek: περὶ κατανύξεως; referring to spiritual sorrow or "piercing of the heart"</note>) was omitted by Photius. Photius 20, "sayings of those who grew old in ascetic practice" <note>original Greek: ἀποφθέγματα τῶν ἐν ἀσκήσει γηρασάντων</note>, is in all probability identical to John IV, where the actual heading has been lost. Photius 21 ("discourses of elders on thoughts" <note>original Greek: διαλέξεις γερόντων περὶ λογισμῶν</note>) and 22 ("maxims of Hesychius, Presbyter of Jerusalem" <note>original Greek: Ἡσυχίου πρεσβυτέρου Ἱεροσολύμων γνῶμαι</note>) were certainly added only later.

The work is also preserved for us in Greek manuscripts. Primarily, I will mention here Codex No. 345 of the Moscow Synodal Library (described by Wladimir on page 505). The work begins with a prologue: "Prologue concerning the life and ascetic practice of our blessed and holy fathers" <note>original Greek: πρόλογος περὶ βίου καὶ ἀσκήσεως τῶν μακαρίων καὶ ἁγίων πατέρων ἡμῶν</note>. (Beginning: "The Word of God, who was in the beginning with God..."<sup>1</sup> <note>original Greek: ὁ ὢν ἐν ἀρχῇ πρὸς τὸν Θεὸν Θεὸς λόγος</note>) page 5. After a second prologue<sup>2</sup>, which does not belong here, the work begins: "Exhortations of holy fathers toward the progress of perfection" <note>original Greek: παραινέσεις ἁγίων πατέρων εἰς προκοπὴν τελειότητος</note> (compare Photius Chapter 1: "contains exhortations toward the progress of perfection" <note>original Greek: παραινέσιν εἰς προκοπὴν τελειότητος περιέχει</note>). The first piece noted by Wladimir corresponds to Pelagius I 1. Then follow 18 chapters from pages 10 to 188, which according to Wladimir are said to correspond to the chapters in Codex 344, pages 1–182<sup>3</sup>. In the description of 344, Wladimir refers in turn to Codex 342, pages 192–340<sup>3</sup>. And here we finally find the headings of the 18 chapters. If one removes some additions from Codex 342, they are identical to those in Photius and Pelagius-John. Even the chapter "on compunction" <note>original Greek: περὶ κατανύξεως</note>, which was lost in Photius, is found here again. They thus correspond to the chapters Pelagius I–XVIII + John I and Photius 1–17. There follows (after two interpolated pieces) on page 189 John 2 = Photius 18 ("on miracle-workers"<sup>4</sup> <note>original Greek: περὶ σημειοφόρων; literally 'sign-bearers'</note>). Then (again after a section that does not belong here<sup>5</sup> on page 200) Photius 20<sup>6</sup> = (?) John IV and Photius 21.

Duensing, in *Christian-Palestinian-Aramaic Texts and Fragments* (Göttingen 1906, p. 15), has pointed to further Greek manuscripts of our work. He notes 1. for the earlier parts of the work, Codex Ambrosianus F. 140 sup.; 2. for the later parts, Codex Vaticanus graecus 1984 and Ottobonianus graecus 174; 3. Codex Marcianus graecus 346. ### Chapter 1: The Various Traditions, Their Relationship, and Value

...thoroughly examined these documents, and thus a precise description of them is lacking in his work. Therefore, the question must remain open as to whether they should all be considered textual witnesses of our work or if some are merely closely related to it¹.

The work follows a straightforward organizational plan. The entire material is arranged into individual chapters according to thematic criteria. Within each chapter, the sayings attributed to famous individuals appear first in alphabetical order, followed by the anonymous pieces. — The Latin tradition consists of 21 (or 22) chapters. Since the organizational system characteristic of the work is no longer found in the final chapter (John IV / Photius 20), and since the pieces in this chapter are not arranged according to a single thematic perspective, this section clearly represents a later expansion of the work. This also proves that Photius 21 and 22 were appended even later, and that Codex Vladimir 345 serves as a witness to this later redaction <note>a specific version or edition of a text</note>.

Thus, 20 chapters (Pelagius I–XVIII + John I–III = Photius 1–19) remain as the older core of the collection. These twenty chapters are also found in the table of contents of Codex Vladimir 342, and both versions of the Armenian translation likewise presuppose these 20 chapters².

However, there is a particular circumstance regarding the last of these 20 chapters (John III). In the Latin version, it bears the very general heading "concerning the excellent way of life of various fathers" <note>original Latin: *de conversatione optima diversorum patrum*</note>, and in Photius, "concerning the God-loving life of various fathers" <note>original Greek: περὶ πολιτείας θεοφίλους διαφέρων πατέρων</note>. This also makes it appear as though a supplement of randomly assembled pieces was added here, especially since no consistent, unified perspective can be discovered in the phrasing of the chapter in John III.

Yet perhaps Codex Vladimir 342 offers the solution to this puzzle. On page 343, it provides the heading for the last chapter (following "concerning sign-bearers" <note>referring to those who perform miracles or "signs"</note>): "concerning hermits" <note>original Greek: περὶ ἀναχωρητῶν</note>. And the first piece of this chapter, which the Vladimir manuscript records with its opening words, is identical to John III 11 (!). Furthermore, Nau³ has demonstrated that a small collection of hermit stories (corresponding to John III 11, 12, 9, and 10) existed independently in a whole series of witnesses and has published the Greek text of these pieces based on them. This collection is also found in the Coislinianus 126 manuscript⁴ (discussed below) under the title "concerning hermits"⁵ before the middle section of the collection of Sayings—that is, the part identical to the anonymous material in the Pelagius/John tradition.

It can therefore be assumed with some probability that John III contained an old collection *about the hermits* <note>original: "περὶ ἀναχωρητῶν"</note>, which followed particularly well after the chapters on the visionaries (Pelagius XVIII + John I) and the *wonder-workers* <note>original: "σημειοφόροι", literally "sign-bearers" or those who perform signs</note>¹. This collection was later expanded by an editor with pieces that did not belong there², making the structure obscure and resulting in a neutral heading. However, it is likely that before this happened, the anonymous stories about hermits detached themselves from the chapter and have led an independent existence ever since. Thus, it remains the case that the "20" chapters formed the original contents of the work under discussion.

We possess a series of Sahidic <note>a dialect of the Coptic language</note> fragments³ of the Sayings, the majority of which were already published by Zoega⁴. With the exception of three of these fragments, the rest (95 folio leaves) represent one and the same work, which corresponds exactly to the structure of the Pelagius-John (PJ) collection⁵. In them, we find a whole series of pieces from Pelagius III, IV, VII, X, XI, XIV, XV, XVII, XVIII, and John I, II, III, IV. There can be no doubt that the PJ collection also existed in the Coptic language. Therefore, the judgment we form regarding the relationship between the PJ collection and the Alphabetical collection (G) will also apply to the Coptic collection.

And finally, Duensing (Christian-Palestinian-Aramaic Texts and Fragments p. 15 ff.) has proven that the Aramaic fragments he deciphered coincide with Pelagius V 28–40 and XIII 9, 13⁶. The first three pieces, however, cannot be identified in our collection. The first is a fragment that has not yet been verified; the second has a parallel in the Berlin Codex p. 172 d⁷; and the third is in the Coislinianus No. 82 (in Nau, *Review of the Christian Orient* 1907, 398). It is therefore questionable, at the very least, whether the collection represented by Pelagius and John was the sole basis for the Aramaic fragments.

For instance, the 7 quotes from *Evagrius* could easily have been added from the extensive *Evagrius* literature ⁵) <note>Evagrius Ponticus was a highly influential monastic theologian whose works were sometimes suppressed due to controversy, but his practical sayings remained popular.</note>. Finally, that *PJ* knows five *Poimen* pieces ⁷) not found in *G* is understandable given the massive amount of material handed down from this *Abba* <note>Abba means "Father," a title for a respected elder monk. Poimen is the most frequently cited monk in these collections.</note> (cf. the differences between *Cotelier’s* text and the Berlin manuscript mentioned above). Based on this compilation ⁸), the result already seems to be that *PJ* is an excerpt from *G* and that *G* is essentially the only primary source for *PJ*.

This preliminary result can now be proven with complete certainty. For the purpose of proof, let us first consider the following:

Suppose that *G* were dependent on *PJ*; this dependency would have to be expressed by *G* presenting the subject matter under individual alphabetically arranged names in the same order as the chapters of *PJ*. Under every single Father from whom more extensive sayings are preserved, one would have to encounter the thematic order of *PJ* *in miniature* <note>original: "in nuce", literally "in a nutshell"</note>. However, a glance at *G* shows that this is nowhere the case.

But suppose the author of *PJ* were dependent on *G*; he would likely have proceeded by going through *G* systematically and placing the sayings and stories that fit into the individual chapters *in order*. We should therefore expect that in *PJ*, within individual chapters and for individual Fathers, the numbers would appear in an order corresponding to *G* (even if interrupted). For example, *PJ* 1, 2, 3, 4, 5 would have to correspond to numbers *G* 2, 5, 8, 12, 14 (but not 14, 5, 8, 2, 12 or any other random order). Attention should also be paid to the agreement in alphabetical order between *G* and *PJ*. For in *G*, the alphabetical order was only carried out for the *initial letter*. Within the individual *alphabetical sections* <note>original: "στοιχεία", referring to the sections of the alphabet under which entries were grouped</note>, the arrangement is arbitrary (though the more significant Fathers are placed first). An agreement between *G* and *PJ* in the alphabetical

PJ 48, Syncletica <note>original: "Sygklet."</note>, is found in B 92 d (before G Syncletica 9), then follows 49, a citation from Hyperechius not present in G ⁸); 50 under the name of Hyperechius: Syncletica 11; 51 Orsisios ⁹).

I believe these tables possess a thoroughly convincing evidentiary power. The many cases in which the rule holds true carry much more weight than the nonetheless considerable exceptions. For the former cannot be based on chance. The latter, however, are easily explained by the assumption that the pieces excerpted from G <note>The Greek Alphabetical collection</note> occasionally fell into disorder for the editor, and by the further assumption that he partially encountered a differently ordered text of G—as indeed such a different order actually exists in a number of cases in Codex B. Some pieces missing in Cotelier’s text are found again in B, others in Paulos Euergetinos, who, as we shall yet see, also goes back to G.

Thus we achieve a first important and quite certain result. PJ, in those parts containing the specifically named pieces, was composed on the basis of G; it is therefore a secondary witness. PJ was created by distributing the Alphabetical collection (G) into individual chapters according to thematic criteria and incorporating it along with the anonymous material.

This result is also particularly important for the evaluation of the Coptic fragments mentioned above, which represent exactly the PJ recension. Upon superficial judgment, Coptic fragments of the *Sayings of the Desert Fathers* <note>original: "Apophthegmata"</note> could easily carry the prejudice of being the original tradition. After all, the language of most of the Scetic Fathers from whom the Sayings originate was Coptic and not Greek ¹⁰). Now, however, it follows with compelling—

**Book I. Investigations into the Textual Tradition and Character of the *Sayings of the Desert Fathers* (Apophthegmata Patrum).**

There is evidence that *these* Coptic fragments originate from a secondary reworking of the Greek Alphabetical collection (*G*), meaning they must have been translated from a Greek collection. The detailed proof for this thesis was, incidentally, provided by *Chaîne* in the article cited above through a series of striking linguistic observations (see pp. 559–567), so that the result is secured from all sides. — And what applies to the Coptic fragments naturally also applies to the Aramaic ones. The Coptic and Aramaic versions of the Pelagius and John collection (*PJ cop. aram.*) represent the translations of a secondary adaptation of the Greek collection (*G*)!

### § 4. The Collection of Anonymous Sayings in Coislinian 126 (N) and Berlin Codex 1624 (B).

The material attributed to specific names in the Systematic collection (*PJ*) is thus traced back to its source in an indubitable manner. We may assume that the anonymous material of around 270 items offered by the Latin versions (*P* and *J I—III*) also represents an excerpt from the lost second half of the Greek collection (*G*). This is supported by the fact that the scholar Photios introduces the entire work as a summary <note>original: "apokephalaiōsis"</note> of the "Great Meadow" <note>original: "mega leimōnárion"</note>. This would mean that at least an excerpt of this second part has been preserved for us. Will we be able to further supplement this excerpt, or even rediscover the original contents of the second part of the Greek collection (*G²*)?

A partial answer to these questions is provided by another collection of <term>Apophthegmata</term> <note>Short, pithy sayings or anecdotes from the Desert Fathers</note>, which is currently accessible to me in two witnesses. One witness is the *Codex Coislinianus 126* (10th or 11th century), which François Nau published in the *Revue de l'Orient Chrétien* from 1907 onwards. The first half of the manuscript (folios 1–138) contains Cotelier's Alphabetical collection, followed by the text published by Nau. Nau numbered the individual pieces of the collections consecutively¹, and from now on, I will cite these numbers as N 1, 2, 3, etc. At the end, from number 393 onwards, Nau provides only a selection from the text, though he maintains the consecutive numbering (393–400).

Fortunately, thanks to Nau’s own reference², I was put in a position to gain a clearer picture of the final part of this collection, which Nau had only treated in excerpts. This second witness is the Berlin *Codex Phill. 1624*, the Alphabetical collection of which I have already discussed above. In this manuscript, the Alphabetical collection is followed first by the stories of Daniel of Scetis <note>An influential monk and superior in the Egyptian desert during the 6th century</note>, and then by the collection corresponding to *Coislinianus 126*.

As a comparison with Nau’s edition (N) shows, the Berlin manuscript is preserved very fragmentarily at the beginning³, but it becomes increasingly complete as the text progresses. # Book I. Investigations into the Textual Tradition and Character of the *Sayings of the Fathers*.

**Concerning Hermits** <note>original Greek: "perì anachōrētōn"</note> appears at the beginning of the middle section before N 133. The remaining numbers, which in PJ <note>PJ refers to the systematic Latin collection translated by Pelagius and John</note> were perhaps only added later, are found once again completely scattered throughout our collection $^1$). Only a small number of pieces from PJ have been omitted entirely. And this deficit $^2$) in N will be due, in part, merely to chance—that is, to the negligence of a scribe. For instance, two of the missing numbers appear in their proper place in B, despite the fragmentary character of that manuscript $^3$).

At the same time, however, an important observation must be made: several other numbers from PJ are missing in the middle section of N. Instead, they are found at other points in the collection, either before or after $^4$). Alongside these are several cases in which a number from our section recurs in the rest of the collection, and thus a duplicate exists $^5$).

From these facts alone, one gains the distinct impression that the work N = B grew out of at least two previously independent sections—the middle part and the remaining pieces—and that the duplicates contained in the various sections were then partially eliminated (thus creating the gaps in the parallel with PJ) or partially overlooked and allowed to remain.

And this suspicion is now confirmed by the character of the entire collection. It is visibly a work of secondary compilation. One must assume that the anonymous material from PJ once became detached; that is, the artistic connection in which the editor of PJ had brought the **Alphabeticon** <term>Alphabeticon: a collection of sayings arranged alphabetically by the name of the monk to whom they are attributed</term> into a thematic order was dissolved again. The form of the Alphabeticon, in which one could find each dictum of an individual monk relatively quickly, was preferred over the new attempt in PJ. Thus, there was a return to the system of the Alphabeticon, and the anonymous material was added to it. Since this material appeared too meager, the collection was supplemented at both the beginning and the end from another collection or several collections by about 500 numbers. Thus arose the work as it exists in B and N alongside the Alphabeticon, with about 800 numbers in total. The question arises as to where the editor of BN <note>BN refers to the tradition represented by the Berlin and Nantes/Coislin manuscripts</note> borrowed the material that exceeded what was in PJ. Hardly from the second part of G <note>G refers to a different group of manuscripts</note> which is lost to us (the **Great Meadow** <note>original Greek: "méga leimōnárion"</note>). For its author indicates to us (pp. 1/2) that he arranged the anonymous sayings (consistently) in chapters. Yet, in the surplus material of BN, nothing of an actual chapter arrangement is to be discovered. Furthermore, it is not clear why our editor, if he had such a uniform and extensive collection of anonymous sayings before him as must have existed in G$^2$, would have preferred such an artificial compilation process over simple copying $^6$). ### § 5. The Connection of NB with Later Collections: The Tales of Daniel of Scetis, John Moschus, the Paris Manuscript 1596, and the Tales of Anastasius.

In **B**, as already noted, the tales of **Daniel of Scetis** $^1$)—a collection of eleven legends that could not have been written earlier than the end of the 6th century $^2$)—stand between the *Alphabetical Collection* and our work. The text contains numbers 3, 4, 5 $^3$), 6 $^4$), 2 $^4$), 10, 7, and 9 of Clugnet’s edition. However, the missing numbers 1 and 11 are found right in the middle of our collection of anonymous **Sayings** <note>original: Apophthegmata</note> (No. 1: 218 b, No. 11: 233 c). Here, we see quite clearly how the process of mixing with later material began.

Furthermore, as the fourth piece of the large collection in the **Berlin Codex** (p. 241/249) stands: **The Book of the New Paradise, named the Meadow** <note>original Greek: "hē bíblos toû néou Paradeísou eponomazoménē tò Leimōnárion"</note>. There is a special circumstance regarding the transmission of the work of **John Moschus** presented here. What Cotelier offers in the *Monuments of the Greek Church* <note>original Latin: "Ecclesiae Graecae Monumenta"</note> is only a supplement to a fragmentary excerpt of the complete work as it exists in Migne, *Greek Patrology* Vol. 87 (Latin: Rosweyde, *Lives of the Fathers* X; Migne, *Latin Patrology* Vol. 74). Our manuscript now provides that fragmentary version of Moschus's work which Cotelier supplemented. Thus, **B** and Cotelier together yield approximately the complete text as found in Migne.

# Chapter 1: The Various Traditions, Their Relationship, and Value

"phórion" <note>A term likely referring to a textual fragment or specific contribution; original Greek: φόριον</note> = B 283 a, p. 547–550 the converted Jewish boy in the fiery furnace = B 279 d¹) (with connections to Moschos <note>Johannes Moschos, a 7th-century monk and author</note> both before and after). To this later layer of tradition likely belong the four pieces that appear in B 203 d–204 a under the name of Longinus. All of these are found again in the Armenian translation, and two are also found in the works of Paul the Evergetinos (see Table II, p. 115)²). The pieces concerning Zeno (191 c to 193 a), for which parallels appear in Paul the Evergetinos, also belong here. The mere fact that named pieces appear here amidst purely anonymous material points toward a later tradition, though this perspective is not always correct; in the NB manuscript, genuine ancient material that the G collection <note>G refers to the older, standard collection of the Sayings of the Desert Fathers</note> had overlooked can still be found here and there under specific names.

Finally³) the story B 230 d (concerning the deacon who denied Christ) is identical or at least closely related to piece XLIX in the collection published by Nau under the title "Stories of Anastasius"⁴). Nau is inclined to attribute this circle of stories to Anastasius of Sinai. If this is not a coincidental connection (such as dependence on a common older source), and if B does not contain a later interpolation, then the time of composition for our collection would reach at least until the end of the 7th century. However, even if we set this aside, based on all the observations made, the collection as it stands can hardly have originated before the first half of the 7th century—a date that is quite distant from the golden age of the Scetic Fathers <note>Monks living in the Scetis valley of Egypt during the 4th and 5th centuries</note>.

# Book I. Investigations into the Textual Tradition and Character of the Sayings of the Desert Fathers.

...is a <term>Asketikon</term> <note>A vast collection of ascetic teachings and rules for monks</note> of the greatest scale. It is divided into four books, each containing 50 chapters. Within these two hundred chapters, material from the most diverse ascetic writings is organized by subject matter. Alongside many others, there appear extensive excerpts from the works of Ephrem, from the *Life of Antony* by Athanasius, the lives of Pachomius¹) <note>original: "Pachom"</note>, Euthymius, Sabas, Syncletica, Arsenius, from the *Lausiac History* of Palladius, from the works of Cassian, Mark the Hermit, the sayings and sermons of the monk Isaiah²) <note>original: "Esaia"</note>, from Diadochos of Photike, from the *Dialogues* of Gregory, and so forth. One of the primary sources for Evergetinos, however, is what he calls the *Gerontikon* <note>A collection of the sayings of the "Old Men" or Desert Fathers</note>, from which he cites approximately 1,250 items³).

We can identify with certainty the *Gerontikon* that Paul Evergetinos cites; it is the *Alphabeticon* edited by Cotelier <note>The standard 17th-century printed edition of the alphabetical Sayings of the Desert Fathers</note> along with the collection of anonymous sayings just discussed. Since Daniel the Scetiote⁴) and John Moschos (see Table VIII) are also utilized, Evergetinos may have had access to a collection similar to the one preserved in our Berlin Codex (compare also the structure of the *Coislinianus 126*). According to a rough estimate, at least seven-eighths of the 1,250 items cited from the *Gerontikon* can be traced back to the G + NB <note>The combination of the standard Greek collection and the Berlin additions</note> tradition. But one can assert even more. The method by which Evergetinos produced his compilation can be demonstrated quite precisely. He followed the *Gerontikon* exactly and entered the individual items in their original order into each specific chapter. This becomes clearer the more items are cited by him in succession. I refer to my table for the 45th chapter of the first book (page 277 ff.) or the 2nd chapter of the third book (591 b–598). Here, the sequence of our *Gerontikon* G + NB⁵) still emerges clearly. If fewer pieces are grouped under a single chapter, the evidence is naturally less obvious. Very often, the items are also shuffled together arbitrarily; this is no surprise given such a laborious compilation process and the distribution of material across two hundred chapters. The exceptions even outweigh the rule, yet the cases where this can be established remain nonetheless absolutely decisive. Paul Evergetinos is dependent on a *Gerontikon* that, in content and structure, largely coincides with our work G + NB.

Nevertheless, a "surplus" eighth remains in the work of Paul Evergetinos, and it is unlikely that he himself incorporated new material into the *Gerontikon*. Where might this material have come from? Regarding the approximately 50 cases in which PE <note>Paul Evergetinos</note> stands entirely alone, not much more can be said than that despite all my searching, this or that parallel may have escaped me, and that...

2) See the fragments of Isaiah in Migne *Patrologia Latina* 40.
3) Paul Evergetinos often added a shorter or longer <term>paraenetic</term> <note>Exhortatory or advisory</note> remark of his own to individual items, which then frequently appears with the heading "of the father," or "of the father, that is, of Evergetinos" <note>original Greek: τοῦ πατρός, τοῦ πατρός ἤγουν τοῦ Εὐεργετινοῦ</note>; see pages 599, 652, 792, 794, 846, 914, 1017, 1095. The entire compilation, therefore, seems to have been published in its current form only by the author's students. Such exhortatory remarks are also found without being clearly marked, e.g., 288 c. 483 h.
4) chapter 9: p. 825 a, chapter 11: p. 316, chapter 1: 171 b.

Paul Evergetinos (PE) <note>The 11th-century compiler of the anthology known as the *Euergetinos*</note> evidently possessed a copy of the *Gerontikon* <note>A collection of the sayings of the "Old Men" or Desert Fathers</note> in which he read those specific passages. The most striking feature is the overlap between the unique material in the *Euergetinos* and the two Armenian recensions A¹⁾ and B²⁾, particularly with the complete recension B. There are no fewer than approximately 70 cases in which PE shares a tradition with the Armenian versions A and B that cannot be traced back to the standard Greek alphabetical and "New Berlin" collections (G + NB). Of these, 63 cases relate to Recension B (49 in B alone, 14 in B and A together); additionally, there are 7 or 8 cases where A stands alone. But we have not yet reached the end of the matter. There are further cases where PE overlaps simultaneously with John Moschos <note>An early 7th-century monk and author of the *Spiritual Meadow*</note> and the Armenian translations³⁾. The points of contact that PE shows with the Syriac tradition are far less numerous. PE also shows some points of contact with the tradition of Codex Paris 1596 (see above, p. 14). Thus, a further stock of the tradition present here must have flowed into the redaction of his *Gerontikon*. The process that could already be demonstrated for the "New Berlin" (NB) collection has therefore continued here⁵⁾.

### § 7. The Dependence of Recension B of the Armenian Translation on the Greek and New Berlin Collections.

Our analysis of the collection of Paul Evergetinos has already led us to the Armenian translations, which are closely related to it. In the collective volume titled *The Writings of the Holy Fathers and Their Conduct*, Venice 1855, Vol. I 413–722, Vol. II 1–504, the two Armenian translations of the *Apophthegmata Patrum* are published under the title *Words and Narratives of the Holy Fathers*. The editors employed a somewhat unusual method. They used one of the two translations (A) as the base text, then placed the parallel from the differently ordered Recension B at the bottom of the page for each piece in A. Finally, for each of the 19 chapters of the work, they added the surplus text of B as a single continuous block <note>original Latin: "uno tenore"</note> under the heading *Paralipomena* <note>Things omitted or left over</note>. Consequently, the original arrangement of all the pieces from B that appear as parallels to A cannot be determined from the edition itself. Furthermore, what we have as Recension B (*Paralipomena*) is only a fragment ⁴).

# Chapter 1. The Various Traditions, Their Relationship and Value.
## 2*

Nonetheless, the specific character of Recension B, despite its fragmentary state in the current edition, can be defined with all desirable clarity. The result of this analysis can be summarized in a single sentence: Armenian B (or rather its Greek source) can be traced back to almost exactly the same *Gerontikon* <note>A "Gerontikon" is a collection of sayings and stories of the "Old Men" or Desert Fathers</note> that was also used by Paulos Euergetinos—that is, an expanded copy of the Greek collections G and NB. The only difference is that the compiler of the Armenian version (or its Greek basis) did not scatter the material in question across two hundred chapters, but instead organized it topically into the 19 (or 20) ¹) chapters with which we are already familiar.

In all probability, we even still possess the Greek original of which Armenian B is merely a translation, namely in the *Codices Coisliniani* 127 and 108 <note>Refers to a specific collection of Greek manuscripts held in the National Library of France, originally from the collection of Henri-Charles de Coislin</note>. Nau (in *Revue de l'Orient Chrétien* 1907, p. 44) characterizes these as follows: "they are very often recent compilations of all origins which have refashioned the alphabetical *apophthegms* <note>Short, pithy sayings of the Desert Fathers</note> with others under various commonplaces" <note>original French: "ils sont bien souvent des compilations récentes de toute provenance qui ont fondu à nouveau les apophthegmes alphabétiques avec les autres sous divers lieux communs"</note> (that is, according to the note in that same source, the very familiar chapters listed by Photius—Migne, *Patrologia Latina* 73, col. 852). "One recognizes this by the fact that the fathers cited are arranged in alphabetical order, and that the stories of Daniel of Scetis (6th century) are already merged among the others" <note>original French: "On le reconnaît à ce fait que les pères cités sont rangés par ordre alphabétique, et que les récits de Daniel le scétiote (VIᵉ siècle) sont déjà fondus parmi les autres"</note> ²) Based on this, I consider it very likely that *Coisliniani* 108 and 127 represent the Greek archetype <note>The original manuscript from which others are copied</note> of Armenian B.

However, we return to the accessible text of the Armenian version to prove the proposed thesis in detail. Recension A contains about 875 pieces ³), of which it shares roughly 620 with B. Recension B alone counts about 880 pieces, making a total of approximately 1,500 entries, thus representing one of the most extensive collections. Of these 1,500 entries, about 11/12 can be traced back to the collections G + NB + PE. Of the remaining 1/12 (120–130 individual cases), about half ⁴) is "special material" unique to the Armenian tradition, which I have not yet been able to find in any parallel source. Added to this are a series of pieces from Isaiah ⁵), which could likely be identified in his surviving works (see above p. 16 note 2) with some searching. Daniel of Scetis has been almost entirely incorporated into our collection ⁶). Connections with manuscript 1596 ⁷) are rarer, while those with John Moschus ⁸) are more frequent. The few cases where the Armenian version aligns solely with the Syrian tradition ⁹) deserve special attention. I shall return to them—

# Book I. Investigations into the Textual Tradition and Character of the Sayings of the Fathers.

I will return to this once more during the discussion of the latter ¹). In addition, there are a few other points that would hardly be worth discussing in detail here ²). I would, however, particularly point out the large Zosimus collection ³) found at the end of the first book (1, 142 p. 466–492) and the Sayings of the 12 Anchorites <note>monks who lived in total isolation</note> at the end of the entire work 19, 54 ⁴).

We may therefore rightly judge that the source of Armenian B (or rather its Greek original) is a known quantity for us in all major respects. And not only this. In his division of the entire material into nineteen chapters, the editor also adhered much more faithfully to the sequence of his source than Paulos Euergetinos did with his distribution of the material into 200 sections. Thus, every single chapter offers a faithful reflection of the foundational text used for the excerpts; we were even able to assign the parallels added by the editor of Recension A to their original place in Recension B with great certainty. One peculiarity of his method may be pointed out: he first assigned a place in the Alphabetical Collection <note>The "Alphabeticon," where sayings are arranged by the name of the monk, from Alpha to Omega</note> to the named pieces that were exceptionally found among the anonymous material in the "NB" collection ⁵). Even with borrowings from John Moschus <note>author of the "Spiritual Meadow"</note> and Daniel of Scetis, he followed this procedure, though not consistently. Based on these observations, a further conclusion can be drawn. Namely, if the close connections between Paulos Euergetinos and our Recension frequently appear at the end of each chapter ⁶), it can be inferred that the material these two witnesses preserved in common was once actually found at the end of the expanded edition of G + NB—the version from which both Paulos Euergetinos and the Armenian’s source originated.

Thus, a clear picture of the entire development emerges: at the base lay the older collection: G + NB. This likely underwent a subsequent expansion at the end no earlier than the seventh or eighth century ⁷). Paulos Euergetinos distributed the material into 200 small chapters, while the source of the Armenian Recension B reached back to the well-known classical chapter division and thus brought order to the mass of text.

# Chapter 1: The Various Traditions, Their Relationship, and Value.

### § 8. The Structure of Recension A of the Armenian Translation.

The picture presented by Armenian Recension A <note>A "recension" is a specific version or edition of a manuscript text</note> is not quite as clear. To be sure, there can once again be no doubt that a close relationship exists between it and the manuscript groups G + N + B + PE ¹). Out of its approximately 875 items, only a good fifth (170–180 cases) cannot be traced back to these sources. Its unique material <note>original: "Sondergut," referring to content found only in this specific version</note> is considerably larger than that of Recension B; I count about 80 such cases. These consist of long legends and detailed narratives that likely grew into our tradition quite late, perhaps added only by the Armenian translator himself. Recension B shares in this unique material with only 13 pieces, which are often the smallest and most insignificant. Very often, these large additions appear precisely at the end of a book; see specifically the narratives 5, 76–81; 8, 17 (the second to last piece); 13, 16 (followed by a parallel with manuscript 1596); 14, 17; 19, 28. The borrowings from the *Historia Lausiaca* ²) <note>A collection of biographies of the early Christian monks of the Egyptian desert, written c. 419–420 AD</note> are also a peculiarity of our recension, but above all the numerous points of contact ³) with John Moschos <note>A Byzantine monk and author of the "Spiritual Meadow," a famous collection of edifying stories</note>; compare in particular the entire cluster of Moschos pieces in 18, 24–50. On the other hand, it can already be observed here that the relationship with the Syriac tradition is somewhat stronger than that of Recension B ⁴), and that parallels can also be found in the small Latin collections which have not been demonstrable anywhere else until now ⁵).

The *arrangement* of the pieces within the individual books is entirely arbitrary. Attributed and anonymous material stands haphazardly mixed together. There is no trace of alphabetical order. In this regard, one further observation must be discussed. When we look through the table, a certain relationship in the arrangement of the material between our edition and *PJ* <note>The Latin translation by Pelagius and John</note> becomes apparent. A strikingly large series of items appeared in the same chapters in both (though in *PJ* they appear in the known order, while here they are shuffled together colorfully). Now, this is not particularly surprising for the anonymous material. However, it remains noteworthy in the case of the material attributed to specific names, because the arrangement of this material is specifically the work of the editor working here on the basis of B. Could there be some relationship between *Armenian A* and *PJ*? This question cannot be decided. One would hesitate to answer in the affirmative. The differences between the two sources are simply too considerable, and the possibility remains that if two editors distribute a set of material under the same practical viewpoints, a high degree of agreement in its arrangement must necessarily result.

# Book I. Investigations into the Textual Tradition and Character of the *Apophthegmata Patrum*. <note>The "Sayings of the Desert Fathers," a collection of spiritual wisdom from early Christian monks.</note>

It remains to determine the relationship between the two Armenian recensions <note>A "recension" is a specific version or edition of a literary text</note> to one another. I assume that both arose independently of each other. At first glance, however, the close relationship of their content seems to argue against this. With about 620 of its 875 items—roughly 7/9ths—Recension A is contained within Recension B! Yet this fact is easily explained by the reality that both were crafted upon a common foundation. If one were to assume that A was an excerpt of B, it would be impossible to understand how the beautiful order of the source could have been so thoroughly destroyed here. If B had used Recension A (alongside its main source, of course), it would be unclear why he would have missed out on the many fine long narratives in A and most of the borrowings from John Moschos ¹).

A final judgment on Armenian Recension A must remain in suspense for the time being. The simple formula—that the manuscript groups G + NB <note>Technical shorthand for the Greek and related Latin/Syriac manuscript traditions</note> form the essential basis of this redaction—cannot be established here. While the vast majority of its material can indeed be derived from there, its arrangement remains inexplicable. It remains incomprehensible that, if Armenian A represents a revision of G + NB like Recension B and PE, every trace of alphabetical order and the separation of named traditions from anonymous material would have vanished here. Furthermore, the points of contact noted above with the Syriac tradition and the smaller Latin collections—an observation that will be strengthened in the course of our investigation—cannot be so easily overlooked. However, we would do well to postpone further investigation of this question until we are in a position to survey the entire body of traditional material.

### § 9. The Smaller Latin Collections (Lat.).

The material available to us for the history of the transmission of the *Apophthegmata* is still not exhausted. We now come to the witnesses that possess independent value alongside G and N[PJ]B: namely, the smaller Latin collections and the Syriac translation.

Of the smaller Latin collections, two are very closely related: *Vitae Patrum* III and VII ²) <note>Lives of the Fathers</note>. *Vitae Patrum* III is of anonymous origin and an entirely uncertain date. Rosweyde <note>Heribert Rosweyde (1569–1629), a Jesuit hagiographer</note> erroneously attributed it to Rufinus because of certain echoes in the prologue to Rufinus’s *History of the Monks* ³). Paschasius dedicated his work to "the father Martin, priest and abbot." This Martin is identical to Abbot Martin of Braga <note>also known as Martinus Dumiensis, a 6th-century bishop and monastic founder</note> († 583), whose own small collection belonging here we will also discuss shortly. I designate these two collections as **R** and **Pa**.

**R** contains 220 items in Rosweyde’s edition; some of these contain multiple pieces, so that in total about 240 pieces emerge.

---

1) B contains only about a fifth of the entire unique material of A (see above). If B and A are independent of each other, one may assume that the shared unique material already originated from their common textual foundation.
2) Compare Salonius, *Vitae Patrum* pp. 11–39.
3) Compare Salonius, as cited above, pp. 12–31.
4) Compare Sigebertus, *On the Illustrious Writers of the Church* 118: <note>original Latin: "Martinus episcopus transtulit per manum Paschasii diaconi interrogationes et responsiones plurimas sanctorum Aegyptiorum patrum in Dumiensi coenobio"</note> "Bishop Martin translated, by the hand of Paschasius the deacon, many questions and answers of the holy Egyptian fathers in the monastery of Dume." Compare Rosweyde’s *Prolegomena* chapter XIV in Migne 73, 50. There is also the evidence regarding Martin's date of death. — It is, moreover, not clear whether Sigebertus's remark refers to *Vitae Patrum* VII or to the collection under Martin's name.

### Chapter 1. The Various Traditions, Relationship, and Value.

In Pa <note>A specific manuscript collection, likely the *Collectio Palatina*</note> I count 154 pieces. R <note>Recension R</note> and Pa are, as already stated, closely related. This is proven less by the fact that R and Pa share 72 pieces in common than by the observation that these are found in almost the same order in both collections. Furthermore, it appears from Pa, in which the chapter divisions and headings are preserved, that we are dealing here with a collection organized according to thematic criteria. This thematic arrangement is also presupposed by R, except that in its case everything that outwardly indicates this has disappeared, and the individual pieces follow one another <note>original: "uno tenore"</note> in one continuous flow. It therefore becomes probable that R and Pa represent excerpts from an older collection. Since Pa dates no later than 583 (see above), and both Pa and R represent Greek texts that go back to a common foundation, we possess in R and Pa a witness of our collection of great age and value. Also, the circumstance that we encounter here a thematic order that is completely independent of the canonical 20 chapters speaks for the independent value of the collection.

I will go into somewhat more detail regarding the structure of the collection and its treatment in R and Pa <note>1)</note>. In R 1–43 (with the exception of R 22 and 38), no parallels are found between R and Pa. This section, therefore, likely does not originate from the common source. A certain thematic order is already evident here, which in part touches upon PJ <note>2) PJ refers to the collection of Pelagius and John</note>. R 1–7 could be titled <term>concerning self-restraint</term> <note>original: "de continentia"</note>, 8–16 deal with unchastity, and 17–29 with humility and obedience. There follow, from 31–35, anecdotes intended to illuminate the relationship of the monk to his relatives. Note here the parallel to the *Lausiac History* 31 a and the *Life of Pachomius* 34–35 <note>3)</note>. R 36 (= I* 3) concerning worldly and spiritual conversation stands quite alone. Then follow—contrary to the usual thematic arrangement of the collection—37–40, stories of Arsenius, and 41–43, anecdotes of Macarius.

Now the parallels with Pa begin (R 44 = Pa 1, 1). Pa chapter 1 has the heading <term>against gluttony</term> <note>original: "contra gastrimargiam"</note>. According to the context, this corresponds to R 44–R 66 <note>4)</note>. Pa chapter 2 reads: <term>against the love of money</term> <note>original: "contra philargyriam"</note>, and chapters 4–5 actually belong to it as well, even if they bear their own individual headings <note>5)</note>. It is possible that these smaller divisions, which disturb the overall clarity, were added only later. The parallels extend over R 65–74. Chapters 6–10 also belong closely together, to which one could give the shared heading from Pa 6, <term>against anger</term> <note>original: "contra iram"</note> <note>6)</note>. This corresponds to the section R 76–99. There follows Pa 11, <term>against the spirit of sadness</term> <note>original: "contra spiritum tristitiae"</note> <note>7)</note> = R 100–109; Pa 12, <term>against the spirit of vainglory</term> <note>original: "contra spiritum vanae gloriae"</note>; and Pa 13, <term>against the spirit of pride</term> <note>original: "contra spiritum superbiae"</note>, which is followed by chapters 14–16 <note>8)</note>.

If we pause here for a moment, the organization of these sections is crystal clear despite the many small subdivisions in Pa. The schema followed here is that of the **eight monk-vices**. <note>The "eight vices" or "eight evil thoughts" were a precursor to the seven deadly sins, codified by early monastic authors like Evagrius Ponticus.</note> However, the chapter "on sexual immorality" <note>original Greek: "peri porneias"</note> is missing from the common stock of R and Pa. But R alone offered such a chapter in its first part, sections 8–16. Here, it likely preserved the beginning of the work. We then obtain the eight monk-vices in the following order: **sexual immorality, gluttony, greed, anger, sorrow, spiritual apathy** (see above the remark on R 104 ff.), **vainglory, and pride!** <gloss>1)</gloss> <note>original Greek terms: "porneia, gastrimargia, philargyria, orgē, lypē, akēdia, kenodoxia, hyperēphania"</note>

In the following section, the common source of R and Pa and the logic of its arrangement can no longer be recognized with the same certainty, especially since the two witnesses now begin to diverge again. It is clear, first of all, that the related chapters 17–20 <gloss>2)</gloss> "on the renunciation of one's own will" correspond to sections 141–158. Alongside the eight primary vices, the recommendation of the **monastic cardinal virtue** would then appear here <gloss>3)</gloss>. In this context, there was talk of the blessing of illness and weakness. This might have been followed by thoughts on death. Thus, R has a series of death scenes and words of the Fathers on their deathbeds in sections 159–163. There follow in Pa chapters 21–25, which can be given the common heading "on repentance" <note>original Latin: "de poenitentia"</note> = R 164–167. Again, Pa 25–28 belong together, concerning the struggle against demons and vices, "on perseverance" <note>original Latin: "de perseverantia"</note>, and "on labor" <note>original Latin: "de labore"</note> = R 172–182. It is titled: *Sentences of the Egyptian Fathers, by an uncertain Greek author, translated by Martin of Braga, Bishop of Dumio* <gloss>1)</gloss> <note>original Latin: "Aegyptiorum patrum sententiae auctore Graeco incerto Martino Dumiensi episcopo interprete"</note>. I cite these as **App.** followed by the number.

Finally, we must include here the small supplement **J IV**, which we previously separated from the work **PJ**. It comprises 37 items. I cite it as **J IV** or **IV***.

We shall also attempt to briefly illuminate the characteristic peculiarities of these smaller collections.

What must be emphasized above all is the extraordinarily pure character of this tradition. The unique material <note>original term: "Sondergut"</note> in all these collections is vanishingly small. I count only 8 cases for **R Pa**; in addition, there are 6 cases in **R** alone and 6 others in **Pa** (three of which—10, 2; 15, 4; 28, 2—**Pa** shares with **App.**). Martin of Braga shows only 7 items (including 81 = App.) in which he stands entirely alone.

Added to these are borrowings from the *Lausiac History* (R 31 a, Pa 19, 3–5 a), from the *Life of Pachomius* (R 34, 35), from Rufinus's *History of the Monks* <note>original Latin: "Histor. Monach."</note> (R 41–43), from Jerome (R 218–220), from Cassian’s *Institutes* <note>original Latin: "Instit."</note> XXIV 9 = App 7, from the *Practical Treatise* <note>original Greek: "Praktika"</note> of Evagrius (IV* 16–19), and from the *Life of Syncletica* (IV* 23 = chapter 35).

But that is all. Otherwise, we everywhere encounter material that is already present in **G + N + PJ + B**. A slight overlap of our witnesses with the Armenian and **PE** traditions was already presented above. A stronger relationship with the Syrian tradition will be discussed shortly.

With this overview, however, a final judgment on the character and value of this Latin tradition has not yet been given. The conclusion—that we have before us only smaller fragments from the large collection **G + NB**—would be premature. Arguing against this, as in the Armenian Recension A, is the fact that in all these collections there is no trace of alphabetical order and no separation of named and anonymous material. Furthermore, and most importantly, we find in **Pa** (**R**) a thematic arrangement (and chapter division) that is entirely independent of the one found in **PJ** and the Armenian tradition. — The close relationship of the content of our collections with **G + NB** could just as easily be explained by the assumption that the Latin collections represent, at least in part, the older layer of the tradition of the *Sayings of the Desert Fathers*, upon which **G**, **PJ**, and **NB** were only gradually built. However, this question can only be discussed after we have addressed the last and most important witness for the history of the Sayings: the Syrian tradition.

### § 10. The Various Syrian Traditions.

The most extensive collection of Syrian "sayings" <note>original: "Apophthegmen"</note> that we possess is preserved for us in the great compilation created by the Nestorian monk Ananjesus <note>also known as Anan-Isho</note> in the Monastery of Beth-Abhe (near Nisibis) during the first half of the seventh century. Thomas of Marga (c. 840 AD) provides a brief sketch of his life in his *History of the Monks* <note>original: "Historia Monastica"; also known as the "Book of Governors," edited by Budge, 1892, Book II, Chapter XI</note>. Among other things, he notes that before beginning his literary activity, Ananjesus undertook a pilgrimage to Jerusalem and from there to the fathers of the Scetic Desert <note>a famous monastic wilderness in Egypt</note>, where he became acquainted with their customs, dwellings, and holy sites. In Book II, Chapter 15, Thomas then gives a precise report on Ananjesus’s work, titled "The Paradise." According to this report, the work comprised two books. The first contained the histories of the holy fathers by Palladius and Jerome; the second contained the questions and narratives of the fathers. Regarding this second part, Thomas specifies that Ananjesus initially collected 615 chapters and divided these in a pleasing manner into "canons" or sections. To these 615 chapters, he added 430 others with teachings "on all types of spiritual virtue" (thus without a thematic order) and finally many others without numbering or thematic organization. At the conclusion, he placed the praise of the Syrian monks from John Chrysostom’s *Commentary on Matthew* and the discourses of Mar Abraham of Naphtharja.

This description best corresponds to the manuscript *Cod. Vat. Syriac. 126*, which Bedjan used as one of the primary witnesses for his edition of Ananjesus’s work <gloss>1)</gloss>. In it, we find the following components: 1. The *Lausiac History* <note>original: "Historia Lausiaca"</note> of Palladius. 2. A collection of individual chapters of the *History* and of "Sayings" (discussed in more detail below), also under the name of Palladius. 3. Under the name of Jerome: Rufinus’s *History of the Monks* <note>original: "Histor. Monach."; that is, the so-called Greek Rufinus</note>. 4. Finally, again under the name of Palladius: the *Sayings of the Holy Fathers*. — In the first section of this fourth part, the manuscript presents 616 items in 14 chapters (more on these further below); Thomas of Marga mentions 615. Following this, a second series begins with 367 items and a third <gloss>2)</gloss> with 161 items. The second sequence is designated as the 15th chapter <gloss>3)</gloss> and bears the heading: "Questions and answers (words) concerning the conduct of the holy men, which they taught publicly and in secret regarding all types of perfection." This expression "regarding all types of perfection" was encountered above literally in the description by Thomas of Marga. The two sections seem to correspond to that part of the work in which Thomas found 434 items and many others without numbers (lacking thematic order). At the end of the Vatican Codex, there is another collection, styled quite differently, of questions and answers <note>original Greek: "ἐρωτήσεις καὶ ἀποκρίσεις"</note>...
