The second complete manuscript of Ananjesus’s work was discovered by Budge in the year 1888 in Mosul <note>a city in modern-day Iraq</note>. In 1907, he made a revised translation, based on new manuscript material, accessible to a wider circle 4).

The Mosul manuscript (M) is relatively old (13th or 14th century). In the first part of Ananjesus's work, it already offers an interesting addition beyond the Vatican Codex (B), namely at the beginning a translation of Athanasius’s *Life of Anthony* and, between the second Palladius work and the Jerome-Rufinus text, the "Asketikon" of Pachomius, that is, the so-called *Paralipomena* <note>original: "Paralipomena"; these are "supplementary" stories about the monk Pachomius</note> 5). M [the Mosul manuscript] provides the *Apophthegmata* in two books. The first book contains 635 entries. These correspond to the 616 in B and the 627 in Bedjan's edition. Then follows a second book with 706 entries. Numbers 1–380 run parallel with the second series in Bedjan (1–373), and 381–534 with the third series 1–154. Numbers 535–540 are identical to Bedjan 155–160. Here, as there, each of these pieces has its own specific heading 7).

Numbers 541–577, which appear in M as Chapter 16—thus following the numbering of the first 15 chapters—correspond to numbers 71–104 in Bedjan (p. 964 ff.). B [the Vatican manuscript] thus confirms the arrangement of M here. Finally, common to both is the narrative of the monk from Antioch (M 599 = Bedjan p. 986). After several concluding pieces (600–603), the numbers 604 follow in an appendix...

created it himself, and it will, in my opinion, be possible to prove that the former alternative holds true: The editorial activity of Ananjesus <note>Enanisho, a 7th-century East Syriac monk who compiled the 'Paradise of the Fathers.'</note> was very modest. He did not even collect independently but merely incorporated ready-made collections into his corpus. Thus we find in Bedjan No. 622 p. 687 (= Budge I No. 630) a short excerpt from the *Acts of Bessarion* (= G 1—5) <note>G likely refers to the Greek Alphabetical collection of the 'Sayings of the Desert Fathers.'</note>, with the concluding remark: "I have meanwhile written all these things in the history of the holy man Bessarion, wherein it was also written that he sat at the gate of the monastery and wept bitterly." This cross-reference refers to the Palladius II collection, Bedjan 265 ff. There, indeed, is the detailed history of Bessarion. That remark, therefore, certainly comes from the hand of the collector of the entire corpus, i.e., Ananjesus. If Ananjesus were an independent collector, he would probably not have included the stories in question at all if he recognized their identity with others already included in his work. If Ananjesus nevertheless provides them in excerpt form, only to break off briefly and refer to the earlier passage, this proves that he was editing a collection that was already finished.

The same applies to the remark found in Bedjan p. 858 between No. 45 and 46 (= Budge II 425. 426). "Here follow in order the counsels of the elder, who spoke against the thoughts of fornication and said: be like the man who went through a street with taverns . . ." Here, too, the editor clearly finds a collection already completed and passes over a piece of this collection with a reference to the duplicate already written down — it is found in Bedjan 589 (first series) Budge 593 — briefly passing it by <margin>1) Ananjesus himself (or his predecessor) also already had various copies of the collections before him. Cf. Bedjan No. 575. 576 two different redactions of the same story, the second introduced as coming from another copy. Bedjan p. 986 the story of the monk of Antioch "from another collection".</margin>.

Also, the (three) collections that Ananjesus presupposes do not, of course, stem from *one* source. Each has had its own history and shows its particular structure. The Palladius 2 collection contains mostly more extensive stories, the character of which is often of a bizarre, frequently questionable nature, and shows how these stories were interwoven with pieces of the *Historia Lausiaca* <note>The 'Lausiac History,' a 5th-century work by Palladius chronicling the lives of the Desert Fathers.</note> and others. The 14-chapter collection is related in its entire design to PJ <note>Refers to the Latin collection of Pelagius and John.</note> and the Armenian recensions; the so-called 15th chapter is of a completely inorganic nature and is probably a "gleaning" or after-crop to 1—14. The material that Ananjesus included in his collection thus already had a long history behind it. This is also proven by the duplicates, which are particularly numerous here (see Table No. VI A). A comparison of the duplicates also seems to show that the entire tradition also involves different translations.

If such an analysis of Ananjesus's work shows us that various larger and smaller collections already existed in Syriac tradition in his time — Ananjesus will also hardly have been the translator of these collections — then the picture becomes even more colorful and diverse when we consider the as-yet-unpublished Syriac collection of sayings <note>original: Apophthegmensammlung</note> preserved elsewhere in manuscripts. # Chapter 1. The Various Traditions, Relationship, and Value.

A characteristic of our collection is clearly the connection of the so-called Greek Rufinus <note>Rufinus of Aquileia was a 4th-century monk and translator; the "Greek Rufinus" refers to a Greek version of his *History of the Monks in Egypt*.</note> with series of *Apophthegmata* <note>The "Sayings of the Desert Fathers," short anecdotes or wisdom from early Christian hermits.</note> 1). The title of the collection (*The History of the Monks in Egypt* <note>original Greek: "ἡ κατ’ Αἴγυπτον τῶν μοναχῶν ἱστορία"</note>) likely also stems from the Greek Rufinus. Furthermore, there appear to be several series of *Apophthegmata* within the four manuscripts; in two of our witnesses, 14 648 and 12 173 (17 176), the first is separated from the second by a work of Euagrius <note>Euagrius Ponticus, a highly influential ascetic teacher and writer whose works were sometimes controversial.</note>, while in three witnesses, the second is separated from the third by the Greek Rufinus or excerpts from him (though the arrangement is different in 17 176).

It is significant that the beginning of the first series corresponds exactly to the beginning of the 15th chapter of the *Apophthegmata* in Ananjesus <note>A 7th-century monk who compiled the "Paradise of the Fathers," a definitive Syriac collection of monastic lore.</note>, or rather, to the second series beginning with No. 1 in his work. Furthermore, according to Dietrich's data, the interesting narrative G Daniel 7 (Migne 65, 156) <note>Migne refers to the *Patrologia Graeca*, a standard 19th-century collection of Greek church writings; G Daniel 7 refers to the 7th saying under the name Daniel in the alphabetical Greek collection.</note> was found in 14 579 on Folios 103—104; 14 648: Folio 28 a; 12 173: Folios 19 b—20, thus within this first smaller collection. This is also found in a corresponding manner in S <note>S stands for the Syriac systematic collection.</note> second series No. 25. — Finally, according to Dietrich's note, the *Logion* <note>A holy saying or utterance.</note> G Gregor 1 (Migne 65. 145) is found in 14 579 Folio 108; the saying stands in S second series No. 31. Everything seems to tempt one to the conclusion that the first part of the 15th chapter of Ananjesus’s collection is more closely related to the first series of *Apophthegmata* in our manuscripts. Unfortunately, an observation stands in the way of this. In his edition of the manuscript Cod. Coislinianus 126, the scholar Nau added parallels from manuscript 12 173 to his Greek text alongside parallels from Ananjesus. There, I now find (cf. the notes in *Revue de l'Orient Chrétien* 1908 60 ff.) among others the following equations: L. Folios 26. 15. 22. 8. 8. 9. 106. 16. 162 = G first (!) series 69. 66. 68. 555. 556. 557. 571. 583. 577. That is to say, eight *Apophthegmata* found in the first series of our collection also have their parallels in the first series (not the second) of Ananjesus's collection. This renders that tempting combination invalid. Some relationship between the first series of our collection and Chapter XV of Ananjesus will, of course, still have to be assumed. In any case, Nau's proof yields the result that the small collections of material presented here are most closely related to Ananjesus's collections in terms of subject matter, even if not in arrangement. Among the 67 numbers for which Nau provides parallels from 12 173 to Coislinianus 126, the relevant piece is also found in Ananjesus in 66 cases. The only exception is No. 189, where no parallel is found in Ananjesus.

# Book I. Investigations into the Textual Tradition and Character of the *Apophthegmata Patrum* <note>The "Sayings of the Desert Fathers," a collection of spiritual wisdom and anecdotes from early Christian hermits.</note>.

...make it possible to find Bedjan's numbers in Budge's edition. I designate the first, second, and third series of numbers in Bedjan as S, S\*, S\*\* followed by the number, and the pieces found in the second volume of Palladius <note>referring to the *Lausiac History* by Palladius, a 5th-century chronicle of early monks</note> (Bedjan p. 193 ff.) as Be. followed by the page number.

If we first examine the external arrangement of the Syriac compilation as it appears in Ananjesus, we have already seen that S is a self-contained piece. It is a collection of 627 items divided into fourteen thematic chapters. Within these chapters, no further consistent order can be identified. Named and anonymous material are mixed together, and there is no trace of alphabetical order. In its arrangement, S resembles Recension A <note>a specific version or "branch" of a manuscript tradition</note> of the Armenian tradition. The series of chapters in the Syriac version is undoubtedly related to the familiar, recurring list, but it deviates significantly (see Table VI). Some smaller chapters from the canonical list are missing in S, such as the very first chapter ("exhortation to progress" <note>original Greek: παραίνεσις εἰς προκοπήν</note>), the seventh ("that one should do nothing for show" <note>original Greek: ὅτι δεῖ μηδὲν πρὸς ἐπίδειξιν ποιεῖν</note>), and the ninth ("that one should not judge anyone" <note>original Greek: ὅτι οὐ δεῖ τινα κρίνειν</note>). In their place, S has two chapters dealing with the theme "on compunction" <note>original Greek: περὶ κατανύξεως; a state of deep spiritual regret or contrition</note> (III) at the fourth and twelfth positions. Furthermore, the chapters "on patience" <note>original Greek: περὶ ὑπομονῆς</note> (VII) and "on forbearance" <note>original Greek: περὶ ἀνεξικακίας</note> (XVI) are combined in the Syriac sixth chapter; the chapters "how one should be hospitable" <note>original Greek: ὡς φιλοξενεῖν δεῖ</note> (XIII) and "on love" <note>original Greek: περὶ ἀγάπης</note> (XIV) are combined in the ninth. Likewise, the chapter "on the need to always be vigilant" <note>original Greek: περὶ τοῦ δεῖ ἀεὶ νήφειν</note> (XI) from the canonical collection appears to be contained in the Syriac eighth chapter, along with the large chapter "on discernment" <note>original Greek: περὶ διακρίσεως</note> (X). The section "on those with foresight" <note>original Greek: περὶ διορατικῶν</note> (XVIII and I\*) does not appear in S, but some <sup>1)</sup> material from it is housed in S XIII, "on the fathers who performed miracles" <sup>2)</sup>. The final chapter in S, "on the greatness of the sublime life of monasticism," seems to correspond to J III according to the heading ("on the God-loving conduct of various fathers" <note>original Greek: περὶ πολιτείας θεοφίλους διαφόρων πατέρων</note>), but none of that section's content is found here. Instead, its characteristic sections—the tales of the hermits—appear alongside much else in the small section in Bedjan 200–326 (see p. 5/6). Regarding the content of the individual Syriac chapters, many of the items are found each time in the corresponding parallel section of the other collection, but deviations in the arrangement of the material are at least as frequent. It is hardly possible to decide *a priori* <note>reasoning from theoretical deduction rather than observation</note> on the priority of these different chapter orders. It makes a good impression that in S, the chapter appearing right at the beginning—"on flight from people, and silence, and remaining in the cell"—is so much more extensive than the corresponding chapter (II) of the canonical collection. The anchoritic <note>referring to anachoretes, or monks who live in complete solitude</note> character of the entire work emerges here most clearly from the start. On the other hand, it seems a bold assumption that S alone—compared to all other traditions (PJ, [N] <sup>3)</sup>, Coptic, Aramaic, Armenian translations Rec. A and B)—has preserved the original arrangement.

The "fifteenth" chapter of the Syriac collection, which is present in S\* and S\*\* (I am ignoring the secondary chapter headings at the end of S\*\*), represents, as already stated, not the final chapter of the original collection, but is a large, later addition through which the material that fell by the wayside in the older collection was supplemented.

These numerous unique connections between the Syriac version and the Latin versions (see especially the parallels between S and M)¹) are very noteworthy. They can hardly be explained in any other way than by the assumption that the Syriac and Latin traditions alone have faithfully preserved the contents of the original work, in contrast to all other witnesses.

In this regard, the Syriac also makes an excellent impression because it is almost entirely free from connections with later collections, which already characterized the text of the Greek manuscripts (NB), and especially the Palestinian-Eusebian (PE) and Armenian (Arm. AB) traditions. Parallels with Daniel of Scetis <note>a 6th-century monk and superior of Scetis</note>, Anastasios of Sinai <note>a 7th-century abbot and prolific author</note>, the material of Codex 1596, or the pieces appearing in Vladimir's manuscripts are completely absent. — The Syriac shares entry 574 (PE 467) with John Moschos <note>author of 'The Spiritual Meadow', d. 619</note>, specifically the short saying <note>original: "Logion"</note> from Moschos 217, though this could have been taken from Moschos himself. And in the final part²) S\*\* 44 and S\*\* 152, two more significant parallels with Moschos (chapters 195 and 189) ³) appear.

### § 12. The Superior Tradition in the Syriac and Latin Versions Compared to the Greek.

So far, we have only compared the (smaller) Latin (Lat.) and Syriac (S) collections with the Greek (G + NB) by asking about the material commonly present in both; this clearly produced the impression that we are dealing here with essentially the same core tradition. Now, however, the question must also be raised: Which parts in the Greek collections (G + NB) do not find confirmation in the Syriac or Latin? And furthermore, is this absence based on chance—as is easily assumed in the case of the smaller Latin collections—or are we dealing here with material of a peculiar structure and secondary character? To make it clearer, before I begin the comparison in this direction, I will offer some general considerations. 

As is apparent at first glance, the work before us contains almost exclusively the tradition of the monasticism of Scetis <note>the 'Sketis', a desert region in Egypt that was a major center of early Christian asceticism</note>. It is an exception from the start if an authority appears among the many cited who does not come from Scetis, or if the anonymous material does not reveal a Scetic environment. This Scetic monasticism represents a very specific monastic ideal in its purest form: namely, that of anchoritism <note>living as a hermit</note> and the individual cell (the practice of *eating alone* <note>original Greek: "monositisai"</note> and *sitting still* <note>original Greek: "kathezesthai"</note>; see below). 

The *Cenobium* <note>original: "Koinobion", a monastery where monks live together in community</note> is completely foreign to this circle. There is also no middle ground between communal life and hermit life <note>original: "Anachorese"</note>, whereby particularly chosen and older brothers receive permission from the abbot of the communal monastery to build a cell near the monastery and live there as hermits. And finally: the entire tradition present here is based essentially on oral tradition, as will be proven more precisely below. Extracts specifically of individual sayings and sentences from identifiable literary works are a rare exception. Now, however, it can be demonstrated that precisely in the Syriac and the smaller Latin collections, the vast mass of material that does not belong here from these points of view is still missing!

# Chapter 1. The Various Traditions: Their Relationship and Value.

I begin the detailed proof by first comparing the Greek version (G) with the Syriac (S) and Latin (Lat). Looking at section A—if we set aside the 38 sayings <note>original: "Apophthegmen"</note> of Saint Anthony, who appeared to Scetic monasticism <note>The monks of Scetis in the Egyptian desert</note> as its own hero—we find exclusively Scetic authorities ^1). At the end, under the names Aio-Antianos and Ammonathas, two stories appear from a non-Scetic environment (the Thebaid and Pelusium). These are clearly attached here as additions and are missing in the Syriac as well as the Latin traditions (including the collection of Pelagius and John).

The great Cappadocian **Basil** <note>Basil the Great, a major figure in Eastern monasticism</note> was given a single saying in the Greek version as a mark of honor; it is missing in the Syriac and Latin versions ^2) (also in Pelagius and John).

It is even more significant and decisive that the pieces **Gelasius 2–6** are found neither in the Syriac nor the Latin (nor, for that matter, in Pelagius and John). In these, we have a distinctly non-Egyptian environment. They contain a description of the partisan turmoil that developed after the Council of Chalcedon <note>A major church council in 451 AD that led to significant theological divisions</note> as a result of the appearance of the monk Theodosios and the Empress Eudoxia. In Gelasius 2, Simeon Stylites <note>the famous "pillar-saint" of Syria</note> is mentioned. Gelasius 5 reports on the founding of a monastery by Gelasius after the model of Saint Pachomius. This entire section reflects only the dogmatically argumentative monasticism of the later, post-Chalcedonian period, whereas the older Scetic monasticism shows itself, on the whole, to be dogmatically uninterested (see page 83), and the tradition of the sayings is otherwise consistently pre-Chalcedonian. We may therefore assume with great probability that the Greek version has undergone a later expansion here ^3).

Under the name of **Saint Epiphanius**, who was highly esteemed in monastic circles, there are 17 entries in the Greek version. Of these, not a single one appears in the Latin, and only one (concerning the Syrian prayer canon) appears in the Syriac version, entry 118 ^4). However, there is something peculiar about this saying <note>original: "Logion"</note>. The Syriac version presents it in a text that differs significantly from the Greek, and it can further be shown that the Syriac version drew here from a collection of Epiphanius-sayings that is entirely independent of the one found in the Greek. This is shown particularly clearly in Budge’s Mosul manuscript. Here, our saying (No. 118, as in Bedjan's edition) stands at the head of an extensive compilation of Epiphanius’s words, which are found in various places throughout Bedjan’s collection. # Book I. Investigations into the Textual Tradition and Character of the *Sayings of the Desert Fathers* <note>original: "Apophthegmata Patrum"</note>.

68—72 (73). The situation becomes even more complicated because the text edited by Budge <note>E.A. Wallis Budge, who edited Syriac monastic texts</note> includes almost all of these sayings <note>original: "Logien"</note> (with the sole exception of Bedjan 328 = Budge 120) a second time in the locations corresponding to Bedjan's text <note>Paul Bedjan, another editor of Syriac Christian texts</note>. The editor of the Budge manuscript could hardly have laboriously compiled his collection (numbers 118–125) himself from the work before him, for then he surely would have avoided the numerous duplicates that follow. This state of affairs can only be explained by assuming that he knew of another small collection of sayings by **Epiphanios** and inserted them at the point where he first encountered that name in his primary text. — Such a collection must also have been available to the editors of the individual collections of the work of **Ananjesus** <note>Anan-Isho, a 7th-century East Syrian monk who compiled the 'Paradise of the Fathers'</note>. This explains the numerous duplicates that exist even in Bedjan’s text between the S and S** versions. Consequently, the result is as follows: in both the Greek (G) and Syriac (S) traditions, the original material of the "Sayings" has been increased by a collection of sayings from Epiphanios. The collections used by G and S were entirely different and overlap in only one saying—one which had particular importance for the regulation of monastic life. The older Latin collections are still completely free of Epiphanios material, which does not truly belong in a collection of the sayings of the Scetic monks <note>monks from the Wadi El Natrun in Egypt</note>. On the other hand, it is understandable that sayings of this famous monastic authority were added to the collection at an early date.

The three stories under the name of **Ephrem** (the Syrian!) are entirely missing in S and the Latin versions, while the collection of Pelagius and John (PJ) contains all three. They originate from the Greek text, the Latin translation of which can be found in the *Life of Saint Ephrem the Syrian, Deacon of Edessa* <note>original: "Vita St. Ephraemi Syri diaconi Edessae"</note> in Rosweyde, *Lives of the Fathers* <note>original: "Vitae Patrum"</note> I (Migne, *Patrologia Latina* 73, 321 ff.) ^1). The non-Scetic environment and the literary dependence again point to a later interpolation into the Greek text.

Of the seven sayings of *Evagrius* in G, only the short anecdote No. 7 is found in S 59. It is likely only due to an error that G Euprepios 7 (and also X 19) appears in S 58 under the name of Evagrius ^2). The small Latin collections do not mention the name of Evagrius at all. Now, Evagrius was indeed a prominent *Scetic* authority—the *Lausiac History* and Rufinus prove this—but he is a special case. From the beginning, as an Origenist <note>a follower of the controversial theologian Origen</note> and a learned Greek ^3), he seems to have been a foreign and suspicious figure to the average Scetic monk. Thus, it must be assumed that in the circles from which the tradition of the "Sayings" <note>Apophthegmata</note> originated, he was almost or entirely bypassed. Later, some items from his *literary* legacy were included in the *Sayings of the Desert Fathers*. For several pieces in G, this can be directly proven ^4). The editor of the Greek foundation for the collection of Pelagius and John (PJ) likely found a copy of G that already contained more Evagrius quotes than Cotelier’s text (unless he made the additions himself).

# Chapter 1: The various traditions, their relationship and value.

John Moschos (compare also the *Plerophories* <note>a 6th-century collection of stories about holy men</note>) is accustomed to introducing his stories. Furthermore, Phokas [1] transports us into the post-Chalcedonian era <note>the period after the Council of Chalcedon in 451 AD</note> marked by the struggles between the Dyophysites and Monophysites <note>two groups with differing views on the nature of Christ</note>, where the latter are already regarded as schismatics <note>original: "ἀποσχισταί"</note>! — Finally, the piece preserved in G <note>the Greek tradition</note> alone under the name of *Psentaisios* is an excerpt from the Life of *Pachomius* <note>the founder of communal monasticism</note> [1].

The few women who appear in the tradition of the Sayings <note>original: "Apophthegmaüberlieferung"</note> require a special discussion. The monasticism of Scetis <note>a major center of early Christian monks in Egypt</note> does not seem to have known any prominent female hermits. Thus, only one name appears to be firmly established in the original tradition. In Scetic circles, various stories were told about **Mother Sarra** [2] (8 entries in G; parallels in the table). G knows of two other women. However, the seven sayings <note>original: "Logia"</note> of **Theodora** are entirely missing in *S* <note>the Syriac tradition</note> and *Lat.* <note>the Latin traditions</note> (including *PJ* <note>the collection by Pelagius and John</note>) [3]. Particularly interesting here is the state of the evidence regarding the sayings of **Syncletica**. G contains no fewer than 18 entries here, but of these, only one reappears in S (G 11 = S 509), and even then under the name of **Hyperechius**! This is likely the correct attribution, as it is confirmed by XV 50. In contrast, we find in S 357 a word from *Syncletica* that is not found in G, though it does appear in VIII 19 and Berlin Manuscript 92 b. In PJ, however, almost the entire material of *Syncletica's sayings* is found, including all those pieces which the Berlin manuscript offers beyond Cotelier’s text. Here too, we are dealing throughout with a literary influence from the independently existing *Life of Syncletica* [4], and once again we observe that *S* [5] proves to be almost entirely free of this influence.

Against all this, only one observation unfavorable to S can be made. We saw that the original tradition of Scetic monasticism completely bypassed the coenobiarch <note>the leader of a communal monastery</note> **Pachomius** and his circle [6]. It is therefore clearly to be addressed as secondary when we find reminiscences from the Life of Pachomius in S 109 and 354. Since these are also found in R 35 [7], this must represent a relatively early expansion of the text.

Otherwise, however, *S* has essentially added no new material from a foreign milieu. One find in it almost no single name [8] that we do not already know from G.

# Book I. Investigations into the Textual Tradition and Character of the Sayings of the Desert Fathers.

This result can be further confirmed by a cross-check. If we separate the approximately 120 sayings <note>original: "Logien"</note> just discussed from the text of G <note>the Greek tradition</note>, a wonderfully uniform picture emerges for the remaining content (roughly 830 entries). In fact, we have before us here the tradition of the anchoritic <note>hermit-style</note> monasticism of Scetis <note>a famous desert center of early Christian monks in Egypt</note> in almost complete purity. Admittedly, not all the fathers mentioned here are strictly Scetic authorities, but almost all of them had a specific relationship with the monks of Scetis.

For instance, to start with one of the most instructive examples, we find Abba Silouanos on Mount Sinai (G 4. 5) and in Syria (Mark 4). But from the notes about his student Mark, it is clear that he, like his master, belonged to the Scetic circle (Mark 1). Mark 4 speaks of his journey from Scetis to Sinai, and Mark 5 speaks of Silvanus's relocation from Sinai to Syria [1]. Zacharias, the frequently mentioned student of Silvanus (G 1. 3. 4. 8), is likely identical to the Zacharias whose many sayings our work has preserved; he therefore certainly belonged originally to the Scetic circle. A third student, Zeno (see Zeno 1), also undertook the move to Syria (Palestine) with him (G 3: "he traveled to Syria" <note>original Greek: παρέβαλεν εἰς Συρίαν</note>; G 6: "walking in Palestine" <note>original Greek: περιπατῶν ἐν τῇ Παλαιστίνῃ</note>), but it is just as certain that he also originally belonged to the Scetic circle (G 5: "sitting in Scetis" <note>original Greek: καθήμενος ἐν τῇ Σκήτει</note>) [2]. The same likely applies to a fourth disciple, Netras, of whom we only hear that he was on Mount Sinai and later became a bishop (Netras 1).

The same will apply to Abba Matoës. We hear that he moved from Raithu <note>a monastic site on the Red Sea coast of the Sinai Peninsula</note> to Sinai "to the regions of Magdolon" <note>original Greek: εἰς τὰ μέρη Μαγδολῶν</note> (in the land of Edom [3]). But from entry G 5, we learn that he had friendly personal relationships with the fathers of Scetis (G 7) [4]. Similarly, it is said of Megethios (G 2) that "after becoming a disciple among the Egyptians and meeting many elders" <note>original Greek: μαθητευθεὶς παρ' Αἰγυπτίοις καὶ συντυχὼν πολλοῖς γέρουσι</note> (specifically Sisoes and Poimen), he later stayed on Sinai [5].

The situation is somewhat different with Joseph of Panepho [6]. He does not belong to the Scetic circle. It is told of Poimen (Joseph G 3) that after a visit to him, "having returned to Scetis... he sat down" <note>original Greek: ἀνακάμψας ἐν τῇ Σκήτει ... ἐκάθητο</note>. He is likely identical to the Joseph of Panepho whom Cassian found as a hermit near a monastery at Panepho (according to *Conference* <note>original Latin: "Collatio"</note> XI, 2) and with whom he claims to have had detailed conversations (*Conferences* XVI, XVII). On the other hand, as the *Sayings* <note>original: "Apophthegmata"</note> show, he was in very close contact with Scetis. In Cassian's writings, alongside Joseph of Panepho, two other holy hermits are mentioned who settled near the monastery: Chairemon and Nisteroos [7]. # Chapter 1. The Various Traditions, Relationship, and Value.

...we encounter a saying <note>original: "Logion"</note> in Migne <note>referring to Patrologia Graeca, a massive collection of Greek patristic texts compiled by J.P. Migne</note>. Whether this Chairemon, who is explicitly introduced here as "Chairemon in Scetis" <note>original Greek: Χαιρ. εἰς Σκῆτιν</note>, is identical to the former remains to be seen. The *Apophthegmata* <note>the "Sayings of the Desert Fathers"</note> distinguish between two monks named Nisteroos, the second of whom is explicitly introduced as "Nisteroos in a coenobium" <note>original Greek: Ν. ἐν κοινοβίῳ; a coenobium is a communal monastery</note>. Yet, it is precisely from the former that a saying is preserved which we find again in Cassian's work (p. 42). Perhaps the two Nisterooses could be identical after all. For Cassian's Nisteroos was first a coenobite and then a hermit. In any case, as the tradition under these three names testifies, there was active communication between Scetis and the hermits of Panepho.

The two fathers Theodore and Lucius are designated as "those of the Enaton" <note>original Greek: οἱ τοῦ Ἐνάτου</note>. The Enaton was a colony of hermits near Alexandria (at the ninth mile-marker [1]). Joining these two brothers is Longinos, who appears in G 1 in contact with Lucius and of whom G 3 says: "he resided at the ninth mile-marker of Alexandria" <note>original Greek: ἐκάθητο οὗτος ἐν τῷ ἐνάτῳ σημείῳ Ἀλεξανδρείας</note>. Close relations also seem to have existed between Scetis and the Enaton [2].

It is more difficult to reach clarity regarding Abba Sisoes. It appears as if the Greek tradition (G)—which otherwise likes to list the same authority twice to achieve the highest possible number of names [3]—has here lumped together different hermits of the same name. One of the oldest figures of Scetis must be Abba Sisoes, who is introduced here several times as being on the mountain of Saint Anthony [4]. According to G 28, he is a contemporary of Abba Or (already mentioned in the *Lausiac History*) and is said to have moved to Anthony's mountain shortly after Anthony's death! It is told of him in G 25 that Arians <note>followers of a 4th-century Christian belief deemed heretical</note> once came to him, and in G 48, Meletians <note>a schismatic group in Egypt</note> are mentioned in his vicinity. He seems to have made the name Sisoes especially famous. His connection to Scetis would thus be certain. Alongside him, in the same section of the *Apophthegmata*, a "Sisoes of Petra" (G 23. 36) and a "Sisoes the Theban" [5], whose residence is given as Kalamon in the Arsinoite district (G 32), are mentioned. These two are most definitely distinguished from one another [6]. However, how they relate to the "Sisoes on the mountain of St. Anthony" is not stated. When G 48 says, "Abba Sisoes went out from the mountain of St. Anthony to the outer mountain of the Thebaid and dwelt there" <note>original Greek: ἐξῆλθε ὁ Ἀ Σισόης ἐκ τοῦ ὄρους τοῦ Ἁ. Ἀντωνίου εἰς τὸ ἐξώτερον ὄρος τῆς Θηβαΐδος καὶ ᾤκησεν ἐκεῖ</note>, one might be inclined to identify the elder Sisoes with the Theban. This would leave two anchorites, of whom the elder Sisoes started out from Scetis...

[1] See the remarks of Nau in *Patrologia Orientalis* VIII, 1 regarding the *Plerophoriae* c. 13, p. 28 3.
[2] Cf. the account of Daniel the Scetiote in *Revue de l'Orient Chrétien* 1900 p. 61: "And all of Scetis went up—likewise also the Enaton and the Cells, and those on the mountain of Nitria, and all the monasteries <note>original Greek: λαῦραι (lavrae)</note> near Alexandria." Here the Enaton appears in the midst of the three locations of Scetis in the broader sense.
[3] Cf. above: John the Theban, the student of Ammoes, who appears in Migne 240 as a distinct authority, is none other than the well-known John Kolobos <note>John the Dwarf</note>. ## Book I. Investigations into the Textual Tradition and Character of the *Apophthegmata Patrum*.

...it would be the case that the younger Sisoes (G 36) ¹) would be directly identified as a Scetic authority (Petra <note>original: "Πέτρα"; a specific rocky locality within the desert of Scetis</note> is a place in Scetis).

Finally, the fact that some sayings <note>original: "Logien"</note> of Patriarch Theophilos of Alexandria appear in G <note>the Greek tradition</note> is not surprising, given the close relationship these church leaders had with Scetis ²).

After all these considerations, one may indeed judge that the original tradition of the *Apophthegmata* <note>the "Sayings of the Desert Fathers"</note> represents exclusively the milieu of Scetic monasticism. To illustrate this, I will summarize the following figures ³) once more. Alongside approximately 60 Fathers whose belonging to Scetis is immediately certain (accounting for over 600 sayings), I count about a dozen more (including Saint Antony) with just over 150 sayings, for whom a close relationship to Scetis is established. The remaining 50–60 (!) sayings are distributed among 19 Fathers of uncertain origin ⁴) and 14 who do not belong to the Scetic circle ⁵). Even the small number of sayings transmitted under the names of these Fathers proves that we are dealing here with occasional tradition that likely circulated within the circle of the Scetiotes <note>monks living in Scetis</note>.

This corresponds, as already indicated, to the fact that the entire work consistently adheres to the anchoritic <note>hermit-like</note> ideal. The main exceptions are found again in the passages already set aside and have already been discussed above. Additionally, they are found among the Fathers who had only closer or more distant relationships with Scetis. Thus, Siluanos ⁶) gathered his disciples in a coenobium <note>a communal monastery; original: "Koinobion"</note> on Sinai and later in Syria (see p. 40 note 1, the report of Sozomenos). He is described in G 5 as the superior of such a community, with communal meals and shared, regulated work. The monastery garden is enclosed by a fence (G 8). Here we see, side-by-side, the main characteristics by which the monastery distinguished itself from the cell of the anchorite.

Joseph of Panepho and Nisteroos also belong here. Cassian's eleventh *Collatio* <note>one of the "Conferences," a famous work on monastic life by John Cassian</note> gives us a glimpse into the environment relevant to these monks, where he describes his journey that took him to the region of the Nile...

However, they assemble together at meal times and at the times of the regular morning and evening prayers. On the other hand, Poimen (168) describes the characteristics of the cell-dweller as: "manual labor, eating alone" <note>original: "τὸ ἐργόχειρον καὶ τὸ μονοσιτίσαι"; the term "monositisai" is correctly translated by Martin of Braga (Dum. 21) as: *solitarie panem tantum edere* (to eat bread only in solitude), and not "to eat once a day" as in S 540 X 64</note> "and silence and meditation" <note>original: "καὶ τὸ σιωπᾶν καὶ ἡ μελέτη"</note>. > "When I first entered the monastery, I said in my mind: You and the donkey are one. Just as the donkey is beaten and does not speak, is mistreated and does not answer, so also are you"

These are interesting exceptions that show us how, even in circles closely related to Scetis, the cenobitic ideal was beginning to penetrate and take hold. In Scetis, by contrast, the anchoritic ideal consistently prevails. Only quite occasionally is the cenobium mentioned here. Here and there, a monastery superior appears before a brother in Scetis, particularly when it concerns punishment and exclusion or the pardon and reinstatement of a fallen brother. A certain exception seems to exist in the story of Abba Poimen in G Anub 1. Here it is reported that Abba Poimen and his brothers, when they left Scetis due to the raid of the Mazices <note>original: "Mazziker"; nomadic raiders from the Libyan desert who frequently attacked the monks</note>, settled together in a ruined temple near Terenuthis and established rules for a common life. And it was impossible for any of us to say, 'bring us something else,' or to say, 'we do not want to eat this'" ³).

This clearly concerns the practice of communal meals, which leads toward the cenobium. — However, this seems to have been only a temporary measure. Elsewhere, Poimen appears to us until his old age as a follower of the anchoritic ideal. It is mentioned that he never left his cell (G 6. 90). His cell was, of course, among the cells of other monks ⁴), his disciples and brothers, who are always mentioned alongside Poimen.

To a brother who wishes to enter a *cenobium* <note>original Greek: κοινόβιον; a communal monastery</note>, Poimen presents the full weight of his decision: "for you do not even have authority over your own drinking-cup alone" <note>original Greek: τοῦ γὰρ βαυκαλίου μόνου μόνον οὐκ ἔχεις ἐξουσίαν (G 152)</note>. The abbot of a communal monastery, by contrast, commands and establishes laws ²).

Poimen is, however—as we shall see more closely below—one of the last great authorities of Scetic monasticism in its golden age, from which the *Apophthegmata* <note>the "Sayings" of the Desert Fathers</note> originate. Here, the anchoritic <note>hermit-like</note> ideal remained in indestructible vitality until the end, despite the general advance of the cenobium. And the Old Man said to him: 'Go, sit in your cell and perform only one prayer in the morning, also one in the evening, and one at night. And when you are hungry, eat; and when you are thirsty, drink; and if you are tired, sleep. But remain in the desert and do not follow your thoughts.' And he also went to Abba John and told him the word of Abba Paphnutius. And Abba John said to him: 'You do not need to perform any prayer at all; just sit in your cell.' And he stood up and went to Abba Arsenios. And the Old Man said to him: 'Keep it as the Fathers told you; I have nothing more to say to you than that.'" The most renowned Scetic authorities are summoned here to defend the ideal of the cell against the communal monastery ³). One of them, Abba Sisoes (see p. 41), who in his old age had gone to a monastery in Clysma, feels deeply unhappy there and laments the lost freedom of the desert: "for the freedom of my mind in the desert alone did not suffice for me" <note>original Greek: οὐκ ἤρκει γάρ μοι ἡ ἐλευθερία μόνη τοῦ λογισμοῦ μου ἐν τῇ ἐρήμῳ (4)</note>.

The corresponding chapter in the S collection is even more richly developed, appearing there at the very head of the entire work. One searches in vain for a corresponding section on the communal monastery. In the smaller Latin collection found in R and Pa, chapters 31–41 (the division is preserved only in Pa) deal explicitly with the life and ideal of the anchorite. We now set out, from these perspectives, to examine the character and authenticity of the anonymously transmitted material as well. I will first look at the collections G, P, and J (and the smaller Latin collections). From the outset, it is to be expected that among the anonymous material, one might find stories and sayings much more easily that do not originate from Scetis <note>a desert valley in Egypt, the heart of early Christian monasticism</note> and do not belong to the Scetic environment. Thus, the geographic picture here is perhaps somewhat more colorful 2), and we lack the means here to establish with certainty the relationships of individual stories to the circle of the Scetic monks. For the most part, as is emphasized here and there in the introduction, these will be anecdotes that were told within this circle. But on the whole, the Scetic environment remains excellently preserved here as well. One point may therefore be particularly pointed out; here, as in G, the linguistic usage is maintained according to which Egypt appears as the land that already lies outside of Scetis, and thus the Scetiote stands in contrast to the Egyptian. So begins the story of the fasting competition between some monks visiting Scetis and the Scetiotes with the words: *Once, monks went down from Egypt to Scetis to see the elders of that place* <note>original Latin: "Descenderunt aliquando monachi de Aegypto in Scythi, ut viderent seniores loci illius"</note>; and afterward, these monks are called "the Egyptians" in contrast to the Scetiotes, and this linguistic usage can be traced through the entire collection 3). Scetis is the home of the anchorites <note>hermits</note>, and Egypt is already a foreign land.

Correspondingly, the anonymous pieces also consistently reflect the environment of the anchoritic monastic ideal. Only here and there do stories appear that presuppose the communal monastery <note>term: Koinobion; a monastery where monks lived, ate, and prayed together under an abbot</note> and its conditions. The Abbot <note>term: Abbas; the father or spiritual leader of a monastic community</note> of the monastery plays a main role in it (XIV 17 R 145 S 236). ### Book I. Investigations into the Textual Tradition and Character of the Apophthegmata Patrum. 46

However, such stories are among the rather rare exceptions ²), at least within the material that the Syriac and Latin traditions offer in common.

A bit more is found when we look at the unique material <note>German: Sondergut; text found in only one specific tradition or manuscript</note> of the Pelagius-John collection <note>a 6th-century Latin translation of the Sayings</note> and the Syriac collection. For example, Pelagius-John VII 33 (matching R 98) offers the following story: "A brother who lived in a **communal monastery** <note>original Greek: κοινόβιον (koinobion); a monastery where monks live, eat, and pray together</note> was very prone to anger. In order to escape this danger, he withdrew into solitude. It then happened that one day his water jug, which he had just filled, tipped over, and this repeated a second and third time. In his anger, he took the jug and smashed it. When he came to his senses and saw that the passion of anger had defeated him even in solitude, he returned to his monastery." Whether this story, with its directly anti-hermit character and its recommendation of the communal life, was actually passed down in the circles of Scetis <note>the desert wilderness where the most famous hermits lived</note> must be seriously questioned. In any case, it represents an almost total exception. Elsewhere in the tradition not confirmed by the Syriac, there are a few pieces that assume a communal ideal, though in a harmless way and without such a clear agenda ³).

Similar observations can be made, on the other hand, regarding the unique material of the Syriac tradition. For instance, we find the following story in S 129: A hermit who was staying in the monastery of a brotherhood held himself back from communal prayer. He then saw in a dream a house radiating fire that reached up to heaven, and small sparks near that house that soon faded away. It was revealed to him that the light-streaming house represented the prayer of the community, and the small sparks the prayers of the individual (S 129). Here, too, one would have reservations about assigning this story—with its specific anti-hermit tendency—to the original tradition of the Scetic monastic circles. Along with this, there are again a few other stories where the tendency is not so clearly prominent ⁴).

But even if we were to assume that this questionable unique material from the Syriac and Pelagius-John (Latin) collections had belonged to the original tradition, all these cases still appear only as a vanishing exception ⁵).

# Chapter 1: The Various Traditions, Relationship, and Value.

Overall, even with the anonymous material passed down in the Syriac and Latin traditions, we get the impression that we are consistently within the milieu of Scetic-anchoritic <note>referring to the hermits of Scetis who lived in solitude</note> monasticism.

Of the many stories that reflect the spirit of Scetis here as well, let one final one be placed here (S 5 = Berlin 180 b). Two hermits lived together in the desert; of them, one became a monastery leader <note>original German: Klostervorsteher</note>, while the other remained in the desert and became a perfect ascetic, to whom God granted the gift of healing the demon-possessed and seeing the future. The <term>Koinobiarch</term> <note>the head of a "koinobion," or communal monastery where monks live together</note> felt slighted and, in response to his prayer, received a revelation from an angel: "That man sits in the desert and prays to the Lord night and day. — You alone are concerned with the crowd and have social interaction with the many. Let the comfort and satisfaction from people be enough for you."

But we return from this excursion—which has already led us deep into the peculiar character of Scetic monasticism—to the simple literary investigation and seek to draw a conclusion from the observations provided. And here, in my opinion, it can hardly be a coincidence that a whole series of *apophthegmata* <note>the "sayings" or short stories of the Desert Fathers</note>, which are subject to internal critical doubts as being non-Scetic, purely literary, and non-anchoritic, are not found in the common tradition of the Syriac and Latin. It seems to follow from this that in the Syriac and Latin versions, we have a more original tradition of the *apophthegmata* literature than in the Greek (G). — In this regard, there would again be two possible explanations. One could either assume that the Syriac and Latin do indeed presuppose collection G, but knew it in a more original, less extensive form. The comparison of the Berlin manuscript with Cotelier’s text <note>a standard 17th-century edition of the Greek Fathers</note> has already shown us how the tradition of G is in constant flux. Thus, we might assume that the Syriac and Latin go back to a form of G that is not contained anywhere in our current manuscripts. From this point, we could perhaps also explain how it happens that the Pelagius-John collection (PJ) coincides with the Syriac and Latin in so many cases regarding omissions compared to G, while conversely, an increased penetration of specifically literary material¹) could be demonstrated in it. We must imagine that the Greek tradition was distributed in ever-new forms and variations, sometimes provided with new material, sometimes shortened. In this way, the various observations could perhaps be best explained. But there remains another possibility. Namely, that the small Syriac and Latin collections reflect that state of the collection of sayings in which it existed before the editor of G created the great collective work of the <term>Great Meadow</term> <note>original Greek: μέγα λειμωνάριον (mega leimonarion); a famous spiritual anthology or "spiritual meadow" of monk stories</note>. This assumption would be supported by the fact that in the Syriac and Latin, all the material still appears in a chaotic state compared to the Greek, without any trace of alphabetical order, and without any separation between the material transmitted under a name and the anonymous material. Also, the fact that a certain thematic order exists in the Rufinus (R) and *Paradisus* (Pa) collections (see pages 23/24) would not contradict this assumption; indeed, it would rather confirm it, since this order is completely independent of the one that later prevailed in the tradition of the sayings. Only one concern arises here against the Syriac collection (the first series in Bedjan). For its 14 chapters are indeed most closely connected with the chapters in the Pelagius-John, Coptic, Aramaic, and Armenian versions. If one wanted to assume the relative original—

<meta>This page continues the investigation into the manuscript lineage of the Desert Fathers' sayings, specifically debating whether the Syriac (S) and Latin (Lat) versions reflect a more primitive, "pure" source than the standard Greek alphabetical collection (G).</meta>

**Book I. Investigations into the Textual Tradition and Character of the *Apophthegmata Patrum* <note>The "Sayings of the Fathers"</note>.**

If we were to still assert the authenticity of the tradition found in S <note>the Syriac manuscript tradition</note>, one would have to make the following assumptions: 
1. A collection of *apophthegmata* <note>sayings</note> already existed before G <note>the standard Alphabetical Greek collection</note> (alongside others), in which the material was organized by subject into chapters (but without alphabetical order and without separating named and anonymous material). 
2. G used this collection, extracted the alphabetical material, reordered it, and left the anonymous material in that old chapter arrangement in the second, now lost, part of his work. 
3. PJ <note>the collection of Pelagius and John</note> adopted the chapter order from G and reintegrated the alphabetical material into it in the manner already demonstrated. 
4. S is, for its part, a revision of the tradition that existed before G, which was already divided into chapters. 
5. The Latin collections, or rather their Greek prototypes, adopted the *apophthegmata* in a completely disordered state, and the editor created a certain topical order on his own initiative.

As long as we do not obtain more manuscript evidence, we will hardly reach full clarity on this point. We must be satisfied with the general result that, in all probability, S and the Latin traditions represent an earlier stage of the *apophthegmata* tradition than what is available to us in the form of G.

### § 13. The Superior Tradition in S (Latin) in Comparison with NB.

Thus far, we have compared the tradition of S and the Latin versions with G; it remains to carry out the comparison with the anonymous material in NB <note>the collection edited by Nau and Bousset</note>. Here, we will arrive at a much more certain result. In particular, the Syriac tradition can provide us with a benchmark for a critical appraisal of NB. A comparison with PJ would be of no use, as NB is a supplementary collection to PJ, which incorporated this smaller collection into its center. Only in about 20 cases do points of contact appear in NB—that is, items rejected from PJ or duplicates. The contacts with the other Latin versions are too sparse to be considered. PE <note>the Pelagius-Evagrius collection</note> and the Armenian versions are dependent variables. But the Syriac tradition can be compared. And the comparison yields a result that is not favorable for the purity of the tradition in NB. 

The Syriac version offers only about 130–140 parallels to the 500 items in NB (and even if one subtracts the small collection of 70 *if-logia* <note>original: ἐὰν-Logien; these are sayings beginning with the word "if"</note> B 211–217, there are still 430 items). This is barely a third—a completely different percentage than what was found for the relationship between S–G and S–PJ. For in G, about 2/3 of all items reappeared in S; in the underlying source of G reconstructed with the help of S, it was as much as 3/4, while the correspondences between S and PJ amounted to nearly 4/5 of the PJ collection. These numerical ratios alone are decisive. They prove, on the one hand, that NB has preserved genuine anonymous material from the original text beyond PJ; they prove, on the other hand, that a considerable amount of foreign material must have flowed into NB.

And this purely numerical result is now brilliantly confirmed by an investigation of the milieu <note>the social or geographical environment</note> in which the tradition of NB moves. I will first focus on the large section from roughly B page 190 to page 217. A glance at the table shows that parallels with S are almost entirely missing here, with negligible exceptions. And here we now find the following geographical references: 195 b, an inscription found on Sinai; 195 c, a gardener <note>original Greek: κηπουρός</note> on Sinai; 196 d, two brothers from Raithu <note>a monastic site on the Red Sea</note>; 197 b, "an old man living on Sinai" <note>original Greek: γέρων οἰκῶν ἐν Σιναῖ</note>; 197 b, "a brother having a garden on Sinai" <note>original Greek: ἀδελφὸς ἔχων κῆπον ἐν Σιναῖ</note>; 197 d, a brother on the Mount of Olives.

Of another hermit it is told (194 b = N 62) that "he was grazing with the buffalo" <note>original: boskomenos meta tōn boubalōn ēn</note>. He enters a monastery, is mocked and teased by the brothers there, and returns again to his cattle. The *taxeot* of Scythopolis (198 a), formerly a great sinner, first devotes himself to the life of the cell, but then, troubled by many visitors, leaves the cell and goes into the wild solitude: "For to me, the food of the irrational beasts is my bread" <note>original: emoi gar artos hē trophē tōn alogōn</note>. These monks who graze with the "dear livestock," the so-called Graziers <note>original: Bougaloi or Boskoi</note> ⁶), are a characteristic phenomenon of Syrian monasticism. Of another monk it is reported (198 d) that, speaking to no one, he sat continually in his cell with bowed head and shaking it, murmuring to himself: "So, what is happening?" <note>original: ara ti ginetai</note> ⁷). In this entire section, there is repeated mention of heightened compunction <note>original: katanyxis</note>, of streams of tears that specifically announce the approach of death, and of the soul-saving blessing of tears (cf. especially the long explanations of Theodore of Canopus 199 c—200 a). Such things do occasionally occur in the genuine environment of Sketis, but nowhere near as frequently or with such intrusive intensity.

# Book I. Investigations into the Textual Tradition and Character of the *Apophthegmata Patrum*.

Enough; it has been established beyond all doubt through external evidence and internal reasons that this entire large section in manuscript B does not belong to the tradition of Sketis <note>the most famous early monastic center in Egypt</note>, but represents an addition that our collection received on Syrian-Palestinian soil 1).

For other parts of the manuscripts N and B as well, the infusion of foreign material from a non-Sketic environment can be clearly demonstrated. I specifically highlight here section N 32–53. Table II again shows the almost complete failure of Syrian parallels <note>meaning these stories do not appear in the older Syrian versions of the collection</note>. Many of these stories take place in a non-Sketic environment 2). For a number of these specific tales, the secondary sources from which they originate have already been pointed out above. Such stories are also found scattered elsewhere in NB. It will suffice to briefly indicate their locations 3).

Finally, a number of stories that specifically reflect the environment of the <term>Koinobion</term> <note>a communal monastery where monks lived together, as opposed to the solitary life of hermits</note> also belong to the later layer of NB. Stories N 52 and 219 b deal with the <term>apokrisiarios</term> <note>original: ἀποκρισιάριος; a representative or administrative official</note> of a monastery. In N 70, a <term>Koinobiarch</term> <note>the head of a communal monastery</note> asks Cyril (of Alexandria) the question of who is greater: the monastery superior or the hermit. The answer given here is that there is no difference in rank between Moses and Elijah. This resolution of the question was unlikely to have been handed down in originally Sketic circles <note>who generally prioritized the solitary life</note>. In N 74, a fixed terminology already seems to be present, according to which the monastic brother is called a <term>monachos</term> <note>original: μοναχός; monk</note> in contrast to the <term>Anachorete</term> <note>a solitary hermit</note>. When it says there that the <term>monk had a certain anchorite who was dear to him</term> <note>original: μοναχὸς εἶχέ τινα ἀναχωρητὴν ἀγαπητὸν αὐτοῦ</note>, this refers to a hermit living near a monastery who is specifically served by a monastic brother. This combination of monastery and cell-life, familiar to us, is also presupposed in N 370: a brother asks his abbot to release him into the desert; likewise in 228 b: two brothers become monks: <term>as they succeeded, it seemed good to them to build cells</term> <note>original: ὡς κατώρθωσαν ἔδοξεν αὐτοῖς οἰκοδομῆσαι κέλλια</note> 4).

Thus, it is now definitively proven that the original Sketic collection of the "Anonymous Sayings" <note>the *Anonyma*</note> has been lost to us and exists in NB only in a heavily edited and expanded state. Indeed, the editing of NB was much more invasive than was the case with the modest expansion of collection G (by about 1/8th of the material) demonstrated above. Nevertheless, we can still form a clear picture of the collection of the <term>Anonyma</term>. The greater part of them is, after all, preserved for us now in the original Greek text within NB. The most valuable witnesses for their reconstruction are primarily S, then PJ, and then the smaller Latin works. One may establish the rule that wherever the witnesses of the collection S, PJ, Latin, and NB 5) only show two parallels each, with certainty...

## § 14. Recension A of the Armenian Tradition and S.

Only from this vantage point can we now bring our judgment on the Armenian Recension *A*, which we previously had to leave in suspense, to a certain conclusion. The investigation revealed a double nature to it. On the one hand, it proved to be a decidedly secondary adaptation. Extensive sections from *Joannes Moschos* and various other secondary materials had been incorporated into it. On the other hand, within its 19 chapters—just as *S* in its 14 chapters—it showed no trace of alphabetical order and no separation of the material attributed to specific names and the anonymous material; there were also striking contacts with *S* and the *Latin*, which we now see as the best witnesses of our tradition.

The observations we were just able to make initially yielded a decisively unfavorable factor for the Armenian recension. For a glance at the table teaches us that precisely the spurious material, originating from a Palestinian-Syrian adaptation in *NB*, has found its way almost in its entire scope into the Armenian recensions, and specifically into Recension *A*. Thus, *Armenian A* also aligns itself completely with *NB*, *Paulus Evergetinos*, and *Armenian B*.

The question is still not entirely settled. On the other hand, an older layer of tradition must have somehow found its way to Recension *A* of the Armenian. This can only now be made particularly clear at one point, after we have gained a more precise insight into the Syrian tradition.

How might this strange agreement between Armenian Recension A and S—which, incidentally, extends from section 10, 155 to the saying <term>logion; a short saying or teaching attributed to a religious figure</term> 10, 157 (see table)—be explained? I believe that the Syriac text in Budge provides us with the key to solving this riddle. It shows us that we are dealing here with a collection that once existed independently, titled *On Thoughts of Sexual Immorality* <note>original Greek: περὶ λογισμῶν πορνείας</note>. For here, after number 297, the following sentence has been preserved: "Here end the questions concerning the thoughts of sexual immorality and the answers to them and the advice of the holy elder." Now, one might think that this is the concluding signature for the entirety of Book XI (*On Sexual Immorality*) <note>original Greek: περὶ πορνείας</note>, which indeed ends with Budge 597 (Bedjan 590). However, such chapter signatures are not otherwise found in S, and in any case, the last sentence of the signature—"the advice of the holy elder"—refers only to numbers 594–597 (= Bedjan 54 \*\* ff.). This is because the corresponding heading appears before 594: "Excellent advice concerning sexual immorality from one of the holy elders." While Budge lacks any heading at the beginning of our section (588), the keyword *thought of sexual immorality* <note>original Greek: λογισμὸς τῆς πορνείας</note>, which appears in the concluding remark, is found at the start of each of the sayings from 588–593 ⁵). The whole of Chapter XI in S deals with *sexual immorality* <note>original Greek: πορνεία</note>, not specifically with the *thought of sexual immorality*. We thus come to the conclusion that the aforementioned concluding remark summarizes precisely our section in its two parts: 588–593 (*against the thought of sexual immorality* <note>original Greek: πρὸς τὸν λογισμὸν πορνείας</note>) and 594–597 (Advice of an Elder).

We have here, then, a very old, independent little collection of <term>apophthegms; sayings or anecdotes of the Desert Fathers</term>. It contained both attributed and anonymous material. The Greek tradition (G) extracted the two attributed sayings. For Theodore of Scetis, whom he found here, he created a separate category, without realizing that he was none other than the Theodore of Pherme ⁶) who appears in his work with so many other sayings. In the saying that follows in S...

# Chapter 1. The Various Traditions, Relationship, and Value.

(Bu 589 Be 586) <note>These abbreviations refer to the editions of the Syriac text by scholars Budge and Bedjan</note> actually lists alongside Theodore "an elder of Pherme." In the small collection IV* 20. 21, both <term>logia; plural of logion, a short saying or teaching</term> are indeed attributed to the same Isidore (a scribal error for Theodore) of Scetis. Here, therefore, we have an ancient text that we must laboriously reconstruct from the Greek (G), Syriac (S), and the IV* collection. The third saying in S (Bu 590 Be 587) is listed here under the name of Copres of Alexandria. The Greek tradition (G) read "Cyrus of Alexandria" and incorporated this name along with that single saying into its catalog. We will likely have to strike the name here and move the saying under Copres, whom G lists immediately beforehand with his own sayings. Furthermore, in the "Cyrus" saying, G has preserved the keyword of the source: "concerning the thought of sexual immorality" <note>original Greek: πρὸς τὸν λογισμὸν τῆς πορνείας</note>. The anonymous material of our collection then also passed into the PJ and NB collections <note>PJ and NB refer to specific scholarly classifications of manuscript groups</note>. PJ V 15. 16. 17 appear here in exactly the same order as in the Armenian version (though shortened here). It is particularly significant that N 78–81 still represents almost exactly the context preserved in S (Budge 592, 594) and Armenian 10, 155f. g. (see table), whereas in Bedjan's text, it appears fragmented.

Thus, one might assume at first glance that the mysterious agreement between Armenian Recension A and the Syriac (S) in Budge stems from the fact that the Armenian translator still had that old, small collection compactly before him and incorporated it into his collection at 10, 155. 157. But things are not quite that simple. Section 10, 156 also shows a striking connection with S that cannot be explained by this assumption; this entry, exactly like S 33*, contains a combination of two sayings that reappear in PJ in two completely separate places, X 91 and XII 13. Thus, it can no longer be a coincidence that Armenian 10, 158—like S 157—presents the saying from the Greek collection "Cassian 8" anonymously, and that Armenian 10, 159 is identical to the piece S 158! (also = B 168 a*) ¹).

These agreements between Armenian A and S, to which a whole series of special points of contact are added (see p. 21, note 4) ²), can, in my opinion, only be explained in a broader context. It must now be assumed that the editor of Armenian A had, in some way, an older layer of the tradition of the <term>Apophthegmata; the collected "Sayings of the Desert Fathers"</term> directly or indirectly at his disposal, which is also present in the S collections. This would also best explain the archaic arrangement of material within it (see p. 21). Alongside this, however, the observation would remain that the Armenian version is simultaneously dependent on the secondary material in NB and has itself added an abundance of secondary material from its own sources.

The goal to which I wished to lead the investigation is, I believe, achieved regardless, and the text-critical investigation of details can only be undertaken after extensive new collections of material and preliminary work have been completed. It may be left to the future editors of this immense body of material. I am compiling here only a few more observations that may serve once again to highlight the value of the Syriac tradition.

In our Syriac collection, specifically in S* 122–127 under the heading "Words which Abba Moses sent to Abba Poimen," seven numbered <term>logia; short sayings or spiritual teachings</term> are compiled. We find these again in the Latin collection PJ IV* 1–7 as: *seven chapters of words which Father Moses sent to Father Poimen* <note>original Latin: "septem capitula verborum, quae misit abbas Moyses abbati Poimeni"</note>. In the Greek tradition (G), they appear without specific numbering and without an indication of the total count under Moses 14–18. In a heavily revised form, they are found in MD 109, though the number 7 is retained. Individual fragments of the original tradition are offered by MD 2, 35–37 and R 202, 203. I am providing a table here as well, from which the relationship between the various series of traditions will become clear. The table shows at first glance that the Syriac version (S*) alone among all witnesses has faithfully preserved the count of the "seven chapters." In the continuously transmitted text of the Greek (G) and Latin (PJ) versions, there are nine clearly distinct items. PJ maintained the number seven only by grouping two items under number 4 and two items under number 7. Only in S* is the phrase "the end of all these things" <note>original Greek: τέλος δὲ τούτων πάντων</note> found in its proper place, at the beginning of No. 7. In G and PJ, it stands in the middle of a long section (G 18 / PJ IV* 7) and has even received a continuation, the origin of which we will establish shortly. But MD also presupposes the tradition found in G and PJ. The material offered by the R manuscript is too limited for us to build conclusions upon. Yet, since the number 7 for the Moses-Poimen sayings is also preserved in the titles of PJ and MD, S* alone has preserved the original state of the text here.

Then follows in S* under a new number (128) a passage that is found in G 18 and PJ IV* 7 without any recognizable break at the end of a section that has been stretched to an awkward length. However, this piece no longer belongs to the original "seven chapters," but is instead a commentary on chapters 1 and 2: "To die to your neighbor means to bear your sins" <note>original Greek: τὸ ἀποθανεῖν δὲ ἀπὸ τοῦ πλησίον σου τοῦτό ἐστι τὸ βαστάσαι σου τὰς ἁμαρτίας</note>.

The relationship between these three parallel texts is a remarkable one. First, we observe that until almost the very end—aside from a minor variant<note>1) Greek: "zeal" (προθυμία); Latin: "humility" (humilitas). See the highlighted passage above.</note>—there is complete agreement between the Greek text (G) and the Syriac version (S*) against the Latin traditions (MD/Pa). In the concluding sentences, the picture changes completely. Now, the Syriac (S*) runs unmistakably parallel with the Latin versions (MD/Pa). One could assume that S* was compiled from two different texts, but based on the observations made above, this is no longer likely. It is much more probable that the Greek version (G) shortened the text at the end, while the Syriac (S*) and Latin (MD/PA) versions preserved the original foundation. 

And for this suspicion, proof can even be provided! We can now bring in the previously mentioned Coptic Macarius text (Annals of the Guimet Museum, 138 f.) for comparison. This text also runs, by and large, entirely parallel with the Greek and Syriac versions. But here, the final sentence in Amélineau’s translation reads:
> <note>original French: "une possession (?) de ton tombeau..."</note> a possession (?) of your tomb, as if you were ready to throw yourself into it, considering your death near you day after day, lost in the deserts, the mountains, and the holes of the earth.

If we compare this text with the Syriac (S*), it turns out that it comes closer to it than all the others. Here, we even find the mention of the mountains, which the Latin versions (MD and Pa) do not have. Admittedly, the striking concluding parallel between S* and the Latin versions is also missing in the Coptic piece. In the Coptic version, the text may again be somewhat shortened. But our suspicion that the Greek (G) is shortened at the end is most brilliantly confirmed by the parallel Coptic text. Thus, in the Syriac version (S*), all the threads of the textual tradition converge. If we assume the text of S* to be, on the whole, the primary one, all deviations in the other versions are fully explained.

Finally, one last observation can be pointed out. The Latin versions (MD and PA) together offer an even longer elaboration beyond the parallels with S*, G, and the Coptic. If we look closer, this is a reworking of the last piece of the Moses tradition discussed above, which we previously characterized as a commentary attached to the seven sayings. ### § 16. Several Coptic pieces published by Amélineau (*Annals of the Guimet Museum*).

As an appendix, we should also treat several smaller Coptic (<term>Bohairic</term> <note>a dialect of the Coptic language used in the Nile Delta</note>) collections, which Amélineau published and translated in the 25th volume of the *Annals of the Guimet Museum* <note>original: Annales du Musée Guimet</note>, and which likewise belong to the circle of our literature. These are primarily the *Sayings of Antony* <note>original: Apophthegmata Antons</note> pages 15–45 and those of *Macarius* <note>original: Makars</note> pages 203–234 2). A simple consideration can, in my opinion, already make it probable that these pieces are not sources that existed before the Greek (G) and were then adopted by the Greek editor, but are instead individual pieces split off from the Greek tradition. Such extensive collections of <term>sayings</term> <note>original: Apophthegmen</note>, categorized under the name of a single <term>Abba</term> <note>a title for a desert father, meaning "Father"</note>, represent precisely the unique characteristic of the Greek (G) tradition, whose editor boasts as his special achievement that he organized the entire mass of tradition according to the names of the individual fathers in alphabetical order. It remains possible, of course, that small collections of sayings under the name of this or that famous authority once existed outside of the Greek (G). But on the whole, we will always be inclined to consider the former possibility as more likely 3).

Thus, these Coptic collections also show the greatest content-related affinity with the collections in the Greek (G). I will briefly summarize the result of my investigation. I count in Amélineau 54 <term>logia</term> <note>sayings or words of spiritual wisdom; singular: logion</note> of Antony (which are distributed across 48 sections numbered by me). 21 of these numbers are found again in the Greek (G) (which for its part shows 38 numbers) 4); for five others, parallels can be found in the rest of the Greek tradition—here, foreign pieces have simply been attributed to Antony. In 27 5) cases, we are dealing with (often quite secondary) unique material 6) of the Coptic tradition—

### Book I. Investigations into the Textual Tradition and Character of the *Sayings of the Desert Fathers* <note>original: Apophthegmata Patrum</note>.

We see that the oral tradition is still in a state of flux, and new material is being incorporated into the framework of the tradition established by the Greek version (G).

The Coptic collection of the Macarius Sayings proves to be even more closely related to the Greek tradition (G)²). I count 35 <term>Logia</term> <note>individual sayings or short teachings</note> in 34 sections numbered by me in Amélineau’s work; 23 of these numbers are found again under Macarius in the Greek version. However, several cases are particularly noteworthy where it is possible to confirm the Coptic tradition through other parallels outside of the Greek version G. For instance, the small and insignificant saying 10 of Macarius is found only in Paulos Euergetinos 545 b³), still under the name of Macarius! In 29 b (a fragment at the beginning, joined together with 29 a, also a fragment), the prayer overheard by Macarius is also found in manuscript N (Coislinian 126) 16, again under Macarius's name. The story of Macarius’s visit to the two pious women (33) is preserved in Greek in B 237 b and in Latin in version III * 17 (= S * 4), and a parallel to <term>Logion</term> 19 is found only in the Armenian translation 8, 25, though it appears there anonymously⁴). One can see that the Coptic tradition either possessed a more complete text of the Greek version (G) or picked up a few more words of Macarius which had fallen into the collection of anonymous sayings. One must constantly marvel at the persistence of the tradition of these sayings, which enables us to rediscover the same saying under the same name in such distant witnesses of the transmission. Thus, the total number of Macarius's words that can be verified elsewhere in G + NB rises to 27, and only 2 remain as the unique material of the Copt, one of which (No. 7) comes from the Coptic *Life of Macarius*, and a second (No. 27) finds a certain parallel in R 29 XV 86⁵). In other words, the origin of the Coptic collection has been clarified almost down to the individual details.

The situation is quite different, however, with that collection of Macarius's sayings which Amélineau published under the title "Virtues of St. Macarius" <note>original: Vertus de St. Macaire</note> 119–202. Among the 81 numbers in this collection, only 5 (or 4)⁶) recur entirely or partially in the Greek version (G). We also find some pieces here that appear in the large collection under a different name or anonymously⁷). The overwhelming bulk of the material is entirely new and often...

### Chapter 1: The Various Traditions, Relationship, and Value

Admittedly, there is much found among them that points to a much later time; for example, the story of how Abbot <note>original: "A." for "Abba" or Abbot</note> Shenoute, upon his return from the Council of Ephesus, is miraculously transported on a cloud to the monastery of Abbot Macarius (No. 32). Furthermore, the description of the evil ruler, painted in anti-Christian colors in No. 57, could only originate from the Islamic period in its current form. In general, these often quite lengthy explanations already exhibit the style of preaching and <term>paraenesis</term> <note>moral exhortation or advice</note> that is largely foreign to the *Sayings of the Desert Fathers* <note>original: "Apophthegmen"</note> as a whole. 

It may perhaps be mentioned here that the collection of the *Virtues* <note>original: "Vertus"</note> stands in a peculiar literary connection with the well-known *Homilies* of Macarius. *Virtues* No. 58 sounds literally like Homily 33. And pieces 5, 61, and 72 offer long, literal parallels to the first and second letters of the small collection of Macarius's letters, which are usually found together with the homilies in printed editions¹). The many small parables that characterize the tradition of the *Virtues* also recall the many parable sections scattered throughout the homilies. It is further noteworthy that **Evagrius** appears here so often as the sole witness of the tradition or together with other disciples of Macarius (cf. Nos. 17, 39, 42, 69, 76, 77 [= **Evagrius**, *The Praktikos* <note>original: "Praktika"</note> 94], 81)²). — We are dealing here with a side-branch of the literature of the *Sayings*, perhaps a tradition that was cultivated and passed down in the school of **Evagrius**. On the other hand, as we have seen, **Evagrius** was an avoided and suspicious authority in the circles from which the main tradition of the *Sayings* originated.

In our context, the Coptic *Life* <note>original: "Vita"</note> of **John the Dwarf** <note>original: "Joannes Kolobos"</note> (Amélineau 316–410) deserves special interest; it was written by **Zacharias**, Bishop of Sakhâ, who lived around the turn of the seventh and eighth centuries³). **Zacharias** himself cites the *Paradise of the Fathers* as the main source (Amélineau p. 322 f.)⁴). And a comparison of this *Life* <note>original: "Bios"</note> with the Greek tradition **G** indeed yields a highly interesting result. We see how the author, over long stretches of his narrative, does nothing other than string together one piece of the tradition of the *Sayings* after another⁵). We will later...
