## Chapter 2.

# Time of Origin,
# Growth, and Value of the Sayings Literature.

### § 17. Chronology of the Fathers of Scetis.

We must now attempt to gain insight into the character of our source, its age, its origin, and the manner in which it was created. It has already been established that the collection, in its original form, contains the traditions of the monks of Scetis <note>a remote desert valley in Egypt, a cradle of early Christian monasticism</note> and several related circles. In a broader sense, "Scetis" refers to the desert district extending a distance south of Lake Mareotis¹) to near the city of Terenuthis in the western Nile Delta. Here, the anachoretic <note>hermit-like, living in seclusion</note> monks of Scetis settled in various locations that are repeatedly distinguished in the tradition—primarily the Mountain of Nitria <note>original: "Mons Nitria"</note>, the Cells <note>original: "τὰ κέλλια" (ta kellia)</note>, the desert of Scetis in the narrower sense, and also Mount Pherme and Mount Petra²). Our collection comprises the sayings and stories of these monks from Scetis dating from the mid-fourth to the mid-fifth century.

It is not entirely easy to separate the individual generations and establish a somewhat clear chronology, at least for the main figures, within the tangle of names and relationships we encounter here.

**Chapter 2. Period of Origin, Growth, and Value of the Sayings Literature.**

->A brief overview of the "generations" of Scetis <note>the remote desert valley in Egypt that became a primary center for early Christian monasticism</note> may be presented here first.<-

Ammon of Nitria is considered the founder of Scetic monasticism; he was a contemporary of Antony the Great and is mentioned in Antony's *Life* <note>original: "Vita"; a formal biography of a saint</note>. In our collection, he appears under the name **Ammon the Nitrian** <note>original: "Ἀμμοῦν ὁ Νιτριώτης"</note> with only three entries¹). However, entries number 7 and 8 (under the name Ammonas) should also be attributed to this Ammon²). The true spiritual hero of Scetis is then considered to be the Egyptian **Macarius**, of whom the *Lausiac History* <note>a famous 5th-century collection of stories about the Desert Fathers</note> chapter 17 and Rufinus in the *History of the Monks* <note>original: "Hist. Mon."</note> chapter 28 report³), and of whom our collection has also preserved a rich tradition. For Rufinus—whose alleged visit to the Egyptian monks occurred in the year 394—Macarius, as well as his namesake "the Alexandrian" (page 38), already belonged to the past. The author of the *Lausiac History* (end of chapter 17) also states that when he visited Scetis, this Macarius had already been deceased for a year. Unfortunately, the chronology of the travels of that work's author can no longer be established with certainty; indeed, its reliability must be doubted entirely⁴). Nevertheless, we will hardly go wrong if we place his death roughly in the decade of 380⁵)–390.

Alongside Macarius stands an entire circle of older Scetic authorities. An excellent clue for establishing a whole series of older anchorites <note>hermits who live in total seclusion</note> of Scetis is offered to us by the text of **Pambo 11** in the complete version of the Berlin manuscript, page 72 d (the text by Cotelier is fragmentary). Here, the hermits **Pambo**, **Bessarion**, **Isaiah**, **Paesios**, and **Athre** are mentioned in conversation with the **priest of Nitria** <note>original: "πρεσβύτερος τῆς Νιτρείας"</note>. — **Pambo** belongs in any case to the oldest authorities of Scetis. He appears in Rufinus’s *Church History* <note>original: "H. E."</note> II 4, 8 alongside the two Macariuses; the *Lausiac History* (chapters 10 and 46) reports on him in detail and even provides a saying <note>original: "Logion"</note> (G 8) which he is said to have spoken at the hour of his death. According to the collection entry G Pambo 4, he appears as a contemporary of Athanasius⁶). Our collection also has much to tell regarding **Bessarion**, who is named alongside Pambo. That he also belongs to the oldest generation of Scetis is proven by his visit to John of Lykopolis mentioned in G 4⁷). **Isaiah** and **Paesios**, who otherwise do not appear in collection G⁸), are interestingly contrasted with one another in the *Lausiac History* chapter 14 as representatives of two different monastic ideals: the cenobitic <note>communal living</note> and the anchoritic <note>solitary living</note>⁹). And once again, the "blessed" **Pambo** is mentioned here as the one...

...introduced as an authority who understands how to settle the dispute over priority between the two monastic ideals <note>referring to the tension between the solitary life of a hermit and the communal life of a monk</note>. Abba Athre, who is otherwise rarely mentioned, appears in the Greek collection under the name **Pistos** <note>original: "Πιστός"; meaning "Faithful"</note> (Migne 372) as a contemporary of Abba Or. This observation helps us assign the latter his place among the oldest generation as well. The *Lausiac History* <note>a 5th-century chronicle of early monks</note> chapter 9 also counts him among those no longer living. On the other hand, Abba Pior, who also plays a role in the Greek collection, appears in the *Lausiac History* chapter 10 as a contemporary of Pambo and is treated in chapter 39, by all appearances, as a figure of the past. To this generation, we may finally add one of the monks named Sisoes, who is grouped with several others under the name Sisoes in the Greek collection (see pages 41/42). According to the Greek collection (entry 28), if the information is correct, he is said to have left Scetis <note>the famous monastic desert in Egypt</note> shortly after the death of Antony and settled on the **Mount of Antony** <note>original: "ὄρος 'Αντωνίου"</note>. His interactions with Abba Or are explicitly mentioned here, which in turn would agree with the entry in the Greek collection for Pistos, which shows us a Sisoes in contact with Or and Athre.

Thus, the oldest circle of Scetic monks reveals itself to us: Macarius the Egyptian, Pambo, Pior, Isaiah, Paesios, Athre, Or, and the elder Sisoes. It can be proven that most of these Fathers already belonged to the past when the author of the *Lausiac History* collected his reports on Scetic monasticism. With them, we actually reach back as far as the middle of the fourth century.

If we turn once more to the testimony of Pambo in the Greek collection (entry 11), from which we began above, this passage reports that the **elder of Nitria** <note>original: "πρεσβύτερος τῆς Νιτρείας"; an "elder" or "priest" was a leader of a monastic community</note> sought advice from these older authorities on **how the brothers ought to live** <note>original: "ὅπως ὀφείλουσιν οἱ ἀδελφοὶ διάγειν"</note>. The "elder of Nitria" mentioned here is likely none other than Isidore, who is frequently mentioned elsewhere in tradition and whom the Greek collection introduces as **Isidore, elder of Scetis** <note>original: "Ισίδωρος πρεσβύτερος τῆς Σκήτεως"</note> (Migne 220) with a series of sayings <note>1</note>.

Alongside Isidore, I would then place someone like Abba Theodore of Pherme <note>2</note>, who appears in Theodore 1 and Pambo 14 in conversation with Macarius and Pambo—specifically as the younger brother—and in Or 1 alongside Abba Or. He might perhaps be identical to the Theodore who appears as a Scetic authority in Cassian’s *Conferences* <note>original: "Collatio"</note> VI. Alongside this Theodore (Isaac 2) appears a certain Cronius, both serving as teachers to Isaac. A Cronius is mentioned by the author of the *Lausiac History* (chapter 7) among the Fathers he saw on Mount Nitria (cf. also Rufinus, *History of the Monks* 26).

From the priest Isidore, we can certainly identify some slightly younger contemporaries. For instance, it is told of Abba Karion how the priest Isidore decisively intervened in his life's path (Greek collection, Karion 2). Above all, however, Paphnutius must be mentioned here, of whom Cassian (*Conferences* XVIII, 15, 3) explicitly reports <note>3</note> that he was the successor to Isidore in the office of the priesthood and that he was a youth when Isidore held this office. This Paphnutius, with the interesting nickname **Bubalos** <note>4</note> (**Cephalas**) <note>Bubalos means "The Buffalo" and Cephalas means "The Head"</note>, is...

Cassian appearing in his third *Conference* <note>original: "Collatio"; a series of influential interviews conducted by John Cassian with the desert monks</note> with the monks of Scetis. He appears, on the other hand, as a disciple of Macarius and a transmitter of several of his *Sayings* <note>original: "Apophthegmata"</note> (Macarius G 28, 37)¹. Furthermore, Abba Moses (G 1) appears as a younger monk seeking advice from Abba Isidore. Since a conversation very similar to the one here is mentioned in the *Lausiac History* <note>a 5th-century chronicle of early monasticism</note> chapter 19 between Isidore and Moses, we may assume with certainty that the Abba Moses who plays such a significant role in the Greek collection is identical to Moses "the Robber" or the "Ethiopian" reported in chapter 19 of the *Lausiac History*². At the same time, we may suspect that the Abba Moses who appears as an authority in Scetis in Cassian's first and second *Conference* (alongside Paphnutius in *Conference* III) is again this same Moses the Ethiopian. Finally, a sentence transmitted by Poimen (166) is significant: **"From the third generation of Scetis and from Abba Moses, the brothers no longer achieved spiritual progress."** <note>original: "ἀπὸ τρίτης γενεᾶς τῆς Σκήτεως καὶ τοῦ ἀββᾶ Μωυσέως οὐκ ἦλθον ἔτι οἱ ἀδελφοὶ εἰς προκοπήν"</note>. We may further regard Abba Silvanus as a contemporary of Moses³, who, as we have seen, moved from Scetis to Sinai and later to Palestine and had numerous disciples: Zeno⁴ (G 1), Zacharias (Silvanus G 1, 3, 4, 8), Mark (G 1–5), and Netras.

The narrative found in the Greek collection under Serapion 4 is also identical to the one Cassian brings under the same name in *Conference* XVIII, 11; thus, the Serapion in the Greek collection likely coincides with the Serapion to whom Cassian attributes his fifth *Conference*⁵. It remains uncertain, however, whether we have the right to connect Serenus, who features only slightly in the Greek collection, with the Serenus in *Conferences* VII and VIII.

We reach somewhat firmer ground regarding historical dates with one of the most prominent figures in the tradition of the Greek collection, Abba Arsenius. According to tradition (Arsenius 42), he is said to have lived at the court of Emperor Theodosius and served as the tutor to Honorius and Arcadius. He then became a monk in Scetis and later withdrew into the interior and remote parts of the desert. The date of his death can still be determined approximately. The biographer of Saint Euthymius, Cyril of Scythopolis, reports at the beginning of the 5th section⁶ of the life of his hero—which takes place between the Council of Ephesus <note>431 AD</note> and the Council of Chalcedon <note>451 AD</note>—that Egyptian fathers told him then about the life of the recently deceased Abba Arsenius, and that these stories had influenced him in a way that shaped his life. From this, the conclusion seems to follow that Arsenius died around 430 AD. We arrive at approximately the same date from the following traditions based on the information in the *Sayings*. This reflects a common sentiment in later monastic literature that the early "heroic" age had passed.</note>

Standing finally as the last in the series of ascetics appearing in the Greek collection is **Abba Poimen**. He, too, left Scetis during the time of the "desolation," and in *G Anub 1* it is described in an interesting way how he came from there to Terenuthis and lived for some time with his brothers in a kind of communal life in an abandoned temple.

### § 18. Date of Origin of the Apophthegmata.

The *Apophthegmata* <note>The "Sayings of the Desert Fathers," a collection of wisdom and anecdotes from early Christian hermits.</note> thus encompass the tradition of the circle of Scetic monks from approximately the middle or last third of the fourth century to the middle of the fifth century. It should further be noted that the true golden age of this monasticism, from which most memories have been preserved, falls roughly within the era of Patriarch Theophilus <note>Theophilus of Alexandria, reigned 385–412 AD.</note>. This brings us to the main problem of our investigation: How did this comprehensive collection of memories from the lives of the Scetic monks come into being, and what value is to be attributed to this tradition?

We shall first attempt to obtain some data regarding the time of origin of the large corpus, the foundation of which is found in the Greek Alphabetical and Anonymous collections, and which can be recovered from these witnesses with the help of Syriac and Latin translations. We find here, however, only a few pieces that provide a point of reference for dating the collection. One of the most important is the story of the meeting between a monk and Emperor Theodosius II which, according to its attestation in various manuscripts, clearly belongs to the oldest core of our collection. The relevant texts have been gathered and a clever investigation into their mutual relationship has been conducted <margin>3</margin>. I will briefly summarize the most important results insofar as they concern the question of dating our collection. Above all, the scholar Nau succeeded in uncovering the original form of our narrative in the *Codex Parisinus 881*. In this form, it still has no connection to Scetis <margin>4</margin>, but rather deals with the meeting of a monk with Theodosius "in the places near Chalcedon." <note>original: ἐν τοῖς πλησιάζουσι τόποις Καλχηδόνος.</note> It concludes with the remark that after their first meeting, Theodosius met more frequently with the pious father "for the sake of spiritual benefit." <note>original: ὠφελείας χάριν.</note>

Greek 9), there is mention of a village <note>original: κώμη</note> near Poimen’s settlement. In Greek 26 it says: "passing through into Egypt." <note>original: παρερχόμενος εἰς τὴν Αἴγυπτον.</note> The location of Mount Athlibis <note>original: Ἄθλιβις</note> mentioned in Greek 90 is unknown to me. It is stated here that Poimen was known throughout the whole country, although he did not leave his cell.

<margin>2</margin> The remarkable story in Greek 78, that heretics came to Poimen and slandered the Archbishop of Alexandria, claiming "that he received his ordination from elders," <note>original: ὡς ὅτι παρὰ πρεσβυτέρων ἔχει τὴν χειροτονίαν</note> probably falls in the (pre-Cyrillian) early period of Poimen. Cf. Butler, *The Lausiac History of Palladius* I, 213.

The Scetic tradition <note>The tradition stemming from Scetis, one of the most famous early monastic centers in the Egyptian desert.</note> took possession of this tradition in an interesting way. The monk who meets with the King here is transformed into an Egyptian hermit staying in Constantinople. The first question the King directs to him is: "How are the Fathers in Egypt doing?" And finally, it is reported that after the encounter with the Emperor, the hermit immediately fled back to Egypt—an example of humility and modesty ¹). The intent behind these changes is obvious. We have here an interesting contribution to how anecdotes migrate and are adapted to a new environment. Since a certain amount of time must have passed before the story taking place in the year 446 was recorded, traveled to Egypt, and received its "Scetic dress" there, we obtain as the earliest <term>terminus a quo</term> <note>original Latin: "limit from which"; the earliest possible date for an event.</note> for our collection roughly the first decade of the second half of the fifth century.

We arrive at a similar result based on *Poimen 183* ²). Here, a monk named Joannes (John), who visited <term>Abba Poimen</term> from Syria, is given the characterization: "the one exiled by Emperor Marcian" <note>original Greek: ὁ ἐξορισθεὶς ὑπὸ Μαρκιανοῦ τοῦ βασιλέως. This note leads us into the period after the Council of Chalcedon <note>A major church council held in 451 AD which led to significant divisions in Eastern Christianity.</note>. This again would yield the same earliest possible date.

On the other hand, we search for a firm <term>terminus ad quem</term> <note>original Latin: "limit to which"; the latest possible date for an event.</note>. However, the circumstance that we find two further sayings from our collection in the same speech proves that we are no longer dealing with an oral tradition, but rather with a literary borrowing.

Looking over to the West, Butler (*Lausiac History* I 211) has pointed out that the *Rule of Benedict* (around 530 AD) already quotes a written collection of Sayings: *Although we read that wine is not for monks at all* <note>original Latin: "Licet legamus vinum monachorum omnino non est"; this refers to a famous saying about monastic sobriety</note> (= LV 31 = S 80).

This information appears to be extremely important for the dating of "G" <note>The scholar refers to the primary Greek collection as "G."</note>. This is because the saying quoted here is found in none of the small Latin collections, and only in "PJ" <note>A Latin translation of the Sayings attributed to the clerics Pelagius and John.</note> (Poimen G 19 = IV 31 = S 80). We may therefore conclude that a translation of "PJ" was already known in the West at that time. Now, however, "PJ" is certainly dependent on "G." If a Latin translation of a secondary revision of "G" already existed in the year 531, we may set the latest possible date for the creation of "G" at approximately the year 500 AD. Thus, it follows that the composition of "G" occurred in the last decades of the fifth century, roughly between 460(70) and 500 ⁴).

### § 19. Poimen and his School.

In which circles and in what manner might the great collected work of the *Sayings* have arisen during this time? I believe that this question can also be answered with a certain degree of probability. The *Sayings* themselves offer us a name that appears in them again and again: I mean that of <term>Abba Poimen</term> <note>Poimen is Greek for "Shepherd"; he is one of the most frequently cited fathers in the collection.</note>, with whom I concluded the overview of the series of fathers from Scetis above.

This suggests that for many smaller sayings—where Poimen’s name was not explicitly repeated in the introduction—his name eventually disappeared entirely. It also suggests that for many a <term>logion</term> <note>a "logion" is a short, pithy saying attributed to a religious teacher</note> of older Fathers whose original witness was Poimen, this fact was later obscured.

This leads us to a further observation. Not only is a vast mass of sayings transmitted from Poimen, but according to current tradition, he appears more than any other as the mediator of the sayings and stories of older authorities. A later witness, the author of the Life of John the Dwarf <note>original: "Joannes Kolobos"</note> preserved in Coptic, gives us an extraordinarily interesting testimony for this mediating activity of Poimen, which I include here in Amélineau’s translation 2):

> "The great discerner <note>original French: 'Le grand diacritique'; referring to the gift of spiritual discernment</note>, the exceedingly wise, our father saint Abba Poimen . . . . told of many great righteous deeds of a multitude of luminaries among our fathers, . . . . he then, the truly wise and all-holy Abba Poimen, wrote of the multitudes of righteous deeds of him who is our father, Abba John the Dwarf, informing us word for word in what he said about him, that he was masterfully strengthened in the habit of perfection."

Whether Poimen himself already passed down the tradition of the earlier Fathers in written records may remain an open question. However, the Greek collection <note>referred to as "G"</note> also confirms his mediating role in the tradition for many pieces of the <term>Apophthegmata</term> <note>the "Apophthegmata Patrum" or Sayings of the Desert Fathers</note>. On the one hand, his name appears as the witness for the most diverse Fathers 3). On the other hand, among the 187 Sayings of Poimen in the Greek collection, we find a whole series of sayings that actually belong to older authorities and are only mediated through Poimen 4).

And Abba Poimen is, for his part, surrounded by a whole circle of students and followers, to which his brothers also belong. Here, within the circle of Poimen's students, the memory of him would have been cherished alongside the entire tradition of Scetis <note>Scetis, or Wadi El Natrun, was the heart of early Christian monasticism in Egypt</note>. Poimen himself had still maintained active personal relationships with the leading authorities from the golden age of Scetis; he lived until the middle of the fifth century. With his students, we descend further into the second half of the century—that is, the time in which, in all probability, the great collection of the <term>Apophthegmata</term> <note>literally "sayings"; short stories and wisdom from the monks</note> originated. Naturally, the entire material of the collection does not stem solely from the tradition of Poimen and his school. Small records likely arose in other places as well; as we shall soon see, some of these must be much older. However, for a vast mass of these memories, Poimen and his school seem to have been the primary source.

### § 20. Socrates, John Cassian, and the Apophthegmata.

It has just been suggested that the collection of <term>Apophthegmata</term> material represents a long process, at the end of which stands Poimen and his school. We shall attempt to penetrate a little further into the history of this process and trace it back to its beginnings. A first milestone on this path is provided by the chapter on monks in the *Ecclesiastical History* of Socrates (Book IV, Chapter 23). After Socrates has provided a detailed account of the life of Ammun, the legendary founder of Scetic monasticism, he describes how, following Ammun’s example, <note>original: "κατὰ μέρος ἐπληρώθη τὸ τῆς Νιτρίας ὄρος καὶ τὸ τῆς Σκήτεως"</note> "the mountain of Nitria and that of Scetis were filled bit by bit." He cannot describe the lives of all these saints, but wishes <note>original: "ἐκ πολλῶν ὀλίγα ἐγκαταμίξαι τῇ ἱστορίᾳ"</note> "to weave a few items from many into his history." He then names the following personalities: Didymos, Arsenios, Pior, Isidore, Pambo, Piterus (likely G Pityrion), and the two Macarii, giving one or two sayings or a short characterization of each. With the exception of Didymos, all the names mentioned here are known to us from our collection. And of the quoted sayings, at least three recur almost word-for-word within it: Pior 2, Isidore 3, and Pambo 4. Now, it is entirely within the realm of possibility that Socrates was used as a source for our collection. On the other hand, the question must be raised: from where did Socrates himself obtain the material for his depiction of Scetic monasticism? The answer can hardly be anything other than that he already had before him a small collection of memories of the heroes of Scetic monasticism, organized exactly in the manner of our later <term>Apophthegmata</term>. The correspondences pointed out above could then be explained by the assumption that a portion of that smaller collection—which Socrates presupposes at the end of the first half of the fifth century—was incorporated into the larger one.

Perhaps even further progress can be made by examining the descriptions given to us by John Cassian in his two great works, the *Institutes* and the *Conferences* <note>original: "Institutionen und Collationen"</note>, regarding the life and activities of the North Egyptian and Scetic monks. Cassian's *Institutes* and *Conferences* show a related literary character in that the author's own explanations in the first work, and the long, continuous discourses which he attributes (in question-and-answer form) to the Egyptian Fathers in the *Conferences*...

---

When one compares these two versions of the same story, the conclusion seems almost inescapable that Cassian’s text is secondary and the *Apophthegmata* <note>The "Sayings of the Desert Fathers," a collection of wisdom from 4th and 5th-century Egyptian monks</note> are primary. The scribe of **G** <note>The Greek alphabetical collection of Sayings</note> or his source would have had to be a master of formulation if he had constructed such a simple and well-phrased story out of Cassian’s account, which is presented with rhetorical bombast. A number of Cassian's literary idiosyncrasies—the emphasis on the "rule of the elders," the embellishment of the story with biblical quotations—are missing in **G**. Almost all the concrete features of the story in Cassian reappear in **G**, and are even increased by a few; compare the sentence in **G**: "And he made him taste [the food]; and the elder also began to eat," and the necessary conclusion of the story, which Cassian omits because he is only interested in the speech of Serapion. One may therefore venture the assumption that Cassian was already familiar with such a story, and indeed in a literary <gloss>1)</gloss> tradition like the one preserved in **G**, and that he "dressed up" this story with his rhetorical style, which he likely brought back to his homeland from the East.

And such observations can be multiplied. Near the stories just discussed, in *Conference* XVIII 15, another is found. It reports how, during the time when Isidore the Priest was in Scetis <note>A famous center of early Christian monasticism in the Egyptian desert</note>, his later successor Paphnutius was accused of theft through an intrigue; he took the punishment imposed on him innocently and in silence until the demon of the brother who had maliciously waylaid him unmasked both himself and the truth. Paulos Euergetinos <note>An 11th-century monk who compiled a famous anthology of monastic wisdom</note> provides the same story from the *Gerontikon* <note>Literally "The Book of the Old Men," another name for the Sayings collection</note>, and he must have actually read it there <gloss>2)</gloss>, although all other parallels fail us here. For it is, to all appearances, independent of Cassian. In place of Paphnutius, an unnamed deacon of the Priest Isidore appears here. And a closer comparison of the texts shows that exactly the same relationship exists here between Cassian’s rhetorical style and the simple, plain narrative of the Sayings as we were just able to establish.

A whole series of further points of contact are added, in which the text of the Sayings can hardly be simply derived <gloss>3)</gloss> from Cassian. Thus we find in **G** under Nisteroos 2 a *logion* <note>A "saying" or divine word</note> from an unnamed elder, whose authority is cited as Nisteroos, the friend of Abba Antony. It concerns the various perfections of the monk as their...

---

1) For the assumption of an oral tradition, the similarities on both sides are too numerous and detailed.
2) Paulos Euergetinos has numerous citations from Cassian’s works alongside those from the *Gerontikon*. However, he specifies his source exactly every time.
3) Absolutely unable to be derived from Cassian is the introduction in **G**, which includes precise information about the witnesses to the story.

<meta>This page continues the detailed textual comparison between John Cassian’s monastic writings and the "Sayings of the Desert Fathers" (Apophthegmata Patrum), arguing that Cassian adapted existing oral or written traditions for his own rhetorical purposes.</meta>

74 Book I. Investigations into the Textual Tradition and Character of the *Apophthegmata Patrum*.

The types of Abraham (<term>hospitality; philoxenia</term>), Elijah (<term>stillness or silence; hesychia</term>), and David (<term>humility; tapeinophrosyne</term>) are mentioned. It is likely no coincidence that Cassian, in his *Conference* XIV.4, provides a very similar explanation, in which Elijah (and Elisha) are again named as models of <term>stillness (hesychia)</term>, while Abraham (and Lot) are named as models of hospitality.

In PJ V 39 = S 624, there is a very charmingly told legend. One of the elders of the Thebaid <note>A region in Upper Egypt famous for early monasticism</note>, who was the son of a pagan priest, recounts how in his youth he once secretly entered a pagan temple. There, he eavesdropped on a meeting of the Devil and his demons, in which each subordinate reported the atrocities they had recently committed. The Devil was dissatisfied with the performance of almost all of them and had them fiercely punished. However, when finally one demon told him that after forty years of work he had succeeded that very night in tempting a monk into sin, the Devil kissed him and placed his crown upon the demon's head, saying: "You have performed a great deed bravely." <note>original Latin: "magnam rem fortiter gessisti"</note> — At that, the boy thought to himself: "The order of monks is truly great." <note>original Latin: "valde magnus est ordo monachorum"</note> Now, if one compares this with the parallel story in *Conference* VIII.16, one finds it told again with bombastic rhetoric, while a number of individual details have disappeared. Finally, in Cassian's version, the son of the pagan priest has been turned into a monk who enters a cave in the wilderness to hold his worship service and then experiences that vision; in other words, the story has been robbed of its actual point.

Furthermore, the narrative in *Conference* XIV.7 is identical to the one provided in the Greek collection under the heading of Eucharistos (= S* 1): the story of the hidden holiness of a secular person living in the world. Again, there is hardly any evidence of a direct dependency of the Greek on Cassian; indeed, Reitzenstein (*History of Monks* and *Lausiac History*, p. 40) already suspected, based on a close comparison of both texts, that Cassian was dependent here on an older text of the *Apophthegmata*. — The parable of the "over-tightened bow" <note>An image used to argue that monks need occasional relaxation to avoid breaking under pressure</note>, which Cassian brings in *Conference* XXIV.21 under the name of the Evangelist John, is attributed in the Greek collection (G 13) to Saint Antony and has a completely different introduction. The story of a monk who is ready, at the command of his superior, to throw his son into the river (G Sisoes 10), appears with all the same details in Cassian, *Institutes* IV.27. Here, the obedient monk is named Patermutius, whereas in the Greek collection he is not named; the superior in Cassian is a <term>monastery elder (senior coenobii)</term>, while in the Greek text it is <term>Sisoes</term>. In the former we have a communal (coenobitic) environment, in the latter a hermit (anchoritic) setting. A second story of a well-endured test of obedience (the motif of watering a dry wooden stick until it leaves) is found in the Greek text under John the Dwarf (Joannes Kolobos) 1, while in Cassian, *Institutes* IV.24, it appears alongside two other tests of obedience under the name of John of Lykopolis. The comparison of monks to a bee, which is found in a lengthy elaboration under the name of Antony in *Institutes* V.4, appears as an anonymous parable in B 167 b = S* 104 = III 187. — Finally, I would point to the important sentence in *Conference* VII.23: "It is customary for the elders to say to them: sit in your cells and eat, drink, and sleep as much as you like, as long as you remain in them continually." <note>original Latin: "(solet) eis a senioribus dici: sedete in cellulis vestris et quantum libitum fuerit, manducate et bibite atque dormite, dummodo in eis jugiter perduretis."</note> Indeed, we read such a saying very frequently in the *Apophthegmata*. Compare, for example, Arsenios 11, Paphnutius 5, Sarmata 3 and 4, Herakleios, and Hierax 1. The phrase "it is customary for the elders to say to them" thus matches exactly, and here again it looks very much as though Cassian had an extensive collection of Sayings before his eyes.

## Chapter 2. The Time of Origin, Growth, and Value of the Sayings Literature. 75

The following consideration also justifies the assumption that written collections of stories and sayings of the fathers of the <term>Scetic Desert</term> <note>The Wadi El Natrun in Egypt, one of the most famous sites of early Christian monasticism</note> must have already been in circulation. The *Institutes* and *Conferences* were written roughly between the years 420 and 428 ¹). However, Cassian’s stay in Egypt could not have lasted much longer than the beginning of the fifth century (402) ²) . Accordingly, there is a period of a good 20 years between Cassian's stay in Egypt and the creation of his works. Nevertheless, we find in them an extensive amount of such reminiscences, including detailed stories that often correspond literally, down to the smallest details, with the tradition found in the *Apophthegmata* <note>The "Sayings of the Desert Fathers"</note>. One can hardly assume that Cassian still mastered the entire material from memory. He must have had a written record of the tradition before him when composing his work ³).

### § 21. *Historia Lausiaca* and Evagrius.

For the *Historia Lausiaca* <note>A famous history of the Egyptian monks written by Palladius</note>, which was also written about two decades after the author's stay in Egypt, observations can be made that indicate the author occasionally adapted "Sayings" material that was already available to him in literary form. I have already pointed this out in my essay on the composition and character of the *Historia Lausiaca* ⁴). I will not return to this in detail because the material here is indeed much less productive.

And finally, the beginning of the literary collections of Sayings can be traced back another 2–3 decades. For this, we have the testimony of **Evagrius** (died 399). At the end of both his "*Praktikos*" and his "*Gnostikos*" ⁵), he appended a small collection of Sayings. Whether Evagrius began this type of collection of the tradition, or whether he himself already had predecessors, cannot be decided with certainty with the means at our disposal. But a suspicion suggests itself. **Evagrius** imprinted the form of the Sayings literature upon almost his entire literary legacy—I mention his *Praktikos*, *Gnostikos*, his *Centuries*, and his *Rules for Monks and Nuns*. In order to present as many Sayings of his own as possible, he excerpted his own letters (as I intend to demonstrate) and, in a quite questionable manner, plundered Origen’s interpretation of the Psalms. How might he have come to this strange kind of literary activity? Likely because even in his time, the "words and stories" of the Egyptian fathers were widespread, whether in fixed oral tradition or already in small written collections.

What is new is that this highly educated Greek man of letters <note>Referring to Evagrius Ponticus, a 4th-century monk known for his intellectual approach to spirituality</note> collected his own sayings for posterity. ### Chapter 3.

## The Literary and Religious-Historical Significance of the Sayings.

### § 22. Character of the Sayings.

Thus, we have followed the history and growth of the literature of the <term>Apophthegmata</term> <note>The "Sayings of the Desert Fathers," from the Greek word for a concise, pithy utterance</note> through several generations: from the very first beginnings of collecting the sayings and deeds of the Fathers at the end of the fourth century, to the emergence of the massive body of the *Great Meadow* <note>original: μέγα λειμωνάριον (mega leimonarion)</note> or the *Paradise of the Fathers* at the turn of the fifth and sixth centuries. And what we have here is a work of a highly peculiar nature and significance. It is the monument of remembrance that the monasticism of the <term>Scetic Desert</term> <note>The Wadi El Natrun in Egypt, a cradle of early Christian monasticism</note> created for itself. Its entire character is determined by the fact that it originates from a completely unliterary environment. Most of the monks who appear here speaking were uneducated Coptic <term>fellahin</term> <note>Egyptian peasants or farmers</note>; we know of the most famous among them—Anthony ²), Macarius ³), and Poimen ⁴), and we may also mention Pachomius and his disciple Theodore, who strictly speaking do not belong here—that they were not masters of the Greek language. None of them left us anything in writing. Evagrius and his circle, so celebrated by Rufinus and especially in the *Lausiac History*, stand recognizably apart from the circles from which the *Sayings* originate. Two sayings <note>original: Logia</note> illuminate this contrast. Evagrius is said to have asked Abba Arsenius:

> “How is it that we, who come from such an education and wisdom, possess nothing, while these peasants <note>original: ἀγροῖκοι (agroikoi)</note> and Egyptians have acquired such virtues? Arsenius says to him: We have nothing of worldly education, but these peasants and Egyptians have acquired the virtues through their own labors.”

In response to a question directed by Abba Arsenios to an Egyptian elder, someone looked at him and said:

> “Abba Arsenios, how can you, who possess Roman and Greek education, ask these peasants about your thoughts? But he spoke to him: I do possess Roman and Greek education. But the alphabet of this peasant I have not yet learned” ⁵).

And precisely because we have a completely unliterary layer before us here, the *Sayings* are such an excellent—

<page-num>77</page-num>

...a perfect paradigm of the nature and essence of oral tradition. It is not as if we, in our great collection, now have nothing but material that flowed directly from oral tradition. The editor of the Greek collection <note>Referring to the "G" or alphabetical-anonymous Greek collection discussed in previous chapters</note> himself indicates the path of laborious literary collecting through which his work came into being. And behind him, according to his own account, there already lay smaller collections whose history we have been able to trace this far back. But on the other hand, the oral tradition continued to flow alongside its literary fixation. While the latter began as early as the turn of the fourth and fifth centuries, the living oral "tradition" lived on at least until the middle of the fifth century in <term>Poimen</term> <note>Abba Poimen (c. 340–450 AD), one of the most frequently quoted Desert Fathers, known for his practical wisdom</note> and his school. Poimen specifically belongs to the non-literary men; in the authentic tradition, it is never claimed that he left behind anything in writing. And the state of our various collections clearly shows how, even into later times, new tradition constantly crystallized onto that which had already been handed down in writing. There is no witness to this tradition who does not show considerable unique material.

Furthermore, we could demonstrate a specifically literary process on the part of the editor of the Greek collection. He also extracted apparent <term>apophthegmatic</term> material from literary works. But we could simultaneously show that this is indeed secondary material, added only later, from which the older tradition was still free. Fundamentally, with the great mass of the material, one receives the impression that it contains a more or less immediate deposit of oral tradition. No literary spirit has come over this material to create an artistic whole out of this unshaped raw material with creative power, as *Athanasios* accomplished in the *Life of Antony* <note>The *Vita Antonii*, written c. 360 AD, which established the "monk-hero" genre</note>—to the detriment of historical accuracy. We find almost no long speeches, dialogues, or subjective reflections, which stamp their character upon the *History of the Monks* by *Rufinus* and especially *Cassian’s Conferences* (and *Institutes*) <note>John Cassian’s works (c. 420 AD) which organized Egyptian monastic wisdom into structured lessons for Western monks</note>. What we have here is, in fact, the raw material of oral tradition.

A comparison with our <term>Synoptic Gospel</term> <note>The Gospels of Matthew, Mark, and Luke, which share a similar viewpoint and material</note> literature can make this particularly clear. We are generally convinced that in them we have before us the fairly immediate deposit of oral tradition. But how much more "formed" this tradition already is. In the Gospel of Mark, we already possess a quite artistically designed *Life* (*Vita*). In the *Logia* <note>original: "Logien"; a hypothesized collection of the sayings of Jesus</note>, we have speeches whose conglomerate-like composition from individual sayings is indeed clear, but they are still mostly speeches, not individual sayings. A fairly extensive literary process already lies between the original oral tradition and our Gospels. In the *Apophthegmata*, however, the raw material of oral tradition encounters us in a far more tangible form. What we must first search for as the bedrock of our Gospel tradition—the individual anecdote, the individual saying (*Logion*), the individual small dialogue, the individual parable—all of this meets us here in tangible reality. Unconnected to one another, thrown together in arbitrary arrangement, only gradually compiled later into smaller and larger thematic groups, but almost always in such a way that the individual small units remain intact—there stand the hundreds and hundreds of fragments of the oral tradition.

I shall attempt to give a brief picture of the richness and uniqueness of this oral tradition. First, we have the characteristic...

...small individual anecdote, a true child of the moment, born from the instant, capturing the instant, without any intrusive agenda, full of vitality, told with the narrator's full joy in the subject matter. I cite one or another example, picking them at random. Even a somewhat exhaustive treatment of the material would have to lead to a depiction of <term>Sketic</term> <note>Referring to Scetis, a remote desert valley in Egypt that was a center for early Christian monasticism</note> monasticism itself and would exceed the scope of the present work. Daniel, the disciple of Arsenius, relates (Arsenius 23):
> I once found myself near Abba Alexander. He was seized by pains and stretched himself out in pain and looked upward. It so happened, however, that the blessed Arsenios came to speak with him, and he saw him (from afar) as he was stretching. As he now spoke with him, he said to him: "Who was the world-man <note>original: *κοσμικός* (kosmikos); refers to a secular person or layman as opposed to a monk</note> whom I just saw?" Abba Alexander spoke to him: "Where did you see him?" And he said: "As I was descending from the mountain, I looked at the cave here and saw someone stretching and looking upward." And he fell down before him <note>original: *ἔβαλεν αὐτῷ μετάνοιαν* (ebalen auto metanoian); a physical gesture of prostration to ask for forgiveness</note> and said: "Forgive me, it was I. The pain overcame me." And the old man said to him: "So it was you!? Excellent! I thought that it was a world-man and therefore I asked."

— In Anthony 18, the following lively little story is told. Brothers from Scetis come to Saint Anthony and meet an unknown old man on the way. They talk much with one another about the words of the Fathers, from the Scriptures, and about their handiwork, while the stranger brother remains silent. When they come to Anthony, he says to them: "You have had an excellent traveling company <note>original: *συνοδία* (synodia)</note> in this old man." But he also spoke to the old man: "You have found excellent brothers, Abba." The old man answered: "Excellent they are, but their stall has no door, and whoever wishes goes in and unties the donkey!" <note>A metaphor suggesting that the brothers speak too freely and do not guard their inner thoughts/souls</note> Regarding Macarius, it is told (G 31):
> When a brother came to him with fear, as if to a holy and great old man, then he would not speak with him. But if someone came and treated him with contempt: "Abba, when you were a camel driver and stole natron <note>A naturally occurring salt used for cleaning; Macarius was said to have been a salt-trader before becoming a monk</note> and sold it, did the guards not beat you then?" — if someone spoke to him like that, he answered with joy when they questioned him.

— "Abba Peter and Epimachus were companions in Raithou <note>A monastic site on the Sinai Peninsula</note>. When they were eating in the church (an <term>Agape</term>! <note>The 'Love Feast' or communal meal of the early Christians</note>), they were forced to come to the table of the elders. And with much reluctance, Abba Peter went alone. And as they stood up, Epimachus said to them: 'How did you dare to go to the table of the elders?' But he answered: 'If I had sat down at the table with you, then the brothers would have exhorted me as an elder to say the prayer of thanks first, and I would have been regarded as the greater among you. Now that I went to the Fathers, I was the smallest of all and became humble in my mind.'" (Peter Pionites 3). — "Abba Theodore once stayed with the brothers of Scetis ¹). ...and spoke of spiritual matters. Again the old man said to his disciple: "Prepare us a small dish of lentils, my son." He replied: "I already prepared it yesterday." And so they stood up and ate. Sisoes 27: "Abba Sisoes once sat in his cell. And when his disciple knocked, the old man cried out: 'Away with you, Abraham, do not enter; the matters here brook no delay!'" <note>original Greek: *ἄρτι οὐ σχολάζει τὰ ὧδε!* — literally: "now there is no leisure for the things here!"</note>

I could continue in this way indefinitely. Dozens upon dozens of examples would pour in. ¹) But I think the impression I intended to achieve has already been made. With tangible vitality, the life and activity of the <term>Sketic</term> <note>Referring to the monks of Scetis, a remote desert valley in Egypt that became a foundational center for Christian monasticism</note> monks stands before us in these little "instantaneous photographs." We see them before our eyes: in the solitude of the cell, visiting one another, immersed in spiritual conversation, in all their merciless austerity and devotion to the cause, yet again not averse to a robust jest; the disciple in reverent humility before the master; we eavesdrop on them at the solemn communal meal with its developed ceremony... One can truly wander through long stretches of the *Life of Anthony*, the *Historia Lausiaca*, the *Historia Monachorum*, or Cassian's *Conferences* before finding even one of these completely concrete and intimate sketches. It would be an extraordinarily attractive task to shape the material hidden in the <term>Apophthegmata</term> <note>Literally "Sayings of the Fathers," a collection of wisdom and anecdotes from early desert monks</note> into a vivid and coherent picture, both from the perspective of the history of religion and cultural history.

Alongside the anecdote, the individual <term>Logion</term> <note>A short, authoritative saying or spiritual teaching</note> appears in our tradition. The Logion plays an immense role within the circle of the Sketic brothers. Countless times we read in the tradition that the younger brother comes to the elder with the request that he "speak a word" to him. Time and again the same stereotypical formulas are encountered: ²) "speak a word to me that I might be saved" <note>original: *εἰπέ μοι λόγον ἵνα σωθῶ*</note> — "what must I do that I might be saved" <note>original: *τί ποιήσω ἵνα σωθῶ*</note> — "give me one commandment" <note>original: *δός μοι μίαν ἐντολήν*</note> — "speak a word to me that I might be saved" <note>original: *εἰπέ μοι ῥῆμα ἵνα σωθῶ*</note> — "asked concerning life" <note>original: *ἠρώτησεν περὶ ζωῆς*</note> — "requesting some concise and saving word in the manner of an inheritance" <note>original: *ἀξιουντες λόγον τινα σύντυμον καὶ σωτήριον ἐν κλήρου τάξει*; "in the manner of an inheritance" refers to a spiritual legacy left behind for them, as in Cassian 5</note>. The request is presented with enormous urgency: "Abba Poimen besought him (Saint Macarius) with many tears: 'Speak a word to me that I might be saved'" <note>original: *παρεκάλεσεν ὁ Ἀ. Ποιμὴν αὐτὸν μετὰ πολλῶν δακρύων· εἰπέ μοι ῥῆμα ἵνα σωθῶ*</note> (Macarius 25). And the Abba addressed in this way often allows himself to be entreated for a long time before he speaks the <term>Logos</term> <note>The Word; here, the spiritual utterance</note>. He allows himself to be disturbed in his work only reluctantly: "do what you see me doing." He points to the Scripture, in which everything is written. He leaves the brother standing and begging for the Logos for days on end. ³) There is a special significance to this Logos. Behind it lies the conviction that it is a gift of the Spirit when a brother knows how to speak an effective Logos. When the younger brother comes to the older: "Abba, speak a word to me," he thereby recognizes him as a <term>Pneumatic</term> <note>A person filled with the *Pneuma* or Holy Spirit; a "spirit-bearer"</note>. He listens to the oracle of the Pneumatic. A characteristic story makes this quite clear: "Abba Moses once spoke to the brother Zacharias: 'Tell me what I should do.' When he heard this, he threw himself to the ground at his feet and said: 'Do you ask me, Father?' The old man said to him: 'My child Zacharias, I saw the Holy Spirit descend upon you and therefore I will [ask]...'"

"...I am forced to ask you" (Zacharias 3). It is meant to be established here that, as an exception, the elder asks the younger brother <note>See footnote 1</note>, the **Abba** (Father) asks the **brother**. He does this because he is convinced that the brother is a spirit-bearer, a <term>pneumatikos</term> <note>from the Greek *πνευματικός*, describing a person acting under the direct influence of the Holy Spirit</note>. The word of the Abba is regarded as an oracular word. Germanus says in Cassian's *Conferences VII, 7*, that the brothers could not withstand the countless hostile demons "unless... we were animated by your words as if by heavenly oracles" <note>original Latin: *nisi ... vestris sententiis velut coelestibus animaremur oraculis*; see footnote 2</note>. In the collection *Verba Seniorum* (PJ) X, 95, it is told: "Certain fathers told of a certain great old man, that if someone came to ask him for a word, he said with great confidence: 'Behold, I take on the persona of God and sit in the seat of judgment; what then do you want me to do for you?'" <note>original Latin: *Narraverunt quidam patrum de quodam sene magno, quia si veniebat aliquis interrogare eum sermonem, ille cum magna fiducia dicebat: ecce ego suscipio personam Dei et sedeo in sede judicii, quod ergo vis ut faciam tibi*; see footnote 3</note>. This respect for the "pneumatic" word also reflects the word of Esaias to Ammoe: "Even if you speak a good word to me, I hold it like a sword" <note>original Greek: *κἄν λόγον μοι λαλήσῃς ἀγαθόν, ὡς ῥομφαίαν αὐτὸν ἔχω*; Ammoe 2</note>. And such a <term>Logion</term> <note>a "saying" or "word" of spiritual wisdom</note> is, on the other hand, received by the brother who hears it with the greatest reverence. It is told of Poimen that he once came to an old man and asked him about three matters. As he returned to his cell, he noticed that he had forgotten one of the three answers. He then withdrew his hand, which was already on the door latch, and hiked the very long way back to the old man. "And the old man said to him: 'Poimen [Shepherd] of Angels; and your name shall be spoken in all the land of Egypt'" <note>original Greek: *ἔlegεν δὲ αὐτῷ ὁ γέρων· Ἀγγέλων Ποιμήν· καὶ λαληθήσεταί σου τὸ ὄνομα ἐν πάσῃ γῇ Αἰγύπτου*; Poimen 1, see footnote 4</note>.

From this perspective, one can easily understand why the Logion plays such an immense role in the tradition of the <term>Sketic</term> monks. One can understand how these Logia, however insignificant they may often seem to us, were faithfully kept and passed on. One grasps the remarkable tenacity with which individual Abbas had their Logia preserved in the tradition, so that in the widely branched transmission, duplicates and transfers—or the complete disappearance of a name—as often as all that occurs, still represent the exceptions in the mass of material. Very soon, written tradition must have been added to the oral tradition. People would have entered the "words" <note>original Greek: *ῥήματα* (rhemata)</note> of the fathers on tablets and in diaries <note>see footnote 5</note>. Of Theodor von Pherme (3) it is told that he refused to speak a word to a brother who begged him for three days: "By nature I did not speak to him; for he is a businessman, and wants to be glorified in the words of others" <note>original Greek: *φύσει οὐκ ἔλεγον αὐτῷ· πραγματευτὴς γάρ ἐστι, καὶ εἰς ἀλλοτρίους λόγους θέλει δοξάζεσθαι*</note>. Here we already encounter a professional collecting of the Fathers' words. Thus, the Logion is characteristic of the tradition of Sketic monasticism, and specifically for this circle. This abundance of word-tradition is never repeated elsewhere outside of this group. Compare now with the Apophthegmata—

### Chapter 3. The Literary and Religious-Historical Significance of the Apophthegmata.

<meta>Bousset, Monasticism.</meta>

...sayings, one need only compare them to the *Religious History* <note>original: "Historia Religiosa"</note> of Theodoret, the *Assurances* <note>original: "Plerophorien"</note> of John Rufus, the *Spiritual Meadow* <note>original: "Leimonarion"</note> of Moschus, or the *Monastic Histories* of John of Ephesus (*Commentaries on the Blessed Easterners* <note>original: "commentarii de beatis Orientalibus"</note>) and so many others, to recognize the distance between them. In those works, miracle legends, reports of visions, descriptions of dogmatic struggles, and detailed accounts of the most bizarre ascetic practices have almost everywhere pushed aside the <term>Logion</term> <note>a brief, inspired saying</note> and the concrete little anecdote. It is characteristic how in the writings of John Moschus the old form of the tradition of sayings reappears quite often, especially when his report reaches the territory of the monasticism of Scetis ¹), and how Cyril of Scythopolis feeds the speeches of his heroes with borrowings from the Scetic <term>Gerontikon</term> <note>a collection of the wisdom of the "old men" or elders</note> ¹).

In order to visualize this oral tradition in its full breadth, we point to several forms or sub-forms of the saying. Alongside the <term>Logion</term>, of course, there very frequently appears the short conversation in question and answer. The brother does not only express the plea: "Give me a word" <note>original: "Sage mir einen Logos"</note>, but he asks a specific question and the elder answers. "Questioned by a brother—the elder answered," is how we read it countless times. A small dialogue ²) can then develop from speech and counter-speech. However, these never become too extensive. There, of course, the powers of oral tradition fail.

The parable also encounters us here as a special form of the <term>Logion</term>. The parable is that form of oral tradition in which even longer discourses by a speaker can be preserved. The sharply polished parabolic form provides the possibility of preservation through memory. The art of speaking in parables is a characteristic of folk speech, especially in the Orient. So it was in the age of Jesus, and so it is also among the monks of the Scetic desert. It is astonishing how rich their tradition is in accurate and effective little parables. And it would be worthwhile to examine the parabolic language of these monks more closely; the environment in which these Egyptian <term>fellahin</term> <note>peasant farmers</note> lived would appear before our eyes in vivid plasticity. The 187 sayings of Poimen alone offer abundant material. The Coptic collection *Virtues of St. Macarius* <note>original: "Vertus de St. Macaire"</note> published by Amélineau (pp. 58/59) is, for long stretches, a collection of parables. And the homilies attributed to Macarius (p. 59 note 1) must also originate from the same circle as this collection; they too are full of parables and parable-like turns of phrase. Of Horsisius <note>original: "Horsisi"</note>, the second successor of Pachomius, it is explicitly emphasized in the Pachomian tradition ³) that he was particularly well-versed in parabolic speech, and two of his parables passed from there into the collection of the *Apophthegmata*. In this world full of Oriental liveliness, we also find the "parabolic action"—the symbolic enactment—which is familiar to us from the Old Testament, whereas it plays no role in the life of Jesus. Once, when Abba Moses was summoned to the assembly that was to judge a fallen brother, he filled a basket full of holes with sand, hoisted it onto his shoulder, and appeared in the assembly. They said to him: "What does this mean?" The elder, however, said to them: "My sins flow [out behind me...]"

...behind me from my back and I do not see them. And so I came today to judge the sins of others!” ¹) The parable naturally very often slides into allegory. And particularly bizarre allegories can then, in turn, be told as a dream, or may have actually arisen from dream experiences or visionary encounters. A good example is provided by, for instance, Arsenios 33. —

The parable, like the spiritual saying <note>original: "pneumatische Logion"</note>, is considered the intellectual property of the Abba <note>Father/Elder</note> who spoke it. On page 343 we find the report: An elder met a brother while he was presenting a parable among his brothers that was not his own, and he said: “How can you, Father, walk in a place that does not belong to you!”

This note may lead us to the realization that among the parables of the Scetic monks, much material may be hidden that was not coined by them personally but was taken over from the outside world. The subject of the “wandering parable” <note>a story motif that travels across different cultures</note> still awaits comprehensive treatment—for example, also regarding the parables of Jesus. Only one interesting observation shall be shared here. One such genuine wandering piece is the parable of the three friends who escort a man on his way to the royal palace, Poimen 109. It is found among the parables of the *Romance of Barlaam and Josaphat* ²), thus representing Indian material. The interpretation of the three friends varies, of course, according to the environment. In the Greek manuscripts of *G*, two variants are already found. According to one, the three friends are: <term>asceticism</term> <note>training/discipline</note>, <term>purity</term>, and <term>almsgiving</term>; according to the other (the Colbertinus codex): <term>asceticism</term>, <term>purity</term>, and <term>obedience</term> (!) It is noteworthy, by the way, that the parable is explicitly put into the mouth of a <term>layperson</term> <note>original: "κοσμικός" - a person living in the world, not a monk</note>, thereby making the borrowing clear.

A further genre of sayings <note>original: "Logien"</note> concerns itself with Scripture, presenting a scriptural quote or an interpretation of Scripture. But it must be emphasized that sayings of this kind are not all too frequent. One must always keep in mind that many of these monks were <term>unlettered</term> <note>original: "ἄγροικοι" - literally "rustics" or peasants</note>, hardly capable of reading. What they knew of the Scripture will have largely originated from what they heard in the liturgical readings. Above all, the Psalms were familiar to them from their <term>liturgical assemblies</term> <note>original: "συνάξεις"</note>. However, there is already fairly frequent mention of books and the possession of books, but especially in cases where the renunciation of even this precious possession is recommended ³). There is a warning against the mere possession of magnificent books: “Prophets wrote books, but our fathers came after them... and again their successors committed them to memory. But this generation that exists now has written them on paper and parchment and laid them aside idle on window-shelves.” <note>original Latin: "Prophetae conscripserunt libros, patres autem nostri venerunt post eos . . et iterum successores illorum commendaverunt eos memoriae. Venit autem generatio haec, quae nunc est, et scripsit ea in chartis atque membranis et reposuit in fenestris otiosa."</note> — But in contrast, a series of characteristic expressions are found which show that people were suspicious of scriptural study and its dangers, and preferred to nourish or build themselves up spiritually on the simple words of the fathers. In Ammun of Nitria 2 it says: “If there is a need to speak with one's neighbor, do you wish me to speak from the Scriptures or from the words of the elders? The elder said: ‘If you cannot keep silent, it is better [to speak] from the words of the elders rather than from Scripture; for the danger is not small.’” <note>original Greek: "ἐὰν οὖν γένηται ἀνάγκη λαλῆσαι... κίνδυνος γάρ ἐστι οὐ μικρός"</note> ⁴). It is characteristic how even the educated Roman Arsenios tuned himself into this environment: “And he related...” <note>original: "διηγήσατο δὲ"</note>

Abba Daniel said of him <note>Arsenios</note> that he never wished to speak on any question from the Scripture, although he was capable of speaking if he had wanted; nor did he ever readily write a letter. (Arsenios 42). To a foreign visitor who begins to speak with him from the Scripture "about spiritual and heavenly things" <note>original: περὶ πνευματικῶν καὶ οὐρανίων</note>, Poimen does not grant a single word. "He is from above, I am from below!" Only when the brother asks how he can master his passions does he enter into the conversation (Poimen 8) ¹). Zenon (4), when asked for the interpretation of a passage from the Book of Job, first replies: "The brothers have abandoned [concern for] their sins and are investigating the heavens" <note>original: ἀφῆκαν οἱ ἀδελφοὶ τὰς ἁμαρτίας αὐτῶν καὶ περὶ τῶν οὐρανῶν ἐρευνῶσιν</note>. Evagrius, in *Praktika* 92, records that Saint Anthony answered a wise man who asked him how he endured without the comfort of books: "My book, O philosopher, is the nature of things, and it is present whenever I wish to read the word of God" ²). Saint Anthony likely did not express himself in such a modern way, but the answer characterizes the mood of these monks not entirely inaccurately. This piety of the Scetic monks does not live by the book, and accordingly, the scholarly <term>logion</term> <note>a short, pithy saying or maxim</note> is still relatively rare. It almost seems as if one can observe that in later times, the engagement with Scripture became stronger. Among the sayings of Poimen, a whole series of this kind can be found ³).

And one more thing must be mentioned. In the sayings <note>logia</note> and stories of these monks, dogma plays no role at all. This monasticism of the Scetic desert is still entirely undogmatic. In general, value is placed on <term>orthodoxy</term> <note>right belief or adherence to established church doctrine</note> and one wishes to be orthodox. It is told of Abba Agathon (G 5) that he easily bore every insult, except for the accusation: "You are a heretic." Of him it was therefore said: "He possesses great discernment" <note>original: μεγάλην διάκρισιν ἔχει</note>. But as for what exactly was orthodox, people in these circles cared little. When Theophilus’s fight against <term>anthropomorphism</term> <note>the belief that God has a physical human form</note> caused such a great stir among the Scetic monks (Cassian, *Conferences* X), this was not actually about dogma, but about a question of life for an <term>enthusiastic piety</term> <note>a form of spirituality emphasizing direct, emotional, or visionary experience of the divine</note> that lived from the vision of God. Here and there, the well-known speculations about Melchizedek seem to have interested the minds of the Scetic monks. It is reported in Kopres 3 ⁴) that he was once called to a gathering in Scetis where this question was being disputed. "But he, striking his mouth... said: 'Woe to you, Kopres! For you have abandoned what God commanded you to do, and you investigate what He does not seek from you.'" — Here and there, "heretical" monasticism is also fought—ascetic Meletians, Euchetes, and Messalians ⁵). But such stories of dogmatic struggles, as told in Gelasios 2–4, demonstrably belong (p. 35) to the latest layer in the collection and are an entirely foreign element in our tradition. To the likewise certainly late vision of Phokas 1, in which a monk is granted a revelation concerning the orthodoxy of the <term>dyophysite</term> <note>the doctrine that Christ has two distinct natures, divine and human, as opposed to one nature</note> Church...

The unique character of <term>Scetic monasticism</term> <note>monasticism practiced in the Scetis valley of Egypt, known for its austerity and simplicity</note> is excellently summarized in the saying <note>logion</note> B 203a: "To speak about faith and to read dogmas dries up the heart; but the lives and the words of the elders enlighten the soul." <note>original: τὸ λαλεῖν περὶ πίστεως καὶ ἀναγινώσκειν δόγματα ξηραίνουσι τὴν καρδίαν· οἱ δὲ βίοι καὶ οἱ λόγοι τῶν γερόντων φωτίζουσι τὴν ψυχήν.</note> At this point, one should also compare the *Apophthegmata* with the *Plerophoriae* of John Rufus, the monastic stories of John of Ephesus, and the biographies of Euthymius and Sabas—on one side and the other, we are in entirely different worlds. Only the struggles brought about by the Council of Chalcedon <note>A major church council in 451 AD that caused significant theological division</note> seized the broad mass of monasticism and made it dogmatic.

Finally, the fact that miracles and, above all, elaborate miracle stories play a very small role in this collection speaks to the quality of our tradition of the *Apophthegmata*. If one opens the chapter in PJ where such miracle stories are collected (II*), how extraordinarily small its volume is (only 17 entries!) compared to so many other chapters. And the elaborate miracle legend, properly speaking, is still almost entirely absent. Miracles are, of course, told here and there. That the perfected monk, the <term>Abba</term> <note>father</note> and <term>pneumatic</term> <note>a person filled with and guided by the Holy Spirit</note>, performs miracles is a firm conviction. But these miracles often remain within very modest limits. Exorcisms <note>casting out demons</note> also play a special role here; but with these, we are not far from historical reality. Exorcism was naturally the primary field in which belief in miracles and the miraculous power—which these monks believed they possessed—was exercised. Otherwise, it seems people particularly adorned the lives of the older fathers, who already belonged to the past, with miracles. Thus, the memories of Macarius especially received the halo of the miraculous. Such strings of miracle stories, as found under Bessarion 1–5, are however a rare exception in our tradition. — Every now and then, the tradition still enables us to follow the birth and growth of a miracle story. Thus, Agathon 27 tells how he once, having gone to the city to sell his handiwork, found a sick man on the street. The old man stayed with him, rented a small cell, supported himself and the sick man by the work of his hands, and remained for four months until the sick man was restored to health. The same story is told in Agathon 30. But here, the sick man has become an angel who reveals himself to Agathon at the end: "Blessed are you, Agathon, by the Lord in heaven and on earth; and lifting his eyes, he saw no one." <note>original: εὐλογημένος εἶ, Ἀγάθων, ὑπὸ κυρίου ἐν οὐρανῷ καὶ ἐπὶ γῆς· καὶ ἄρας τοὺς ὀφθαλμοὺς αὐτοῦ οὐδένα εἶδεν.</note> — In Theodore 29, it is told that three robbers broke into his cell and stole his things. When they tried to take his books and his monk's garment, ¹) he stretched out his hand and threw two of them to the ground, but then kindly shared his remaining possessions with them. Of the same Theodore, G 27 tells that he once bound three demons who wanted to break into his cell by a magic spell, but then released them at their request. I suspect that this expe—

Other such miracle legends can be seen migrating and attaching themselves now to this name, now to that. For example, to pick out one or two examples, the motif of the speaking corpse is a very popular one. At the request of a holy Abbas <note>Abbas: a title for a monk, similar to "Abba" or father</note>, a deceased person begins to speak in order to name his murderer or to reveal where he has hidden a pledge entrusted to him that is being reclaimed ²). Also widespread is the story of how a saint falls under the unjust suspicion of having sinned with a girl, and how divine justice then unmasks the slanderers through a miraculous intervention ³). That rain pours down from heaven upon the prayer of the saint is reported of the holy monastic fathers just as readily as in Jewish miracle tales of the Rabbis ⁴). And as was just indicated, these motifs are for the most part not invented within monasticism; they have discernibly migrated and been adopted from the outside. And so, not only are individual motifs taken over, twisted, and adjusted to names famous in monastic circles; here and there it also happens that an interesting story from a foreign milieu is simply taken over by putting it into the mouth of some holy father as a narrative. This is perhaps most clear in the legend of the gemstone of the High Priest B 177 b = S** 43. We are dealing here with a distinctly Jewish legend, which in turn works with older known motifs. It is put into the mouths of the monastic fathers Abraham and Ares, at least in S** ⁵).

But all this can only be briefly touched upon here, although much of it tempts a closer examination. Here, above all, the negative aspect should be emphasized: what a small role the miracle and the miracle legend told for its own sake play in the *Apophthegmata* <note>The Sayings of the Desert Fathers</note>. Compare, for example, the stories of the *Historia Lausiaca* <note>A collection of biographies of early Christian monks, written c. 419-420 AD by Palladius</note> and Rufinus <note>Tyrannius Rufinus, a monk and historian known for translating Greek Christian works into Latin</note> about the two Macarii <note>Macarius the Egyptian and Macarius of Alexandria</note> with the Macarian *apophthegmata* preserved in Greek (and Coptic), or our entire collection again with the *Plerophoriae* <note>A 6th-century collection of stories and miracles intended to support the anti-Chalcedonian theological position</note> or with John Moschus <note>A Byzantine monk and author of the "Spiritual Meadow," a travelogue of monastic wisdom</note>; the difference is striking. We are in a different world on either side.

We make the same observation in another field. Characteristic of all monastic literature is the report of visions experienced by the monks. Here we are again very close to historical reality. The "pneumatic" <note>spirit-filled or spiritually gifted</note> monk is also a visionary. It is part of his equipment that he knows how to look into people's hearts, that he has <term>prognosis</term> <note>original: πρόγνωσις; foreknowledge or spiritual discernment</note>, that he knows how to uncover hidden secrets, that he is caught up and sees the secrets of heaven and hell. From this, a specific literary genre develops: the detailed vision report about the conditions in heaven and hell, about the...

the fate of souls and their separation from the body. Alongside the report of visions stands the "Apocalypse"—the visionary unveiling of the future destiny of humanity. Very little of this type of literature is yet found in the *Apophthegmata*. The spirit in which these mysterious matters were handled in the circles of Scetic monasticism <note>Scetic: referring to Scetis, or Wadi El Natrun in Egypt, one of the most important early centers of Christian monasticism</note> was much more delicate and chaste. A few examples may illuminate this claim. In the section on Titoes 1, it says: "They told of Abba <note>Abba: a title of respect for a monastic father</note> Titoes that, if he did not quickly lower his hands after rising for prayer, his spirit was snatched upward. Whenever it happened that brothers were praying with him, he hurried to lower his hands quickly so that his spirit would not be snatched away and remain (up there)." "When Abba Titoes once sat (in his cell), a brother was near him. And unconsciously he sighed <note>original Greek: στενάζειν - *stenazein*, a spiritual or "pneumatic" groaning</note>. He did not notice that the brother was nearby. And he asked for forgiveness and said: 'Forgive me, my brother, I am not yet a monk, because I sighed in your presence!'" (Titoes 6). Siluanos (G 2) experiences a vision in the presence of the brothers; when he awakens from it, he bursts into tears. He gives only a brief hint of his experience. He saw many monks <note>original Greek: πολλοὺς τοῦ γένους ἡμῶν - *pollous tou genous hēmon*, literally "many of our kind"</note> wandering into damnation and laypeople reaching the kingdom of heaven! "His disciple Zacharias finds the master in ecstasy <note>original Greek: ἐν ἐκστάσει - *en ekstasei*</note>, his hands stretched up toward heaven. He closes the door again, returns at the sixth and ninth hour, and finds him in the same posture. At the tenth hour, he finds him resting in silence <note>original Greek: ἡσυχάζοντα - *hēsychazonta*</note>. To his question, 'What is the matter with you today?' <note>original Greek: τί ἔχεις σήμερον - *ti echeis sēmeron*</note>, he answers: 'I was sick today.' At the urgent request of his disciple, he confesses: 'I was snatched up into heaven and saw the glory of God, and I stood there until now and was only just released'" (Siluanos 3). Even Poimen, overheard by his disciple during an ecstasy, only reluctantly allows himself to reveal his secret: "My spirit was there where the holy Mother of God, Mary, stands and weeps at the cross of the Savior" ¹) (Poimen 144).

This is the chaste and delicate way in which Scetic monasticism, in its classical period, speaks of the mysterious experiences of ecstasy; reverence for the reality experienced prevents chatter about it. In this soil, the broad narrative of visions does not yet thrive. The detailed vision reports with dogmatic tendencies (Phokas 1, Daniel 7, 8) belong to the latest layer of the tradition. The long tales of the virgin to whom the fate of her parents in the afterlife is revealed (I* 15) and of the bishop who is granted the gift of "reading hearts" <note>reading hearts: the spiritual ability to know the secret thoughts or sins of another</note> during the distribution of the Holy Eucharist (I* 16) did not arise in the circles of Scetic monasticism, but are legends picked up from a different milieu. This is evident from the fact that the subjects of the stories are not Scetic monks. The stories of the mysterious travels of anchorites <note>anchorites: hermits or monks living in total seclusion</note> to distant, wondrous regions, in which the visionary plays a major role (III* 10—12) and which are then partially associated with the name—

### Chapter 3: The Literary and Religious-Historical Significance of the *Apophthegmata*. 87
