The collection of sayings found in the PJ <term>PJ: The *Pelagius-Johannes* collection, a major Latin translation of the Sayings organized by theme.</term> already contains a chapter (XVIII + I*) "concerning foresight or contemplation" <note>original: *de praevidentia sive contemplatione*</note>, which is considerably more extensive than the chapter on miracles; however, if we disregard the critically questionable material just discussed³), which is spun out here with particular fondness, most of the remaining pieces contain no visionary narratives at all, but only brief hints of visionary experiences. — And it must be emphasized in conclusion that the actual visionary prophecy of the future is still entirely missing from the *Apophthegmata*. Here too, in order to grasp the distance in time and the milieu, one should compare our collection with the *Plerophories* <note>A 6th-century collection of miracle stories and visions promoting Monophysite views.</note> and John Moschus <note>Author of the *Pratum Spirituale* (The Spiritual Meadow), a late 6th/early 7th-century collection of monk stories.</note>.

And finally, just as the literarily stylized legend and the literary vision report are rare exceptions in our tradition, the sermon—the long speech—is also almost entirely absent. This follows from the very nature of oral tradition. A speech or a sermon cannot be transmitted orally. — We can almost establish it as a rule <gloss>postulate</gloss> that whenever such a long sermon piece appears in our collection, we are dealing with later material and literary borrowing. Thus, the long explanation in "Evagrius 1" comes from Evagrius’s *Rerum monacharum rationes* <note>original: "Reasons for Monastic Affairs," chapter 9. Evagrius Ponticus was a 4th-century ascetic and prolific writer.</note>. Likewise, it is surely no coincidence that the long sermon on judgment in "Theophilus 4" is preserved only in G <note>G: the Greek "Alphabetical" collection.</note> and is missing from all older witnesses. The same applies to "Isidore 9." The parainesis <term>parainesis: a speech of exhortation or advice</term> in "John the Dwarf 34" is a late "migratory piece" <note>A story that moves between different saints or collections over time.</note> that appears in the Latin tradition under the name Moses-Silvanus and in the Coptic *Virtues of St. Macarius* under that name. The short speech in "Theodora 3 a" is placed before an anecdote, 3 b, whose separate existence we can prove with the help of the Armenian version. Thus, upon closer inspection, these minor exceptions often disappear⁴).

Also interesting are the few cases in which the appearance of a longer, continuous discourse was created through the conglomerate-like assembly of several small pieces—cases that remind one of how the "mosaic stones" of oral tradition were assembled in our Synoptic Gospels <note>The Gospels of Matthew, Mark, and Luke, which often share similar small units of tradition arranged differently.</note>. I will place a particularly striking example here and mark the individual small sections of the conglomerate in "Arsenius 40": As Abba Arsenius <note>Arsenius the Great (c. 350–445), a former imperial tutor who fled to the desert.</note> was about to die, his disciples were troubled; and he said to them: "The hour is not yet; but when the hour comes, I will tell you."

And they said: "What then shall we do, for we do not know how to bury you?" And the old man says to them: "Do you not know how to tie a rope to my foot and drag me to the mountain?"

The parallels (see Table I) show that this conglomerate consists indeed of individual sayings (<term>logia: short, pithy utterances of spiritual wisdom</term>) which appear scattered here and there in the tradition of other witnesses <gloss>1)</gloss>. Similar observations can be made, for example, with Nisteroos 5. This is also true of the conglomerate of sayings found in Appendix 5 (Migne 74, 378) and Armenian 10, 155 (see Tables V D and VII A <gloss>2)</gloss>).

From every angle, our examination has repeatedly demonstrated the very peculiar value of the tradition of the *Apophthegmata* <note>The "Sayings of the Desert Fathers."</note>. In it, we truly have, over long stretches, the often almost immediate record of oral tradition. We find the individual saying (the spiritual utterance), the individual short conversation, the relatively brief dialogue, the individual parable, the individual character anecdote, and the short miracle report—in the vast majority, these are pieces whose preservation through memory is the primary mode of transmission. Detailed legends, literarily polished vision reports, speeches, and sermons are almost entirely absent or at least take up very little space.

I have often asked myself whether we might not have before us shattered fragments of a continuous literary tradition in our collection, just as the G manuscript group <note>The "G" group refers to the alphabetical Greek collection of sayings.</note> partly shows the process of intrusion by existing literary material. Could there perhaps be a series of <term>vitas: biographies or "lives" of saints</term> of the various monks in our collections, and these sayings represent fragmentary excerpts from them? I must, in general at least, answer this question in the negative. All these hundreds of small pieces stand so much on their own, requiring no introduction before or continuation after; they are so self-explanatory and well-rounded in themselves that such a hypothesis becomes very unlikely for that reason alone <gloss>3)</gloss>. In any case, we do not possess such sources, as far as I can see. The Coptic pieces collected by Amélineau <note>Émile Amélineau (1850–1915), a French Coptologist and archaeologist.</note> in the 25th volume of the *Annales du Musée Guimet* contain either sayings of individual fathers that already point back to G (pp. 57–60), or parallel collections to G, or secondary material <gloss>4)</gloss>. <meta>This page continues the discussion on how the individual "Sayings of the Desert Fathers" (Apophthegmata) were eventually woven together into longer, structured biographies or "Lives" (Vitae), and addresses the question of whether the original language of these traditions was Coptic or Greek.</meta>

### Chapter 3: The Literary and Religio-Historical Significance of the Sayings. 89

The work is, by the author’s own admission, dependent on the *Paradise of the Fathers* <note>A famous collection of stories about the early desert monks</note>. Conversely, it demonstrates in a truly classic fashion how a *Life* <note>original Latin: *Vita*</note> could be constructed from the material of the *Sayings*. We found most of the individual pieces of this *Life* in our collection. Furthermore, the author transferred a series of foreign and anonymous pieces—again from the *Sayings*—to his heroes. He arranged the whole work somewhat chronologically by placing the stories in which the teacher of Kolobos <note>John the Dwarf, a 4th-century desert father</note> plays a role at the beginning, up until his death. Then, he compiled stories in which John's brother plays a role alongside him. He grouped the stories here and there according to subject matter, placed some traditions he found regarding the childhood and youth of his hero at the start, and added the edifying description of his death and burial. And thus, the *Life* is complete. In a similar way, the Evangelist Mark composed the life of Jesus from the oral tradition available to him (which he perhaps already found in writing as a very loose sequence of material). The only difference is that here, somewhat more artistry and literary intent are already evident ¹).

If the *Sayings* are thus the sometimes indirect, sometimes direct sediment of oral tradition, another problem arises which we have already touched upon previously: In what language are we to imagine this tradition originally existed? Amélineau ²) in particular has taken up this problem and repeatedly pointed out that the original language of the *Sayings* was Coptic. From this, he concluded that the surviving Coptic sources he provided have an inherent claim to priority. In my opinion, the answer is not difficult. In Amélineau’s arguments, truths and falsehoods are mixed together. It is correct that we should imagine the great mass of these sayings and stories as originally being in Coptic. The majority of the monks in Scetis <note>A center of early Egyptian monasticism</note> were Coptic **peasants** <term>original Greek: ἀγροῖκοι (agroikoi)—meaning rural or unlearned folk</term>, and their sayings <note>original: *logia*</note> and stories were spoken in Coptic. Thus, we should not be surprised that a language expert like Amélineau occasionally succeeds in proving that specific turns of phrase belong to the Coptic language ³).

...the narrator presents himself in the first person, it is immediately suspicious. The older sources (Athanasius, the *Lausiac History*, Rufinus) know nothing of a close relationship between Macarius and Anthony. Our collection (Macarius G 4) admittedly assumes such a relationship. However, the Anthony tradition in our collection is entirely unreliable. The report that Macarius received the monastic habit from Saint Anthony is, in my opinion, clearly an anachronism. Anthony did not distribute the monastic habit like the abba <note>The spiritual father or leader</note> of a well-organized **communal monastery** <term>original: koinobion</term>. — Furthermore, the entire presentation makes a secondary impression; it is already spun out to a tedious length. The same motifs (the vision of a calling, the visit to Anthony, the battle with demons) are processed twice or three times. How drastic, by contrast, is the description of Macarius’s past when he was a camel driver in the soda mines of the Nitrian desert (G 31; see above, p. 78). And how the author of the **Life** <term>original Greek: Βίος (Bios)</term> has struggled to paper over this "disreputable" past of his hero. The concrete individual traditions of the *Life*—which are not very numerous compared to the length of the narrative—can at least mostly be found in the *Sayings* or in the *Lausiac History*. Even if the *Life* cannot be reduced solely to these sources, it is nonetheless of a decidedly secondary character. Chaîne (loc. cit. p. 567₁) has proven a translation error which demonstrates its origin from the Greek.

<header>Book I. Investigations into the Textual Tradition and Character of the *Sayings of the Desert Fathers* <note>original Latin: *Apophthegmata Patrum*</note>.</header>

have also been preserved in our Greek tradition. It cannot be otherwise. But the claim must also be stated just as firmly that only Greeks took the first larger written collections from this oral tradition. The collection G + NB <note>Manuscript designations used by the author</note> was made by a Greek collector; he collected the vast material according to the Greek, not the Coptic, alphabet. The idea to organize the material into individual thematic chapters <note>original: *Sachkapitel*</note> must also have originated in a Greek mind. G <note>The "Great" or "Greek" collection</note> had already begun this; the collection PJ, which carried out this perspective most consistently, was developed on the basis of G. It is possible that smaller Coptic collections existed before the Greeks set to work. That escapes our observation. But we have already seen <sup>1)</sup> that all Coptic material preserved for us is, with the greatest probability, to be addressed as secondary and thus as a translation from the Greek. It happened here as it did everywhere: Only the Greek brings the <term>formal talent</term> <note>original: *Formtalent*; the innate ability to structure raw oral data into a cohesive literary work</note> to shape a literature, even if the literary collecting activity remains within such modest limits as with the *Sayings*. Athanasius wrote the *Life of Anthony* <note>original: *Vita des Anton*</note>, and alongside it, no memories of any kind from the original Coptic circles of his disciples have been preserved for us. The *Lausiac History* <note>A 5th-century collection of stories about monks by Palladius</note> is and remains a thoroughly Greek work. The *Life of Pachomius* <sup>2)</sup> was first shaped by the Greek brothers of the order; the tradition preserved in Coptic, which indeed added some valuable material <sup>3)</sup>, adhered closely in its entire structure—and that is what matters—to the Greek model and used it from beginning to end as the framework of the presentation.

And again, the comparison with our Synoptic Gospels <note>The Gospels of Matthew, Mark, and Luke, which share a similar "synopsis" or view</note> forces itself upon us. They originate from the Aramaic oral tradition. The literature that is preserved for us is, after all, Greek. The Gospel of Mark is and remains a Greek Gospel; an Aramaic <term>Proto-Mark</term> <note>original: *Urmarkus*; a hypothetical earlier Aramaic version of Mark's Gospel</note> is a dream and a fantasy. Only a Greek, or rather a Jew grasped by Greek culture, had the formal talent and the creative power to write a <term>Life of Jesus</term> <note>original: *Vita Jesu*</note>. Even the Sayings <note>original: *Logien*; referring to the "Q source" or "Sayings Source" used by the Evangelists</note>, as we know them and as they appear in Matthew and Luke, are a Greek writing and not a pure translation. And we cannot go beyond this with the means at our disposal. What we know of the *Gospel of the Hebrews* and the *Gospel of the Ebionites* <note>Early Christian texts that survived only in fragments</note> is sufficient for the claim that we are dealing here with generally secondary material that primarily originates from the Greek.

It is always the same phenomenon: The Greek first creates the literature; the simple Oriental circles from which the tradition originates were not capable of it. And so, in individual cases as well, the Greek has left the final stamp on this literature. For one should not really speak of "translation" during the transition of this tradition from one language to another, but rather of a free treatment and passing on of a still fluid material. And from the outset, one will therefore...

### Chapter 3: The Literary and Religious-Historical Significance of the Sayings <note>original: *Apophthegmata*</note>.

We may assume that we will encounter genuine translation errors only very rarely <sup>1)</sup>. But admittedly, this stamp only touches the surface. Beneath it remains the character of the original oral tradition of another language. We are dealing here with a highly simple tradition, with plain stories, with simple short sayings <note>original: *Logien*; from the Greek *logia*, meaning short, pithy utterances or divine sayings</note>. This tradition does not lose all that much of its character through the transition into another language. But once again, in both cases, nothing of the original tradition in its original language is truly preserved for us.

This brings me to the final question regarding the historical word and the significance of our Sayings literature <note>original: *Apophthegmenliteratur*</note>. One will not easily be able to value this literature too highly. Regarding the historical value of the tradition, one must, however, keep one thing in mind. We must not expect to gain faithful character portraits of the many individual monastics <note>original: *Mönchsväter* (Monk-Fathers)</note> named within it. For most of these fathers, the tradition is far too meager for that. We must also always keep in mind how fluid the character of this tradition is. It is not just wonder-legends and vision reports that travel, but also the inconspicuous anecdote and the individual saying, attaching themselves now to this <term>Abba</term> <note>A title of respect for a spiritual father, from the Aramaic word for "father"</note>, now to that one. And even if we must often marvel at the tenacity with which the names of individual authorities remain connected with the most inconspicuous sayings <note>original: *Logien*</note> in the most remote sources of our tradition, we must not forget that all the tradition we possess is already fixed in writing, and behind it always stands an age of much more fluid oral tradition. Furthermore, the individual monks of Skete <note>original: *sketisch*; referring to Wadi El Natrun in Egypt, a center of early monasticism</note> are mostly not original character figures whose development would even be worthwhile. Here and there, one gains the impression of a unique personality standing behind individual sayings—I might mention Arsenius, the noble Roman—but basically, one of these ascetics looks like the next. — However, what our source really provides us is the image of this Scetic <term>anchoritic</term> <note>Refers to hermits or monks who live in seclusion rather than in a community</note> monastic life as a whole. The life and activities of original, classical anchoritism, which has not yet entered into a compromise with the <term>cenobitic</term> <note>original: *koinobitisch*; referring to monks who live in a community under a rule</note> ideal—as happened so soon and everywhere later—stands before us with an almost unsettlingly vivid clarity and tangibility. I repeat that I consider it one of the most charming and important tasks, from both a religious-historical and cultural-historical perspective, to work out this overall picture from our source, which has been neglected beyond measure until now. I confidently place Athanasius’s *Life of Antony* <note>original Latin: *Vita Antons*</note>—that artwork in which historical reality was lost—the travel stories of Rufinus and Palladius and even of Sulpicius Severus, the complete works of Cassian (from whose long dialogues we learn much more about Cassian’s own ascetic piety than about that of Scetic monasticism), and the later excellent biographies <note>original Latin: *viten*</note> of Euthymius and Sabas (representatives of a refined monasticism that cannot be understood at all without knowledge of the Egyptian), I place all of that in one scale and in the other the *Sayings of the Desert Fathers* <note>original Latin: *Apophthegmata Patrum*</note>, and I believe I see the latter sink <note>meaning they have more "weight" or historical substance</note> and the former shoot upwards. I state for the history of the—

What has been presented here as translation errors remains in the vast majority of cases of a questionable nature. I suspect that the same result would be found for the Sayings.

# Book I. Investigations into the Textual Tradition and Character of the *Apophthegmata Patrum*.

In the study of the oldest form of monasticism, there is only one source of equal importance alongside the *Sayings of the Fathers* <note>original: *Apophthegmata*</note>, and that is the *Life of Pachomius* (along with the *Rules of the Pachomian Order*), which still needs to be reconstructed from various sources. What the *Sayings* mean for the historical understanding of the earliest Egyptian <term>anchorite</term> <note>From the Greek *anachōreō*, meaning "to withdraw"; refers to hermits living in isolation</note> life, the *Life* and *Rules of Pachomius* mean for the history of the <term>cenobium</term> <note>From the Greek *koinobion*, meaning "communal life"; refers to monastics living together in a community</note>. Alongside these, I would also place the ascetic works of **Basil**, as well as the writings and personality of **Evagrius** <note>Evagrius Ponticus (345–399 AD), a highly intellectual monk whose systematic writings on prayer and the "eight evil thoughts" deeply influenced later Christian mysticism</note>—that truly Greek figure among the Scetic monks, shaped by the spirit of **Origen** and the **Cappadocians**, who was the pioneer and creator of actual Christian mysticism—and finally the *Religious History* <note>original: *historia religiosa*</note> of **Theodoret**, which provides a good description of the original, wild Syrian asceticism, free from later Egyptian and Asian Minor influences. — But among all these sources, I give the "crown and the palm" to the *Sayings of the Fathers*. None can quite compete with them in terms of the sheer mass, breadth, diversity, and faithfulness of the material.

And so, the significance of this work for the entire history of ascetic piety has been extraordinary. This is already evident in the external history and dissemination of the collection, or rather, the collections. We encounter a wide-reaching tradition in various versions in the Syriac and Latin languages as early as the sixth century. We find the *Sayings* in Coptic, Ethiopic, Aramaic, and two Armenian translations. In the great *Asceticon* of **Paulos Euergetinos**, the excerpts from the *Gerontikon* <note>Greek for "Book of the Elders"; another title for the collection of Sayings</note> take first place in terms of volume. How the stories of the Egyptian elders influenced the development of Syrian monasticism is shown by **Cyril of Scythopolis** in his account of the life of **Euthymius**. And in the West, **Saint Benedict** cites the writings of the Fathers as an authority. The *Sayings*, in one form or another, frequently became the primary reading book in many monasteries. **John Moschus** already mentions here and there that the fathers in the monasteries read from the "Lives and Sentences of the Fathers" <note>original Latin: *Vitae et sententiae Patrum*</note> (chapters 55, 212). When the custom later arose from Cappadocia to read "sacred lessons" <note>original Latin: *sacras lectiones*</note> at the table (*Cassian, Institutes IV, 17*), as mentioned above on page 67 note 2, the Book of the Fathers likely played its part in these readings ¹).

Furthermore, individual monasteries continued to work on the *Gerontikon*. Codex 1596 (page 652) ²) has preserved an extraordinarily interesting note for us regarding this. At the end of a miraculous story, it says: <gloss>“And I told the abbot in secret what the elder had done and said to me; therefore, seeing they were worthy of being written down, Saint Isaac commanded that they be recorded and placed in the book of the wonder-working fathers for the edification and benefit of those who read them.”</gloss> <note>original Greek: καὶ διηγησάμην λάθρα τῷ ἡγουμένῳ τὰ ὑπὸ τοῦ γέροντος δραθέντα καὶ λαληθέντα πρὸς μὲ, διὸ καὶ ὡς ἄξια γραφῆς ‧ ἐπέτρεψεν ὁ Ἁ. Ἰσαὰκ γραφῆναι καὶ τεθῆναι ἐν τῇ βίβλῳ τῶν σημειοφόρων πατέρων πρὸς οἰκοδομὴν καὶ ὠφέλειαν τῶν ἐντυγχανόντων.</note> This story shows us that the monastery in question possessed a *Gerontikon*. It was the specific collection whose eighteenth "book" (chapter) indeed bore the title "Concerning the Wonder-Working Elders" <note>original Greek: περὶ σημειοφόρων γερόντων</note> (according to Photius). At the same time, we see how the material was still fluid, and how new material was inserted into the existing framework. This glimpse into the history of the tradition first makes it clear to us where the nearly overwhelming—

...the sheer variety and almost hopeless confusion in the transmission of the *Sayings of the Fathers* <note>original: *Apophthegmata*</note> stems from this.

Thus, the monastic communities and monasteries of many centuries and regions lived off these *Sayings* and, for their part, enriched and expanded this literature. It is true not only for the monks of Scetis <note>A desert region in Egypt famous as a center of early Christian monasticism</note>, but far beyond it, that the *Gerontikon* <note>A collection of sayings and stories of the 'Old Men' or Desert Fathers</note> came to be valued alongside and even above the Scriptures: "Let us delight in divine words and celebrate in the narratives of the holy fathers." <note>original Greek: ἐν λόγοις θείοις τρυφήσωμεν καὶ ἐν διηγήμασιν ἁγίων πατέρων ἑορτάσωμεν</note> "To speak of faith and to read dogmas dries up the heart; but the lives and the words of the elders enlighten the soul." <note>original Greek: τὸ λαλεῖν περὶ πίστεως καὶ ἀναγινώσκειν δόγματα ξηραίνουσι τὴν καρδίαν· οἱ δὲ βίοι καὶ οἱ λόγοι τῶν γερόντων φωτίζουσι τὴν ψυχήν</note>

# Book I. Investigations into the Textual Tradition and Character of the *Apophthegmata Patrum*. <note>The *Apophthegmata Patrum* is a collection of spiritual wisdom and anecdotes from the 4th and 5th-century Christian hermits living in the Egyptian desert.</note>

# Book II. Investigations into the *Life of Pachomius*.

### [Sources and Manuscript Traditions]

...have brought to print. This *Life of the Holy Pachomius* <note>original Greek: "βίος τοῦ ἁγίου Παχουμίου"</note>, with its 96 chapters, encompasses not only the life of Pachomius (chapters 1–75) but also that of his first successors: Petronius, Theodore, and Horsiesios. I designate this text as **G**.

Two secondary compilations are currently available only in Latin translation. The first, the *Life of our holy father Pachomius* <note>original Latin: "Vita sancti patris nostri Pachomii"</note>, was translated by Hervet based on a text that—likely incorrectly—was attributed to Symeon Metaphrastes <note>Metaphrastes was a famous 10th-century Byzantine hagiographer known for "rewriting" lives of saints into a more polished style.</note>. This translation is found in Surius, *On the approved lives of the saints* <note>original Latin: "de probatis sanctorum vitis"</note>, Cologne 1617, Volume III, pages 195 ff. Nau (in *Patrologia Orientalis* IV. 5. 409) has collated five Greek manuscripts and declares that the manuscript *Vaticanus graecus 819* is most closely related to Hervet's translation. A German translation of this manuscript can be found in Mertel (cited above), pages 20–122. (The *Life* printed in Latin by Lippomanus in *Lives of the ancient holy fathers*, Venice 1551–1560, is, according to Mertel p. 15, identical to Vatican Greek 819.) I choose the designation **G¹** for this text.

Dionysius Exiguus <note>A 6th-century monk best known for inventing the AD/BC dating system; he also translated many Greek church documents into Latin.</note> translated a Greek text that has since been lost to us. This translation is found in Migne’s *Patrologia Latina* Volume LXXIII, Columns 229–272. I name it **G²**. The structure of G¹ and G² will be discussed shortly.

Alongside G, a series of Coptic-Arabic versions must be considered as primary sources for the Life of Pachomius; their structure and material largely run parallel with G.

A series of fragments from various manuscripts have been preserved in the Thebaic dialect <note>Thebaic, now commonly called Sahidic, was the dialect of Coptic spoken in Upper (Southern) Egypt where Pachomius’s monasteries were located.</note>. These were published in text and translation by Amélineau in the *Memoirs of the French Archaeological Mission in Cairo* IV 2, 523–608, 800–810, and in the *Annals of the Guimet Museum* XVII 295–334. Among the texts of Egyptian origin, these deserve the first place because a life of Pachomius (and his successors) would naturally have been written first in this southern Egyptian dialect. I designate these fragments as **T** (followed by the page numbers of Amélineau's editions).

In the Memphitic dialect <note>Memphitic, or Bohairic, was the Coptic dialect of Northern Egypt; it later became the official liturgical language of the Coptic Church.</note>, a life of Pachomius and a life of Theodore are preserved in Code 79 of the Coptic manuscripts in the Vatican (10th–11th century). A small piece is missing from the beginning and a considerable part from the end of this *Life of Pachomius* (Codex 79, pages 94–306). (The *Life of Theodore* is found there as well, on pages 459 to 546, also mutilated at the beginning and the end.) The edition and translation were provided by Amélineau in *Annals of the Guimet Museum*, Volume XVII, pages 1–214 (Life of Theodore 215–294). The siglum **M** shall serve as its designation.

Finally, Amélineau published an Arabic version of this *Life of Pachomius* in *Annals of the Guimet Museum* XVI, 337–712. It represents the most extensive version compared to all others; like G, it contains not only the *Life of Pachomius* (in the narrower sense) but also—continuously <note>original Latin: "uno tenore"</note>—the history of his first successors. As is now generally conceded, it is a compilation of several sources. Its structure and value shall be discussed in detail further below. Designation: **A**.

To these sources, which can collectively be addressed as the actual *Lives*, is now added a further work that bears the character of a subsequent, supplementary collection. These are loosely connected narratives that begin in the middle of Pachomius's life and break off suddenly without any conclusion. For this reason, they have received the name *Paralipomena* <note>A Greek term meaning "things left out" or "omitted," often used for supplements to historical books.</note> in the tradition, although that may not have been their original name...

# Chapter 1. The various traditions, relationship, and value.

...seem to be, and in the introduction they openly present themselves as an appendix to one of the great Lives <note>A "Life" or "Vita" refers to a formal biography of a saint.</note>.

For this work, we have previously known of two witnesses <note>In textual criticism, a "witness" is a specific manuscript or version that provides evidence for the text.</note>. The first and, as we shall demonstrate, more valuable one is preserved in a Syriac translation. It is found in a collection of stories <gloss>1)</gloss> about the Egyptian Fathers in a manuscript dating as far back as the 7th century, London British Museum add. 17 173 (compare Nau, *Eastern Patrology* <note>original: "Patrol. Or."/Patrologia Orientalis</note> IV 411; for other manuscripts, see Nau 4112). This small collection—which, incidentally, shows strong variations among its individual witnesses (compare the overview in Butler, *Lausiac History* I 79)—was later incorporated into the great compilation of Anan-Isho <note>A 7th-century East Syriac monk who compiled the "Paradise of the Fathers."</note> (second half of the 7th century) and appears there as the second part (a supplement to the *Lausiac History* <note>A famous collection of biographies of early desert monks written by Palladius.</note>, which constitutes the first part). From this compilation, the text was edited by Bedjan, *Acts of the Martyrs and Saints* <note>original: "Acta Martyrum et Sanct."</note> Paris 1895, V 122–176, 701–704, and edited and translated by E. A. Wallis Budge, *The Book of Paradise of Palladius*, London 1904. It bears the heading: *Asceticon of those around Pachomius, the monks of Tabennisi* <note>original: "Asketikon derer um Pachom..."</note> and the concluding remark: *End of the history of those around Pachomius, whose name in Greek is: Asceticon of those around Pachomius.*

The corresponding Greek text was edited by the Bollandists <note>A group of Jesuit scholars who have published critical editions of saints' lives since the 17th century.</note> in the *Acts of the Saints* <note>original: "Acta Sanctorum"</note> 1738, p. 814–825, 1866 Appendix p. 44–53. One of the manuscripts in which it is preserved confirms the title of the Syriac translation: *Life from the Ascetic Works* <note>original Latin: "Vita ex asceticis"</note>. The Greek text offers exactly the same pieces as the Syriac. However, a slight rearrangement has taken place. In the Greek, after numbers 1–6 (which match the Syriac), the numbers 7, 8–11, and 12 are placed, which only reappear in later sections of the Syriac translation. Thus, the Syriac contains the Greek numbers in the following order: 1–6, 13–16, 7, 17–23, 8–11, 24–33, 12, 34–36. The very poor connection between § 7 and § 6 in the Greek text makes it probable that the Greek version, with its different order, is secondary. Furthermore, at the end of the Greek version, § 37–41 contains a long polemic against idolatry. But this addition does not even seem to have belonged to its original text. Nau (*Eastern Patrology* IV 410) suspects that it represents a later revision, represented by the Florence Codex. I finally mention that both witnesses, the Greek and the Syriac, agree in the characteristic preface (prooemium) by which our text is characterized as a supplement; I designate both witnesses with the common siglum **P** (*Paralipomena* <note>Greek for "things left out" or "omissions," commonly used for supplements to a main text.</note>), the Greek as **P<gloss>g</gloss>**, and the Syriac as **P<gloss>s</gloss>**.

A further document, very interesting in several respects, is a *Life of the blessed Pachomius* <note>original Greek: "βίος τοῦ μακαρίου Παχουμίου"</note>, which Nau edited and discussed in detail in *Eastern Patrology* IV 5 from the Paris Codex (10th century) No. 881 p. 222–225, and which I will call **N** (Nau) in the following. This *Life of Pachomius* begins with a section (1–8) that corresponds to the *Lausiac History* chapter 32, the relationship of which to the *History* still presents a problem. Then, with a phrase also found in the preface of **P<gloss>g,s</gloss>**, the text transitions into the context of **P**. Specifically, **N** § 9–52 + 66–68 correspond exactly in scope and sequence to **P<gloss>s</gloss>**, thereby confirming at the same time...

---

1) The manuscript includes the *Sayings of the Fathers* <note>original Latin: "Apophthegmata Patrum"</note> folio 82, then our text, the *Asceticon of the monks of Pachomius* folio 90, the *Life of Malchus* folio 109, and *John of Lycopolis* folio 115. Compare the report provided by Butler regarding this and the related section of the *Paradise of Anan-Isho* from the Budge manuscript in his edition of the *Lausiac History* I 79.

<meta>This page continues the technical analysis of the various manuscript traditions of the "Life of Pachomius," specifically focusing on the Greek manuscript "N" and its relationship to other versions like the Paralipomena (P) and the primary Greek Lives (G, G1, and G2).</meta>

## Book II. Investigations into the *Life of Pachomius*.

...its text compared to P^g <note>The Greek version of the *Paralipomena*, a collection of supplementary stories about Pachomius.</note> 1). N 53–65 present themselves as an expansion from a specific part of G^1; in the order found in N, chapters G 40 (end), 35, 38b, 39a, 41, 43, 47, 45, 50a, 44, 51a, 65b, 57, and 55a have been imported and reworked. N 69–71 provide the account of Pachomius's death, roughly following G 74–75. N 72–73 contain editorial concluding remarks that frequently agree with the literary remarks in G 62, 31, and 32, while also appearing to have blurred the characteristic features of those pieces.

All of this suggests that the editor of N discovered a copy of P and attempted to expand this fragment of a *Life* into a full biography. To do this, he utilized the beginning of the *Lausiac History* <note>A famous 5th-century collection of biographies of Egyptian desert monks by Palladius.</note>—or a report on Pachomius upon which that work also draws as a source—and used G for the middle and end. This suspicion of a rather superficial compilation is further confirmed by two observations. In the first 51 chapters, the name of the saint is always written as **Pachoumios** <note>original: "Παχούμιος"</note>; then it disappears (by chance), and starting with chapter 57, the form **Pachomios** <note>original: "Παχώμιος"</note> appears and is maintained until the end (Nau 422). This agrees with the source findings outlined above, except that in the numbers 66–68 (see above), which originate from P, the form **Pachomios** <note>original: "Παχώμιος"</note> is nonetheless found once, which may have been adapted to its surroundings here <gloss>2)</gloss>. — From this point, one could indeed try to argue for the original belonging of N 1–8 to what follows. However, a second observation stands in the way. Only in N 1–8 is Pachomius referred to throughout quite simply and plainly by his name. In the following sections, he is always called: **the holy** (or **most holy**) <note>original: "ὁ ἅγιος (ἁγιώτατος)"</note>, or **the blessed Pachomius** <note>original: "ὁ μακάριος Παχ."</note>. **The Great** <note>original: "ὁ Μέγας"</note> is also very popular. Incidentally, the compiler seems to have preserved a good—perhaps the best—text of P. I designate the section of numbers 9–52 + 66–68 in the following as P^n.

2) This is roughly the view of Nau. According to him, N (1–52, 66–68?) is supposed to represent the original text. In P^g.s, there is then an excerpt from N for the purpose of supplementing the *Lausiac History*, and therefore N 1–8 was omitted as a duplicate of the *Lausiac History* (410₃). However, I cannot consider the proof established that P was originally intended as a supplement to the *Lausiac History* rather than to G. I also believe that the observations brought forward above decide against N. — One fact should be pointed out here that I cannot entirely explain to myself. Are there hidden connections here between P^g in its secondary form and N, or is this just a playful coincidence?

3) According to Nau 416, G^1 is supposedly an expansion of G^2. I do not know how he intends to prove that. I believe that Ladeuze’s thorough investigation remains correct here. For the whole, this difference is of little consequence.

G³ has established. We find in manuscript A exactly the formation of the text that Nau <note>François Nau (1864–1931), a French priest and Syriac scholar who specialized in Christian Oriental texts.</note> postulated for G³: A² = G 1—50 a <note>The note clarifies: "This solves the riddle of why A 599—605 offers excerpts at the beginning that can be traced in sequence within G 1—50 a."</note>) + Pⁿ + G 50 b—96, therefore = G³.

Should Nau’s thesis also be confirmed—that G³ contained the text of N 1—8 (= *Historia Lausiaca* 32) <note>The *Historia Lausiaca* is a collection of biographies of early Egyptian desert monks written by Palladius of Galatia around 419–420 AD.</note>? I believe that is the case. Although N 1—8 is not found in the second half of A, this is because A has already incorporated this text into the first half of its report, where it belongs according to its position in the life of Pachomius. We find N 2 (end) 3—5 in A 366—369, and N 6—8 in A 377—382. And what provides decisive proof is that we find this text in the form of N, not in the form of *Historia Lausiaca* 32. I will highlight several observations that are particularly convincing.

N differs from the *Historia Lausiaca* primarily because, while the latter provides a list of the number of monasteries and their inhabitants, N § 6 actually tells the story of the founding of the monasteries by Pachomius in historical sequence following the angel’s delivery of the tablet of laws. Accordingly, *Historia Lausiaca* (Butler 93, 7) begins with the general summary statement: <note>original: "ἔστιν οὖν ταῦτα τὰ μοναστήρια πλείονα κρατήσαντα τοῦτον τὸν τύπον συντείνοντα εἰς ἑπτακισχιλίους ἄνδρας."</note> "There are, therefore, many of these monasteries following this rule, amounting to seven thousand men." N first lists the (first) three monasteries that Pachomius founded and then concludes, <note>original: "ἐκ τούτων καὶ ἄλλα πλεῖστα ἐγένοντο μοναστήρια κρατήσαντα τὸν αὐτοῦ τύπον συντείνοντα εἰς ἑπτακισχιλίους ἄνδρας."</note> "From these, many other monasteries also arose, following his rule and amounting to seven thousand men." Although A 378 has heavily remodeled this section—reporting much more extensively on the founding of the first four (!) monasteries based on G 35 a—it brings that specific sentence at the end of this report on page 380 exactly in the form of the N-text.

Furthermore, A 369 and N § 5 share the important (and more original) statement that in the Pachomian monasteries, six prayers were prescribed for the evening time (the *lychnikon* or lamp-lighting service), <note>original: "τὸ λυχνικόν"</note> whereas the *Historia Lausiaca* (92, 5) specifies twelve prayers. And while the *Historia Lausiaca* incorrectly applies the rule that a psalm be added to every prayer only to the prayer at mealtime, N § 5 and A 368 correctly apply the rule to every prayer. Also, the lists of trades in the Pachomian monastery of Tabennisi (according to N and A, while the *Historia Lausiaca* gives the details for Panopolis) agree almost in every detail against the *Historia Lausiaca* (N 7—A 377 f.). And for the unintelligible word *phylakas* <note>original: "φυλακάς," meaning "watches" or "guards."</note> in *Historia Lausiaca* 94, 10—which was misplaced in another section—A and N have in their list the logically consistent "ten guards"! <note>original: "δέκα φύλακας"</note> This should suffice as proof. Regarding the relationship of N 1—8 to the *Historia Lausiaca*, I claim for the time being: <note>Concerning this, compare Bousset's explanations in the *Journal for New Testament Science* 21, 1922, 81—98.</note> the parallels in A to N 1—8 were not taken by A from the *Historia Lausiaca*, but originate from G³.

Thus, A also gives us information about where in the compilation of G³ <note>Also, page 382, within the report on the monastery founded by Pachomius’s sister, A clearly shows a borrowing from N (G³). He first brings the story in agreement with G and M, including the report on the manner of burial of the sisters (which, incidentally, coincides with *Historia Lausiaca* 32 a), but then has a clearly recognizable duplicate on 382 a. And this duplicate is literally identical with N 8! A then, of course, adds the story of the slandered nun (contrary to M and G), which is found in *Historia Lausiaca* 32 b. He probably borrowed it from there if it was not already in his source and thus omitted by M. It is unlikely to have been mediated through G³, as N shows no trace of it. Or could it have been broken off in the compilation of M? Be that as it may, in any case, the existence of N 8 in source A is proven.</note> this piece N 1—8 might have stood. ## Book II. Investigations into the *Life of Pachomius*.

The editor of G³ <note>G³ refers to a specific reconstructed branch of the Greek manuscript tradition of the Life of Pachomius.</note> has inserted here the story of the angel delivering the tablet and the report on Pachomius’s monastic institutions. Further confirmation of this theory is provided by the observation that G² (Dionysius Exiguus, chapter 22) <note>Dionysius Exiguus was a 6th-century monk famous for inventing the Anno Domini calendar system; he also translated Greek hagiographies into Latin.</note> inserted the story of the angel delivering the tablet at the very same point. The editor of G² either arrived at the same—admittedly quite obvious—idea as the editor of G³, or was dependent on him <note>1</note>.

Based on this established result, we now seek to penetrate a little further into the structure of A <note>A represents the Arabic manuscript tradition of the Life of Pachomius.</note>. We have just observed that G³ also influenced the composition of the first half of A in certain places. In general, however, A presents a text here that by and large—again, particularly closely in the first chapters—agrees with M <note>M refers to another manuscript family, likely the "Mittel" or middle Greek tradition.</note>. We should certainly not say that A <note>2</note> can be explained simply by M. The relationship between A and M, as further detailed investigation will show, cannot be understood through a simple scheme of one being dependent on the other. Rather, A and M represent two witnesses of a common archetype <note>An "archetype" is the lost original manuscript from which later copies or versions descend.</note> which could be reconstructed with all desirable certainty over long stretches (see also the attached table). To M and A are often added, as we shall see and as is to be expected, the Theban fragments (T) <note>T refers to fragments written in Sahidic Coptic from the Thebaid region of Upper Egypt.</note> as confirmation, though these certainly do not all originate from the same archetype.

In comparing the texts, A is initially particularly valuable because M is also only a fragment and has not preserved the conclusion of the *Life of Pachomius* for us. It seems, however, as if this conclusion could still be recovered from A. In my opinion, this suspicion can be proven through an investigation of the reports of Pachomius’s death. Here, A offers two interleaved reports: one corresponds exactly to G 74–75 (here identical with G³), while the other, if we strip away the G/G³ text from A, emerges quite cleanly. Finally, a Theban fragment undoubtedly confirms the independent report in A. We may therefore assume that in A and the fragment T, we have the conclusion of a *Life* which the now-lost report of M would also have followed. The source extracted in this way can then be shown to be relatively independent of G. For within it, as we shall see, was a *Life* that contained only the life of Pachomius and had not yet directly connected it with those of his successors, as G (G³) does. A comparison of the texts will make this clear.

| ->G 74—75<- | ->A 643 ff.<- |
|-------------|---------------|
| And after Easter, a disease from the Lord seized the brothers, and in all the monasteries about 100 brothers or more fell asleep [died]... <note>original Greek: "καὶ μετὰ τὸ πάσχα νόσος κατέλαβεν τοὺς ἀδελφοὺς παρὰ κυρίου καὶ ἐν πάσαις ταῖς μοναῖς ἀδελφοὶ ἐκοιμήθησαν ὡς ρ' καὶ πλεῖον ἐπὶ τὸ"</note> | After Easter, God sent the brothers a sickness that became general for them; more than 100 brothers in the monasteries succumbed to it. |

---

1) This piece seems to originate here not from G³, but directly from the *Historia Lausiaca* <note>A 5th-century collection of biographies of the Desert Fathers by Palladius.</note>, as a precise textual comparison proves.

2) A surprising confirmation of these combinations is offered to me by Mertel's report (Library of the Church Fathers, Athanasius II, Appendix p. 11) regarding the *codex Monacensis graecus 3* <note>A Greek manuscript held in Munich.</note>. Here, in the Greek text, we have a report that runs directly parallel to the complicated composition of A 366 ff. First, the delivery of the tablet by the angel and a part of the Rule written upon it (= N 2–5) = A 366–369; then Pachomius’s remarks about the clergy (= G 18 b) = A 372 (in between in A is the report about the first followers [G 17–18 a], which in the Munich manuscript, it seems, stands earlier); then the first monastic regulations that Pachomius gave his followers = A 372–373; finally, the conclusion of the angel’s speech (= N 6–7) = A 376–378 (A 374–375 previously correspond to a section in G 17). It would not surprise me if the Munich Greek manuscript 3 were a witness for G³.

# Book II. Investigations into the Life of Pachomius.

And two days before he died <note>original: "τελευτῆσαι αὐτὸν"</note>, he summoned the other fathers of the monasteries and the other superiors and said to them: "Behold, you see that the Lord is visiting me <note>A biblical idiom for the arrival of death or a divine reckoning</note>. Choose therefore for yourselves someone who is able in the Lord to govern you."

And he called one of them from the monastery of Chenoboskion <note>A significant early monastery in the Pachomian system</note>, named Horsisius (and he was strong in faith, humble-minded, and good) and said to him: "Go around and examine whom they choose." And as he was troubled by the giving up of his spirit <note>original: "ἀποδοῦναι τὸ πνεῦμα" — dying</note>, he took hold of Theodore's beard in a supplicating manner and said to him: "If they hide my bones, carry them out from there."

<column-break/>

It was the time of the Khamsin <note>A hot, dusty Egyptian wind; original: "Khamson"</note> ^1). Three days before his death, he had the great brothers brought and said to them: "I am going to the God who created me and united us to fulfill His will. Tell me now, my brothers, whom you want as your superior." They all wept and no one answered him due to their sadness, for they were to become orphans after him, like sheep without a shepherd. Thereupon he spoke with Horsisius and said to him: "Speak to the brothers so that they tell me who it is they want for a father." They answered him weeping: "If it stands thus, then we know no one but God and you, and the one you designate for us, with him we will be satisfied and obey him in everything he tells us." Immediately the man of God spoke to them: "The man whom God has revealed to me to raise your souls in fear is Abba Petronios, father of the monastery of Aschmini <note>The Coptic name for Panopolis</note>, and he will lead your souls in the fear of God, especially because of the purity of his heart; for he often sees visions and has a good nature in every respect. But I must tell you that he is ill. If he remains alive, he will be your father." Immediately Pachom <note>Pachomius</note> had him brought by some of his entourage.

Now, before he called the brothers together and spoke to them, they had persisted for three days in prayer to God and with tears, that He might spare him for a while longer so that he might teach them the fear of the Lord. At the end of the 3 days, our father sent Theodore to say to them: "Speak to the brothers, it is enough of the weeping, for regarding me the command of God has gone forth that I should go to Him, before my holy fathers." The brothers then came to the place where he was bedded. They wept with burning hearts.

He then turned to Theodore and spoke to him: "When God has visited me, do not leave my body in the place where you will have buried it." Theodore said to him, "I will do everything you tell me." Theodore thought that he spoke to him thus out of fear that people would come to take his body to build a church for him, as was the custom for the martyrs. For he had often rebuked those who acted so and said that the saints would not be satisfied to be treated thus, and that whoever does that to someone drives a trade with the body of the saint <note>Pachomius was strongly opposed to the commercialization of relics</note>.

And our father Pachom grabbed Theodore’s beard a first and a second time and spoke to him, "Leave my body indeed there where it will be buried." Theodore said to him, "I will do according to your word." Then Pachom took him by the beard for the third time and said to him: "Theodore, do what I have told you, and awaken them in the Spi-" <note>The German text breaks off mid-word: "Ge-" for "Geist" (Spirit)</note>

> Therefore the Saints . . . the Apostles . . . the Prophets . . . the Martyrs . . . the Teachers of the Church . . . the Lord of the Angels and the God of the Saints have received him, because he kept his commandments with all steadfastness, and so God has given him what no eye has seen, no ear has heard, and what has entered into no human heart—that which God has prepared for his friends and those who keep his commandments. To Him be glory for eternity, now and for all time and all ages. Amen!

I believe this compilation speaks clearly enough; it requires only a few explanatory words. Version A has indeed provided the conclusion of the "Life of Pachomius" based on two different sources. One can see very clearly here the crude and superficial editorial work of the final compiler. The death of Pachomius’s companions with a list of names, the description of the plague, the death of Pachomius himself—the entire beginning is simply told twice.

In the following scene—the story of how Pachomius refuses to accept a lighter blanket—the two sources are more closely intertwined. It is clearly visible that in version G, an unnamed brother appears as Pachomius’s nurse, while in the second source of A, Theodore has taken his place. In the final compilation, naturally, only Theodore is mentioned. I assume that in the second source there was no mention of a request from Pachomius. It was likely told here that Theodore brought the better blanket to Pachomius of his own accord and that Pachomius indignantly rejected it. Only in this way can the contradictions in A be explained. The section describing how Pachomius appoints his future successor and the instructions he gives regarding his burial are again reported twice. Indeed, astonishingly, it is even told twice that Pachomius dies. The second tradition also provides a striking introduction here: "the elders tell." This source, therefore, still drew from oral tradition.

Finally, we even receive an explicit confirmation that our observations have not deceived us; a short Thebaic <note>Thebaic: referring to the region of Thebes in Upper Egypt, often used interchangeably with Sahidic Coptic</note> fragment confirms for us in a gratifying way the conclusion of the narrative regarding the end of Pachomius’s life, which the source we reconstructed (beyond version G) has preserved¹)! There can be no doubt about it. Here we find the important numerical data regarding his age and the course of his life; here too we find the characteristic justification for his early death!

1) To what extent these details are historically reliable is not relevant to our context. — Ladeuze (p. 254) rejects them categorically. The statement that Pachomius had been a monk for 39 years would contradict G 2, M 5, and A 342. For according to the former calculation, Pachomius must have entered the monastic state in 307/308 (calculating from the year of his death, 346), but according to the latter, he was only pressed into military service after the end of the Christian persecutions in Egypt (late 312) and only became a monk after that. However, the details regarding Pachomius’s conscription into military service by Constantine, who was waging war against a tyrant, are quite unsuitable as a starting point for chronology. How difficult, indeed how impossible, it is to reconcile these details with the known dates of secular history is shown by Ladeuze’s own laborious attempt (p. 234 ff.). The note that this happened after the cessation of persecution is likely a simple case of tendentious "history-faking" <note>original German: "Geschichtsklitterung," meaning a biased or distorted rewriting of history</note>: the monks appear as the successors to the martyrs (cf. the Prologue of the *Vita*).

The Theban fragment serves another purpose for us. In the source material for versions A and T, there exists a distinct *Vita* <note>Life/Biography</note> of Pachomius with its own solemn conclusion. This conclusion, it seems, is preserved in version T only in a revised form, as a strange bit of folklore has been inserted there: that the monks who died before Pachomius must wait at the feet of the Apostle Paul until they can enter the heavenly city with him ¹). Meanwhile, version A announces the solemn reception of Pachomius himself into the heavenly realms in a sustained, ceremonial style.

From these facts, an important result seems to emerge with total clarity: the "second" source of version A was a *Life of Pachomius* that ended with the death of the hero and, unlike version G <note>The Greek recension</note>, did not narrate the activities of Pachomius's first successors ²).

Amélineau ³) claims, of course, that the fragment just discussed—along with fragments 5–12, 19, 20, 22, and 23—comes from the same manuscript which, under the title "The Great Life of Pachom," contained the biographies of Pachomius and his successors Theodore, Petron, and Horsiesios. This presentation is misleading. The title "The Great Life of Pachom," as shown by the analysis of the fragment at the end of which it stood, can only refer to a text containing the life of Pachomius up to his death. Alongside it, the same manuscript would have contained a *Life of Theodore*. The fragments, as Amélineau presents them, are jumbled together. Fragments 5–11 contain scenes from the life of Pachomius (in a sequence corresponding to version G) ⁴). By fragment 12, we have already arrived at the death of Theodore ⁵); 19 describes Theodore’s assumption of office; 20 contains some monastic rules; 22 features scenes from Theodore’s tenure; and 23 describes the raid on the monastery of Phbôu by the imperial official Artemios. Pachom thought at that time that the Lord would come to visit him with death. For that reason, he fasted for four days until Friday, weeping and sighing for the community <note>original: "Gemeinschaft," referring to the Koinonia or monastic federation</note>, that it might not be scattered. And on Friday evening, that is, on the third day since the Angel had appeared to him, he gathered all the brothers and spoke to them, as Samuel had once spoken to the people, and proclaimed to them all the judgments of God. Now Abba Paphnutius the Steward <term>Economos: the monk responsible for the physical and financial administration of the monastery</term>, the brother of Theodore, became ill; on the evening of the Saturday of the feast of the Resurrection, he died in peace. Pachom immediately remembered the word: "A great sacrifice will be demanded from your house." He gathered the brothers and spoke to them—now follows a longer farewell speech by Pachom in 597–599—"And as our father Pachom spoke thus to the brothers sitting around him, Theodore sat a little to the side. His tears flowed from his face onto his knees, and he wept bitterly. And a great number of the brothers wept with him, because they knew the strength of Pachom’s piety and the humility he had shown among them, his numerous devotions, and his gentleness . . . This report does not agree with the report from G <note>The Greek recension of the Life of Pachomius</note>. We will therefore have the beginning of the second report here, which then continued roughly as follows (see the comparison above): "And after the Easter festival, many brothers fell ill" ¹).

We see, moreover, how the independent report appearing here is connected to the dismal experience of Pachomius in Latopolis, which is also pointed out here as his martyrdom. It can further be demonstrated that this event in the life of Pachomius—the so-called Council of Latopolis—exists in *A 590–595* in a tradition that is independent of, and indeed more original than, *G*. Thus, we have followed the thread of this tradition through *542–543* ¹), *591–595*, *596–599*, and *643 f.* And we must conclude that *A*, in this section, is in agreement with *M*, which breaks off earlier as a fragment.

Thus, the preliminary result can be established that *A*, in its second half, represents *G³*, while in the first half—aside from the influence of *G³* in a specific section—it exhibits an <term>archetype: the original source manuscript from which later copies are derived</term> together with it, which *A* alone has preserved at the end. This second source, from which most of the Theban fragments <note>Theban fragments: Coptic manuscript remains from the region of Thebes in Egypt.</note> also originate, in all probability contained only the Life of Pachomius, and not, like *G*, the lives of his successors. In the report on the death of Pachomius, the two sources in *A* are compiled so superficially that they are almost separable with scissors.

And finally, in this overview of sources, it may be pointed out that *M* also shows a distinctly compilatory character here and there. We find two proofs for this. In *M 109 f.* and *114–116*, there is a clear doublet <note>Doublet: the same story appearing twice in the same text due to the use of different sources.</note>. In both instances, the story is told of the monks who gossip in the bakery and thereby arouse Pachomius’s anger. A comparison of the texts makes it immediately clear ²) that *M 109 f.* runs parallel with *G 57*, while *M 114–115* finds its parallel in *A 446–448*. The difference between the narrative in *A* and *G* arose because *G*, or its predecessor, biasedly removed everything that was unfavorable to Theodore <note>Theodore: Pachomius’s favorite disciple and eventual successor, whose leadership was initially controversial.</note>. Therefore, the subsequent transfer of Theodore from Tabennisi to Phbôu <note>The headquarters of the Pachomian movement.</note>, which is connected to the event, is also missing (see the note below). *M* did not recognize the identity of the stories and placed both side by side ³).

A second case occurs in the episode of the ten rebellious brothers, which *M* tells twice in *151* and *178–181*. In the first instance, it goes with *G*; in the second, with *A*. The fact that the two identical reports are so far apart is due to the fact that *G* placed Theodore's report in *152–168* be—

In fact, in the basic report of *A* and *M*, only a few visions and miracles and the long account of Theodore’s revolution stood between Pachomius’s illness and the prophesied martyrdom of Latopolis.
2) To clarify the source relationships even more precisely: *M 109 f. = G 57* [*G 58 a = A 450–454*]; *M 110 = 58 b*; *M 110–112 = 58 c (= A 455–458)*. — On the other hand, *M 112–114* (Throne vision of Pachomius and Theodore) *= A 445 f.*; *M 114–116 = A 446–448*; *M 116 = A 448 f.* (Transfer of Theodore to Phbôu); *M 117–119 = A 449 f.* (+ *458 f.*). — *G* has condensed the entire context of *M 112–119* and *A 445–450* into one short chapter. Then the sources run parallel again.

## Chapter 2.
### Circumstances of Origin.

And with this, we find ourselves in the heart of the primary problem regarding the transmission history of the *Life of Pachomius* <note>The *Vita Pachomii*, the foundational biography of Saint Pachomius (c. 292–348 AD), who established the first organized Christian monasteries.</note>. Having recognized that the *Paralipomena* <note>original: "Pg.n.s" refers to the *Paralipomena*, a collection of supplementary stories about Pachomius that were added later.</note> is a largely secondary supplement to the *Life*, and that the versions known as N, G¹, G², and G³ are clearly compilations <note>Works assembled from various pre-existing sources.</note> that utilize material already well known to us, we are left with G, T, and M—and despite its compiled nature, A—as the primary sources of the first rank. But where should we look for the true and original *Life of Pachomius*? In the tradition represented by G <note>The Greek manuscript tradition.</note> or that of M and A (and T) <note>These represent the Coptic and Sahidic manuscript traditions.</note>? This leads to the accompanying question: was the life of Pachomius originally recorded in Greek or in Coptic?

After Amélineau ¹), in the initial excitement of discovery and based on a few isolated observations, granted priority to the Coptic tradition over the Greek—claiming the Arabic translation (which he derived directly from the original <term>Theban: a dialect of Coptic from Upper Egypt</term> text) was the best source of all—and after Grützmacher ²) essentially agreed with him, the tide seems to have turned completely ⁵). In particular, Ladeuze ³), in his fundamental investigation, has argued for the priority of the Greek tradition in the form of G. He has been joined in the main by Schiwietz ⁴), while Butler ⁵) has reinforced this position with new evidence. Ladeuze primarily relied on the self-testimony of the Greek authors, which appears in several places (chapters 6, 11, 31, 62 f.). According to these passages, the authors of the *Life*, who introduce themselves as "we" <note>original: "$\dot{\eta}\mu\epsilon\tilde{\iota}\varsigma$" (hēmeis)</note>, claim they were the first to write the biography based on the oral traditions of those who had actually seen Pachomius himself. They explicitly state that they had frequently heard those men of the older generation saying that "the life" <note>original: "$\tau\grave{o}\nu$ $\beta\acute{\iota}o\nu$" (ton bion)</note> of Pachomius must be written, "but perhaps the time was not yet [right]" <note>original: "$\dot{\alpha}\lambda\lambda\grave{\alpha}$ $\tau\acute{\alpha}\chi\alpha$ $o\overset{\prime}{\upsilon}\pi\omega$ $\kappa\alpha\iota\rho\grave{o}\varsigma$ $\tilde{\eta}\nu$" (alla tacha oupō kairos ēn)</note>. But now, they say, it has become necessary to set to work (chapter 62). These remarks appear strangely scattered throughout the entire work, so much so that they often nearly interrupt the narrative flow. Upon closer inspection, they appear every time the author or authors intend to report something of particular importance regarding their master: such as the account of his extraordinary <term>asceticism: severe self-discipline and abstention from all forms of indulgence</term> (chapter 6), his battles with demons (chapter 11), Pachomius's own statements about his miracle-working (chapter 31), or a striking instance of his <term>prognosis: the spiritual gift of foreknowledge or prophecy</term> (chapter 62). Although, as mentioned, these explanations often almost disrupt the continuity,

### Chapter 2. Circumstances of Origin.

...one will find it very difficult to decide to dismiss these passages as the late additions of an interpolator <note>A person who inserts unauthorized or later material into a historical text.</note>. In general, it is hard to assume that these notes are a fraud or a literary fiction. A forgery or a work of literary fiction would likely have been more heavy-handed and would have established a direct relationship to Pachomius himself. Thus, we may assume that a genuine historical tradition exists in that passage. The author or authors were truly convinced they were writing the *Life of Pachomius* for the first time, and they wrote it, on the other hand, based on the stories of men who had personally known Pachomius. However, these passages are only found in the Greek tradition in G and partly in the versions dependent on it <gloss>1) See N 72 f. (above) and the concluding chapters of G 1 and G 2.</gloss>. Therefore, Ladeuze <note>Paul Ladeuze (1870–1940), a scholar who argued for the Greek origin of the Pachomian documents.</note> concludes that G contains the original first draft of the *Life*, that it was written in Greek, and that the dependency lies on the side of the Coptic tradition. But is the matter really decided by Ladeuze's argument, and has what needed to be proven actually been proven?

And this conclusion now seems to be confirmed by a very important report preserved consistently in the fragments T 299–302 and M 249–259. Here it is told that Theodore—the most significant successor and student of Pachomius—appeared within the circle of monks and delivered an inspired eulogy for his master. He tells them that the one thing they have which places them ahead of other coenobia <note>Communal monasteries where monks lived and worked together, as opposed to living as hermits.</note> is precisely this: the character and the image of Father Pachomius. He calls upon them to join him in the blessing:

->**"Praised be the God of our father Pachomius."**<-

And in this context, he suggests to them that it is absolutely necessary to record the memories of their father’s life to preserve his memory. The length of his explanations here likely shows that there were various misgivings within the circle of his listeners regarding such a literary undertaking. It may have seemed like a profanation <note>The act of treating something sacred with a lack of respect or making it "common" by publishing it.</note> to the monks to reveal their holy memories to the public in a book. We still find an echo of these concerns in G 63. By pointing to various precedents—including Athanasius's *Life of Antony*, Pachomius's own writings, etc.—the authors seek to justify their undertaking. — But in a certain circle, Theodore does find obedient listeners:

> "And when the interpreter-brothers—who translated his (Theodore’s) words for those who did not understand Egyptian, because they were friends or people from Rakoti <note>The Egyptian name for Alexandria.</note>—had heard him speak repeatedly about our father Pachomius's way of life, they set their hearts upon everything he had truly proclaimed about him and wrote it down. For when he had finished praising him, as well as his sufferings, he used to sigh and say to the brothers: 'Take these words to heart, for a time will come when you will find no one left to proclaim them to you' (M 258)."

I believe that Ladeuze is entirely correct when he places this report in the closest connection with the self-testimony of the author of G. Here we indeed learn who the "we" (<term>ἡμεῖς</term> <note>original: "ἡμεῖς" (hemeis), the Greek word for "we."</note>) speaking in G are. They are none other than the Greek brothers of the Pachomian community, who served as interpreters during the monastery assemblies for their countrymen who were ignorant of the Coptic language. ## Book II. Investigations into the Life of Pachomius.

...wrote the <term>Life</term> <note>original: "βίος" (bios); a standard biographical genre in late antiquity.</note> of Pachomius first. It is also likely from the start that only Greeks, and not Copts <note>The native Egyptian Christians who used the Coptic language.</note>, possessed the artistic talent for structure required to create such a comprehensive outline of a real "Life" as is found in the Greek manuscript G. One might object to this, however: according to the report from the Coptic fragments MT, it seems as though this recording of Pachomius’s Life occurred while Theodore was still alive<sup>1</sup>). Yet G also includes the life of Theodore, so it could only have been written after his death. The way in which Ladeuze (p. 35 f.) attempts to resolve this difficulty is unsatisfactory. Perhaps the solution can be found in another way. Those literary notes in G are only found in the first half of the work—the actual Life of Pachomius. Should we not consider the possibility that the first half of G represents a Life of Pachomius written during Theodore's lifetime, which was only later expanded with a second part detailing the work of his first successors<sup>2</sup>)?

For Ladeuze, these <term>a priori</term> <note>Deductive reasoning based on theoretical deduction rather than observation.</note> observations decide the entire state of affairs. And the thorough investigation<sup>3</sup>) in which he compares the sources in detail clearly operates with a preconceived opinion and, in my view, does *not* do justice to the facts. Ladeuze has evidently failed to seriously consider two further questions. First: Do we have any guarantee that G truly presents us with that first, unprocessed Life of Pachomius to which those scattered remarks in G point? The observation that these remarks were adopted word-for-word by such secondary revisions as NG<sup>12</sup> should urge caution. Furthermore, we have already encountered the suspicion that the second part of G was actually added later, and that the common source of M and A represented only a Life of *Pachomius*, without the expansion found in G. Ladeuze should have further asked whether the notes about the Life of Pachomius exclude from the outset any other prior literary records about Pachomius and his circle. We shall yet see that the assumption can be made quite probable that individual records (or fixed oral traditions)—perhaps concerning the foundation of monasteries, the rules of his brotherhood, Pachomius’s miracles and visions, and perhaps the personality of his student Theodore—existed within the circle of Pachomian monasteries before the creation of the full "Life." Such an assumption would by no means contradict the self-testimony of G. A literary "Life"—a composed book intended for publication—is one thing; occasional, accidental records of individual events from the life of Pachomius, perhaps stored in monastery archives, are another. With this assumption, the claim of the Greek brothers to have written the first Life of Pachomius (which, however, was not...

# Chapter 2. Circumstances of Origin.

...to simply assume, as Ladeuze does, that it is identical with the Greek manuscript G) remains undiminished. One could, of course, point out that the Coptic report just cited names Theodore’s oral lectures as the sole basis for the recording of the <term>Life of Pachomius</term> <note>The "Life" (or Vita) refers to the standard biographical account of a saint's deeds and teachings.</note> and that Theodore’s own presentations exclude any prior written records. However, that would surely be overestimating an <term>argument from silence</term> <note>original Latin: "argumentum e silentio"; a logical fallacy where one assumes something is false simply because there is no mention of it.</note>. What was requested of Theodore was a true "Life"—a complete picture of the Master—and that, we must conclude, was indeed not available at that time.

But if our suspicion is correct, then we could imagine that the Coptic <term>Vitas</term> <note>plural of "Vita," the biographical accounts of the Saint.</note> found in the manuscripts TMA were designed in dependence on a once-existing Greek outline of Pachomius’s life (or its <term>archetype</term> <note>The original manuscript from which later copies or versions are derived.</note>). Nevertheless, they might still preserve older traditions that were already lost or buried in manuscript G. Added to this would be the "freely flowing stream of oral tradition"—as even Ladeuze must admit—which continued to flow specifically on Coptic soil. And even if such a source of later oral tradition is not entirely beyond suspicion from the start, it should not be rejected <term>out of hand</term> <note>original Latin: "a limine"; literally "from the threshold."</note>. Under these conditions, it remains possible that all sorts of original traditions were preserved in sources that are—from a literary perspective—later and dependent. In any case, it is evident that these <term>theoretical</term> <note>original German: "apriorischen"; referring to knowledge or deductions that exist prior to looking at the actual evidence.</note> observations decide very little about the relationship between manuscript G and the group AMT; everything remains to be settled by individual investigation.

How complicated the source relationships are in detail, and how one cannot get by here with the simple formula of the priority of manuscript G, can be made particularly clear by comparing the various reports of Pachomius’s monastery foundations. I shall now begin the individual investigation with these.

G reports on these monastery foundations in two different places, in chapters 35 and 50–52. Whether the author of G found a summary report here, from which he then distributed the events—which actually happened at different times—to various places in the biography, or whether manuscripts M and A only later piled the reports together in one place, may remain open for now¹). In any case, the <term>compilatory</term> <note>Created by gathering material from various different sources.</note> character of manuscript A becomes very clear here. Specifically, A provides a report on the first monastery foundations corresponding to G 35 at a much earlier point (pages 378–80). Its report here follows G very closely. The names of the monasteries, which are recorded consistently in G and A (some of which are <term>Hellenized</term> <note>Greek-influenced versions of Egyptian names.</note>), already prove this: <note>original Greek: "Πρόου"</note> Proou = Bafua; <note>original Greek: "Χηνοβόσκια"</note> Chenoboskion = Schinubeskia; <note>original Greek: "Μούνχωσις"</note> Monchosis = Mankuschim.

Furthermore, as we have already been able to prove, the report in manuscript A showed clear traces of influence from manuscript N. We could conclude from this that A does not stem directly from G, but rather from a collaboration of G and N (referred to as G³ above).

Alongside this, a summary report of all monastery foundations is found in manuscript A (pages 567 onwards) and manuscript M (pages 70 onwards). ## Book II. Investigations into the *Life of Pachomius*.

(Did the philosophers of Akhmim <note>German: Akhmin; a center of Greek learning in Egypt</note> appear above?) We can also see clearly that the two reports discussed in **T A$^1$ G** and **M A$^2$** are identical. The discrepancies, however, are considerable. In the former, the narrative takes place in Panopolis <note>Modern Akhmim</note>; in the latter, it occurs in southern Egypt at Latopolis <note>Modern Esna</note>. That **M A$^2$** are correct in their tradition is evident from the fact that the text of **T A$^1$ (G)** mentions events in Panopolis twice in a row in a very confusing manner. What does it mean that after Pachomius has already founded two monasteries in the vicinity of Panopolis, the Bishop of Panopolis now directs him to another monastery foundation and assigns him a site for it? Regarding the most significant variant of these reports—that in one, the Bishop himself invites Pachomius to found a monastery, while in the other, the Bishop or bishops seek to disrupt the construction already begun—we shall return to this in a broader context, where the full significance of this variant will become clear. The variations in the names given are less significant. In **T A$^1$ G**, the name of the monastery is not mentioned; in **M A$^2$**, it is called **Phenum** ¹). There, **Samuel** is the first abbot; here, it is **Surius** ²) (= Severus).

This also yields a reliable result regarding the monastery foundations of Pachomius. He founded seven monasteries: 1. **Tabennisi**, 2. **Phbôu**, 3. **Schenesit**, 4. **Tmuschus** ³), 5. and 6. **Tsi-Taschmine** and **Thebiu** near Panopolis, 7. **Pichnum** near Latopolis. To these, one could add as an eighth the restored earlier small *koinobion* <note>A communal monastery</note> of Pachomius near Schenesit (see above). This result agrees excellently with a note found in the *Letter of Ammon*, chapter 13: "of all the monks in the ten monasteries gathered by Theodore in Phbôu" <note>original Greek: πάντων τῶν μοναζόντων τῶν ἐν τοῖς δέκα μοναστηρίοις ὑπὸ Θεοδώρου ἐν τῇ Βαῦ συνηγμένων</note>. For Theodore himself, according to **G 86**, founded three more monasteries, and this makes exactly ten when added to those listed above ⁴). If **G 72** (the Trial of Latopolis) and **M 78** count nine monastery foundations by Pachomius, this is not a counter-argument. Either the two convents for women (**G 82**) are being counted as well, or it could be that **G** is following his own incorrect calculation here, which will be illuminated immediately below. For he does indeed count 9 monasteries for monks belonging to Pachomius (4 in chapter 35 + 5 in chapter 52).

But we return to the discussion of the sources. We see that we are dealing here with a very complicated tradition. **A** has compiled two parallel traditions without recognizing their identity. To be sure, he provides the opening passage (pages 567 f.) only once, following **T**. But then he added the various reports together. The following sections are identical:
