# Chapter 3. The Account of the So-called Council of Latopolis.

The parallel accounts vary significantly from one another. In the end, account **M A** (574–575) is decidedly the more original, while **T G A** (570 to 573) has been tendentiously revised <note>Revised with a specific bias or agenda</note>. It is a stroke of luck that both sources have been preserved for us here. The character of the author of **A** as a superficial compiler is thus proven once again and definitively. Nevertheless, we can see at the same time how much valuable material **A** has preserved for us precisely through his mechanical method of working.

However, **G** <note>The Greek version of the Life of Pachomius</note> appears in the most unfavorable light from the very beginning. His account shifts back and forth between the opposing sources and, moreover, has significantly shortened the report of his source at one point (see the comparison in 50 b). Most damning for him, however, is the list of all the monastery foundations he provides in Chapter 52. From a text that is admittedly transmitted in a confused state, it emerges with some clarity that **G** (besides the four mentioned earlier in Chapter 35) lists five monasteries here: the (unnamed) monastery of Panopolis <note>Modern Akhmim</note>, Tasē, Tebēue, Tismēnai, and Pichnum <note>1</note>. Here, **G** has stuck to the monastery of Panopolis, which was likely invented by a secondary editor, as that corresponds to his preceding account. Additionally, at the end, he mentions the monastery of Pichnum near Latopolis <note>Modern Esna</note>, even though he omitted it in his main report. Finally, he has turned the single monastery of Tasē = Tismēnai into two, apparently based on different source traditions. Thus, from the three monasteries of Pachomius—the two near Panopolis and the one near Latopolis—**G** has successfully made five <note>2</note>. In his list in Chapter 52, **G** therefore assumes the two sources we reconstructed above and has, moreover, jumbled, shortened, and misunderstood them, ultimately preferring the inferior account to the better one. Furthermore, this single example sufficiently demonstrates how complex the source relationships of the *Life of Pachomius* are. An old monastic report about the foundations of the Pachomian monasteries appears before us in ever-new variations of tradition.

## Book II. Investigations into the *Life of Pachomius*.

"Some" bishops and monks gather together to expel the Pachomian monks from their districts. "For we have been told that your father speaks words that have never been spoken by a human." Pachomius is informed of this. Surrounded by numerous monks from his monasteries, Pachomius arrives in Esne <note>Modern Esna, historically known as Latopolis</note>, carried on a sickbed. In the church of Esne, where a large crowd of (hostile) monks, laypeople, and soldiers has gathered, the meeting or the interrogation of Pachomius takes place. The bishops put the question to him: "We have heard that you say of yourself that you have ascended to heaven and claim: 'I know what goes on in the hearts of men.'" A monk who is present confirms this accusation. In essence, Pachomius does not wish to deny its accuracy at all. He first appeals to four of his present opponents who had formerly been monks in Tabennisi; they were forced to testify that he was a pious and righteous man. Then he corrected the situation slightly. He had not said he had ascended into heaven, but rather that he had been **carried away into Paradise by the command of the Lord**. He had not said he knew what went on in human hearts; rather, he had said that the Lord had given him the grace to distinguish the wicked from the good (during the admission of monks). After this explanation, the impression among his opponents remains: "Have you ever heard such a word from a human?" An indescribable tumult breaks out. One of his monks has to carry Pachomius out through a side door on his shoulder. Only with the support of an influential man, Sabinus, do the monks—who people have already begun to beat—manage to escape with their lives. They bring their father back to the monastery on his mount, proud and boasting of the wounds and injuries they sustained. And when they arrived at the monastery, they all kissed our father Pachomius.

Ladeuze (89₂) has briefly dismissed this important narrative—which strikes the unbiased reader with an impression of almost photographic accuracy—in a footnote. Compared with the Greek version, he finds in it all the hallmarks of a legend. "The opponents of Pachomius are made to look bad, and he himself is glorified." Here, Ladeuze has made his proof a bit too easy for himself. I would venture to say that with the critical principle he has established, one could discredit any source report, even the very best¹).

However, let us examine the account from G 72 <note>The Greek version of the *Life of Pachomius*</note> in contrast. I first emphasize that G generally confirms the basic features of the account in A <note>The Arabic version</note>. G also places the event in the church of Latopolis. Pachomius appears with some senior brothers, while monks and bishops appear as his opponents. A *dispute arises regarding the claim that he possessed the gift of discernment* <note>original: "ἀμφιλογία περὶ τοῦ διορατικὸν αὐτὸν λέγειν" — a conflict over his alleged ability to see into the souls of others</note>. (The two accusations in A are thus initially condensed into one here). Two bishops, mentioned by name, grant him the floor for his defense. He appeals to those bishops who were once monks in his monastery and who themselves witnessed a healing of a demoniac performed by him. The bishops confirm this experience to him and state that they consider him a man of God, *but as for the gift of discernment, since it is a great thing, defend yourself again* <note>original: "ἀλλὰ τὸ διορατικόν, ἐπειδὴ μέγα ἐστίν, ἀπολόγησαι πάλιν"</note>. Now Pachomius points to his great successes, to his nine monasteries, and to the fact that he has the gift...

### Chapter 3: The Account of the So-called Council of Latopolis.

[Pachomius claimed] to have received from God the ability to distinguish among those pressing in: "which of them is the one walking well and which is a monk in hypocrisy" <note>original: "τίς αὐτῶν ὁ πορευόμενος καλῶς καὶ τίς ἐν ὑποκρίσει ὢν μοναχός"</note>. He asked why this should not be possible "either by discernment of the Holy Spirit, or by vision" <note>original: "ἤτοι διακρίσει πνεύματος ἁγίου, ἤτοι ὀπτασίᾳ"</note>. For he did not possess the gift whenever he wished, but rather when God, who directs all things, entrusted it to him. — Up to this point, the two accounts are essentially identical. However, in the description of how the scene ends, version **G** deviates significantly. For here it now states: "As they heard this, they admired the frankness and humility of the man." But of course, it must still be reported that someone "driven by Satan" <note>original: "ἐνεργούμενον ὑπὸ τοῦ σατανᾶ"</note> attempted to kill Pachomius with a sword. But the Lord saved him through the brothers who were present. Then a clamour arose in the church, some speaking one way and others another: "and after the brothers were saved (!) he went to their furthest monastery, the one called Pachnum" 1) <note>original: "καὶ διασωθέντων (!) τῶν ἀδελφῶν ἦλθεν εἰς τὴν μονὴν αὐτῶν τὴν ἐσχάτην τὴν λεγομένην Παχνούμ"</note>.

The difference between the accounts of **A** and **G** is striking. According to **A**, the event at Latopolis is of decisive significance in the life of Pachomius. What he endured here was his martyrdom (see above). In all its force, the contrast—so interesting from the perspective of religious history—reveals itself here between the pneumatic <note>A "pneumatic" refers to a person led by the Spirit or possessing charismatic spiritual gifts</note> and visionary Pachomius and the organized episcopal church and its official representatives. And while **A** allows us to look into the full severity of the contrast present here, **G** has turned it into a relatively harmless scene that proceeds without any discernible result.

I now assert that the reporting on the life of Pachomius was also influenced by the after-effects of this contrast. There is a perceptible effort within it to smooth over the conflicts that open up here. Accordingly, we may establish the principle that a secondary report is present in those sources where the tendency toward reconciliation with the episcopal church—and the related suppression of the visionary element—clearly emerges. It will be shown that this judgment applies to the report in **G** and not (or at least much less so) to the one in **M A** (**T**).

We shall first consider the position of Pachomius and his circles regarding the organized church and episcopal authority. An observation we have already made now immediately moves into the proper context and receives its full light here. We saw above how the original report was preserved in **M A**; that the Bishop of Latopolis sought to disrupt Pachomius's construction of the monastery in Pichnum in the midst of a great crowd of people, but was prevented from his undertaking by God Himself. In **G**, this detail is suppressed. The author knew the story of the founding of the monastery of Pichnum near Latopolis. But he follows another report that retouches the events, indeed completely reversing them into their opposite. Bishop Arius of Panopolis (!) himself requested the Holy Father to found a monastery and assigned him the location for it. But wicked, lawless people sought to destroy the monastery walls during the night. The angels of God, however, protected them through a miracle. The two accounts from Latopolis-Esne according to **M A** now fit together excellently. From beginning to end, Pachomius here had the episcopal power and authority against him.

### Book II. Investigations into the Life of Pachomius.

The sources agree that Pachomius built a church in the village located near his monastery of Tabennisi to give the villagers an opportunity to hear the word of God. The Greek version <note>referred to as "G"</note> explicitly adds (chapter 20): He did not do this on his own initiative, but on the advice of Serapion, the Bishop of Tentyra (Dendera) ^1). Building churches is the business of the bishop, and it must not appear as though the monk had acted high-handedly. The friendly and mediating role previously taken by the Bishop of Panopolis is here assigned to his colleague from Dendera. Our sources agree that Pachomius performed the office of a <term>Reader</term> <note>original: "Anagnostes," a minor clerical rank responsible for reading scriptures during services</note> in this village church. Version G 20 feels compelled to remark that no (ecclesiastically appointed) Reader was available and that he administered the office until a priest was appointed there. — On the other hand, version G also seems to have preserved the original account in one instance (chapter 18). It simply reports that when they wanted to present the offering <note>original: "προσφορά" (prosphora), referring to the Eucharist</note> in the monastery, Pachomius brought a priest from the neighboring churches "and in this way he celebrated the feast for them" <note>original: "καὶ οὕτως ἐποίει αὐτοῖς τὴν ἑορτήν"</note>. Version M 33, by contrast, reports in agreement with version A that when the number of brothers reached one hundred, Pachomius built a church inside the monastery. He then reportedly went with the brothers to the village church for service on Saturday, for which the clergy then came to the monastery on Sunday for the Eucharist. This depiction seems to reflect already advanced circumstances. — The report in G 20 does not yet assume an organized clergy in the village church; not even a lector was present there. Indeed, even during the later founding of Phbôu, Pachomius seems to have built not a church, but only a meeting room for the monastery ^2). Through a comparison of the sources, we see here into the early days of the Pachomian monastic foundations, in which divine service and the relationship to the Church of the Sacrament were still very little regulated.

Connected to this in our sources is a discussion of Pachomius’s position regarding the priesthood. In Pachomius’s monastery, there was initially no priest; Pachomius also did not want any of his companions to strive for the priesthood, for that would be a source of ambition, strife, and greed (G 18). The report of our sources, however, already has a later time in view, as Pachomius could not avoid admitting priests who applied for admission into the monastic association. But he emphasized that the priest also had to submit unconditionally to all monastic rules. Here too, we find several additions in G. Version G has Pachomius exhorting his monks that if someone from other monastic associations were ordained as a priest, the brothers should not despise him as a "lover of money" <note>original: "φιλάργυρος" (philargyros)</note>. One should not judge a blameworthy priest at all; God and the successors of the Apostles are there for that purpose. Thus, here too, Pachomius is depicted as a degree more submissive and accommodating toward the priesthood than in the other sources. And through this conclusion, the fatal impression that the Saint's sovereign position toward the clergy could awaken is somewhat mitigated. In the story of Theodore’s entry into the monastic association, it is emphasized more strongly in M that the bishops (in M, the one from Esne-Latopolis is explicitly named on page 53, alongside the clergy on page 55) were on the side of...

The detail that the clergy help the mother see her son once more through a ruse (55) is suppressed in *G* <note>the First Greek Life of Pachomius</note>. Once again, or for the third time, the clergy of Latopolis appear in the better sources as opponents of the monastery and its demands. The fact that the story of Pachomius's vision—in which he sees a <term>catechumen</term> <note>a convert in training for baptism</note> who died unbaptized being baptized by angels—has disappeared in *G* (ch. 59), or rather is distorted and mutilated beyond recognition, is also explained in this context. Not only a distaste for all things visionary, but also specific ecclesiastical interests are asserting themselves here. The entire report in *M* 142 ff. and *A* 473 ff. contains a sharp critique of the worldly Alexandrian priesthood. In *G*, this has fallen victim to ecclesiastical bias ¹). Finally, the anti-ecstatic and ecclesiastical tendencies clearly unite in the broad explanations of Theodore in *G* 87, which will be discussed more precisely below. One may already point to the characteristic words in this context: "Nevertheless, let us all pray to be sheep" ²).

At this point, however, an observation must also be recorded in favor of version *G*. This concerns, admittedly, the second half of the *Vita* <note>the biography of the saint</note>. It is noteworthy that *G* does not yet know anything of the particularly intimate contact between Theodore—the student and successor of Pachomius—and Athanasius <note>the powerful Bishop of Alexandria</note>. *G* initially reports on a journey by Theodore (accompanied by Zacchaeus) to Alexandria. It clearly emerges from the report (end of ch. 70 and ch. 73) that things were going poorly for the church in Alexandria at that time, and that the <term>Arians</term> <note>followers of a doctrine that denied Christ's full divinity, which Athanasius opposed</note> were in control. There is not a word in *G* about Theodore meeting Athanasius in Alexandria. This also fits with the time of the visit. That journey took place before the death of Pachomius, which occurred in May 346. Athanasius, however, did not return to Alexandria until October 346 ³). Then *G* (ch. 77) reports on the visit of some monastery brothers (led again by Zacchaeus) to Anthony <note>the famous desert hermit</note> and to Athanasius shortly after the death of Pachomius. It is explicitly noted that Theodore was not present during this reception of the brothers by Anthony—upon which special weight is laid in the context of the *Vita*—and by Athanasius. When *G* 92 shows Athanasius actually meeting with him and the Pachomian brothers, the report clearly assumes that the two men had never seen each other before. The presentation in the Coptic sources is quite different. Already *M* 167–169 and *A* 588–591 report that Theodore meets Athanasius himself on the journey to Alexandria (before Pachomius's death) and that Athanasius gives him a letter of recommendation full of undisguised admiration. Then the report in *M* ends. However, we find the continuation of this account in the Memphitic Life of Theodore (297–299) as well as in the Theban fragments. undertaken jointly after the death of Pachomius. The meeting of the Pachomian monks with Anthony <note>Saint Anthony the Great, often considered the father of Christian monasticism</note> is depicted in a most vivid and edifying manner. They then travel to Athanasius in Alexandria, to whom Anthony hands a letter of recommendation (578). Athanasius provides the brother with a letter of recommendation for the new <term>abbot</term> <note>the head of a monastery</note> Orsisius. Here in Alexandria, Theodore's account falls upon a saying of Pachomius regarding the three heads of the Church: Athanasius, Anthony, and the Pachomian community; whereas in version *G* (ch. 87), Theodore is reminded of this word of their master upon the occasion of the brothers' return from the journey (for he himself was not present <note>original Greek: "αὐτὸς γὰρ οὐκ παρῆν"</note>) to this saying of their master. — These are all new constructions, and one will hardly go wrong in assuming that in this significant reshaping, an interest was at work to bring Theodore into a closer relationship with Athanasius than with Anthony. The endeavor to bring the leaders and the history of the Pachomian monastic association into closer connection with the <term>hierarch</term> <note>a high-ranking religious leader</note> Athanasius belongs to the chapter of ecclesiastical-political tendency, which is thus proven not only in *G*, but also in other sources of the Life of Pachomius.

### Chapter 4.
## The Visionary Element in the Tradition.

All these reports, especially the fluctuations and corrections in the traditions, are so interesting because they allow us to look into the initial conflicts between the clergy and monasticism. In the ecclesiastical province of Egypt, this <term>antagonism</term> <note>hostility or opposition</note> disappeared very quickly, much faster than in other church provinces — I recall the struggles in Asia Minor over the person of Eustathius of Sebaste, the opposition to monasticism and the person of Jerome in Rome, Martin of Tours, and the execution of Priscillian in Gaul — it vanished. Here, Athanasius, the great biographer of Saint Anthony, immediately took the lead; he recognized the importance of monasticism for the Church and knew how to harness it to his wagon and use it for the struggle for <term>orthodoxy</term> <note>the authorized or generally accepted theory, doctrine, or practice</note>. It is characteristic that Athanasius tried to make Pachomius a priest at their very first meeting (G 20), although he did not succeed in this. That was also the proven method in other districts to bridge the gap between <term>pneumatic</term> <note>spirit-led or charismatic</note> monasticism and the clergy: by making someone from the midst of the monastic community itself a bishop or priest of the district or monastery. The stories just touched upon from the later time of Pachomius and those of Theodore show how well the great church politician succeeded in his policy, even toward the association of the Pachomian people.

However, if the reconciliation of the clergy and monasticism were to be lasting, the latter had to temper its pneumatic-ecstatic nature, which was always perceived by the clergy as revolutionary. Thus, these two tendencies are constantly linked: the push for greater harmony between clergy and monasticism and the suppression of the visionary. In the Life of Theodore in *G* 87, we read the following inter-

And the successor of the "man of God" <note>original Greek: "ἄνθρωπος τοῦ θεοῦ"</note> had as his main wish: "Nonetheless, let us all pray to be sheep."

## Book II. Investigations into the Life of Pachomius.

...is led by pride. He wants to show them a great vision: to see a holy and humble person—that, he says, is the true **vision of God**. Then Pachomius will, at most, allow that holy men possess **the gift of discernment of souls to see their inner thoughts** <note>original Greek: "τὸ διορατικὸν τῶν ψυχῶν τὰ ἐνθυμήματα ὁρᾶν"</note>. Characteristically, ecstasy is here—as in the Greek report on the Synod of Latopolis—restricted to the reading of thoughts, while actual visions are removed 1). This gift of **discernment** <note>original Greek: "διορατικόν" — the spiritual ability to perceive hidden things or read minds</note>, it continues, is granted to men by God. Thus they become **discerning** <note>original Greek: "διορατικοί"</note>; without His revelation, they are **like all other men** <note>original Greek: "ὡς πάντες ἄνθρωποι"</note>! But there is another way to be **discerning**. It is hinted at in the word of the Psalm: *I saw the Lord before me always!* (Psalm 16:8). A person is not held accountable for whether they possess the gift of vision (in the first sense), but rather for whether they "see" God in the sense of the Psalm. Children should be raised in this [type of] vision of God.

In connection with what precedes it, the tendency of the presentation here also becomes unmistakable. Pachomius was certainly not such a good-natured and comfortable "average pious man" as the one expressing himself here. The anti-ecstatic tendency is clearly evident, though it is forced by tradition to grant a limited recognition of the **gift of discernment**. Otherwise, however, the visionary and ecstatic elements are visibly reduced to general religiousness.

The observations can be expanded. In G 61, in agreement with the other sources (M 103 f., A 471), a story is told concerning the **gift of discernment** of Pachomius. A monk, contrary to the rule, has obtained a supply of figs and keeps them in a vessel to make fasting easier for himself. Pachomius "sees" this from the distant monastery of Phbôu, comes therefore to Tabennisi, and exposes the brother by hinting in a speech held before the assembly of brothers that he knows his secret. G has used the mention of an assembly speech in the primary report to actually insert a longer address by Pachomius. And in the middle of this very speech, one finds a polemic against ecstasy. The "enemies" (demons) try to tempt the monks: **"if he finds one who is not sober... if he does not keep watch as he should"** <note>original Greek: "ἐὰν εὕρῃ τινὰ μὴ νηφάλαιον ... ἐὰν μὴ νήψῃ ὡς δεῖ"</note>. Many have already taken their own lives; one threw himself from a cliff **as if in a state of ecstasy** <note>original Greek: "ὡς ἐκστατικός"</note> (!), another slit open his own body with a sword. It is especially condemned if one does not report such conditions to an experienced brother: **"for it is a great evil not to report this quickly to the one who has knowledge, before the passion becomes long-standing"** <note>original Greek: "μέγα γὰρ κακὸν τὸ μὴ ἀναγγεῖλαι τούτο ταχέως τῷ ἔχοντι τὴν γνῶσιν, πρὸ τοῦ χρονῆσαι τὸ πάθος"</note>. All of this no longer has anything to do with the "sin" of the fig-loving monk. At most, one could say that the thought of the monk who shuns fasting triggered the discourse on **being sober** <note>original Greek: "νηφάλιον εἶναι" — referring to spiritual sobriety or mental alertness</note>. It would be more accurate, however, to judge that according to the tendency of G, at the moment Pachomius provides a special proof of his **gift of discernment** <note>original Greek: "διορατικὸν χάρισμα"</note>, he must simultaneously deliver a speech against demonic ecstasy. Even after the exposure of the fig-thief, it says again: **"And finally he says to them: 'See then, that we do not see when we wish to know secrets for the sake of salvation, but when the providence of God wills.'"** <note>original Greek: "καὶ λοιὸν λέγει αὐτοῖς· ἴδετε οὖν ὅτι οὐχ᾿ ὅτε ἡμεῖς θέλωμέν τι εἰδέναι τῶν κρυπτῶν διὰ σωτηρίαν βλέπομεν, ἀλλ᾿ ὅτε ἡ πρόνοια τοῦ θεοῦ βούλεται"</note>

### Chapter 4: The Visionary Element in the Tradition.

However, the tendency in G <note>The Greek version of the Life of Pachomius.</note> does not only come to light in such reflections. It is also shown in the actual suppression of the visionary element within the narrative itself. A particularly characteristic scene is reported to us in M 119–129 and A 460–467 <note>M and A refer to the Coptic versions of the Life of Pachomius.</note>. A catechumen <note>A person receiving basic instruction in Christianity before being baptized.</note> in the neighboring monastery of Tmuschus is deathly ill. Pachomius and Theodore decide to travel there. While they are soaking the bread they intend to eat beforehand in water, an angel already appears to Pachomius, exhorting them to give him their prayers so that he might bring them before the Lord. When they arrive at the monastery, the unbaptized catechumen is at the point of death. They had been unable to bring him to Phbôu <note>Pabau, the central monastery of the Pachomian federation.</note> for baptism because he was too ill, nor could they baptize him on-site because no priest was present ¹). Then Pachomius and Theodore behold angels coming and baptizing the catechumen before he dies. This is followed by a report of a vision Pachomius had concerning the fates of the righteous soul after death, containing extraordinary, primitive, and interesting eschatological material.

-> “Our father Pachomius saw this vision in the monastery of Tmuschus on the occasion of the brother catechumen, who was secretly baptized before his death” (M 127). <-

Then Pachomius asks to be allowed to see the fate of an unjust soul as well, and this too is granted to him ²).

G 59 has condensed this entire report—which is problematic in two respects, as the vision of the catechumen's baptism also endangers the ecclesiastical interest in the sacrament <note>By suggesting an "angelic" baptism, the story bypasses the formal role of the Church and its priests in performing the sacrament.</note>—into just a few sentences:

-> “And another time, when both sat with a brother (!) who was distressed at having to die, the manner of the soul's departure from the body was revealed to them by the Lord. And they voluntarily told this to no one while they lived, for these are mysteries, but the great brothers <note>Senior or elder monks.</note> present became aware of how they watched with wonder the saints (angels) present in silence at the hour when the sick man gave up the ghost” ³). <-

It is certainly true that the report in M and A, as it stands, is legendary. Furthermore, Pachomius’s visions regarding the fates of the good and evil souls—which no longer have anything to do with the specific case and certainly originate from literary tradition—were only attached here later, following the law that related materials attract each other. But what we have here is nonetheless a folk-like presentation that may have arisen very early in the circles of the brothers based on certain visionary experiences of Pachomius. On the other hand, G bears all the marks of literary reflection and tendentious editing. The offense—that Pachomius sees how the unbaptized catechumen is subsequently baptized in heaven—is removed. At the same time, in contradiction to what we otherwise know (see above), it is emphasized how anxiously Pachomius and Theodore guarded the secret of their visions; in response to this, the reflective question arises as to how anything at all is known of that process under such circumstances. None of this is folk tradition. This is not how the Coptic monks told stories of Father Pachomius. Here, the Greek...

He reports in detail the earthquake, the testimony, and Theodore's flight—that is, the entire objective realization of the subjective experience. But he glides over the characteristic vision itself with just a few sentences ¹). And at the end, we find once again a sentence characteristic of the reflective nature of G: <note>original: "καὶ ἐθαύμαζον οἱ ἀκούοντες αὐτοῦ καὶ μάλιστα ὅτι τοῦ κυρίου θέλοντος, ἐὰν ἴδῃ τι τῶν κρυπτῶν, οὐκ ἐδήλου αὐτοῖς, εἰ μὴ τὰ φθάνοντα εἰς πίστιν καὶ οἰκοδομήν."</note> "And those who heard him marveled, and especially because, by the will of the Lord, if he saw anything of hidden things, he did not reveal it to them, except for those things which contribute to faith and edification."

I believe that with all of this, the character and tendency of G’s reporting has become clear on this point as well. In contrast, the pneumatic-enthusiastic <note>Refers to a style of spirituality focused on the direct, overwhelming presence of the Holy Spirit and ecstatic experiences.</note> element in the person of Pachomius and his circle comes to light with full clarity everywhere in the Coptic sources.

This brother prayed to God to calm his heart and make it believe that the **actions of men often became visible to our father Pachomius**, for he did not believe it and doubted it. Accordingly, it can also be clearly seen that the visions of **Pachomius** were a main component of his tradition from the very beginning. Even **G** <note>The Greek version of the Life of Pachomius.</note> reports (see above) that the brothers came to **Pachomius** and asked him to tell them a **vision** <note>original: "ὅραμα" (horama)</note> (32). Through the valuable notes that **G 63** provides regarding written sources that already existed during the composition of the **Life** — this seems to be directly confirmed. The section begins: "And since Abba Pachomius often spoke the word of God to them, some who heard him and loved him exceedingly wrote down many of his interpretations of the Scriptures." <note>original: "καὶ ἐπειδὴ ἐλάλει αὐτοῖς πολλάκις τὸν λόγον τοῦ θεοῦ ὁ ἀββᾶς Παχούμιος, τίνες ἀκούοντες ὑπεραγαπῶντες αὐτὸν ἔγραψαν πολλὰ περὶ αὐτοῦ νοήματα τῶν γραφῶν."</note> Even this sentence is not entirely clear. In any case, it is intended to say that written records about **Pachomius** had already begun before the authors of **G**. It is only not quite clear what was recorded; it likely concerned Pachomius’s thoughts on Scripture (one might read something like: "concerning <the> thoughts on the Scriptures"). Then **G** continues: "so that if he ever saw a vision or a manifestation of the Lord’s will <and>¹⁾ spoke of it privately to the great [monks], for the faith and benefit of those hearing..." <note>original: "ὥστε καὶ εἴ ποτε ὅραμα εἶδεν ἢ ὀπτασίαν τοῦ κυρίου βουλομένου <καὶ> κατ ἰδίαν τοῖς μεγάλοις εἴρηκεν, εἰς πίστιν καὶ ὠφέλειαν τῶν ἀκουόντων . . ."</note> Here the sentence breaks off, and the general remark follows: "**For God will always glorify His own servants, as He also speaks to Moses, saying, 'so that they may believe in you forever.'**" <note>original: "ἀεὶ γὰρ ὁ θεὸς τοὺς ἰδίους δούλους δοξάσει, ὡς καὶ λαλεῖ τῷ Μωυσῇ λέγων, ἵνα πιστεύσωσίν σοι εἰς τὸν αἰῶνα."</note> Then follows without a conjunction: "**But we, having learned at that time that faith is not for everyone, especially for a monk, even though he walked the path of the saints—for this reason, we have blended these things in our writing so that we might be able to bring the benefit of what was said without harm.**" <note>original: "ἡμεῖς δὲ μαθόντες κατὰ τὸν καιρόν, ὅτι οὐ πάντων ἐστὶν τὸ πιστεύειν μάλιστα μονάζοντι καίτοι γε τῶν ἁγίων τὴν ὁδὸν ἐπορεύετο, — διὰ τοῦτο συνεκεράσαμεν ταῦτα γράφοντες πρὸς τὸ δύνασθαι ἡμᾶς φέρειν ἀζημίως τῶν λεγομένων τὸ κέρδος."</note> Now one could try to put the general remark (**For God always...**) in parentheses and seek the main clause in the words **we... for this reason, we have blended these things in our writing**. This would result in the meaning: And therefore we—even if (**Pachomius**) saw a dream or a vision... and told it specifically to the great ones (for God will always glorify His own...) in the realization that faith is not everyone's business...—have also included this (the visions) while writing... But the sentence structure and meaning remain highly confused in this interpretation. It seems better to me [to see] that broken-off sentence...

## Book II. Investigations into the Life of Pachomius. ##

to be understood as an aposiopesis <note>a rhetorical device where a sentence is abruptly broken off</note> and to be completed from what preceded: "And therefore if he saw a dream or a vision according to God’s will and told it particularly to the great elders for the faith and benefit of the listeners, <**they recorded it**>"<sup>1)</sup>. Then we would have here a testimony of extraordinary importance: the authors of **G** <note>The Greek version of the Life of Pachomius</note> would have accordingly already found a collection of visions of **Pachomius** in written tradition and incorporated <note>original: "συνεκεράσαμεν" (synekerasamen) — literally "blended together"</note> some of it into their account. But unfortunately, the text is not certain. However, this much at least emerges with certainty: that when the life of **Pachomius** was written by the brothers, a collection of **Pachomius's** dreams and visions was available to them, either in oral tradition (fixed through frequent storytelling) or perhaps even already in written records.

And now, on the other hand, the observation can be made that such collections of vision reports, as the text of **G** suggests, are actually present in the Coptic sources of the *Vita* <note>The "Life" or biography of the saint</note>; and we may suspect that these pieces, which were initially largely suppressed in **G**, were subsequently re-incorporated into the Coptic recensions of the *Bios* <note>The Greek word for "Life"</note>. The first piece to be considered here begins with the already mentioned vision of the baptism of the catechumen <note>a convert undergoing instruction before baptism</note>. This is followed by the two visions regarding the departure of the good and the bad soul (**M 119–129, A 460–468**). Then it is told how **Theodore**, who in this discussion throughout the *Vita* simply stands alongside **Pachomius**, hears the heavenly music at the reception of a soul into heaven<sup>2)</sup>; how **Pachomius** and **Theodore** see during the **Eucharist** <note>the service of Holy Communion</note> that the angel of the worthy gives the holy elements during the ceremony itself; and how an angel entrusts **Theodore** with the care of his flock (**129–131, 468–469**). From a distance, **Theodore** hears exactly the catechesis <note>religious instruction</note> that **Pachomius** is giving to the brothers in **Pibohu** <note>also known as Phbow, the headquarters of the Pachomian monastery system</note>. **Pachomius** sees how the Lord sits enthroned in the assembly hall of the brothers and communicates His words to him, which he from then on always proclaims from the spot where he saw the Lord (**132–133, 469–471**). **Theodore** reads the thoughts of a brother who cannot decide to commit to a harder asceticism (**133–135, 471–473**). **Pachomius** has a vision about the torments of hell (**135–141**; **A** has this piece in its own collection of visions, **548–552**).

We have here, therefore, a unified context that extends in **M** from page 119 to 141. And this context can be traced even further back. Not far from this piece (**M 104–109, A 442 ff.**) stands the already discussed vision in the Sanctuary of **Phbôu**. There follows the story of the monks gossiping in the bakery, in which **Pachomius's** clairvoyance <note>literally "far-seeing"</note> again plays a role (**G 37**, **M** and **A** doublets **109–110, 114–116 = A 446**). After a story that does not belong here, there follows the vision in which **Pachomius** sees the throne of God and presents the present **Theodore** to God as his gift (**M 112f., A 445**). And again separated from this by a few small stories, in whose tradition **M** and **A** moreover partly diverge, stands the discussed corpus of visions! **G** has only included a few broken fragments of this entire corpus (**56, 57, 59**) and of these included pieces, one contains no actual visions, but only samples of the miraculous clairvoyance of **Pachomius**.

### Chapter 4. The Visionary Element in the Tradition. ###

A second series of visions is preserved for us only in **A** <note>A Coptic Sahidic version of the Life of Pachomius</note> (in a context already partially discussed above), because **M** <note>A Coptic Bohairic version</note> breaks off as a fragment at this point. It begins with that vision in which martyrdom in Latopolis <note>a city in Upper Egypt, modern Esna</note> and death are prophesied to **Pachomius** (541 f.). Attached to this are a series of related visions: the appearance of Satan in the form of Christ, a journey by **Pachomius** through Paradise (543–545), a story of how **Pachomius** watched the fate of two monks in Paradise (545–548), and finally a description of Hell and its locations, which **M**, as we saw, had placed within the first collection. **G** <note>The Greek version of the Life</note> has included from this entire series only the single story of the appearance of Satan in the form of Christ <sup>1)</sup>. For this story, which was followed by discussions on the discernment of the spirit so as to distinguish the evil spirits <note>original: "διάκρισις τοῦ πνεύματος ὥστε διακρίνειν τὰ πονηρὰ πνεύματα" (diakrisis tou pneumatos hōste diakrinein ta ponēra pneumata)</note> (somewhat in the style of the *Life of Antony*), contained at the same time a critique of the visionary element and an exhortation to caution.

It is equally characteristic that almost the only vision (apart from the unavoidable vocational visions) preserved fairly fully in **G** is the sight with which **Pachomius** warns against heresies and schisms in the Church (**G** 65, **A** 180–185, **M** 498–502, cf. **N** 28–31, **Pg** 17–19, **A** 613–620). **G** also did not let this edifying exhortation pass by. He did, however, shorten it a bit here too. And at least one interesting feature remained only in **A** and **M**. It speaks here of bishops who, while holding the orthodox faith, live in communion with the schismatics (**A** 500) <sup>2)</sup>, an allusion that can only refer to the **Meletians** <note>A 4th-century schismatic group in Egypt who disagreed on how to readmit Christians who had lapsed during persecution</note>, who also play a role elsewhere in the life of **Pachomius**. Furthermore, for **G**, one should note the vision that **Pachomius** had while gathering rushes regarding the moral dangers threatening his monks (**G** 45, **M** 92 f., **A** 413), and some examples of **Pachomius’s** clairvoyance and thought-reading, against which the authors of **G** do not seem to have had such strong reservations as they did against the actual visions <sup>3)</sup>.

**Ladeuze** (p. 84) simply dismissed this entire surplus, which the reports of **M** and **A** have over **G**, under the verdict of legendary overgrowth. He places these reports alongside the other miracle accounts—vanishingly few in number and unimpressive—that **M** and **A** offer beyond **G**. He argues that everywhere the same impulse prevailed: the tendency to embellish the Saint's life with the marvelous.

This very equating of vision and actual miracle is misleading. The vision does not belong to the realm of legend in the same way as the actual miracle does. It cannot be emphasized enough that in all the traditions under consideration, the actual miracle and the report of miracles play almost no role. Conversely, we saw above in an interesting case how **G** [suppressed] the entire [account] increased into the externally miraculous...

<meta>This page continues the comparison between the Coptic and Greek versions of the Life of Pachomius, specifically arguing that the Coptic tradition (represented by manuscripts M and A) preserves the original visionary and charismatic atmosphere of the early monastic community, whereas the Greek version (G) has been "distilled" to present a more conventional, cautious image of the saint.</meta>

## Book II. Investigations into the Life of Pachomius. ##

...presentation of a vision has been maintained, but the powerful visionary details have been purged. In this consideration, both areas—the actual miracle and the vision—must be more sharply separated. Now, in contrast to Ladeuze <note>Paul Ladeuze, a scholar of Pachomian monasticism</note>, it is certainly not my intention to take all these vision reports directly as historical fact or at face value. It is quite clear how these often simply pass on well-formed material from visionary ideas and experiences. Amélineau¹⁾ once attempted to prove the presence of numerous ideas from Egyptian eschatology <note>theology concerning death and the afterlife</note> in them. Ladeuze has—probably with greater justification—pointed to direct contact with later Christian apocalyptic literature, specifically with the *Vision of Paul*²⁾. Anyone who is somewhat familiar with monastic literature will very soon discover what a role the once-coined wandering motifs <note>recurring themes or plots found in folklore and legends</note> play even in this realm of visions. Without question, many individual details reported here must be abandoned and addressed as "poetry" from the circle of Pachomian monks, or as wandering legends adopted here.

What I contend, however, is that all these reports—seen as a whole—lie quite close to reality. Pachom <note>Pachomius, the founder of communal monasticism (c. 292–348 AD)</note> was truly an outspoken visionary. Dreams, visions, clairvoyance, foreknowledge, thought-reading, and the seeing and proclaiming of the secrets of the brothers' hearts belong to the very core of his personality. A part of his power and the authority he possessed among the brothers rested upon this. They simply believed him capable of anything³⁾. In the circles of the brothers, people loved most of all to tell stories of the mysterious visions of our father Pachom. Indeed, even the proof that many of these stories work with inherited material and shaped eschatological ideas does not make them simply unhistorical. Pachom was not an original mind; what he absorbed of eschatological ideas through hearsay or reading followed him into his dreams and visions, or offered him the means to give shape to the unformed matter of his experience when retold in narrative form.

What I must assert after all this is that the Coptic tradition lets us look better into the entire atmosphere surrounding the life of Pachom and his followers than the everywhere anxiously and cautiously weighing, reflecting, and restraining reporting of the Greek brothers who take the lead in **G**. If one wants to know what was told of Father Pachom from the beginning in the circles of the Pachomian brothers in deep reverence, in murmurs and whispers, one must read the popular reports in **M** and **A**, not the distilled <term>Life</term> <note>original: Βίος (Bios)</note> of **G**. Beyond that, it will often no longer be possible to determine what Pachom actually experienced in each individual case. He certainly was not such a cautious and prudent "average Christian" devoted to the Church as **G** portrays him.

<header>Chapter 5. Book-Piety.</header>

## Chapter 5.
# Book-Piety.

Ecstasy and vision on one hand, and scriptural and biblical piety on the other, are two things that exist in a state of strong tension with one another; when one takes the lead, the other typically recedes. It would be worth presenting a systematic account of how "book-piety"—contemplation leaning on the Scriptures, edifying Bible study, the joy of complex allegorical interpretation, and with all that, a degree of scholarship—only gradually made its way into the enthusiastic, visionary world of monasticism, with its desert wanderings, its battles with demons, and its fantastic exercises of penance in solitary cells. Here, we are dealing with a small excerpt of this broad development: the few things that the various versions of the *Life of Pachomius* <note>The "Vita Pachomii," the biographical accounts of the founder of communal monasticism</note> teach us in this regard. Here, one might postulate from the outset: to the extent that the ecstatic element is pushed into the background in version G <note>The primary Greek recension of the Life</note>, the written word and book-piety will, on the other hand, gain increased importance. This suspicion will indeed be confirmed. It is not as if literature and book-piety played no role at all in the original life of Pachom <note>Saint Pachomius (c. 292–348 AD)</note>. However, it can be clearly proven that these elements of piety play a stronger role in G than in the Coptic versions M and A.

Thus, for example, in G 17, in the important report about the first monastic rules that Pachom gave to his followers, it is said: "and thus he prescribed for them... from the Divine Scriptures" <note>original: "καὶ οὕτων ἐκανόνισεν αὐτοῖς . . . ἀπὸ τῶν θείων γραφῶν"</note>. The exact parallel in M 33 does not contain this emphasis on the Scripture, which does not even seem to fit properly with the monastic rules <note>1</note>. When the first disciples come to Pachom (G 16), it says: "and they, being well taught by him according to the Scriptures, bore fruit" <note>original: "καὶ αὐτοὶ διδασκόμενοι καλῶς ὑπ’ αὐτοῦ κατὰ τὰς γραφὰς ἐκαρποφόρουν"</note>. Pachom exhorts them: "Strive to attain that for which you were called, brothers: to meditate on the psalms and the lessons from the other books, and especially the Gospel" <note>original: "ἐφ’ ᾧ ἐκλήθητε ἀδελφοὶ ἀγωνίσασθε τυχεῖν αὐτοῦ, ψαλμοὺς μελετᾶν καὶ τὰ ἀπὸ τῶν ἄλλων βιβλίων μαθήματα, ἐξαιρέτως δὲ τὸ εὐαγγέλιον"</note>. In the parallel M 30 f, we again find not a word of this emphasis on Scripture and scriptural study. According to G (and M), Pachom survives his battles with the demons "having learned from the Divine Scriptures and especially from the Gospel" <note>original: "μαθὼν ἐκ τῶν θείων γραφῶν καὶ μάλιστα ἐκ τοῦ εὐαγγελίου"</note> <note>2</note>. Even the long and edifying story of how Pachom serves in the office of a <term>Reader</term> <note>original: "Anagnostes"—a minor clerical rank responsible for reading the scriptures during the liturgy</note> in the village church he built (chapter 20) is exclusive to G. M 33 and A 71 pass over it with a single sentence.

In G 24 f., it is claimed in all seriousness that Theodor <note>Theodore of Tabennese, Pachomius’s successor</note> was drawn to Pachom and his monastery with irresistible force because he heard a brother of Pachom give an allegorical interpretation of the Temple and its ritual objects, and this brother identified the interpretation as coming from Pachom. Was this really the historical occasion for Theodore's entry into the monastery <note>3</note>? One is reluctant to accept this, although the report in G is even confirmed here by M 42 ff.

The report from **A** 386 ff. is quite different. Here, too, it is told that it was the custom among the brothers to gather every evening <note>1)</note> after the meal to speak of the Holy Scriptures "and to say what each knew of them, whether he had learned it by heart or had heard it spoken of." But the exhortation of the Pachomian monk sounds completely different:

> Listen to me, and I will tell you the following word with its interpretation. I heard it from our father Pachom, the man of God. It is written in the Proverbs that God loves the pure, and whoever is pure is chosen in His eyes. This means that He loves those of a pure heart just as He loves those who walk in the law of the Lord. — And when it says that all the righteous are chosen by Him, this applies only to those who have fulfilled the law without fault, as is fitting for the Gospel of the Son of God. And when the brother had spoken this word and its interpretation, he said: May God forgive me for speaking at this moment of the righteous man and of what I heard from him.

And when Theodor heard that, **his heart burned like fire**. I believe that anyone who impartially compares these reports <note>2)</note> must grant greater originality to the one in **A**. There is no mention here yet of an elaborate, allegorizing exploration of Scripture, but only of an edifying <term>paränese</term> <note>an ethical exhortation or sermon</note> based on a passage of Scripture.

The reworking of the story regarding the visit Pachom made with several disciples to the monastery of Tmuschus (<term>Monchosis</term> <note>original: Μόνχωσις</note>) on his Nile boat is particularly significant. Here it is first reported that Pachom is very distressed by the overly abundant food the brothers are consuming. To lead them toward proper <term>asceticism</term> <note>the practice of self-denial and spiritual discipline</note>, he challenges them to keep watch with him through the night and persist in prayer. One of the brothers cannot withstand the exertion and lies down to sleep. When the brothers arrive in Tmuschus, they complain about the lesson Pachom has given them. Corne-

2) An investigation of the reports present here in **G M** leads, moreover, to the result that in **M A** two reports are again running side by side. The <term>patchwork</term> <note>German: Klitterung; a compilation of different sources into one text</note> emerges most clearly in **M**. **M** runs parallel to **G** 24 f. in sections 41–44, and like **G**, it brings the report about Pachom’s allegorical scriptural interpretation, following the report found in **G** up to the introduction of Theodor into the monastery of Pachom by Pegôsh (Pekysios) 44–45. Then, in 46–48, it seemingly reaches back to **G** 23. However, the fact that a patchwork of sources exists here is proven by the double mention of the brother Pegôsh (see above) p. 44 f. and 48. With the second mention of Pegôsh, **M** then steers back into the report corresponding to **G**. — **A** has been designed more uniformly this time. For it essentially sticks to the one source independent of **G**, and consequently has not joined in the strange rearrangement of material found in **G**. It begins immediately with the keyword of the second source, "We must begin the story of our father Theodor," after briefly reporting the arrival of the Pachomian monk in the monastery of Esne, through whom Theodor is won (= **M** 41). It then brings the same material regarding Theodor’s youth as **M**, going beyond **G**, and then leads the report uniformly to its conclusion. And in this report—that is, in the second source—stands the account of Pachom’s sermon that interested us above, which is independent of **G**. **A** has evidently preserved the <term>archetype</term> <note>the original form of the text</note> of **M A** purely, while **M** is a patchwork of **G** (or a report corresponding to **G**) and **M A**.

Cornelius, the Abbot of Tmuschus, mocks them, suggesting they would surely not fall behind an older man in ascetic practice. What has version **G** <note>The Greek recension of the *Life of Pachomius*</note> now made of this story? It has shattered and torn it apart by inserting a long lecture in sections 36—37, and even an excerpt of Pachomian monastic rules in 38 a ¹). It does not explicitly state that Pachom held the lecture on that very night; it only says that he held such lectures often: "And finally he interpreted for them the words of the Divine Scriptures, especially those which were not easy to understand and were deep." <note>original Greek: καὶ λοιπὸν τὰ λόγια τῶν θείων γραφῶν ἡρμήνευεν αὐτοῖς μάλιστα τὰ μὴ εὐνόητα καὶ βαθέα</note> The scholar Pachom has here strongly overshadowed the figure of the great man of prayer and vigils ²).

But it should be emphasized that this tendency to stress "scriptural piety" in **G** does not emerge as strongly as the tendency to suppress visionary elements. Often, a sentence leaning in this direction is also confirmed in the parallel versions. Thus, **G** 76 has Horsisi <note>Orsisius, Pachom’s successor</note> say: "We know that through the Scriptures our father has strengthened you in perfect knowledge." <note>original Greek: οἴδαμεν ὅτι ἀπὸ τῶν γραφῶν ὁ πατὴρ ἡμῶν τῇ τελείᾳ γνώσει ἐστήριξεν ὑμᾶς</note> Not only is there a parallel for this in **A** 653, whose presentation here is directly dependent on **G** (specifically G³). Also in the Memphitic *Life of Theodor* (291) it says: "Our father Pachom has strengthened us in the holy scriptures and the perfect wisdom of God" (from Horsisi’s funeral oration on the death of Theodor). Likewise, the sentence in **G** 91: "Let us also consider this benefit, which we heard from our father from the meanings of the Divine Scriptures" <note>original Greek: νοήσωμεν δὲ καὶ τοῦτο τὸ κέρδος, ὅπερ παρὰ τοῦ πατρὸς ἡμῶν ἠκούσαμεν ἐκ τῶν νοημάτων τῶν θείων γραφῶν</note> is confirmed by the exact parallel in **M** 232. And the expression "meanings of the Scriptures" <note>original Greek: νοήματα τῶν γραφῶν</note> reminds us of the exposition in **G** 63, which we already discussed above.

On the other hand, we find that **M** 18, where **G** only speaks of them "keeping vigil" <note>original Greek: ἀγρυπνούντων αὐτῶν</note>, adds "and meditating in the heart on the holy scriptures" (**A** 353 describes them reciting what they had learned by heart), while the report earlier in **G** 4, in the description of Palaimon’s asceticism, mentions the "meditation on the words of God" <note>original Greek: μελετὴ τῶν λόγων θεοῦ</note> and again finds its parallel in **M** 12.

One might therefore say, at most, that in **G** the tendency toward emphasizing scriptural piety emerges somewhat more strongly than in the other accounts. It would thus be necessary to extend the investigation to all sources to see how far a stronger emphasis on "book-piety" might have only penetrated these texts at a later stage.

However, that does not belong to our task for the time being, and we now turn to a field of stories in which the state of affairs is once again quite clear.

## Book II. Investigations into the *Life of Pachomius*.

...are suited to cast a poor light on the conditions within Pachomian monasticism. They are actually most faithfully preserved in the Arabic tradition, already less so in the Coptic, while the Greek version has removed almost everything. Ladeuze <note>Paul Ladeuze, a scholar who argued that the Greek versions were the most authentic and that the Coptic/Arabic versions added later "romantic" embellishments.</note> reversed the assessment of these sources here, specifically wanting to see only interesting and "novelistic" embellishments in the Arabic *Life*. The assumption of such a perverse reporter, who—out of interest in the scandalous—would have burdened the older report with scandalous and sordid stories, is in itself extraordinarily unconvincing. This theory fails, however, when comparing the details.

I will first pick out the story preserved for us in **A** 418 ff., **M** 95 ff. (= **T** 317 ff., **G** 47 f.). In **A**, the narrative begins with a general description of how Pachomius fought with demons for the souls of his brothers. He hears the conversation of two demons; one of them tells how the person he wanted to haunt burned him through prayer, while the other says he was received quite kindly by his target. He sees the angels quarreling with the demons over the temptation of men and rejoicing over the conversion of sinners (418–421) ¹). One day, however, he observes (424) a <term>demon of impurity</term> <note>This refers to a demon associated with sexual lust or "unclean" thoughts.</note> sneaking among his brothers. He gathers them in the evening and gives them an exhortation. If a man has a hundred rooms in his house and sells one of them, he cannot prevent the buyer from entering all the others. So it is with the human heart. One should not allow the evil spirit even the slightest space. The reward for this struggle will not fail to come ²). In connection with this warning, Pachomius gives the brothers rules for their behavior: No one shall stay alone with his companions in a room unless work requires it; no one shall take the hand of his companion or touch any part of his body without necessity (e.g., if he is sick or falls); no one shall sit down on the same seat with another to speak with him; no one shall sleep on a bed that does not belong to him; no one shall enter the cell of his comrade without a command or sufficient reason. When the brothers hear these regulations, they grumble: "Is there perhaps a woman among us?" They grumble all night and refuse to go to work in the usual way the next morning. Then, the next morning, two monks arrive who were sent by a bishop with a letter; one of the revolting brothers, named Mauo (Mauos), urges Theodore <note>Pachomius's successor and favorite disciple.</note>—who has to decide on the matter in Pachomius's absence—to receive the monks well. One of the two in particular seems to him to have the form of an angel. When Pachomius returns, he reads in the letter that the monk was caught trying to commit a transgression with a boy. Pachomius imposes a heavy penance on this brother. Mani <note>The text likely means Mauo here, the brother mentioned previously.</note> falls into a great rage over how he allowed himself to be deceived. On the same day, however, other monks—presumably in the Pachomian monastery itself—are caught in the same act. Pachomius drives the older one out of the monastery and beats the younger one. When the brothers, after these experiences, for the...

---

1) The following story (421–424) of the ascetic who was proud of his achievements is inserted here at the wrong place in **A**, as a comparison of parallels shows (at the word "demons").
2) Here, the two other sources insert a sentence that could well be original and which reads in **G**: "For there are rich rulers in the spirit; and there are those like leaders of ten, leaders of fifty, leaders of a hundred, leaders of a thousand, and perfect kings," etc. **G** 47 c. <note>original Greek: εἰσὶν γὰρ πλούσιοι ἄρχοντες τῷ πνεύματι· καὶ εἰσὶν ὡς δεκάδαρχοι, πεντηκόνταρχοι, ἑκατόνταρχοι, χιλίαρχοι καὶ βασιλεῖς τέλειοι κ. τ. α.</note>

### Chapter 6: Reports of Sexual Sins of the Monks.

...gathered for prayer, the rebellious monks prostrate themselves before their abbot and ask him for his intercession in prayer.

This is a good, coherent narrative that is beyond reproach. However, in all other traditions—even the Hebrew one—it is now thoroughly corrupted. In these versions, the unchaste monk sent by the bishop has **become a thief instead**. Naturally, the individual parts of the story now fall apart. One no longer knows what the grim premonitions (the conversation between the demons) or the solemn exhortations of Pachomius refer to. What is the point of all this in this context, if it were merely a case of theft by a foreign monk? The mention of specific regulations against <term>unchastity</term> <note>This refers to sexual misconduct or "impurity," a major concern in early monastic rules.</note> naturally had to be omitted. But these rules were indeed likely given by Pachomius; they are found in Jerome’s <note>Saint Jerome, the 4th-century scholar who translated Pachomius’s rules into Latin.</note> tradition of the *Codex Regularum* <note>original: "codex regularum"; a collection of monastic rules.</note> under numbers 93–95. The narrative, preserved faithfully only in the Arabic *Life*, provides us with a very valuable commentary on them ¹) and shows us quite clearly at one point how such rules originated. The other sources, which omit them, betray themselves, as it now remains unclear in their versions why the monk Mauo (the other rebellious monks are not mentioned) actually becomes so enraged by the very general warnings left in the reports that he refuses to go to work the next morning. Furthermore, the Greek version (G) most clearly allows the original state of affairs to shimmer through when it has the rebellious monk ask: "Why then does the old man hand down so many safeguards to us? Are we then about to fall every hour?" ²) <note>original Greek: "τί οὖν τοσαύτας ἀσφαλείας (!) παραδίδωσιν ἡμῖν ὁ γέρων; μέλλομεν ἆρα καθ' ὥραν πίπτειν;"</note>

We have here, then, evidently once again an interesting case for <term>source criticism</term> <note>The scholarly method of analyzing different versions of a text to determine which is the oldest or most accurate.</note> where the Arabic tradition alone, against all other sources—which here even includes the Thebaic fragment that matches the Memphitic *Life*—has preserved the original account ³). Other observations support this. The Arabic version (A) tells us (435) a story about the pious father Titoes (Duiduna). He has to care for a young, beautiful boy during an illness. And his heart inclines toward him. He cannot explain the stirrings of his own mind. Then, at night, the <term>demon of unchastity</term> appears to him and tells him that he is tempting him through this boy. The Greek version (G) has turned this (53) into a harmless story that is hardly recognizable. In that version, Titoes, who has to care for the sick, falls into the temptation of taking some of the sick-food for himself. Only the similarity of the name...

---

1) There is no reason to assume here that the Arabic version (A) is a later borrowing from the *Book of Rules* (*Codex Regularum*). Although A externally incorporated the Rule—which is preserved in the *Lausiac History* <note>original: "Historia Lausiaca"; a 5th-century work on the desert fathers.</note>—into its report from G 3 in sections 366–369, the regulations in question here are quite different and are internally connected to the report. The same likely applies to the extensive communication of monastic rules in A 502 ff. (cf. also 447). By contrast, G 38 a (A 601 f. see above page 214) shows clearly what an interpolation from the *Codex Regularum* looks like. According to G 63, the authors of the *Life of Pachomius* already found written rules (cf. A 502, rules of which some were written and others were given orally). Why should the original *Life* not report here and there on the origin of individual rules? Cf. also G 27 a.

2) Ladeuze <note>Paul Ladeuze, a historian of early monasticism.</note> (page 41) must himself admit regarding the report in G: "*His account seems to be from a man who is not always very well-informed about the details of the facts he recounts*" <note>original Latin: "Son exposé semble être d'un homme, qui n'est pas toujours très au courant des détails des faits qu'il raconte."</note>. Nevertheless, Ladeuze declares G to be primary and A to be secondary even here. From what has been stated above, however, it becomes clear why G appears not to be "very well-informed about the details of the facts."

3) On the other hand, G 58, M 110, and A 454 f. really do concern a theft. A 454 speaks generally of "a dishonest action" <note>original French: "une action malhonnête"</note>. This is only an accidental generalization, to which one must not attribute a specifically sexual meaning.

# Book II. Investigations into the Life of Pachomius.

...and the placement of the narrative within the context ¹) prove that we are dealing here with identical stories.

We note, moreover, that the two stories being discussed are located quite close to one another in the Arabic *Life* (418–430, 435 f.) ²). — Another group of such stories has been preserved for us by A <note>Manuscript version A, representing a Coptic or Arabic tradition</note> near the very end of its old source. This involves the entire section from 509 to 536, of which only fragments remain in M <note>Manuscript version M, often referring to a Latin or Bohairic source</note> 193–210, while G <note>The standard Greek version of the Life of Pachomius</note> omits them entirely.

The presentation here initially links back to the verse from Matthew 13:38: "the weeds are the sons of the evil one" <note>original Greek: τὰ δὲ ζιζάνιά εἰσιν οἱ υἱοὶ τοῦ πονηροῦ</note>. With the keyword <term>weed</term> <note>original Greek: ζιζάνιον (zizanion); referring to the biblical parable of the wheat and the weeds</note>, the monk who is burdened with unnatural passions is identified. Ladeuze (90) <note>Paul Ladeuze, a 19th-century scholar of Pachomian monasticism</note> now places great emphasis on the fact that the Arabic tradition here, right at the beginning, quotes the scriptural passage in a coarsened manner: "The unchaste are the sons of the evil one, as it is written in the Gospel." It must be conceded to *L.* <note>Ladeuze</note> that A is secondary here and later, where he once again renders the keyword <term>weed</term> as "the unchaste (fornicator)," <note>the original text uses the French 'fornicateur'</note>. But it is entirely incorrect to assume that A only introduced the reference to <term>sexual immorality</term> <note>original Greek: πορνεία (porneia)</note> into the entire context.

Anyone who attentively reads the account in M 193 ff. cannot be in doubt about what is at stake here either. One day—it is said—Pachomius <note>The text uses "P.", referring to Pachomius, the founder of communal monasticism.</note> receives a revelation regarding the passages in Jude 16 and 18 ("walking according to their own lusts" <note>original Greek: κατὰ τὰς ἐπιθυμίας αὐτῶν πορευόμενοι</note>) and Matthew 13:38; it is meant to refer to people "who have *defiled the* image of God (the human body)." Even if this expression already points to the sin of unchastity, the following regulations concerning the treatment of sinners clearly distinguish between the older seducer and the younger seduced: "If someone, seduced by one of the ‘sons of the evil one,’ felt his inferiority and showed a little understanding, Pachomius cared for his soul and healed it." And on the other hand: "Those whom he recognized as ‘sons of the evil one,’ he stripped of their monastic habit, dressed them in worldly clothing, and drove them from the midst of the brothers" ³). This is truly clear enough. It also fits well when it is emphasized in this very context that Pachomius, due to the Spirit of God within him, recognized the "desires of the heart" <note>original Greek: ἐπιθυμίαι τῆς καρδίας</note> even before they were carried out; that he forced such brothers to confess and drove them out; and that if a brother voluntarily confessed his fault and he saw the possibility of salvation, he saved him. — It really serves no purpose to pick out individual phrases with Ladeuze and demonstrate that these are also used in cases where it is not specifically about the vice of unchastity. The meaning of the entire section is beyond doubt even in M.

And now, in M and A, these general principles are illustrated with a specific case (M 194, A 510). It is told that three men from Alexandria arrive and want to be accepted as monks. One of them—

3) It seems he has already turned these general remarks into a specific case: One day he found "a young boy in a bad state of impurity," and then he took off his monk's clothes and drove him away (509 f.).

# Chapter 6: Reports of Sexual Sins of the Monks.

...is recognized by Pachomius, through his gift of *discernment* <note>original Greek: διάκρισις (diakrisis)</note>, as a *weed* <note>original Greek: ζιζάνιον (zizanion); a reference to the biblical parable of the wheat and the weeds</note> (this man is a bad weed by his actions since his childhood <note>translated from a French quotation of the source text</note>). Pachomius, however, does not want to reject him, so as not to scare off the two others who came with him. But he admits him only under certain conditions and precautionary measures. He is to be watched, "so that he does not commit the same bad actions among us" that he did before. — What is meant here is, again, quite clear from the context, and source A <note>The Arabic/Coptic version of the manuscript</note> is factually correct when it paraphrases the keyword *weed* with "fornicator" <note>original Greek: πόρνος (pornos)</note>. — It is furthermore fitting when, in both sources, right in this context, a long discourse is inserted regarding the good nature of man and the possibility of resisting sin through free will (M 196-199, A 512 f.). The following explanations also only then become truly understandable. Pachomius justifies himself here as to why he has rejected so many who applied to enter the monastery. They were all *weeds*. They would not have been able to sustain themselves in the monastic life because of the passions that dominate them. Had he revealed their deeds to the brothers and asked them to pray for them, the brothers would have turned away from them in disgust. If he alone had taken care of them, he would have had an infinite amount of work. For he would have had to visit them very often by day and by night (!) and thus he would have had to neglect the other brothers; he would have cultivated the bad field with infinite effort and not cared for the good one. Such people did not belong in the <term>Koinobion</term> <note>a communal monastery where monks lived together</note>, but should become <term>Anchorites</term> <note>hermits who live in isolation</note> in solitary penance and extinguish their passions through continuous ascetic exercises, in fasting day and night, and in tears. — All of this only gains its true meaning if Pachomius is thinking of people with strong sexual inclinations and not just any sins in general. Now (M 206), the story of that *weed* who was nonetheless admitted is followed further. Pachomius subjects him to unheard-of ascetic exercises. He is regarded in the monastery as particularly holy. But after nine years of ascetic exercises, he nonetheless falls. And now it says quite clearly: "he inclined, through his impure will, to set snares for a soul to kill it" (206) (less clearly in A 518). But the clairvoyant Father forces him to confess and drives him out of the monastery.

The story of the youth Silvanus, which source A (518 ff.) places exactly in the right spot (cf. also T 557 f.), while source M has omitted it, takes a different turn. For the story is a counterpart to the preceding one. Pachomius recognizes that this youth, contrary to his first very promising beginnings, has "given room to Satan" and makes the decision to remove him from the monastery. At the urgent pleading of Silvanus, he does not carry out this decision, but subjects the youth to an unheard-of system of penance and mortification <note>1</note>. And this time, the system is fully successful. Pachomius can finally declare to the brothers that no other among them reaches him in piety (53 a). Then the brothers begin to revere him like a saint (a man of the Spirit): "O our father Abba Silvanus, tell us..."

---

1) Note especially how Pachomius subordinates Silvanus to an older monk, Sanamon (Greek: Ψενάμμων), who is to direct his penitential exercises: "Behold, there is your father (in second place) after God; do everything he tells you; when he sits down at the table to eat, you shall also sit, until the moment he rises, and then you rise as well." Unconditional subordination to the <term>man of God</term> <note>original Greek: ἄνθρωπος θεοῦ (anthropos theou)</note>, the mortification of one's own will, is Pachomius's most powerful means of discipline. One obscures what is characteristic if one mixes in the modern expression "pastoral care" here.

# Book II. Investigations into the *Life of Pachomius*.

...a word <note>original footnote 1: A "pneumatic" or spiritually-gifted person is, as occurs in many places in the *Apophthegmata* (Sayings of the Desert Fathers), asked for a spiritual word or "logos."</note> that can benefit us.” However, the story also has its tragic downside. It concludes with the brief remark: “The suffering he had endured among the brothers, until the day our father Pachomius <note>original: Pachom</note> sang his praise, had lasted 3 years. After that, he died at the home of Abbot Paul, the leader of Tmuschus, in the peace of God. Amen!” (533) <note>original footnote 2: In Source G 67, the penance lasts 7 years; in Source Ps 4, it lasts 8 years.</note>.

As mentioned, the story is missing in Source M. Instead, this time the Theban fragment 557 ff. stands alongside the report from Source A. Source G also preserved the story (66–67), but how cruelly he has distorted it. He summarizes the sins of Silvanus in the sentence: “Father Pachomius had given him certain instructions when he entered the monastery, <note>original Greek: καὶ μετὰ ταῦτα ἀμελοῦντος αὐτοῦ καὶ πολλὰ γελῶντος...</note> and after these things, he was negligent and laughed much...” And yet we are expected to believe Source G, that the unprecedented years of penance performed by Silvanus were intended merely to drive the laughter out of him. Somewhat more motivated is the report found finally in Source N 12–16 and Ps 2–4. According to this, Silvanus had been an actor <note>original Greek: ἀπὸ μίμων (apo mimon), meaning from the mimes or stage-performers</note> before he became a monk. Here, his main sin is emphasized accordingly (alongside the general accusations of <note>original Greek: σπαταλιᾶν καὶ στρηνιᾶν (spatalian kai strenian)</note> “living in luxury and wantonness”) as having begun: <note>original Greek: τὰ τῆς θυμέλης ἄσεμνα ῥήματα ἀδεῶς μεταξὺ τῶν ἀδελφῶν ἐκτραγῳδεῖν</note> “to boldly recite the unseemly words of the stage <note>The Greek "thymele" refers to the altar or platform in the center of an orchestra in a theater.</note> among the brothers.” The concrete detail that Silvanus had been an actor may contain a valuable memory. But the idea that Pachomius imposed years of asceticism that ended in death for the purpose of curing Silvanus of reminiscences of his acting days is also quite unbelievable.

And Source A brings yet a third story in this context (533 ff.). In one monastery, there was a monk who had a reputation for special holiness. When Pachomius visits the monastery, the monk seeks in every way to hide from him. They finally force him to come to him. And Pachomius unmasks the "saint": <note>original French: "cet homme a en lui l’âme d’un loup, et certes il a tué un grand nombre de frères."</note> *“this man has the soul of a wolf within him, and certainly he has killed a great number of brothers.”* — Through a hideous smell, he sensed the demon of unchastity within him. Then the bad monk was driven out of the monastery (533–536).

Incidentally, Source A has already included a duplicate of this story in 477–480. Here, it is not just any brother, but even the superior of a monastery named Apollonius <note>original footnote 3: In Source M 75, an Apollonius is named as the deputy of Abbot Petron.</note>. Again, Pachomius discovers the criminal act by smelling a terrible odor. Also, the boy seduced by Apollonius <note>original French: "pour lequel Satan avait tué cet homme"</note> (*“for whom Satan had killed this man”*) comes and confesses. Apollonius is not immediately excluded; Pachomius initially wants to save him through prayer, but then receives strict instructions to cast him out.

As stated, the two stories are likely originally identical. The latter is the original. The former covered up the fact that this concerned the abbot of a monastery. In Source T, the story of Apollonius stands directly next to that of Silvanus (555 f. 557 f.). I point out here once more in conclusion the observation that in Source A we find a series of these stories immediately next to one another <note>original footnote 4: Compare A 509–536 (separated 477–80) = M 88–99. Additionally, it may be pointed out that the unprecedented harshness with which Pachomius once prevented the burial of a deceased monk, burning his clothes, and leaving the corpse unburied...</note>

## Chapter 7.

# Summary Discussion of the Sources and the Origin of the *Life*.

I shall now attempt to summarize the result of our investigation. The main thesis of Ladeuze <note>Paul Ladeuze (1870–1940) was a Belgian scholar who argued that the Greek version of the *Life of Pachomius* was the original source.</note> must be recognized as correct. The Greek-speaking brothers in the monastic community of the Pachomians—perhaps even during Theodore’s lifetime and at his instigation—wrote a <term>Life</term> <note>original Greek: Βίος (Bios)</note> of Father Pachomius, which was then supplemented after Theodore’s death by an account of the work of his first successors. This <term>Life</term> was composed in the Greek language, and its outline is preserved in Source G (sections 1–74). This established outline of the life of Pachomius then dominated all subsequent accounts, just as the Gospel of Mark dominated the Synoptic literature <note>The "Synoptic Gospels" (Matthew, Mark, and Luke) share much of the same material; scholars generally believe Mark was written first and used as a source for the others.</note>. A comparison of the sources shows this clearly: it is always the same outline that forms the basis of the individual accounts.

However, the source question is by no means settled by this, and it would be a grave error if we were to treat the parallel Coptic (and Arabic) *Lives* throughout as merely secondary material—an error similar to taking the Gospel of Mark as the sole source for the life of Jesus simply because one has proven Mark's priority over Matthew and Luke. Rather, we are dealing here with a highly interesting case of a complex history of transmission. For undoubtedly, original and primary material has been preserved for us in the Coptic sources (T, M, A), and undoubtedly Source G is secondary in a whole series of reports. The riddle is solved, on the one hand, by the assumption that Source G has not preserved the original Greek <term>Life</term> in its pure form, and on the other hand, by the realization that the...

Perhaps the entire section G 64–67; M (151) 178–210; A 495–536 was originally grouped under this same dominant perspective.

He believes that the closing word of Pachomius, which is recorded in G 2 (M 2; A 340; Th. 314), refers only to the first of the three temptations (the expulsion of Pachomius from the pagan sanctuary) and that therefore the (third) temptation standing in between is secondary. But G has misunderstood the context. It is a matter of "persecution" by the demons in general, not the expulsion from the sanctuary (<term>to be persecuted/pursued</term> <note>original: διωχθῆναι (diōchthēnai)</note>, not, as further above, <term>to be driven out</term> <note>original: ἐκδιωχθῆναι (ekdiōchthēnai)</note>). In that case, the word fits all three temptations. Admittedly, Sources M and A misunderstood the passage as wrongly as Ladeuze did, by adding "from that place" to the word <term>persecuted</term>.
