# Book II. Investigations into the *Life of Pachomius*.

The composition of a comprehensive <term>Life</term> <note>original Greek: Βίος (Bios)</note> is something quite different from the written recording of specific details from the life of the Saint; the claim of the Greek brothers that they were the first to write the <term>Life</term> does not exclude the existence of **such** literature prior to that <term>Life</term>. We were able, for instance, to provide definite proof that Source G <note>Source "G" refers to the primary Greek manuscript of the biography.</note> already presupposes several connected reports of Pachomius’s monastery foundations and that one presentation here bears the character of a secondary compilation. In Source G itself, it is specifically handed down to us that even before the composition of the <term>Life</term>, some brothers had recorded <term>thoughts on the scriptures</term> <note>original Greek: νοήματα τῶν γραφῶν (noēmata tōn graphōn)</note> from Pachomius. Indeed, with a certain probability, a note could be extracted from G suggesting that a written collection of Pachomius's visions already existed back then, and the findings in the Coptic-Arabic tradition confirmed this suspicion in an almost compelling manner. — We were finally able, on the basis of an analysis of Sources A and M <note>"A" and "M" refer to the Amélineau and Musée Guimet Coptic manuscript traditions.</note>, to propose the hypothesis that a collection of stories also existed in which it was reported how Pachomius exercised monastic discipline in particularly difficult cases—notably in offenses of a sexual nature—with wisdom, but also with almost barbaric strictness. Theodore used to tell the brothers how Pachomius had snatched the souls of those whom the Lord had entrusted to him from the demons (M 249). Such stories will have received a fixed form very early, whether in oral or, what is more likely, in written tradition. And even after the Greeks had written the life of the holy father, the oral tradition in the monasteries of Pachomius certainly continued to flow quietly. And while it naturally washed along much sand and debris <note>The author uses "sand and debris" as a metaphor for legendary or unreliable additions that accumulate in oral tradition over time.</note>, it nonetheless preserved valuable material that had not entered the literary presentation. One observation may be briefly suggested here: the detailed account—preserved in M 152 ff. and A 578 ff. (heavily condensed in G 69 b–70)—of the fall of Theodore, his ambitious plans to take the master's place at the end of Pachomius's life, and his punishment, reveals itself by its entire character as a half-accusing, half-excusing account of the whole fatal incident from the mouth of Theodore himself.

Indeed, the tradition in Source A even tells us the point in time at which Theodore began to speak of this shameful experience to the brothers <note>1)</note>. — Thus, when the Coptic monks set about placing a parallel work (or even several) alongside the <term>Life</term>, they could draw upon a rich material of older tradition. Externally, they adhered to the framework of the Greek <term>Life</term>; they did not possess the talent for form <note>The author suggests the Coptic writers were less concerned with polished literary structure than the Greek writers.</note> that was characteristic of the Greeks to create such a whole anew. But into that framework, they worked much new and valuable material. On the other hand, the fixation of the <term>Life</term> of Pachomius in Source G signifies a major shortening of the tradition concerning Pachomius. In true Greek fashion, subjective reflection and a tendency toward eloquence appear everywhere here. The entire work is permeated by numerous literary reflections that reveal more to us of the spirit of the authors than that of Pachomius. These Greeks are writing in a time when the full reconciliation and harmony between the Episcopal Church and monasticism, clergy and

### Chapter 7. Summary Discussion of the Sources and the Origin of the Life.

Once <term>asceticism</term> <note>The practice of self-discipline and abstention from indulgence, often for religious reasons.</note> was established, the authors themselves promoted this development through their work. They were therefore anxiously striving to eliminate or reinterpret all those features from the older period that might point to a stronger tension between original monasticism and the clergy. Nothing, however, was as concerning to the organized Church as the <term>pneumatic enthusiasm</term> <note>A form of religious fervor characterized by a belief in direct inspiration by the Holy Spirit, often involving visions or ecstasies.</note> of the earliest monasticism. The events at the Synod of Latopolis <note>A gathering of bishops in 345 or 346 AD where Pachomius was called to answer for his spiritual gifts, particularly his ability to read hearts.</note> prove this. Thus, in the presentation of the <term>Bios</term> <note>original Greek: Βίος; "Life" or biography.</note>, the visionary and ecstatic elements had to be pushed into the background. It could not be eliminated entirely, as the tradition stood too powerfully against such a move. Consequently, they sought to surround it with all sorts of reflective remarks, warning of the need for caution, thereby rendering it harmless. Everywhere, the supposedly wise caution and circumspection of Pachomius in these matters were described. They sought to transform the enthusiastic "pneumatic" into a wise pastor of souls. In doing so, they relied—whether rightly or wrongly may remain an open question—on an explicit statement by Abbot Theodore (see above) that revised earlier views. Finally, the "Greek spirit" <note>Referring to the more refined, Hellenistic sensibilities of the biographers in Alexandria or other Greek-speaking centers.</note> did not care for the many "unrefined monastery stories," which, according to their original intent, were only meant to illuminate the strictness and wisdom of Father Pachomius. Here, too, the original abundance of such tales had to be reduced, and the few items selected from the tradition had to be toned down.

The Coptic tradition appears little or not at all tainted by these considerations. It has preserved for us the fuller stream of the oldest tradition without the cuts found in G <note>The primary Greek manuscript tradition.</note>, and therefore remains of invaluable worth to us.

The entire history of the transmission of the *Life of Pachomius* is, moreover, of almost paradigmatic significance. If we understand and interpret it correctly, we see deep into the process of how a <term>Vita</term> <note>Latin for "Life"; a hagiography or biography of a saint.</note> of a religious hero arises within a pious community as its most sacred possession. Here we can eavesdrop on the process in its becoming, its individual stages, and its phases.

We look deep into the driving motives of this process when we read the large speech of Theodore already cited (M 248 ff.), which he delivered to the large monastic community gathered at Phbôu <note>The headquarters of the Pachomian monastic federation in Upper Egypt.</note> during Easter week:

> “In a multitude of places, people wear the same clothes as we do, for the glory of God and His grace have filled the whole world. But what the Lord has given us more abundantly is that He has gifted us our righteous father—he who followed entirely the life of the prophets and the service which the Lord fulfilled according to the Gospel.” “Therefore, let us all now say, my brothers: blessed be the God of our righteous father, who through his sufferings and prayers has become a guide for us to eternal life. Then all the brothers answered with one mouth and one voice: Blessed be our God-loving and righteous father, our father Pachomius, in all things and in all his works.” “Then—it is stated previously—Theodore began to tell them the life of our father Pachomius since his childhood, with the sufferings he had endured for them since the beginning when he founded the <term>Coenobitic life</term> <note>original Greek: κοινόβιον (koinobion); a communal form of monastic life where monks live together under a rule.</note>, the temptations of the demons, the way he snatched from them the souls which the Lord had entrusted to him, and the visions which the Lord had revealed to him; for he had learned these from the mouth of the saint himself and everything he had seen with his own eyes.”

Theodore was indeed the primary carrier of the oral tradition, whose...

# Book II. Investigations into the *Life of Pachomius*.

The character of the text confirms this, for it often reads like a report on the lives of Pachomius and Theodore. However, he was not the only transmitter of these stories. The opening chapters of the *Letter of Ammon* are very instructive here. A new arrival to the monastery immediately asks the Greek brothers **Elurion** and **Ausonios**—he does not yet dare to approach the leader of the "Greeks," **Theodore of Alexandria**—about the wonderful man of God, Theodore, who was the head of the monastery at that time. These brothers report on him, but in direct connection with this, they also tell of various events from the life of Pachomius (chapters 5–7), and at the conclusion, they cite their source:

> "And these things Pekusios, having heard them from Pachomius, passed them on to us after his falling asleep <note>original: *καὶ ταῦτα ἡμῖν Πεϰούσιος παρὰ Παχουμίου ἀϰούσας μετὰ τὴν ϰοίμησιν παραδέδωϰεν*. "Falling asleep" is a traditional Christian term for death.</note>."

In the literary reflections of the Greek source (G) already discussed, there is a repeated reference to the **ancient fathers** <note>original: *ἀρχαῖοι πατέρες* (archaioi pateres)</note>, the guarantors of the oral tradition.

> "This we have learned from the ancient fathers who walked with him for a long time (ch. 6)."

> "Therefore, what we have seen and heard, and what the fathers have told us, must not remain hidden from the following generation (ch. 11) <note>1) Compare again the remarks in chapters 31, 59, and 62.</note>."

Similar phrases are found in the traditions of manuscripts **M** and **A**:

> "and when the old elders heard this, they were filled with great joy and said: these holy ones are like those who are in heaven" (**M 109**).

The "old elders" here are clearly the carriers of the tradition. Likewise, source **A 648** reports that the elders had told of the miraculous appearances at the death of Pachomius. Here, as in the earliest days of Christianity, there is a circle of **Presbyters** <note>From the Greek *presbyteros*, meaning 'elder'; here referring to the respected senior monks who guarded the community's memories.</note> upon whom the tradition rests. And this knowledge of Pachomius's life was not just passed on privately from mouth to mouth. Above all, the liturgical assembly of the brothers was the place where these memories were nurtured. The sermon of Theodore, cited in detail above, was delivered on the occasion of the great Easter assembly of the entire brotherhood in **Phbôu** <note>The administrative heart and headquarters of the Pachomian monastic federation.</note>. Source **G 79** expressly records that at their meetings—where they also searched the Scriptures—the brothers often used to ask Theodore to interpret a **spiritual word** <note>2) original: *πνευματιϰὸν ῥῆμα* (pneumatikon rhēma). This likely refers not to biblical verses, but to mysterious prophetic sayings or charismatic utterances of Pachomius.</note> for them or to tell a dream of Father Pachomius. Indeed, even during Pachomius’s lifetime, it had become a custom for the saint himself to tell the brothers stories from his own life during the assemblies **after the reading of the divine scriptures** <note>original: *μετὰ τὰ εἰρημένα τῶν θείων γραφῶν*</note> (**G 6**).

Thus, the still-oral tradition gradually had to take on a fixed form. Certain related materials clustered together through association and were then retold in the same context. Eventually, people likely began to unofficially write down such longer sequences, which were organized according to indefinite viewpoints, and keep them in the monastery archives. Individual pieces that were first written down in this manner can still be specifically identified. To the pieces identified above, I add a reference to **G 276–31, M 56–67, M 553–565**. Here lies a small collection of miracle reports from the life of Pachomius. It is only strange that this collection turned out so meager. In the circles of the Pachomian brothers, more weight was placed on Pachomius’s visions and clairvoyance than on healing miracles and exorcisms. An existing collection of stories about Theodore may also have already existed in a fixed form. **M 41–55** and **A 386 ff.** seem to represent such a series, recorded on the occasion of Theodore's entry into the monastery...

### Chapter 7: Summary Discussion of the Sources and the Origin of the Life.

...to include collected **memoirs** <note>original: *ἀπομνημονεύματα* (apomnemoneumata)</note>. The section concerning the struggles of Pachomius with demons (G 11 a, 12–13, M 27–29, A 363–366, compare Theodore’s speech mentioned above) perhaps also belongs here. An important note regarding such memoir-like records of the experiences of the holy fathers has been preserved for us from an entirely different environment—that of the Scetic monks of Lower Egypt $^1$—and may be used to illustrate what has already been said. There, following the report of a miraculous experience, it says: "And I told what I had seen before the old man, and it was reported secretly to the Abbot. And so Abbot Isaac commanded that it be written down as worthy of written record in the **Book of the Wonder-working Fathers** <note>original: *τῶν σημειοφόρων πατέρων* (tōn sēmeiophorōn paterōn)</note> $^2$ for the edification and benefit of the readers." In the same way, various diaries or books may have been kept in the Pachomian monasteries, in which the individual experiences of Pachomius were preserved in writing. There may have even been differently edited collections in the individual monasteries. This might explain, for example, why several different reports concerning the founding of the order's monasteries already existed in the Greek source (G).

From that point to the composition of an actual literary **Life** <note>original: *Βίος* (Bios)</note>—a book intended for publication—is still a long road. An organizing hand had to be laid upon the confused mass of the resulting tradition. And that hand was not easily found among the masses of Pachomian monks who spoke only Coptic. It was the Greek brothers who first created this literary whole. It also seems that all sorts of resistance to such an undertaking made itself felt within the circle of monks. They guarded the memory of the master's life like a mysterious treasure entrusted to the monastery. To turn all of this into a book accessible to the whole world seemed like a profanation, like a display and boasting of the most sacred things. In the frequently mentioned speech of Theodore, he addresses such concerns in detail. The authors of the Greek source (G) must justify their undertaking (in chapter 63) with a lengthy explanation, appealing to precedents—above all to the **Life of Antony** written by Athanasius, and to the master's own writings (monastic rules and letters). Now we also understand why they emphasize so anxiously: "And even now in writing, we have written it not as a formal Scripture, but as a kind of memorial, just as letters were written by the holy bishops and fathers for our benefit" <note>original: *ϰαὶ ἄρτι δὲ γράφοντες οὐϰ ὡς γραφὴν ἀλλὰ ὡς μνήμην τινὰ ἐγράψαμεν, ὡς ϰαὶ ἐπὶ τῶν ἁγίων ἐπισϰόπων ϰαὶ πατέρων ἐπιστολαὶ ἐγράφησαν εἰς ὠφέλειαν*</note>. They want their work to be viewed not as a formal book $^3$, but merely as a memoir, comparable to the personal letters of bishops and fathers that are preserved.

With the overview of the whole—the composition of a **Life**—literary reflection and a specific "tendency" or perspective are introduced. As long as the tradition remains focused on individual details, reflection and perspective may already be present, but they can only express themselves randomly here and there and cannot achieve a unified effect. But with the composition of a formal **Life**, subjectivity begins to play its role and a specific narrative purpose begins to dominate. This is also evident in the composition of—

### Chapter 8.

## The Life of Antony and the Life of Pachomius.

Finally, one question invites closer investigation. The Greek *Life of Pachomius* <note>Vita Pachomii</note> stands in close relationship to the *Life of Antony* <note>Vita Antonii</note> written by Athanasius <note>Athanasius was the powerful Bishop of Alexandria in the 4th century</note>. Its authors undoubtedly knew this work. Already in the introduction <note>prooemium</note> of the Greek text (G), there is a direct reference to the "most holy Archbishop Athanasius, who wrote the life of Antony" $^1$. In section G 63, the undertaking is justified by a reference to the **Life of the blessed Antony [written] for the monks and brothers in foreign lands who requested this of the most holy Father Athanasius.** The question arises: to what extent did this famous work of Athanasius, with its spirit and intent, also influence the portrayal of the Life of Pachomius?

Traces of this influence can be recognized at first glance. It shows itself particularly clearly in the treatment of the question of miracles and visions. We read in G 30 (compare M 66, A 566): **"And many other healings the Lord performed through him . . . but if again, when he prayed for someone's health, the Lord did not grant the request, he was neither surprised nor grieved as if he had not been heard . . . and he himself prayed, saying: 'Thy will be done, and not mine.'"** In the *Life of Antony* (chapter 56) it says: **"And many times and in many things the Lord heard him, and being heard he did not boast, nor being not heard did he grumble; but he always gave thanks to the Lord himself."** The parallel in the discussions about Pachomius’s visions, which section G 32 attributes to Pachomius himself, is even clearer. I recall once more the connection already outlined above: visions are given by God alone; they should not be demanded by the sinner. The true and genuine <term>vision</term> <note>original: *ὅραμα* (horama)</note> is the sight of a good man. **"Likewise, let us also consider it a great thing to see the thoughts of souls with discernment, as in the case of Elisha and Gehazi <note>A reference to the biblical story in 2 Kings 5 where the prophet Elisha perceives the hidden actions of his servant Gehazi</note>. For when the Lord who is in them . . . reveals [it] to them, they have the gift of <term>discernment</term> <note>original: *διορατικός* (dioratikos), the spiritual ability to perceive hidden or future truths</note>."** But the true "seeing" is that described in Psalm 16:8: **"one is not judged for not seeing hidden things; but one is judged if one possesses the likeness of those... condemned in the Psalm"** (Psalm 54:8) $^2$. And Antony expresses himself quite similarly in Athanasius’s work (chapter 34): **"One should not <insert>need to</insert> practice <term>asceticism</term> <note>spiritual discipline and self-denial</note> and labor for these things [foreknowledge], but in order that we may please God by living well. And one must pray not so that we may have foreknowledge."** But if we want to have <term>foreknowledge</term> <note>original: *πρόγνωσις* (prognosis)</note>, let us purify our minds. **"For I believe that a soul being pure . . . is able, having become discerning, to see more and further than the demons, having the Lord who reveals [things] to it. Such was that of Elisha, seeing the things concerning Gehazi."** Here, not only is the train of thought parallel, but there is also a literal overlap (compare the mention of the example of Elisha and its surrounding context).

<header>Chapter 8. The Lives of Antony and Pachomius. 259</header>

In the Greek source G 2 (see also the parallel accounts), it is emphasized regarding Pachomius that the demons did not pursue him during his youth because they possessed a <term>foreknowledge <note>original Greek: πρόγνωσις (prognōsis)</note></term> of his later deeds; rather, they had already seen his moral goodness even then. **"Therefore, guessing <note>1</note> whether the boy would later be god-fearing . . . they did not pursue me."** <note>original Greek: διὰ τοῦτο στοχασάμενοι μὴ ἆρα μετὰ ταῦτα ὁ παῖς ἔσται θεοσεβής . . . ἐδίωξαν με</note> Likewise, in chapters 31–34 of the *Life of Antony*, Antony explicitly denies the demons the gift of <term>foreknowledge</term>. He states that they cannot know anything about things that have not yet happened. **"For they know nothing of themselves, but like thieves, what they see among others, they report . . . and they are guessers <note>original Greek: στοχασταί (stochastai)</note> rather than those with foreknowledge."** — Note the use of the keyword "guessers." Furthermore, where G 2 (and its parallels) says: **"For God made man upright,"** <note>original Greek: ὁ γὰρ θεὸς ἐποίησεν τὸν ἄνθρωπον εὐθῆ</note> we read in the *Life of Antony*, chapter 20: **"But [human nature] has become very good and upright."** <note>original Greek: γέγονε δὲ (die Physis der Menschen) καλὴ καὶ εὐθὴς λίαν</note>

These are all undeniable points of contact between the two biographies. Words and thoughts that Athanasius puts into the mouth of his hero Antony appear in the Greek text as the personal property of Pachomius. And we are dealing here with more than just isolated similarities; rather, it is the adoption of coherent fundamental perspectives. It has recently been excellently demonstrated <note>2</note> how Athanasius, through his *Life of Antony*, consistently follows a specific agenda: he intended to use it to purify and clarify the "lower" <term>pneumatics <note>German: Pneumatik; refers to a form of spirituality focused on the "pneuma" or spirit, often involving visions and miracles</note></term> prevailing among average monks—where all weight was placed on miracles, the struggles of the pious against demons, visions, and miraculous foreknowledge—and to lead them toward a higher spiritual ideal of the godly life. It also emerges clearly as an agenda of the *Life* and its structure that it strives above all to portray its hero as a devoted follower of the Church, who endeavors to place all his strength in its service.

And now we see quite clearly that these are roughly the same tendencies that emerge everywhere in the Greek text (G) where the reflective "we" speaks up in the *Life*. We can thus understand the remarkable agreement that appears here and there in the utterances of Antony on one hand and Pachomius on the other. Even the external literary technique was learned from Athanasius. Here, too, we encounter long inserted speeches, though not to the same extent as in the *Life of Antony* <note>3</note>. In the brothers who recorded the life of Pachomius, the spirit and agenda of Athanasius were at work, and they did not merely model themselves superficially on the work known to them.

Only one difference must be emphasized. In our case, the original popular tradition has not been suppressed, rendered unrecognizable, or worn down to the same degree as in the *Life of Antony*. I would judge that we gain about as much or as little historical insight into the hero's life from the latter as we do from the Fourth Gospel <note>The Gospel of John, often seen as more theological than biographical</note> for the life of Jesus. On the other hand, in the transmission of the *Life of Pachomius*, the comparison with the Synoptic literature <note>The Gospels of Matthew, Mark, and Luke, which share a similar "view" and are often considered more historically descriptive</note> has repeatedly suggested itself to us, whether explicitly or implicitly.

There is indeed a difference here. This is partly due to the nature of the transmitted material. Athanasius simply—

<header>Book II. Investigations into the *Life of Pachomius*.</header>

...yet possessed no intimate connection with the life of his hero. He had seen him once or twice in passing, but had not lived with him. It is likely correct that he possessed no more direct information about Antony’s life than what he had been able to hear narrated from time to time, and of tangible material, only an <term>aretalogy <note>a collection of stories celebrating the miraculous deeds and virtues of a hero or divinity</note></term>, a collection of miracle stories. With great skill, he managed to compensate for this significant lack, ingeniously interpreting a sense of development into the course of his hero's life. Through speeches—which make up about half of the entire content—he placed his own new spiritual ideal into Antony's mouth. He even plundered a biography of Pythagoras and adorned his hero with shimmering borrowed feathers. The effect was grand and unique. But it is no longer Antony himself who wanders through the inhabited world in his <note>original Greek: Βίος (Bios), meaning "Life" or biography</note>.

In contrast, the Greek brothers to whom we owe the origin of the source known as "G" stood in the very center of the life and traditions of the Pachomian community. This explains the overwhelming abundance of authentic tradition that the *Life* of Pachomius possesses in contrast to that of Antony. They had a foundation of popular folk tradition behind them that was so powerful that it even regained control over the written *Life*, despite its later edits and distortions. Accordingly, they were bound to their material in a completely different way; they changed and retouched things only tentatively and did not dare to invent freely. They were certainly much lesser minds than the Archbishop of Alexandria <note>referring to Athanasius, the traditional author of the Life of Antony</note>. They did not even dare to place themselves alongside him, wanting only to write a <note>original Greek: μνήμη (mnēmē), a "memorial" or "remembrance"</note> and not a pretentious <note>original Greek: γραφή (graphē), a formal "writing" or "treatise"</note>. We should be glad that the tradition followed this path here. A precise and accurate image of Abbot Antony—the rough hermit and lonely desert wanderer—is irretrievably lost to us. However, we have been granted a very direct insight into the life and work of Pachomius and the beginnings of <term>cenobitic monasticism <note>a communal form of monastic life where monks live together, as opposed to the solitary life of a hermit</note></term>.

<summary>The author argues that while the *Life of Antony* is a literary masterpiece by Athanasius, it is historically unreliable compared to the *Life of Pachomius*, which remains rooted in authentic community tradition. This makes the Pachomian sources more valuable for understanding the early development of communal monastic life.</summary>

## Appendix I.

### I. Christological-Dogmatic Corrections.

As an appendix, we may finally point to a widespread corruption in our <term>manuscript tradition <note>the history of how a text was copied and passed down through the centuries</note></term> that affects all of our texts. This is related to another set of facts important for understanding the character of the *Life of Pachomius*. When one reads through the *Life*—specifically in the version known as "G," which strangely has been least affected by later revisions—one is repeatedly astonished by how little a role <term>Christology <note>theological study of the person and work of Jesus Christ</note></term> and faith in Christ play in it, let alone "Christ-mysticism." Instead, a simple faith in God the Father dominates the text. I will highlight only the most significant observations:

With very few exceptions, all the visions experienced by Pachomius and his successor, Theodore, are visions of God, not visions of Christ. God’s voice speaks to Pachomius through an angel; God’s form, God upon His throne, appears to him; the fear of God or His mercy descends upon him, and so on ¹). Furthermore, all prayers in the *Life of Pachomius* are addressed to God, not to Christ. Proof of this will be provided by the textual criticism of the manuscript tradition following below; I will only note in advance that I have examined every single passage where a prayer to Christ appears in any witness.

Indeed, even praying "in the name of Jesus" is at the very least extraordinarily rare, and even in those instances, the various manuscripts disagree. It almost seems as though an appeal to the saints, and especially to the <term>intercession <note>prayer on behalf of another</note></term> of "Father Pachomius," has here and there taken its place ²). Otherwise, the "Christ-mysticism" that is so common in later monasticism is entirely absent. The monks have the "commandment of God," they stand in the "fear of God"—such phrases are infinitely more frequent than any thought of Christ. Even when looking toward the afterlife, Christ is occasionally forgotten, it seems. One thinks of beholding God, of beholding the saints; only later <term>glosses <note>marginal or interlinear notes added by later scribes</note></term> introduced the thought of Christ. Here and there, one finds mention of the Crucified One and allusions to the Cross ³). Otherwise,

A strange fantasy in A 464 and M 125 may be noted here: according to this, only the entirely pure souls behold God Himself in His glory in the afterlife. The less worthy are meant to behold the <note>original: "Sohn Gottes in seiner Menschlichkeit, die der Gottheit geeinigt ist"</note> "Son of God in his humanity, which is united to the divinity." **Book II. Investigations into the *Life of Pachomius*.**

This too is characteristic: Christ is mentioned only where his words are quoted and where other New Testament citations and reminiscences appear ¹). God the Creator and Lord of all creatures, God the Judge, who fills souls with both fear and mercy, is the figure who stands before the eyes of the authors of the *Life*, as well as the ancient <term>Pachomian monks <note>the followers of Pachomius, who established the first communal monasteries in Egypt</note></term> in general.

If this is the case, one can postulate from the outset that the tradition of the *Life of Pachomius* likely retouched and suppressed the original perspective at this point. Egypt became the classic land of heightened <term>Christology <note>the theological study of the nature and role of Jesus Christ</note></term>, of <term>Monophysitism <note>the doctrine that Christ has a single, divine nature rather than two distinct natures (human and divine)</note></term>, and of exclusive <term>Christolatry <note>the specific worship of Christ, sometimes emphasizing his divinity over the Father</note></term>. Later monasticism was the champion in all of these developments. The native <term>Coptic liturgies <note>the structured public worship services of the Egyptian Church</note></term> distinguish themselves from all other liturgies by the fact that almost all of their prayers become prayers to Christ.

The actual state of the evidence is reflected in our sources. They are all corrupted in this direction—the <term>Memphitic tradition <note>manuscripts written in the dialect of Coptic used in Lower Egypt</note></term> most of all, the Arabic tradition somewhat less, and the Greek tradition the least. Furthermore, comparison reveals how consistent the theological atmosphere was in the original Pachomian tradition in this regard.

A difficulty arises in the textual comparison because the title **Lord** <note>original: <term>κύριος</term></note> can, in the *Life of Pachomius*, naturally refer to both God ²) and Christ. In many cases where our better texts have a simple "Lord," perhaps in place of "Lord Jesus Christ," the decision as to whether a shift in the sense mentioned above has occurred remains uncertain at first. However, such a conclusion can then often be reached based on the surrounding context of the text.

In the following, I arrange the observations so that I place the witness that is most productive for our investigation in the first position, namely **M** <note>the Memphitic Coptic manuscript</note>. In this list, I also include the relatively rare cases in which **M** happens to coincide with **A** <note>the Arabic manuscript</note> or **G** <note>the Greek manuscript</note> in such a change. Then the changes in **A** will be noted, followed by those in **G** (and **P**).

2. **M 6** = **A 343** (Prayer of Pachomius before he even meets Christians): My Lord Jesus Christ, Your will be done. **G** > <note>The symbol > indicates the text is missing in this version.</note> But **T 316**: My Lord, your will be done.

2) The fact that the simple title **Lord** <note>original: <term>κύριος</term></note> in the *Life* often refers to God can be explicitly proven. **G 4** **meditation on the words of God** <note>original: <term>μελετὴν λόγων θεοῦ</term></note> = **M 12** "word of the Lord." — **M 19 f. # Appendix I. Christological-Dogmatic Corrections.

20. M 184 (Vision concerning <term>heretics<note>Those holding beliefs contrary to established church doctrine</note></term> and <term>schismatics<note>Those who split from the main church over authority or practice rather than doctrine</note></term>): "Those who let go of the hand of the brothers are the bishops who are in the orthodox faith of Christ and who have communion with the heretics" (followed by Ephesians 4:13). A 500: "the bishops who have the orthodox faith and stand in communion with the schismatics." In G 65, the entire vision is greatly shortened. At the conclusion of the vision, M 185 speaks of the "eternal life of the Lord Jesus." A 501 does not include this sentence, providing instead a discussion on free will.

21. M 191 (Speech of <term>Pachomius<note>Saint Pachomius the Great (c. 292–348 AD), the founder of Christian communal monasticism</note></term> on the relationship between <term>Anchorites<note>Hermits living in isolation</note></term> and <term>Coenobites<note>Monks living in a community</note></term>, G 7): "For the reward for his fasts, prayers, and deeds, which the Coenobite has done for us out of love for him in the **name of Christ**, as well as out of fear toward him, will be multiplied many times by Christ in the future life and in his kingdom." A 508: "For he will receive the reward of his deeds and his prayers in the **name of the Lord** and **his fear** and receive numerous rewards in the other world."

22. M 194 "When he had asked them about the state of the holy catholic church of Christ." A 510 omits the sentence, and it is missing in G. However, compare the parallel passages in G 73: "how the church is" <note>original Greek: πῶς ἡ ἐκκλησία</note>. K 169: "what is the church doing" (and afterward twice more: church, catholic church). G 18 b = M 34 = A 372: "church of God" <note>original Greek: ἐκκλησία τοῦ θεοῦ</note>. Also M 168 (Prayer for the catholic church)¹).

23. M 204 (Prayer of Pachomius): "my Lord Jesus," A 517 "my Lord." Immediately preceding this in A is the sentence "I have very often satisfied God." Afterward in M and A, God is mentioned: "so that God may see your humility and your suffering," "fear of the Lord."

24. M 207 (Pachomius's prayer for a brother who had sinned): "Lord God, Creator of all things, Father of our Lord Jesus Christ." The story is either parallel with A 533 ff. or 477 ff. In both places, no such prayer is found.

25. M 212 (Healing of a <term>demoniac<note>A person believed to be possessed by an evil spirit</note></term>):
> "Then our father stretched out his hands, prayed to the Lord, and said: I implore You, my Lord Jesus Christ . . . O God, you who love mankind, that You heal him from this evil demon. And to You alone belongs the glory and the honor and the power with Your all-good Father and Your Holy Spirit, now and always and unto all eternity. Amen. And when he had said the Amen, he sealed the person in the name of the Father, the Son, and the Holy Spirit; he rebuked <note>original Greek: ἐπετίμησεν</note> the evil spirit, which immediately departed from the person, and he was healed through the power of Christ and the prayers of our father Pachomius."

— A 561: "Father Pachomius spread out his hands and rebuked <note>original Greek: ἐπετίμησεν</note> the demon, which left the person immediately." (Previously, according to both sources M 211 = A 560, Pachomius asks the demon who gave him power over the sick man, and at the answer "the Crucified," he demands that the demon tell him the number of nails with which He was crucified.)

26. M 213 (during a second exorcism): "He asked Christ for the brother." A 561: "He asked the Lord" (cf. further below "he was healed in the name of the Lord") and in another healing "the healing that God gives them," though later "servants of Christ."

### 2. Alterations in A <note>The Arabic version of the manuscript</note> ²).

29. A 363 "God (M 27 the Lord) knows that I said until this day: I am older than You. But now I will call You not only my father, but my master because of the strength of Your faith in the Christ" (M: in the Lord).

30. A 392 (Pachomius to Theodore): "Do not weep, my son; the one to whom you have taken refuge is the Lord J. Chr." — M 45: "Do not weep, my son, for I am the servant of Your Father (i.e., God)."

33. Especially significant are the variants of A in the large prayer of intercession by Pachomius, which originates from the church liturgy (M 173—178, A 486—491). In M, this prayer characteristically begins with an invocation of God: "God, Lord, Creator of all things, God highly praised." According to A 487 as well, the prayer is addressed to God: "O Lord God, Master (<term>master</term><note>original Greek: "despota"</note>) of all things, highly praised . . ." But then in A 188 we find the phrases: "through the intercession of Your beloved Son J. Chr." In the mention of the widows it says: "the promise which they have made to Your only-begotten Son," and finally at the conclusion of this part of the prayer: "Lord God, highly praised, God of glory, protect us through the blood of Your only-begotten Son . . . through your <term>Logos<note>The "Word" or second person of the Trinity, Jesus Christ</note></term>, who became incarnate for our salvation and through your Holy Spirit." Instead of all these phrases, which are unheard of in the *Life of Pachomius*, we find in M only the sentence: "through Your mercy, (O God), who loves mankind!"

34. A 496 — "That is my will; I will endure by praying for them to the Lord J. Chr." Missing in M.

### Appendix II.

#### **Invasion of a Philosophical-Mystical Linguistic Usage into the Sources.**

It is noteworthy and interesting to see how a semi-philosophical and dogmatically reflective language gradually penetrates the various sources of the Life of Pachomius—a language that was certainly entirely foreign to the original, Coptic-speaking circle of Pachomian monks.

Here, G again provides some interesting contributions in which it stands alone. I count among these especially some passages where <term>gnosis</term> <note>Gnosis: a Greek term for "knowledge," often implying a deep, spiritual, or mystical understanding.</note> is strongly emphasized. G 14: <term>and before he had perfect knowledge, he seemed to have such perfect faith from the Lord as to openly tread upon serpents and scorpions.</term> <note>original Greek: "kai pro tou autou tēn teleian gnōsin echein, para tou kyriou toiautēn edokei teleian pistin echein tou patein epanō opheōn kai skorpiōn phanerōs."</note> — <term>and he did not yet do these things in the perfection of knowledge.</term> <note>original Greek: "kai oupō en teleiotēti tēs gnōseōs epoiei tauta."</note> ³) It is said of Theodore <note>Theodore (c. 314–368 AD) was the favorite disciple of Pachomius and eventually his successor as head of the monasteries.</note> that he his...

---

1) For comparison, I point to the end of the special source of A (see above, p. 242) 650. Here it is described how Pachomius is received in heaven by the apostles, prophets, martyrs, etc., and finally by the Lord of the Angels and the God of the Saints. One also misses the mention of Jesus here.

2) Prayers to God are also to be noted for the second half of G. G 81, the prayer of Horsisi <note>Horsisi (c. 305–390 AD) was another early leader of the Pachomian monastic order.</note> (A 667: "Lord, God, Creator of all creatures"). G 85: <term>Lord, the God of glory</term> <note>original Greek: "kyrie ho theos tēs doxēs"</note> (compare the phrasing in the chapter before). — Theodore heals the sick in God’s power: <term>he prayed for the will of God and what was beneficial to happen.</term> <note>original Greek: "ēucheto to thelēma tou theou kai to sympheron genesthai."</note> — G 85 b, compare A 675: "Lord, fulfill Your will in the name of the prayers of our father Pachomius"; compare G: <term>but he did these things in the memory of the father who raised him, Abba Pachomius.</term> <note>original Greek: "tauta de epoiei tē mnēmē tou anatrepsantos auton patros tou Abba Pachōmiou."</note> Compare also G 84: <term>insofar as we sought God, so much more His goodness appeared, sweetening our souls</term> <note>original Greek: "kathoson ezētoumen ton theon, tosouton hē chrēstotēs autou mallon ephaineto glykainousa tas psychas hēmōn."</note> (similar to A 672).

3) By <term>pistis</term> <note>Pistis: Greek for "faith."</note> is meant here the bestowed power to work miracles; Pachomius only receives perfect <term>gnosis</term> with the completion of his monastic state.

### Appendix II. The Penetration of Philosophical-Mystical Terminology into the Sources. 269

[He] might see [his] mother <note>original Greek: "meta tēn tosautēn gnōsin" — after such great knowledge</note>¹) G 26. In the great sermon of Pachomius, it says in chapter 36 (at the end) regarding the 15th chapter of the First Epistle to the Corinthians: <term>and speaking about the resurrection, Paul said certain things which we need to perceive with true knowledge</term> <note>original Greek: "kai peri anastaseōs lalōn Paulos tina eirēken, haper chreian echomen met' epignōseōs alēthinēs noein"</note>²). <term>But one word of his is enough: if the dead are not raised, neither has Christ been raised.</term> <note>original Greek: "all' arkei eis logos autou: ei nekroi ouk egeirontai, oude Christos egēgertai"</note> In the following section (beginning of chapter 37), the <term>spiritual resurrection</term> <note>original Greek: "pneumatikē anastasis"</note> is discussed. In chapter 61, the brothers are exhorted by Pachomius that if they fall into ecstatic states, they should <term>announce this quickly to the one who possesses knowledge</term> <note>original Greek: "anaggeilai touto tacheōs tō echonti tēn gnōsin"</note> (here referring to the gift of <term>discernment</term> <note>original Greek: "diakrisis" — the ability to distinguish between divine and demonic spirits</note>) <term>before the passion becomes chronic.</term> Of Horsisios <note>A successor to Pachomius as leader of the monastic koinonia.</note>, it is judged in chapter 76: <term>that even if he had not yet received much knowledge of God, yet he spoke a parable to them</term> (note the contrast between <term>knowledge</term> and <term>parable</term>) <term>and God worked through it.</term> Horsisios himself remarks: <term>we know that through the scriptures (see above) our father established us in perfect knowledge.</term> In the speech of Theodore <note>Another key disciple and eventual leader of the Pachomian order.</note>³) chapter 87, the following sentence is found: <term>And God the Word appeared to us, having been revealed in human form, and saved us, granting us the knowledge of faith</term>⁴).

If we can again identify these observations as proof of the secondary and reflective character of the Greek Biography (G), then such echoes can be detected even more strongly in the sources N P (G¹) <note>These represent different manuscript families or versions of the Vita.</note>. I will only cite two striking passages here. First, the explanations in N 52 (compare P 12): one of the brothers asked him: why is it that before the onset of a troubling demon, while we possess a <term>healthy rational disposition</term> <note>original Greek: "sōon echontes to tēs dianoias phronēma"</note>, we <term>philosophize</term> <note>original Greek: "philosophoumen"</note> about self-control, humility, and other virtues; but when the time comes to demonstrate those <term>philosophical principles</term> through action—such as patience in a moment of anger—we lack the strength? Pachomius answers: because we do not perfectly pursue <term>virtue</term> (P [the manuscript P] says <term>practical virtue</term>!), for this reason we do not understand the entire <term>habit and entanglement</term> <note>original Greek: "hexin te kai metemplokēn"</note> of the demons, so as to be able to repel the presence of the one troubling us through the <term>sharper contemplative power of the soul</term> <note>original Greek: "oxutera tē theōrētikē dunamei tēs psuchēs"</note>... therefore it is necessary, every day and hour, to pour the <term>fear of God</term> like oil into the <term>contemplative part of the soul</term> <note>original Greek: "theōrētikō merei tēs psuchēs"</note>; for this fear is the <term>maker of practice</term> <note>original Greek: "praktikēs pōiētikos"</note> and serves as a <term>lamp for the contemplation of what is suggested to us</term>. It makes our <term>mind</term> <note>original Greek: "noun"</note> unshakable and does not allow it to be snatched away toward anger or wrath... or any other of the passions that leverage us toward vice. Making the soul <term>contemplative and uplifted toward the region of the incorporeal</term> <note>original Greek: "theōrētikon te kai metarsion pros tēn tōn asōmatōn chōran"</note>, it encourages one to despise the work of such demons and prepares one to <term>trample</term> (as it is written in P) <term>upon serpents and scorpions and over all the power of the enemy.</term>

---
1) This refers to the entry into Pachomius's monastic order.
2) The term <term>epignosis</term> (higher knowledge) refers here and in other mentioned passages to (allegorical) scriptural interpretation. This passage is interesting because it shows that one read the explanations of 1 Corinthians 15 with some hesitation.
3) See the characterization of Theodore in chapter 50: <term>for the word of God set him on fire and established him in thinking on things above</term> (compare G 79: <term>whom the Lord set on fire [instead of "tested"] through Saint Pachomius in the spirit</term>).
4) In this context, I would also point out some remarkable reflections on <term>free will</term> and the original "goods" of human nature, which we encounter in our sources, though not in G alone. Compare G 17 = A 374. — G 2 = M 5 = A 342 (<term>for God made man upright</term> <note>original Greek: "ho gar theos epoiēsen ton anthrōpon euthe"</note>, see above regarding the connection between this passage and the Life of Anthony). Particularly detailed considerations of this kind are found in A 512, M 197, and again particularly striking ones in A 402 f. Here it is stated that every human being possesses conscience, free will, discernment, and a certain knowledge. When a person follows their conscience, the Holy Spirit descends upon them like a vessel set in gold. When the Holy Spirit descends into a person in this way, he makes the "members" of the soul manifest and allows the conscience to rise high. Those who do not possess the Spirit of God have these "members" within them—I mean their conscience and their reason—but they are not visible. For the idea of the "members of the soul," compare the homilies of "Macarius" I 4 and 6. See also A 502 for a polemic against the <term>doctrine of predestination</term>.

It highlights how these later Greek texts transformed simple monastic stories into sophisticated theological reflections on the soul and free will.</summary>

## Book II. Investigations into the *Life of Pachomius*.

I place a second passage alongside it, P 20 = N 32¹). Pachomius <note>The 4th-century Egyptian founder of cenobitic (communal) monasticism.</note> warns that one should always keep the eternal punishments of judgment before one's eyes: <term>through which the intellect comes to perception and the soul trembles and weeps, and it makes the soul contemplative, making it soar from earthly things toward God...</term> <note>original Greek: "di' hōn eis aisthēsin ho nous erchetai kai phrittetai men dakryousa hē psychē kai theōrētikēn de katergazetai autēn, apo tōn gēiinōn ameteōron kataskeuazei autēn pros ton theon..."</note> <term>let the soul, therefore, practice philosophy</term> ²) <note>original: "philosopheitō" — here referring to the monastic life as the "true philosophy" or spiritual discipline</note> <term>daily toward the densest body...</term> <note>original: "pros to pachytaton sōma"</note> <term>for instead of ten thousand teachers, the Word of God "dwelling in you more abundantly"</term> (absent in N), <term>teaches you and makes you wise "rather in the knowledge of Himself"</term> (absent in N).

These last two cited passages are especially interesting because of their language. The use of the term <term>to practice philosophy</term> <note>Greek: "philosophein"</note> with reference to monastic asceticism; the distinction between <term>practical</term> and <term>contemplative virtue</term> <note>Greek: "praktikē" and "theōrētikē aretē"</note>; phrases such as <term>contemplative power</term>, <term>the contemplative part of the soul</term>, <term>contemplative and uplifted</term>; the distinction between <term>intellect</term> <note>Greek: "nous"</note>, <term>soul</term>, and the <term>densest body</term>; the concept of a <term>perception of the intellect</term>; and the idea of the indwelling of the divine <term>Logos</term> — and here again the mention of <term>Gnosis</term> <note>spiritual knowledge</note> — all of this reminds anyone familiar with the development of monastic language and mysticism of the milieu and surroundings of someone like Evagrius <note>Evagrius Ponticus (345–399 AD), a monk whose writings synthesized Christian theology with Neoplatonic philosophy</note>. It is clear, in any case, that the monks of the Pachomian monasteries did not speak this way or tell stories of their founding father in such terms. Indeed, we find almost none of these phrases (aside from the emphasis on <term>Gnosis</term>) in the accounts of Pachomius's life drafted by the Greek monks and students of Theodore <note>Pachomius's successor</note>.

This leads us finally to a conjecture regarding the origin of the secondary sources P, N, and G ³. I suspect that their home is already in Alexandria. We know that Theophilus of Alexandria (died 384 AD) had already settled a colony of Pachomian monks in Canopus ³). It is here in Alexandria that those later additions to the *Life of Pachomius* may have originated. It can be proven that the two regulations regarding prayers and prayer times, as they appear in N 5 and its parallels, correspond approximately to those that Jerome <note>The Latin Church Father Hieronymus</note> found in the Rule of the Order which he translated. This Rule, however, was sent to him along with other writings of Pachomius from the monastery of Canopus. Here, far from the original environment of Pachomius, the legend may have arisen of the angel who handed Pachomius the written monastic rule in a <term>cave</term> <note>Greek: "spēlaion"</note>. Here, the author of the *Lausiac History* ⁴) may have become acquainted with it and, based on a report such as the one in N 1–8, shaped his remarks on the Pachomian monasteries in his chapters 31–32. Indeed, in the middle of his report in chapter 32, he mentions that he met one of these Pachomian brothers in Alexandria. Here also may have originated the baroque legend which tells how Pachomius could not communicate with a <term>Roman</term> <note>Greek: "Rōmaios"</note> who had come to him, and how he was enabled by a "heavenly letter" sent down to him to converse with the Roman in his own language (N 44 f.). The priest Silvanus, who asked Jerome to translate the Greek rule into Latin, speaks of the large number of Latins who were present above all (though he also mentions the Thebaid) <term>in the monastery of Metanoia, which was changed from [the name] Canopus into "repentance" by a happy conversion of name</term> ⁵).

---

1) I provide the text here according to source P; source N lacks the beginning. However, P is largely confirmed by the Syriac version (Nau 453).
2) Here the parallel with source N begins.
3) Ladeuze, work cited, p. 202.
4) See my article on the composition of the *Lausiac History* <note>A collection of biographies of early desert monks by Palladius</note>.
5) Migne, *Latin Patrology* Vol. XXIII, column 65 f. <note>original Latin: "in monasterio Metanoae, quod de Canopo in poenitentiam felici nominis conversione mutatum est"</note>

These later versions influenced major historical works like Palladius's Lausiac History and Jerome's Latin translations.</summary>

<header>Appendix III. On the Chronology of Pachomius.</header>

## Appendix III.

### On the Chronology of Pachomius.

In this investigation, I initially assume that Ladeuze <note>Paulin Ladeuze (1870–1940), a theologian who wrote a definitive study on Pachomian monasticism.</note> (p. 321 ff.) succeeded in correctly establishing the following dates: the death of Theodore, Pachomius’s successor, in 368; Theodore’s assumption of office (alongside Horsisios) in 350/51; and the death of Pachomius on May 14, 346.

I seek to carry the investigation a bit further from this point. We must start with the passage M 265 <note>References like M, G, and A refer to different manuscript traditions of the "Life of Pachomius" (M for certain fragments, G for Greek, A for Arabic).</note>, according to which Theodore declares that he was in office for 18 years (350–368) and had lived as a monk under Pachomius for 18 years. It is surprising why Ladeuze (240) places so little weight on the second of these statements and passes over it so quickly in favor of other inferior notes, given that the first statement has been so excellently confirmed. I believe that this tradition, too, can be proven to be authentic.

Regarding Theodore’s life in Pachomius’s monastery, the various branches of tradition provide the following specific figures. According to the *Letter of Ammon* 5, Theodore was 22 years old when he shared that remarkable ecstatic experience with Pachomius, which we have frequently referred to above as the vision in the assembly room of Phbow <note>The administrative headquarters of the Pachomian monastic federation.</note> (G 56, M 104 ff., A 440 ff.). At that time, Theodore would have been in the monastery for 8 (or 9) years, since according to firmly consistent tradition, he entered the monastery at about 14 years of age (G 25, A 392; Ammon 5 says 13 years)¹). Now, immediately following this scene in our reports is the story that Theodore, out of excessive rigor against Pachomius (regarding monks chatting in the bakery of Tabennisi <note>The first monastery founded by Pachomius.</note>), raised his hand against him in anger. For this, he was punished by Pachomius and, likely in connection with this, was removed from his independent position in Tabennisi and sent to Phbow. Here he worked under the direct supervision of Pachomius as his "right hand" in managing the entire federation. We then learn from the reports A 492 = M 153 that Theodore—before he allowed himself to be led by ambition to strive for the leadership of all the monasteries during an illness of Pachomius—had worked for **seven years** under Pachomius. Following his lapse, he was sentenced by Pachomius to penance in solitude. This time, G 69 provides the duration of this penance: it lasted **two years**²). At the end of this period of penance occurred Theodore's journey to Alexandria, which he made with Zacchaeus (G 70 c + 73 = M 168 f. = A 642 f. + 590 f.). This journey took place during the events of Latopolis, which Pachomius reported to Theodore upon his return, according to G 73. Finally, the reliable old report A 595 explicitly tells us that in "the same year," while the brothers were once again preparing for a journey to Alexandria, Pachomius definitely predicted to Theodore that the end of his life...

---

1) Only M 44 f. gives 20 years (14 + 6). With this singularity of M, its other statement related to this age calculation also collapses: that Theodore was 33 years old when Pachomius made him a <term>catechist</term> <note>A teacher of the faith; a "katechētēs" in the monastery was responsible for the spiritual instruction of the monks.</note> (M 100). The story itself does not agree with this age, as it shows the brothers taking offense at the extraordinary youth of the new catechist. Ladeuze (240) placed far too much weight on this figure.

2) A 591 admittedly gives a penance period for Theodore of 7 years (including the journey to Alexandria). There must be an error in the transmission here.

The author uses internal evidence to argue that Theodore entered the monastery as a young teen and served in various leadership and penitential roles before Pachomius's death.</summary>

had arrived, and immediately following this is the account of the death of Pachomius <note>Saint Pachomius the Great, the founder of Christian cenobitic (communal) monasticism.</note> at Easter in 346. We may therefore assume approximately one more year between the incident at Latopolis <note>A city in Upper Egypt, modern Esna, where a council was held to investigate Pachomius.</note> and the end of Pachomius's life.

We thus obtain the following partial figures for Theodore’s stay in the Pachomian monastery: until the occurrence of the vision in Pibohu <note>Also known as Phbow, the headquarters of the Pachomian monastic federation.</note>, 8 years (during which Theodore was in Tabennisi); Theodore under the leadership of Pachomius in Pibohu, 7 years; Theodore’s rebellion and subsequent penance, 2 years; and from then until the death of Pachomius, 1 year. — In other words, the partial figures 8 + 7 + 2 + 1 = 18 exactly confirm the total sum given in manuscript M 256 for Theodore’s life under Pachomius. Thus, all the data are confirmed as reliable.

If Pachomius died at Easter 346, then Theodore’s entry into the monastery occurred around 328¹). Now, according to manuscript A 323, Theodore entered the community five years after the founding of the monastery in Tabennisi. This would yield approximately the year 323 as the founding year of the Pachomian monastery. If the report from manuscript A T. (see above, p. 220) is reliable—that Pachomius had been a monk for 39 years, thus since approximately 307/8—there remains a large period of his life about which we know very little. One must account for those approximately 16 years by looking at Pachomius’s stay in Schenesit <note>A village in Upper Egypt where Pachomius first lived as a hermit after his military service.</note>, his period of instruction under Palaimon <note>An elder hermit who served as Pachomius's first spiritual mentor.</note>, and the time of his shared life with his brother. For the actual founding of the monastery is likely to be dated only after the death of his brother, roughly at the point where the appearance of Pachomius’s specifically named disciples (manuscript G 16 and parallels) is reported. For the stay of Pachomius in Schenesit, manuscript A gives 3 years; for a portion of the time he remained with Palaimon (until the recurrence of the baptismal vision), it again gives 3 years (manuscript 352 M gives 4 years). There we already have 6–7 years for this period. It should not be difficult to account for the remaining 9 years within this timeframe.

1) In our sources, immediately before Theodore’s entry into Tabennisi, a visit by Athanasios <note>Athanasius the Great, the Bishop of Alexandria and a major figure in 4th-century Christianity.</note> to Southern Egypt is reported (cf. Pachomius’s life is first followed to a certain conclusion before the second main hero <note>Referring to Theodore.</note> enters the narrative.

### Book III.

# Studies on Evagrius.

### Introduction.

Through the new publications by Frankenberg $^1$) and Gressmann $^2$), the figure of Evagrius—the fascinating monk of the Scetic desert <note>The Scetis, or Wadi El Natrun in Egypt, was one of the three great centers of early Christian monasticism.</note> whom we may call the pioneer of monastic mysticism—has become more tangible and clear to us. However, a comprehensive treatment of all the currently available material has been lacking until now $^3$); the present investigation intends to make a beginning in this regard.

The following writings of Evagrius are used primarily in this study:

1. The *Chapters on Practice* addressed to Anatolius <note>original Latin: *capita practica ad Anatolium*; this work outlines the ascetic struggle against the "eight thoughts" or vices.</note>. The Greek text in Migne <note>Patrologia Graeca (PG) 40, columns 1219–1251. Migne is a massive 19th-century collection of writings by the Church Fathers.</note> 40, 1219–1251, is pieced together from two manuscript copies that contain the chapters in different arrangements. The first copy (p. 1219–1244) contains 71 entries. A series of entries from a second collection, which has preserved the original count of one hundred chapters, was added later (p. 1244–1252). Frankenberg (p. 4) reports on the original structure of the work based on a Syriac translation, which confirms the arrangement and chapter count of the second collection $^4$). It appears as though the second collection (chapters 6–15 according to the Syriac) also included the smaller work of Evagrius on the eight vices (Migne 1271–1275) $^5$). On the other hand, numbers 63–71 of the first collection did not belong to the original redaction of the work; they contain a mosaic-like conglomerate of mostly genuine Evagrian fragments. I cite the work (abbreviated as *Pract.*) of necessity according to the Migne edition, and the second collection as *Pract. II* (with numbers).

2. Immediately following the *Practika* <note>The Practical Chapters</note>, at least in the Syriac tradition, is the *Gnostikos* <note>The Gnostic; the second part of Evagrius's trilogy, aimed at the monk who has attained "knowledge" (gnosis).</note> with numbers 104–151 (originally 50 chapters). Text and translation are found in Frankenberg 546–553.

3. Closely related to the *Gnostikos* in nature are the *Prognostic Problems* <note>original Greek: προβλήματα προγνωστικά (problēmata prognōstika)</note>, also known as the *Centuries*. One might say that together with the *Gnostikos*, they represent the "gnostic" sayings of Evagrius. Evagrius himself states: "the *Practical* in one hundred chapters, and six hundred and fifty [concerning knowledge]..." <note>original Greek: ἑκατὸν μὲν κεφαλαίοις τὰ πρακτικά, πεντήκοντα δὲ πρὸς τοῖς ἑξακοσίοις (hekaton men kephalaiois ta praktika, pentēkonta de pros tois hexakosiois)</note>.

---

1) Evagrius Ponticus, *Göttingen Learned Proceedings* <note>original: Gött. Gel. Abhandl.</note>, New Series XIII 2. 1912.
2) *The Nuns' Mirror and Monks' Mirror* <note>original: Nonnenspiegel und Mönchsspiegel</note> of Evagrius Ponticus. Texts and Investigations by Harnack and Schmidt, 3rd Series IX. 4 (= Vol. 39) pp. 143–165.
3) An excellent preliminary work is provided by Reitzenstein, *History of the Monks* <note>original: Histor. Monach.</note> and *The Lausiac History* <note>original: Hist. Lausiaca</note> 1916, Chapter 6: "Evagrius and Diadochus of Photiki."
4) The Syriac [version] actually has 103 entries (in secondary tradition) instead of 100.
5) The so-called "Little Refutation" <note>original: *Antirrhetikos*</note>. The "Great Refutation" is available in Frankenberg 472 ff. in Syriac text and Greek translation; it is of less relevance for our purposes.

<summary>This page introduces a study on Evagrius Ponticus, identifying him as the pioneer of monastic mysticism and outlining the primary texts used for the investigation, including the Practical Chapters and the Gnostikos.</summary>

<header>Book III. Studies on Evagrius.</header>

...having divided the gnostic matters concisely <note>original Greek: "τὰ γνωστικὰ συντετμημένως διελόντες"; from the Preface to the *Practicus*, Migne 1221 C</note>. The "Centuries" <note>The *Gnostic Chapters*, one of Evagrius's most influential and controversial works</note> contain six hundred sayings, which strangely are arranged into 6 books with 90 *logia* <note>sayings or oracles</note> each, plus a supplement containing the remaining 60 numbers; it seems this arrangement was already compiled by Evagrius himself. They are available in Frankenberg (pages 8–471) in the Syriac text alongside an excellent Greek back-translation <note>term: retrovertierung; the process of reconstructing a lost original text by translating a preserved translation back into the original language</note>, accompanied by the commentary of the Abbot <note>term: Archimandrite</note> Babai. I cite the *Centuries* (Cent.) by providing the book and number; where no error is possible, I also use a double number (e.g., I 1).

4. *Exhortation to a Virgin* <note>original Greek: παραίνεσις τοῦ παρθένου</note> and *To the monks in communities or associations* <note>original Greek: πρὸς τοὺς ἐν κοινοβίοις ἢ συνοδίαις μοναχούς</note>, cited as the *Mirror for Nuns* and *Mirror for Monks*; the Greek text is in Gressmann (pages 146 ff. and 152 ff.; numbering follows Gressmann).

5. A very valuable collection of letters by Evagrius is likewise preserved only in Syriac and is available in Frankenberg’s edition with the text and Greek back-translation on pages 554–635. I cite these as Let. (number), followed by Frankenberg's page number and the manuscript page numbers noted in the margin. Especially important for our purposes is the long letter from Evagrius to Melania <note>Melania the Elder, a Roman noblewoman and a key figure in early desert monasticism</note> (Fr. 613–620). The last letter published and back-translated by Frankenberg is found (cf. the footnote in Fr. 621 *) as a letter of Basil the Great in his collection of letters under I 8 (Migne 32, 245–268). That this letter belongs to Evagrius and not to Basil will be proven in the final section of these investigations. The result appears so certain to me that I have already frequently drawn upon this letter for the presentation of Evagrius's views. ¹)

Regarding the text of the Evagrian citations, I gratefully use Frankenberg’s back-translation for the pieces preserved only in Syriac. This is, under all circumstances, an admirable achievement and testifies to an astonishing insight into the individuality and linguistic character of Evagrius. Furthermore, the terminology and vocabulary of Evagrius are so peculiar and distinct that one can often reconstruct the original Greek source used by the Syriac translator with great certainty. Wherever I deviate from Frankenberg’s translation based on newly discovered parallels or other considerations, it is noted every time.

However, before I turn to the presentation of Evagrius's views, two investigations must first be presented: one regarding the nature of the composition of the *Centuries* and another on the literary dependence of Evagrius on Origen <note>An early Christian theologian whose complex views on the soul and the cosmos deeply influenced Evagrius but were later declared heretical</note>.

# I. The Composition of the Centuries.

The fourth Century of Evagrius begins with three sentences that deal with the relationship of Gnosis <note>spiritual knowledge</note> to God the Father and Christ. Then we read the sentence:

> 4. An heir of Christ is the one deemed worthy to be a beholder <note>original: "ἐπόπτης"</note> of created things (or perhaps: of beings?) <note>original: "τῶν γενήτων (? ὄντων)"</note>.

This is followed again by three sentences on Gnosis. Then we encounter a sentence stylized exactly like No. 4:

> 8. A joint-heir of Christ is the one who, being in the Monad <note>The "Monad" refers to the ultimate divine unity or the state of the soul returned to God</note>, rejoices (revels) <note>original: "εὐφραινόμενος (τρυφῶν)"</note> with Him (instead of "with it"?) in its contemplation <note>original: "συγκληρονόμος δὲ Χριστοῦ ἐστιν ὁ ὢν ἐν τῇ Μονάδι εὐφραινόμενος (τρυφῶν) μετ’ αὐτοῦ (st. αὐτῆς?) ἐν τῇ θεωρίᾳ αὐτῆς"</note>.

---

1) I am not entirely certain about the attribution of the work *The Reasons for Monastic Matters* <note>original Latin: *Rerum monach. rationes*; original Greek: *τῶν κατὰ μοναχῶν πραγμάτων τὰ αἴτια*</note>, Migne 40, 1251 ff. It is only used occasionally.

If we continue counting in this way, we find under numbers 16, 20, and 24 three closely related sentences.
16 Only-begotten is he before whom another was not born, nor after him another <note>original: μονογενής ἐστι οὗ πρότερον ἄλλος οὐκ ἐγεννήθη οὐδὲ μετ’ αὐτὸν ἄλλος</note>.
20 ^1) Firstborn is he before whom no other was born, but after whom another was born <note>original: πρωτότοκος ἐστὶ, οὗ πρότερος ἄλλος μὲν οὐκ ἐγεννήθη, μετ’ αὐτὸν δὲ ἄλλος ἐγένετο</note>.

If we follow this trail further, we now encounter a whole series of allegorical definitions of Old Testament cult objects. The first reads:
28 Spiritual unleavened bread is the state of a rational soul, etc <note>original: ἄζυμα πνευματικά ἐστιν κατάστασις ψυχῆς λογικῆς κ. τα.</note>.
And so the following are further explained: 32 lobe of the liver <note>original: λόβος τοῦ ἥπατος</note>. 36 fat <note>original: στέαρ</note>. [40 key of the kingdom of heaven <note>original: κλεῖς τῆς τῶν οὐρανων βασιλείας</note>]. 44 Sabbath <note>original: σάββατον</note>. 48 miter of the priesthood <note>original: κίδαρις τῆς ἱερωσύνης</note>. 52 petal <note>referring to the golden plate on the high priest's miter; original: πέταλον</note>. 56. ephod <note>original: ἐπωμίς</note>.

There follow some numbers, 57–60, which group together around the terms "creation" and "creator" <note>original: κτίσις, κτίστης</note>, then with a small irregularity:
61 Instructive revelation is the interpretation of the commandments of God <note>original: ἀποκάλυψις διδακτική ἐστιν ἡ τῶν θεοῦ ἐντολῶν ἑρμηνεία</note>
and now from 63 onwards, every third number again contains allegorical interpretations of Old Testament terms.
63 spiritual ephod <note>original: ἐφὼδ πνευματικόν</note>. 66 spiritual undergarment <note>original: ὑποδύτης πνευματικός</note>. 69 spiritual undergarment. 72 spiritual mantle <note>original: περιβόλαιον πν.</note>. 75 spiritual fine linen <note>original: βύσσος πν.</note>. 79 ^2) belt of the loins of the priest <note>original: ζωνὴ τῶν ὀσφύων τοῦ ἱερέως</note>. 82 place of refuge <note>original: φυγαδευτήριον</note>.

For the conclusion of the book, the compiler has dispensed with the insertion of such definitions. But with the 5th Century, the old procedure begins again. One might indeed doubt whether number 1 belongs here, since the form of the sentence does not quite correspond to the others singled out: Adam is a type of Christ; Eve, however, of the rational nature for whose sake Christ went out from his paradise <note>original: Ἀδὰμ τύπος τοῦ Χριστοῦ. Εὔα δὲ τῆς λογικῆς φύσεως δι’ ἣν ὁ Χρ. ἐξῆλθε τῆς παραδείσου αὐτοῦ</note>.

But then closely grouped together are: 4 archangel <note>original: ἀρχάγγελος</note>, 7 angel <note>original: ἄγγελος</note>, 10 firstborn <note>original: πρωτότοκοι</note>, and furthermore 13: a spiritual cloud is a rational and incorporeal nature <note>original: νεφέλη πνευματική ἐστι φύσις λογικὴ καὶ ἀσώματος</note>. . . There follows, in a somewhat external association: 16 ^3) spiritual darkness is a spiritual contemplation <note>original: ζόφος πνευματική ἐστι θεωρία πνευματική</note> ..., then again very closely related: 19 the small resurrection of the body <note>original: ἡ μικρὰ τοῦ σώματος ἀνάστασις</note>. 22 the small resurrection of the soul <note>original: ἡ μικρὰ τῆς ψυχῆς ἀνάστασις</note>. 25 the small state of the mind <note>original: ἡ μικρὰ τοῦ νοὸς κατάστασις</note>.

Now follow allegorical explanations of *New Testament* symbols:
28 spiritual sword <note>original: μάχαιρα πνευματική</note>. 31 spiritual shield <note>original: θυρεὸς πν.</note>. 34 the spiritual helmet <note>original: ἡ περικεφαλαία ἡ πν.</note> ^4). 37 spiritual fishhook <note>original: ἄγκιστρον πν.</note>. 40 spiritual mountain <note>original: πνευματικὸν ὄρος</note>. 43 the spiritual way <note>original: ἡ πνευματικὴ ὁδός</note>. 46 high priest <note>original: ἀρχιερεύς</note>. 49 new god <note>perhaps "recent god"? referring to Psalm 81:10; original: θεὸς καινός (πρόσφατος?)</note>. 53 ^5) (!) spiritual sacrifice <note>original: θυσία πν.</note>.

Here the arrangement breaks off. 54–64 (cf. in the following still roughly 67, 69, 73, 75, 76, 79, 81) represent a fairly coherent connection.

It is a kind of theory of knowledge <term>epistemology: the study of how we know things</term> that Evagrius develops here. But afterwards, he continues his old method. At number 65, we encounter the sentence:

->A practitioner <note>original: πρακτικός</note> ^1) is one who works with discernment, while a gnostic <note>original: γνωστικός</note> is a helper of wisdom.<-

This is followed by the definitions: 68 Philistine <note>original: Φιλισταῖος</note>. 71 Unsubmissive <note>original: ἀνυπότακος</note>. 74 City <note>original: πόλις</note>. 77 Gates of the city <note>original: πύλαι τῆς πόλεως</note>. 80 Spiritual bar <note>original: μόχλος πνευματικός</note>. 82 (!) Spiritual wall <note>original: τεῖχος πν.</note> 84 Spiritual temple <note>original: ναὸς πν.</note> The interconnectedness of 74, 77, 80, 82, and 84 is correctly highlighted by the commentator in his remark on 84. The series is somewhat interrupted by 86: A monk who is a lover of vainglory <note>original: μοναχὸς ἐραστὴς κενοδοξίας</note>. But 88 follows suit again: Zion, Egypt, Jerusalem <note>original: Σιών, Αἴγυπτος, Ἱερουσαλήμ</note> ^3).

The compiler of the sayings <note>original: logia</note> has not maintained his peculiar "disputation" procedure as strictly in the neighboring centuries. Yet even here, we now find clear traces of it. Compare III 6, 8, 10, 12 (naked mind <note>original: νοῦς γυμνός</note> . . . who has acquired the final garment . . . incomplete . . . perfect). 14, 16 ^4) (a soul that has suffered loss . . . perfect) 18, 20 (trial by fire . . . transformation). 22, 24 ^5), 26, 27! (the first movement of rational nature . . . the knowledge of the first . . . second nature . . . the first contemplation of nature) 28, 30, 32, 34 (sinful soul . . . the spiritual mind . . . image of God . . . the demon). 36, 38, 40 (world . . . the judgment of God . . . the last trumpet.) 42, 44 (contemplation [is] an intelligible sun <note>original: θεωρία ἥλιος νοητός</note>). 46, 48, 50 (the toil of the angels ^6) . . . the spiritual renewal of the righteous . . . the displacement of sinners). 52 Intelligible moon (cf. 44). 56 Spiritual knowledge is the wings of the mind, and a gnostic is a mind with wings ^7). 60 Symbol of the day's dawning. 62 Intelligible luminaries (see 44, 52). From this point, the regular recurrence of such sentences breaks off. They are found only under 72, 83, 84.

The matter emerges even less clearly in Century 6. But here too, compare numbers 5, 15, 17, 19, 21, then 28–32 (Father . . . Father of grace . . . increasing Father . . . begotten/created ^8)). 38. — 39, 40, 42 (The birth of Christ, crucifixion, death.) 44. — 46, 48 (Zither, psaltery) 49 (see above V 88) 53. — 60, 62 (barren, sterile). 65, 66, 68, 70. — 78, 80 (anti-type [likeness] of the body . . . of rational nature).

In the first and second centuries, such definitional sentences are completely absent. In their place, the 60 supplementary chapters that follow the so-called six centuries consist almost entirely of such sentences. Compare 3, 4, (5), 6 (passionlessness <note>original: ἀπάθεια</note> . . . the state of the mind . . . fire-drill <note>original: πυρεῖον</note> ^9)). 8–13 (kiss of the mind . . . good anger, dog ^10) of God, dog of the law of Christ's sheep, discipline, fear. (14.) 16.

7) There follows an addition in which the image is more broadly developed.

9) The "fire-drill" <note>original: πυρεῖον</note> is a symbol of the "pure mind" <note>original: νοῦς καθαρός</note>; see above Century IV 32 ff.
10) The "dog" is the "visible mind" <note>original: νοῦς ὁρατός</note> which watches over evil thoughts, and thus belongs together with "good anger" <note>original: θυμὸς καλός</note>.
