# I. The Composition of the Centuries.

17 (human and practical mind <note>original: ἄνθρωπος κ. νοῦς πρακτικός</note>)^1). 29—33 (prayer, prayer [duplicate], petition, prayer/vow, intercession <note>original: προσευχή, προσευχή, δέησις, εὐχή, ἔντευξις</note>) 34 (Hades). 35. 36 (gnostic <note>the one who knows</note>, practitioner <note>the one who acts</note>). 37—39 (mind, embodied mind, impure mind <note>original: νοῦς, νοῦς ἐνσώματος, ν. ἀκάθαρτος</note>) 40 (desire <note>original: ἐπιθυμία</note>) 41. 42 (practitioner, contemplative <note>original: πρακτικός, θεωρητικός</note>) 44. 45. — 46. 47 (anger, courage <note>original: ὀργή, ἀνδρεία</note>) 48—50. 53—55 (divine mind, embodied intellect, contemplative nature <note>original: νοῦς θεῖος, διάνοια ἐνσώματος, φύσις θεωρητική</note>).

These observations cannot be based on chance. In their form, these definition-sentences stand out so distinctly from all the other sayings <term>logia: short, pithy spiritual utterances</term> that there can hardly ever be a doubt about whether a sentence belongs to this group or not. One should look at all the unlisted sentences once more with this in mind. They all have a different form. Although everything has been preserved for us only in a Syriac translation, the actual state of affairs has remained perfectly clear^2).

How are we to explain this strange finding? One might first think of an editor who organized this peculiar compilation. However, according to the specific self-testimony of Evagrius (see above), there is hardly any other option left but the assumption that Evagrius himself prepared this interesting medley <note>literally "ragout"</note> of his thoughts. We must imagine that he had an older collection of definitions (originating from himself) in front of him. He then mixed these with his other fragments of thought, often following a completely schematic numerical procedure. Every now and then, he added related material to those definitions (see, for example, V 3 ff. regarding the angels). Usually, he broke the connection using completely remote thoughts. On the other hand, he tore apart related chains of thought by inserting the definitions. Occasionally, a series of thoughts was too valuable to him for such a game. In those cases, the series of definitions breaks off (V 54—64; VII 19—28). —

Finally, we find external confirmation of our suspicion. In Migne’s *Patrologia Graeca* <note>a massive 19th-century collection of Greek church writings</note> volume 40, page 1263 ff., we indeed find under the heading "33 Chapters in Sequence" <note>original: κεφάλαια λγ' κατ' ἀκολουθίαν</note> a chain of such definitions, though none of them are found again in the *Centuries*. Perhaps this collection is only a remnant of a much larger one from which the *Centuries* were also supplied.

Moreover, this also solves another riddle: the question of how to understand the strange external arrangement of the "Centuries" into 6 sections of 90, plus 60 <note>6 X 90 + 60</note>. Originally, Evagrius likely only compiled 6 groups of 90 sayings. At the end of the sixth book—at least according to the Syriac translation—stands the concluding exhortation: "Seek my words, brothers" <note>original: ἐπιζητεῖτε λόγους μου ἀδελφοί</note> (Frankenberg 423). Then, he filled out his work with the 60 supplementary chapters. But by then, he had run out of steam. In this supplement, he almost exclusively utilized his old collection of definitions, as shown in the list above.

Even otherwise, it is unlikely that Evagrius created everything from scratch at the moment he wrote his *Centuries*. It is probable from the outset that he frequently compiled material that was already formulated. Among other things, he used his own letters and took striking sentences from them. This can be specifically proven for a few sentences, as the following comparison demonstrates.

---

1) In between these are sentences about intuitive knowledge and specifically about the mystical light-appearances during prayer (see below).
2) One should note the recurring Syriac word "is" <note>original: ܐܝܬܘܗܝ (itawhi), corresponding to the Greek ἐστιν (estin)</note>.

### The Practitioner 70.
When the mind, having stripped off the **old man** <note>original: παλαιὸν ἄνθρωπον; a Pauline term referring to the unregenerate self dominated by passions</note>, has put on the one of **grace**,

then it will also see its own **state** <note>original: κατάστασιν; the stable condition of the soul</note> at the time of prayer resembling **sapphire** or the **color of heaven**,

which Scripture also calls the **place of God** <note>original: τόπον θεοῦ</note> seen by the elders on Mount Sinai.

### 71.
The mind would not see the place of God within itself unless it has become **higher** than all things in the world.

But it will not become higher unless it has stripped off the **passions** <note>original: πάθη; the disordered impulses or emotions that bind the soul to sensory objects</note> which bind it through **thoughts** <note>original: νοημάτων</note> to sensible things;
and it will set aside the passions through the **virtues**, but it will set aside **bare thoughts** <note>original: ψιλοὺς λογισμοὺς; thoughts stripped of emotional charge but still occupying the mind</note> through **spiritual contemplation** <note>original: πνευματικῆς θεωρίας</note>;
and this in turn occurs when that **light** appears to it, which at the time of prayer forms the image of the place of God.

<column-break/>

### Century VII 25. 26.
When the mind puts off the **old man** and puts on the **new** through grace,

then it will also see its own **state of prayer** at that time being made like **sapphire** and the **appearance of heaven**.

This is what was named the **place of God** by the elders of Israel to whom He appeared on the mountain.
(26) The mind is not able to see the place of God in its own soul unless it has been raised **above all thoughts** of visible things;
nor is it raised above these unless it has set aside the passions which, through the memory of these things, bind it to sensible objects;

and it repels the passions through **virtues** and the thoughts through **spiritual contemplation**.

And this light of the **Holy Trinity** rises at the time of prayer.

<column-break/>

### Century VII 2.
Whoever wishes to understand the **state of the mind**, let them tear their soul away from all **reasonings** <note>original: διαλογισμῶν</note>
and then

they shall see their soul like **sapphire** or the **appearance of the heaven**.
[VII 50 The **inner man**, having become a **gnostic** <note>the one who possesses spiritual knowledge</note>, will strip off the old man of the passions; then he will see within himself the **light** of the beauty of his soul, and at the time of prayer he will perceive **heavenly visions** within himself.]

But without **dispassion** <note>original: ἀπαθείας; the state of being free from the disturbance of the passions</note> it is impossible to do this;

it requires the **help of God**, with the need for **light** to empower and fill him. (?)

### VII 4.
The **state of the mind** is the **height of the intelligible** <note>original: ὕψος τῶν νοητῶν; the pinnacle of things perceived by the intellect rather than the senses</note> resembling the appearance of the heaven, over which the light of the **Holy Trinity** shines at the time of prayer.

<column-break/>

### Letter 39, 593.
If, therefore, by the **grace of God** the mind turns away from these things and puts off the **old man**,
then it will also see its own **state** at the time of prayer resembling **sapphire** or the **color of heaven**,
which Scripture also calls the **place of God** seen by the elders on Mount Sinai.

### VII 52.
The **passions** that bind the soul to matter: set them aside in this way through the **labors of the virtues**.

### VII 32.
But set aside the thoughts of the **composite** <note>original: συνθέτου; likely referring to the human being as a composite of soul and body</note> through **spiritual contemplation**,
which rises in its own light after one is raised above the passions and draws the soul to itself with the **sweetness of the ages**.

"...to receive; but of the second (knowledge) the **dispassionate alone** are receptive, who during the time of prayer behold the **proper radiance of the mind** shining around them."

## (Letter 43. 549; 59. 609.)

### The Practitioner 65.
Three types of thoughts are opposed to the **demonic thought**, cutting it off when it lingers in the mind: the **angelic**, the one from our own **free choice** inclining toward the better, and the one arising from **human nature**. According to the latter, even the **pagans** <note>original: ἐθνικοὶ; non-Christians or Gentiles</note> love their own children and honor their own parents. But only two thoughts are opposed to the **good thought**: the **demonic** and the one from our own **free choice** leaning toward the worse. No **evil thought** comes out of nature. For we were not made evil from the beginning, since the Lord sowed **good seed** in His own field.
(Letter 43. 579: "That from the beginning seeds of **virtue** lie within us, but of vice, none"). For it is not the case that if we are receptive to something, we all also have the power—

## II. The literary dependence of Evagrius on Origen.

While leafing through the *Selecta in Psalmos* <note>original: "Selected passages on the Psalms"</note> of Origen (Lommatzsch edition XII—XIV), I immediately noticed a whole series of parallels—some literal, some adaptations—used by Evagrius, particularly in the *Centuries*, but also in the *Praktika*. I have been able to demonstrate these massive points of contact only for the *Selecta in Psalmos*. Here and there, however, *On First Principles* <note>original: περὶ ἀρχῶν; Origen's foundational work on systematic theology</note> also comes into consideration. A precise expert on Origen (and also on Evagrius) will certainly be able to contribute much more here. For my current purpose—to prove how strongly Origen specifically influenced the language of the "mystic" Evagrius—the evidence provided here, together with the following chapter, will suffice. I provide the parallels according to the sequence of Evagrius's sayings in the *Centuries*.

**Century I 13:** Of rational beings, some possess both **contemplation** <note>original: θεωρίαν; spiritual insight</note> and spiritual **practice** <note>original: θρησκείαν (πρακτικὴν)</note>; others possess practice and contemplation; still others are held in hindrance and judgment.

**Lommatzsch XIII 89:** For it belongs to angels to behold the face of God at all times, that is, to have the **contemplation** of Him; but it belongs to humans to be able to act righteously through their actions at all times.

**I 63:** In the holy angels there is an abundance of **intellect** <note>original: νοός; the highest faculty of the soul</note>; in humans, an abundance of **desire**; and in demons, an abundance of **anger** <note>original: θυμοῦ; the "spirited" or "incensive" faculty</note>.

**III 4:** It belongs to the angels to be nourished at all times by the contemplation of existing things; to humans, to be nourished at the proper time; and to demons, never at all.

**IV 65:** **Rational nature is divided into three parts: over one part life reigns, over another both life and death, and over the third, death.**

**VI 69:** Angels see both humans and demons; humans are deprived of the sight of angels and demons; and demons see only humans.

**Lommatzsch XIII 9:** It belongs to demons to work lawlessness at all times; to humans, not at all times; to angels, never.

**XII 144:** It belongs to angels to magnify the Lord at all times; to humans, not at all times; to demons, neither at all times nor in any amount.

I am convinced that if Origen's commentary were better preserved, the evidence of these connections would multiply greatly.
2) This is followed by a reference to **the fathers**.

### Book III. Evagrius Studies.

**XII 313** To always act according to God belongs to the angels; to never do so belongs to demons; to act sometimes well and sometimes not rightly belongs to humans.

**XIII 147** Life shepherds the angels, but death and life shepherd humans, and only death shepherds demons. <note>Evagrius uses "shepherding" as a metaphor for the guiding principle of one's existence.</note>

**I 15** When four are removed, five are also removed; but when the five are removed, the four are not necessarily removed because of this. The last half of this enigmatic sentence is interpreted by the commentary as meaning that even if the five senses of man were suspended, the knowledge of the world of the elements <note>The physical building blocks of the universe</note> remains possible through intense spiritual vision <term>theoria: spiritual contemplation or insight</term>.

Regarding this, Origen (Lo. XIII 147) provides a commentary: It is not for everyone to say: "Bring my soul out of prison" <note>Psalm 142:7</note> unless they are able, through purity and even apart from this body, to apply themselves to the contemplation of created things.

**I 23** Understandings of the rational principles <note>original: λόγων / logoi</note> of things on the earth are called "the good things of the earth." If the holy angels know these things well according to the word of the woman of Tekoa <note>A reference to 2 Samuel 14:20, where the woman praises the King’s wisdom as being like that of an angel who knows all things on earth</note>, and the angels of God eat the "good things of the earth"—according to what is written, "man ate the bread of angels"—it is clear that they also learned the rational principles of understanding on the earth from humans.

Two sentences from Origen provide a parallel and an explanation for this complicated thought.

**Lo. XII 125** If, according to the wise woman of Tekoa, the angels know everything on the earth, the "face of God" (Ps. 29:7) are the rational principles of things on the earth which characterize His creative Word.

<column-break/>

**Lo. XII 98** If it belongs to angels to see the face of God always, and humans also seek to see this face, then humans also seek knowledge <note>original: γνῶσιν / gnosis</note>, if indeed it is possible for man to eat the bread of angels.

**I 25** Those who wish to ensnare us with temptations either seek the rational power of the soul, or they insist on seizing the impassive part <note>original: τὸ ἀπαθὲς μέρος / to apathes meros – the part of the soul reached through 'apatheia' or freedom from passion</note> within it, or the body, or everything concerning the body.

**I 10** Some of the demons oppose the religious observance of the commandments (= the **practical life**), others the recognition of natures; others the rational principles concerning God (= **theology**). Cf. Lo. XIII 62: Some of the demons fought him <note>the pious person</note> as a practitioner <term>praktikos: one focused on ethical action</term>, others as a theorist <term>theoretikos: one focused on spiritual contemplation</term>. **XIII 143:** Through thoughts <note>original: λογισμῶν / logismoi – intrusive or tempting thoughts</note> the demons array themselves against us, sometimes stirring up desires, sometimes rages, and at other times anger and desire together.

**I 41** If death is secondary to life and disease secondary to health, it is clear that vice is also secondary to virtue (cf. I 59). **II 8b** If ignorance is a deprivation of knowledge, it is clear that wealth is prior to poverty and the health of the soul is prior to its disease. Cf. Lo. XIII 8c: Just as cheese existed when it was not yet cheese <note>meaning it was milk first</note>, so the demons once existed when they were not yet evil. If milk is older than cheese, it is clear that virtue was also older than vice.

**I 71** The end of the knowledge of natures is the knowledge of the Holy Unity <note>original: Μονάδος / Monad – often referring to the Trinity or the ultimate oneness of God</note>; but for the Incomprehensible, as the fathers say, there is no end (cf. I 54). **III 88**

## II. The literary dependence of Evagrius on Origen.

Blessed is he who has descended into infinite knowledge <note>original: "gnôsin" (knowledge); the author notes that the Armenian version reads "knowledge" while the Syrian versions read "agnosian" (ignorance/unknowing)</note>. Compare Origen (Lo. XIII 153): "The contemplation of all created things has a limit; but the knowledge of the Holy Trinity alone is infinite."

**I 73** The life of man is the Holy Trinity. The goal of God’s mercy is the contemplation <term>theoria: the spiritual perception of the inner essence of things</term> of existing things. Since many wise men promise knowledge, but the mercy of the Lord is better than lives <note>original: "kreisson to eleos sou hyper zōas," a reference to Psalm 63:3</note>. Compare Origen (Lo. XII 384): "Human life is the holy knowledge. The mercy of the Lord is the contemplation of created things. Many in this age have promised us various kinds of knowledge, but the mercy of the Lord is better than lives."

**I 75** If the crown of righteousness is the knowledge of the Holy Trinity, it is clear that at the end of the race, the saints will be crowned with it. **III 15** If the perfection of the mind <term>nous: the highest faculty of the human soul, intended for the vision of God</term> is spiritual knowledge, as the fathers say, then its crown is the knowledge of the Holy Trinity (compare III 49). Compare Origen (Lo. XIII 6): "The knowledge of God is divided into two parts: practice <term>praktike: the ethical life and struggle against passions</term> and contemplation. The 'shield of favor' belongs to practice, while the 'crown' belongs to contemplation."

**I 81** The glory and light of the **mind** is spiritual **knowledge**; the glory and light of the **soul** is **impassibility** <term>apatheia: a state of holy calm where one is no longer driven by disordered passions</term>. Compare Origen (Lo. XII 63): "Purity of the soul is impassibility through the grace of God." XII 131: "Just as the face of God hides the **soul** . . . . . granting **impassibility** through the practical life, so also the tabernacle guards the mind through true **knowledge** . . . ."

**II 12** The right hand of Christ is also called His "hand"; but His "hand" is not always called His "right hand": because the purpose of the one is in giving, while the other is in discipline. Compare Origen (Lo. XIII 9): "If there is a difference between the 'hand' and the 'right hand' of God, I wonder whether perhaps the 'hand' performs acts against the enemies of the people, while the 'right hand' performs good things for the sake of the people."

In **II 57**, Evagrius provides the enigmatic sentence: "We learn that there are three altars of the height: one is uniform and non-composite, while the other two are composite."

The ancient commentary arbitrarily interprets this as the three levels of believers: the first group consists of those who have entered into the mystical vision of the ineffable light; the second group occupies themselves with psalm-singing, the study of scripture, and (vocal) prayer; the third group focuses on almsgiving, hosting strangers, and visiting the sick.

However, only a parallel with Origen leads us to the correct interpretation. We find in his commentary on Psalm 25:6 the following explanation: "Our mind is the rational altar of God. Upon it we burn . . . every irrational thought that strays from the master’s flock . . . but the altar is the contemplation of bodies and bodiless things, through which the mind is purified."

We now know what Evagrius's three altars <note>original: thysiastêria</note> are meant to represent: 1. the contemplation of physical bodies, 2. the contemplation of bodiless beings (angels/demons), and 3. the Trinity. We see where he took his idea and how he reworked Origen's thought. Furthermore, he used this passage a second time, following it even more closely in **VII 45**: "The altar of God is a pure mind, unmoved by the memory of the world's structure so as not to be troubled."

**II 62** The working soul (engaged in practice) which prospers by the grace of God and is separated from the body, will be in those places of knowledge where the wings of **impassibility** will cause it to arrive. **III 56** Spiritual knowledge is the wings of the mind, and the gnostic <note>gnostikos: the spiritual seeker who has attained true knowledge</note> is the **mind with wings**. Compare Origen (Lo. XII 362): "The wings of the holy dove are the **contemplation of bodies and bodiless things**, through which the mind is lifted up and comes to rest in the **knowledge of the Holy Trinity**."<sup>1)</sup>

---

1) We have here at the same time the classification scheme of true knowledge that recurs again and again in Evagrius; see also Origen (XII 405): "Some have said that the 'lots' and the 'wings' (Psalm 67:13) refer to . . . others to practice and contemplation. Still others to the knowledge of bodies and bodiless things."

**Header: Book III. Evagrius Studies.**

**II 78** Every rank of the heavenly powers consists either entirely of those from the lower realms, or entirely of those from the higher, or from both those above and those below. <note>original: "hekaston tagma tōn ouraniōn dynamōn..." This refers to the Origenist view that angels, demons, and humans are all fallen "rational beings" who occupy different ranks based on their previous choices.</note>

**III 36** The world <note>original: "kosmos"</note> is a constitution of nature, or it consists of separate bodies and contains various principles <term>logoi: the inner divine purposes or "blueprints" behind created things</term> of growth for the sake of the knowledge of God. *Compare Origen (Lo. XII 5):* An age <note>original: "aiōn"</note> is a natural system of various bodies—containing rational differences for the sake of the knowledge of God.

Anathemas of the Fifth Synod <note>The Second Council of Constantinople in 553 AD, which condemned specific "Origenist" doctrines held by followers of Evagrius</note>, Koetzschau *On First Principles* 160, 10: "Every rank of the heavenly powers consists either entirely of those from below, or entirely of those from above, or of those from above and those from below."

**III 60** The symbol of the day's rising is the symbol of the saints, while the setting represents the souls in Hades. *Compare Origen (Lo. XIII 53):* The "east" refers to the intellectual natures in whom the Sun of Righteousness rises; the "west" refers to the souls of men in whom the spiritual and heavenly sun once set. *Origen (Lo. XII 43 f.):* The inheritance of a rational nature is the contemplation <term>theoria: spiritual insight into the essence of reality</term> of the ages that have been and those that are to come. The inheritance of Christ is the knowledge of God.

**III 72** The inheritance of Christ is the Monad <term>Monas: The absolute unity of the Godhead, beyond all division</term> of the holy essence, and all his fellow-heirs shall be partakers with him in this holy knowledge (*compare IV. 4. 8*).

**IV 18** An intelligible anointing is the knowledge of the holy Monad. *Compare Origen (Lo. XIII 29):* The holy oil signifies the knowledge of God, or rather, it reveals essential knowledge. <note>original: "gnōsin ousiōdē"</note>

**IV 36** Intelligible fat <note>original: "stear"</note> is a density that has happened to the mind <term>nous: the highest faculty of the soul</term> as a result of vice. *Compare Origen (Lo. XII 51):* Intelligible fat is the density that happens to the "governing faculty" <term>hegemonikon: the ruling part of the soul</term> as a result of vice.

**V 13** A spiritual cloud is an incorporeal rational nature, which has been entrusted by God to refresh the innocent. *Compare Origen (Lo. XIII 133):* A cloud is a rational nature entrusted with the principles <note>original: "logous"</note> of providence.

**V 22** The "small resurrection" of the soul is the transition from the state of being ruled by passions to the state of passionlessness <term>apatheia: a state of holy calm where one is no longer driven by compulsive emotions</term>. **IV 25** The "small resurrection" of the mind is the change from ignorance to knowledge. *Compare Origen (Lo. XIII 53):* God raises the soul from vice to virtue, but he urges the mind from ignorance toward knowledge.

**V 27** The anger that disturbs the vision causes blindness, but evil desire hides the things that are visible. *Compare Origen (Lo. XII 9):* Nothing blinds so much as a disturbed anger (later: "corrupted according to the deceitful desires").

**V 28** A spiritual sword is the spiritual word which both separates the soul from the body and cuts away the soul's vice of ignorance. *Compare Origen (Lo. XII 326):* This sword separates the soul from vice and the mind from ignorance (*compare XIII 162*).

**V 37** A spiritual hook is the spiritual teaching which pulls the soul up from the depths of vice. *Compare Origen (Lo. XIII 145):* (Of the present age) there is a casting-net of spiritual teaching that leads those who have strayed from godliness back to virtue.

**V 40** A spiritual mountain is the spiritual contemplation situated on high, which the mind reaches to become a beholder of all the principles <note>original: "logōn"</note> concerning nature. *Compare Origen (Lo. XII 39):* A holy mountain is the knowledge of Christ, which is the contemplation of created things.

## II. The Literary Dependence of Evagrius on Origen.

**V 49** A **new god** <note>original: *theos kainos*; Frankenberg adds "recent?" (*prosphatos*)</note> is one who cannot create but is full of hidden malice. *Compare Origen (Lo. XIII 24 on Psalm 80:9):* A "recent god" is one who is unable to give essence to anything, or one who is characterized by malice.

**V 77** The **gates of the city** are the virtues of the rational soul.... *Slightly different in Origen (Lo. XIII 64):* The **gate of knowledge**, which is the contemplation <term>theoria: spiritual insight or "seeing" into the nature of things</term> of created things, both corporeal and incorporeal¹).

**VI 38** The **bed of one sleeping** is the deadening of the body or... it perfects purity in Christ. *Compare Origen (Lo. XII 310):* A **bed of pain** is the body of humiliation.

**VI 46 + 48** A **lyre** <note>original: *kithara*</note> is a practical soul moved by the commandments of Christ. — A **psaltery** is a pure mind moved by spiritual knowledge. *Compare Origen (Lo. XII 133 f.; cf. 368, XIII 165):* A lyre is a practical soul moved by the commandments of God. A psaltery is a pure mind moved by spiritual knowledge.

**VI 53** An **evil arrow** is an evil thought <note>original: *dialogismos*</note> proceeding first from the soul's desire. *Compare Origen (Lo. XII 29):* An **arrow** is a passionate thought, and a **quiver** is a wretched habit filled with impure thoughts²).

**VI 68** The **submission** of a rational nature to the knowledge of God is the harmony of a good will. *Compare Origen (Lo. XII 147):* This submission is the voluntary consent of a rational nature toward the knowledge of God³).

**VII 44** The **kingdom of heaven** is the knowledge of a high and intelligible, super-heavenly contemplation occurring through the mind's sense-organ... **Praktikos 3:** The **kingdom of God** is the knowledge of the Holy Trinity, extending along with the constitution of the mind. *Compare Origen (Lo. XII 27; XIII 148):* For His kingdom is the contemplation of all past and future⁴) ages.

**Praktikos Prologue:** **Dispassion** <term>apatheia: a state of being free from the disturbance of the passions, not merely "apathy"</term> whose offspring is **love**; and love is the door to natural knowledge, which is succeeded by theology and ultimate blessedness. **Praktikos 1:** Christianity is the doctrine of our Savior Jesus Christ, consisting of the practical, the natural, and the theological⁵). **Praktikos 2:** The kingdom of heaven is the dispassion of the soul along with a true knowledge of beings. *Compare Origen (Lo. XIII 121):* Through the **practical**, one acquires Him (Christ) as a master of the house; through **natural contemplation**, as a king; and again, through **theology**⁶), as God. *Origen (Lo. XI 380):* The blessedness of the soul is dispassion along with a true knowledge of beings. *Origen (Lo. XIII 152):* The blessedness of the righteous is the dispassion of the soul along with the knowledge of God.

**Praktikos 40** The perfect man does not practice self-control, and the dispassionate man does not endure <note>meaning they are beyond the struggle where "endurance" is a conscious effort</note>. *Origen (Lo. XIII 122):* The knowledge of God is of a nature to dissolve the labor of the practical life. **Praktikos I 48** (Migne 1233 A): Angels rejoice when malice diminishes, but demons rejoice when virtue does. *Compare Origen (Lo. XII 36):* Angels rejoice over those who repent; demons rejoice over those who sin.

**Praktikos II 47** A symbol of the passions in the soul is either a word spoken or a movement of the body, through which the enemies perceive whether we have their thoughts within us... therefore, only God who made us knows, and not...

needs symbols (cf. 46 for God is the knower of hearts <note>original Greek: kardiognostes</note>). Cf. Lo. XII 366: "learning by observing those things through which we act; for the demons are not knowers of hearts¹)."

In a series of passages, Evagrius cites the Fathers. In two of these citations, we have already been able to establish a dependence on Origen (I 71 III 15). We shall examine a few other passages. In I 27, Evagrius recounts (as the Fathers say <note>original Greek: kathos legousin hoi pateres</note>) the five contemplations <term>theoriai: levels of spiritual insight or "seeing" into the nature of reality</term> through which the believer rises step by step: the contemplation of the adorable Trinity, of the incorporeal beings, of bodies, then as numbers 4 and 5: the contemplation of judgment and providence²).

Where the assumption of the first three contemplations originates, we already know; but even the somewhat awkwardly attached numbers 4 and 5 are borrowed from Origen:

Lo. XII 383: "God spoke the word once (Ps 71~10~), containing the word concerning providence <term>pronoia: God's care and guidance of the universe</term> and judgment." XIII 39: "He wishes to sing the word concerning providence and judgment."

*On First Principles* <note>original Greek title: peri archon</note> I 2, 13 (p. 45~13~): "*through whom the Father works, whether when He creates, or when He provides, or when He judges*³)."

Century V 24 will also belong here:
"The Fathers say that the principles of judgment are secondary to the principles of movement⁴)."

It would be important to know whether a saying about the "sevenfold circumcision," which Evagrius introduces as "the word of the Fathers," goes back to Origen. For we clearly have here (though the commentary is arbitrary) the theory of the seven vices⁵).

## III. Evagrius’s General Outlook in Relation to that of Origen.

> "In his thought entirely dependent on Origen and his school, he nonetheless gives its dogmatic reflections a touch of practical asceticism and monastic mysticism that became very important for subsequent times"—this is how—generally correctly—**Frankenberg** has characterized **Evagrius**, this most interesting figure among the monks of the Scetic desert. If one might initially suspect from the course of **Evagrius’s** life that we would find in his thoughts a reflection of the intellectual world of the great **Cappadocians** <note>The "Cappadocian Fathers" (Basil the Great, Gregory of Nazianzus, and Gregory of Nyssa) were leaders of 4th-century Christian thought; Evagrius was a protégé of Basil and Gregory of Nazianzus</note>, one very soon sees that **Evagrius** cannot be understood from that source alone; rather, one must indeed go back to the great master of his teaching, to **Origen**, and even further back to **Clement** and the **Alexandrian** school, to find the milieu from which **Evagrius** becomes comprehensible.

2) Evagrius also presents the fourfold transformation <term>metathesis: a shift or movement from one spiritual state to another</term> (from vice to virtue . . . from passionlessness <term>apatheia: a state of holy calm where one is no longer driven by disordered impulses</term> to natural contemplation . . . from this to the contemplation of rational natures . . . from all these to the Holy Trinity) "according to the Fathers," and after everything already said, this too refers to Origen.

### III. Evagrius’ General Worldview in Relation to That of Origen.

One fundamental trait of Evagrius’ general worldview makes this connection immediately clear. It is the strong emphasis on Gnosis <note>The Greek term *gnosis* refers to "knowledge," specifically a deep, spiritual understanding of divine realities.</note>, which we encounter at every turn in Evagrius’ work. "Knowledge of the Holy Trinity" <note>original: γνῶσις τῆς ἁγίας Τριάδος</note>, "natural knowledge" <note>original: γνῶσις φυσική</note>, "knowledge of the incorporeal beings" <note>original: τῶν ἀσωμάτων</note>, and "essential knowledge" <note>original: γνῶσις οὐσιώδης</note> are recurring concepts for him. In his writing, the "Gnostic" <term>Gnostikos: the advanced practitioner of spiritual knowledge</term> is still a very living figure, one who stands out even more prominently than the "spiritual man" <note>original: πνευματικός</note>. We no longer find this emphasis to such a degree among the Cappadocians <note>The "Cappadocian Fathers" (Basil the Great, Gregory of Nazianzus, and Gregory of Nyssa) were contemporaries of Evagrius who refined orthodox theology.</note>. Indeed, we must actually go back through Origen to Clement of Alexandria and the teacher of Clement—who speaks in the *Excerpts* and *Eclogae*—to find anything similar. We will even be able to prove that in his description of Gnosis and the Gnostic, new tones unique to him ring out, tones which we do not find in this specific style and abundance even in Clement and Origen. But before we go into these peculiarities of Evagrius, it will be a matter of presenting the great common body of thought that he shares specifically with Origen.

We can formulate it roughly like this: The **content** of what Evagrius presents as Gnosis rests entirely upon the worldview of Origen. Let us visualize this world-picture of Origen. At its peak stands the self-sufficient Godhead, which Origen essentially represents as the "Holy Monad" <note>original: ἁγία Μονάς; the term "Monad" refers to a perfect, indivisible unity.</note> (although he then seeks to understand it within the Trinity of Father, Son, and Spirit). It is "immaterial" <note>original: ἄϋλος</note> and "incorporeal" <note>original: ἀσώματος</note>, without "quality" <note>original: ποιότης</note> or "quantity" <note>original: ποσότης</note>. This Godhead is surrounded by the world of spirits, who were initially without bodies and whom the Godhead creates from eternity in an eternal act of creation. Movement enters this resting world-picture because the created spirits are unable to remain in the blessed rest of the Monad and in their state of bodilessness. This original sin, through which the creature separates itself from the Godhead, becomes the occasion for the creation of the physical world. For depending on the degree of their sinfulness or "negligence" <note>original: ἀμέλεια</note>, the spirits become entangled more or less deeply in physicality (*On First Principles* I 4, 1), and therefore the Godhead has prepared for them various places in the now-emerging "world" <note>original: κόσμος</note>. "What else must one say was the cause of its [the world's] existence . . . than the diversity of the falling away of those who do not flow from the Unity in the same way?" <note>original: τί ἄλλο χρὴ λέγειν αἴτιον γεγονέναι τοῦ ὑποστῆναι αὐτὸν (sc. τὸν κόσμον) . . . . ἢ τὸ ποικίλον τῆς ἀποπτώσεως τῶν οὐχ ὁμοίως τῆς Ἑνάδος ἀπορρεόντων (II 1, 1)</note>.

And from that point on, the entire drama of world history—which plays out over long, successive periods of time—consists of the falling and rising, the descending and ascending of spirits. Origen does not know if this process ever had a beginning or will ever find an absolute end. These spirits form a coherent, never-breaking chain of existence within which there are no absolute opposites; through the infinite course of time, anything can become anything. The chain of the spirit-world gains even closer connection and inner cohesion through Origen’s strongly emphasized assumption that the higher and better spirits teach, promote, and support the lower ones in their attempt to ascend. Indeed, perhaps some of them descended into the world of physicality only to provide this help to others who had fallen and were in need of aid. They are managers and rulers whom the Godhead has appointed for the individual parts of the world. — Thus the great dance of spirits joins together once more into unity and harmony, filling the eons with its labor and its suffering. — Finally, into this fundamental view, Origen also places the fate of the human soul and the biblical doctrine of the Fall. Man, too, has fallen from the original divine unity of his being. He was originally pure "Nus" <term>Nus (νοῦς): the highest part of the soul, the mind or intellect capable of direct contemplation of God</term>—a "naked mind" <note>original: γυμνὸς νοῦς</note>—but through the Fall the essence of the Mind has sunk,

It highlights how Evagrius revives an older, more intense focus on spiritual knowledge that had begun to fade among his contemporaries.</summary>

He has become the Soul <note>original: *Psyche*</note> with its split nature and its lower parts, and as the Soul, man has fallen further into corporeality. His task—or rather, his salvation taking place through divine grace—consists in the return to the lost unity of his being, in the merging of the higher part of his nature with the divine Spirit, in the liberation from the lower parts of the soul and from material corporeality. And thus, human souls also form only one part of the great realm of spirits, caught in an endless ascent and descent.

In general, sketched in broad outlines, this is the worldview of *Origen*. I have intentionally not gone further into the way *Origen* amalgamates this with the beginnings of specifically Christian religious thoughts, because the parallels between him and *Evagrius* show themselves much more clearly within this general milieu than on the ground of specifically Christian theology.

### I.

§ 1. We begin with a detailed comparison between *Origen* and *Evagrius*. Even when we look at the worldview of the Evagrian *Gnosis* <note>The Greek term for spiritual knowledge or insight</note>, the agreement shows itself on the whole. Again and again, it is a threefold division of being that he has before his eyes: that of the Godhead—the *Monad* <note>original: *Μονάς*; the ultimate Unity</note> or the *Holy Trinity* <note>original: *ἁγία Τριάς*</note>—that of the spirits and demons, which he summarizes under the term *incorporeals* <note>original: *ἀσώματα*</note>—somewhat differently, incidentally, than *Origen*—and into which he also includes human souls, the region of the *middle state* <note>original: *μεσότης*</note> between angels and demons; and finally, the corporeal *world*.

The connections become clearer when we go into detail. For *Evagrius* as well, the essence of the Godhead falls quite significantly under the concept of the *Monad*. Again and again, this tone resonates in his work. For him, the highest knowledge is *the knowledge of the holy Monad* <note>original: *ἡ τῆς ἁγίας Μονάδος γνῶσις*</note> (*contemplation* <note>original: *θεωρία*</note> ¹). God the Father is to him: *alone uniform in the Monad* <note>original: *μονοειδὴς μόνος ἐν τῇ Μονάδι*</note>; Christ belongs to this world *according to the union of the Monad* <note>original: *κατὰ τὴν τῆς Μονάδος ἕνωσιν*</note>. The essence of the divine Triad also collapses for him into the formula *uniform Triad* <note>original: *μονοειδὴς Τριάς*</note> (I 54), *the uniformity of the essence of the Holy Trinity* <note>original: *ἡ τῆς ἁγίας Τριάδος οὐσίας μονοειδής*</note> (VI 10, V 62). As the Monad, the Godhead is *undivided* <note>original: *ἄσχιστος*</note>. He is *not divided in those things in which he dwells* <note>original: *οὐ διασχισθεὶς ἐν οἷς κατοικεῖ*</note> (I 3). The highest knowledge that humans reach is *the contemplation of things not split* <note>original: *ἡ τῶν οὐκ ἐσχισμένων θεωρία*</note> (II 67), through which they themselves become undivided beings. This divine unity lacks all composition, all qualities: *the Holy Trinity is not a composite or a quality of any kind* ²) (V 62, V 55). In the letter of *Evagrius*, which has fortunately been preserved in the Greek text under *Basil's* name (Epist. Cl. I. No. 8), it says accordingly in chapter 3 ³): *For "like" and "unlike" are spoken of according to qualities; but the divine is free of quality. We confess the identity of [its] nature.* <note>original: *ὅμοιον γὰρ καὶ ἀνόμοιον κατὰ τὰς ποιότητας λέγεται· ποιότητος δὲ τὸ θεῖον ἐλεύθερον. ταυτότητα δὲ τῆς φύσεως ὁμολογοῦντες.*</note> The *qualities* <note>original: *ποιότητες*</note> belong to the corporeal world. In that [divine realm], there is therefore also no movement: *the Monad specifically does not move* <note>original: *ἡ Μονὰς ἰδίως οὐ κινεῖται*</note>. All movement originates from the (created) Intellect <term>Nus: the mind or spirit</term>, when it turns away from God (I 49, see below). And like quality, all quantity is also excluded from the Monad. The divine Monad or *Henad* <note>original: *Ἐνάς*; another term for absolute Unity</note> lies beyond the world of numbers. That is one of the favor—

Strictly speaking, only *Christ* has the knowledge of the *Monad* III 3. From him the *fellow heirs* <note>original: *συγκληρονόμοι*</note> receive it (III 72).

Thus, he contrasts the knowledge that moves within the realm of the "Four" (the elements) with the knowledge of the One (I 19), and speaks of the bodily world which splits our essence through number (I 8). It is stated quite definitively in VI 10:

-> The Holy Trinity is not like a group of four or five . . . for these are numbers; but the Holy Trinity is an essence of a single form <note>original: *μονοειδής* (monoeidēs); of one kind or uniform</note> (VI 10)¹). <-

A long explanation of how the essence of the Godhead lies beyond number is found in the great Epistle that we already mentioned above (c. 2) ²):

-> For everything that is called "one" in number is not truly one, nor is it simple in its nature; but God is confessed by all to be simple and uncomposite; therefore, God is not "one" in number . . . . For number belongs to quantity; and quantity is joined to the bodily nature. For number belongs to the bodily nature; and we have believed our Lord to be the creator of bodies; therefore every number signifies that which is material <note>original: *ἔνυλον* (enylon)</note> and has a circumscribed nature; but the **Monad** <note>The Monad represents the ultimate indivisible point of origin</note> and the **Henad** <note>The Henad represents absolute oneness</note> are significant of the simple and incomprehensible essence. <-

These same thoughts recur in Evagrius’ great Epistle to Melania (Frankenberg 613 ff.). Here, however, they appear in contexts that will occupy us further below—namely, the teachings on the origin of the created world and of number through *kinesis* <note>original: *κίνησις*; movement or change from the original state of rest</note> and the hope for the complete abolition of number at the end of all things. Thus, these parallels are only pointed out here for the time being.

Suffice it to say, the essence of the highest Godhead is the Monad. Even the relationship between Father and Son is determined by this term: *Christ is he in whom the whole Monad dwells* (III 2), *The Monad is that which is now (?) known only by Christ, whose knowledge is essential.*

One only needs to leaf through the beginning of Origen’s *On First Principles* <note>original: *περὶ ἀρχῶν* (Peri Archon)</note> to find the definition of the Godhead here:

-> a nature simple to the intellect <note>original Latin: *intellectu natura simplex*</note> ³), admitting nothing at all added to itself, so that it is not believed to have anything greater or lower within itself, but so that it is from every part a **Monad** and, so to speak, a **Henad** ⁴), and a mind and source from which is the beginning of the whole intellectual nature or mind. But a mind . . . does not need a bodily place, nor sensible magnitude, nor a physical habit or color . . . it can have nothing of expansion or hesitation, lest the simplicity of the divine nature seem to be circumscribed by such an addition (I 1, 6). <-

To this, one should add the description of the blessed (unfallen) divine world of spirits:

-> that the production of all rational beings happened as incorporeal and immaterial minds without any number or name, so that a "henad" <note>oneness</note> of all these came into being by the identity of essence and power and activity and by the... <-

...to God the Word through union and knowledge <note>1)</note>. Origen [O.] further presents the problem with regard to the state of completion (III 6, 1 p. 281 6): "in which it is asked by some whether the nature of the bodily substance, although purified to the point of clarity... does not seem to stand in the way either of the dignity of likeness or the property of unity" (cf. III 6, 4 p. 286 7)). Finally—what will be discussed more closely below in context—the fall of the spirits (the cause for the emergence of the diverse bodily world) is nothing other than the falling away of created beings from the unity of the Godhead: "the variety of the falling away of those who do not flow equally from the **Henad**" <note>original: *Ἑνάδος*; the state of absolute oneness</note> (II 1, 1 p. 107 4 f.) — and on the other hand, the completion is the return of created beings to unity: "that there shall be **one single unity** <note>original: *ἑνὰς μία* (henas mia)</note> of all rational beings, with their individual existences and numbers being abolished along with their bodies" <note>2)</note>.

§ 2. And this world of the Monad is now, for Origen as for Evagrius, the world of incorporeality and pure spirituality. The Godhead is incorporeal <note>original: *ἀσώματος* (asōmatos)</note>, immaterial <note>original: *ἄϋλος* (aylos)</note>, without form <note>original: *σχῆμα* (schēma)</note> and color <note>original: *χρῶμα* (chrōma)</note>. This actually requires no further proof on either side. With full emphasis, Origen defends this favorite thesis of his—the incorporeality of the Godhead—immediately at the beginning of his work *On First Principles* <note>original: *περὶ ἀρχῶν* (peri archon)</note> and deals with the opposing "unworthy" view of the Godhead (cf. especially I, 1, 7). In his struggle with Celsus, he emphatically stresses this free, spiritual conception of the Godhead. Chapter 23 of *On Prayer* <note>original: *περὶ εὐχῆς* (peri euches)</note> proves at length that the Godhead is not enclosed by space <note>3)</note>.

Similarly, in Evagrius, the contrast between the incorporeal and the bodily world plays a decisive role. The entire schema of his theory of knowledge, which we will treat more closely below, is built upon this contrast. Again and again we find the keywords "contemplation of the incorporeal" <note>original: *θεωρία τῶν ἀσωμάτων* (theōria tōn asōmatōn)</note> and "contemplation of the bodies" <note>original: *θεωρία τῶν σωμάτων* (theōria tōn sōmatōn)</note> <note>4)</note>. And even if he usually includes the angelic world in the field of the contemplation of the incorporeal, for him the true core of the divine bodiless world is the Holy Trinity <note>original: *ἁγία Τριάς* (hagia Trias)</note> and the highest knowledge is the "essential knowledge of the Holy Trinity" <note>original: *γνῶσις οὐσιώδης τῆς ἁγίας Τριάδος* (gnōsis ousiōdēs tēs hagias Triados)</note>.

As in Origen, so too in Evagrius, below the world of the unchangeable Holy Trinity stands the host of created angelic powers, endowed with free will, therefore changeable and belonging only conditionally to the world of bodiless spirituality. While the persons of the Trinity can never step out of the world of the Godhead and are of unchangeable persistence in their essence, this no longer applies to the entire angelic world. They are no longer of undivided essence and will. "Every rational creature is capable of praise and blame; of praise if, according to the reason it has within itself, it advances toward better things; of blame if it turns away from the right reason" (I 5, 2).

<header>III. Evagrius’ Overall Perspective in Relation to that of Origen.</header>

...because goodness in them [created beings] is not substantial, which we have certainly shown to be clearly present in Christ alone and in the Holy Spirit, and undoubtedly in the Father. For the nature of the Trinity has not been shown to have anything of composition, such that these [accidental changes] might consequently seem to happen to it <note>original Latin: *quia non substantiale sit in ipsis bonum...* from Origen's *De Principiis* I 5, 3. Origen argues that only God is "good" by nature; all other beings are good only by choice, meaning they can change or fall.</note>. Evagrius expresses this entirely in the Origenist style as follows:

"Likewise, we shall call an angel 'one' in number, but not 'one' in nature nor simple; for we understand the existence <term>hypostasis; an individual, distinct reality</term> of the angel to be a substance combined with holiness <note>original Greek: *οὐσίαν γὰρ μεθ’ ἁγιασμοῦ* (ousian gar meth’ hagiasmou)</note> (specifically, of the free will)." (Migne 32, 242 D) ¹).

The specifically problematic doctrine of Origen regarding the origin of the physical world based on the fall of the spirit-realm seems not to have been adopted by Evagrius; rather, if one can believe his commentary, he seems to occasionally polemicize against it. But characteristic for both Origen and him is the conception of the spirit-realm as a large, interconnected chain, whose links interlock in an indissoluble connection, so that through the constant sinking and rising of individual spirits, any being can become any other. This is how the Anathema <note>A formal curse or rejection of a doctrine by a church council.</note> of the Fifth Synod (Hahn³ 227 f. Koetschau p. 160 <sub>8—12</sub>) summarizes the teaching **of Origen**:

"From an angelic and archangelic state, a soulish state <term>psychic; relating to the lower soul rather than pure spirit</term> arises; from a soulish state, a demonic and human one arises; and from a human state, angels and demons arise once more; and each rank of the heavenly powers consists either entirely of those from below, or those from above, or of both those from above and below." ²)

Justinian, in his *Letter to Menas*, quotes the sentence of Origen (Koetschau p. 81 <sub>2—10</sub>):

"Since for this reason, by divine judgment measuring out according to the better or worse movements of each, and according to merit, one will have a place in the future arrangement of the world—whether an angelic rank, or a ruling power, or authority over certain things, or a throne... or lordship... while those who have not fallen very far will have the administration under those mentioned... and thus, for the most part, the human race will be constituted from those ranked under the principalities and authorities, thrones and lordships, and sometimes even from those [ranks] themselves."

Finally, Jerome summarizes the teaching of Origen in his *Letter to Avitus* (3, Migne XXII 1062, Koetschau p. 80—83, note) roughly in this sentence:

"From which it follows by logical reasoning to show that all rational creatures can be made from all [others]... and that we shall be both future angels and demons, if we act more negligently, and conversely, demons, if they wish to embrace virtues, can reach the angelic dignity."

One easily recognizes this doctrine of the "circle dance" of spirits in the saying <term>logion; a short, pithy saying</term> of Evagrius, *Century* V. 11:

"From the angelic state, humans slip into the human way of life, and from this they are brought down again into the lowliness of demons... if they turn back to ascend, they return to the ranks from which they fell."

### § 3. A favorite thought of Origen is that this chain of the spirit-world is also connected by the fact that the higher-standing and less-fallen spirits kindly take care of those dwelling below them through help and instruction, drawing them up to themselves and [making possible] the ascent into the...

---

1) Similarly, it says in chapter 10 (Migne 22. 269 D) that Satan fell from true life because his holiness was acquired <note>original: *ἐπίκτητον* (epik tēton); something added or gained rather than being part of one's essential nature</note>. — "Therefore, having fallen from the **Monad** <note>the state of divine unity</note> and having cast away the angelic dignity... he was named the devil." — Cf. also 264 D: "If the Holy Spirit is not simple <note>i.e., not a single, uncomposed substance</note>, he consists of essence and holiness; but such a thing is composite." 261 c: "If it is a servant and has acquired holiness."

2) This sentence is taken literally by Evagrius in *Century* II. 78: "Each rank of the heavenly powers consists either entirely of those from below, or entirely of those from above, or of those from above and from those from below." This is also a beautiful proof of the accuracy of the excerpts in the Anathemas <note>The formal condemnations issued by the Church</note>. Cf. also the interesting commentary, which with its explanations of angel classes and hierarchy leads over to Dionysius the Areopagite <note>A later mystical theologian who wrote the definitive Christian guide to the hierarchy of angels</note>.

It highlights the controversial idea that a human can become an angel or a demon, and vice-versa, depending on their spiritual progress or neglect.</summary>

Or in I 6, 2: <note>original Latin: "Hi vero qui de statu primae beatitudinis moti . . . sunt . . . . . sanctis beatisque ordinibus dispensandi subjecti sunt; quorum adjutorio usi et institutionibus ac disciplinis salutaribus reformati, redire ac restitui ad statum suae beatitudinis possunt"</note> "But those who have been moved from the state of primary blessedness . . . are subjected to the holy and blessed orders for their administration; having used their help and been reformed by their wholesome instructions and disciplines, they are able to return and be restored to the state of their own blessedness" (cf. also I 8, 1.) <header>III. Evagrius’s Overall Outlook in Relation to that of Origen.</header>

...seems to pass over the origin of the physical world. However, he develops his speculative view on the Fall of the first human in great detail, and it is Origenistic through and through.

I will begin here with the presentation of Evagrius, as his statements are available here in sufficient quantity and detail to allow for the drawing of a clear picture. Evagrius's conception of the Fall is primarily linked to a distinct psychology, the characteristic feature of which is the sharp separation of the mind <note>original Greek: νοῦς (*nous*), the highest intellectual or spiritual faculty</note> and the soul <note>original Greek: ψυχή (*psyche*)</note>. I cite the following sentences from I 81: "The glory of the mind is spiritual knowledge <note>original Greek: γνῶσις (*gnosis*)</note>, while the glory and light of the soul is dispassion <note>original Greek: ἀπάθεια (*apatheia*), a state of being free from emotional disturbances</note>" (cf. III 12, 16 for the definitions of the "perfect mind" and "perfect soul"). II 56: "The mind teaches the soul, and the soul teaches the body." ¹) *Practicus* 54: "Just as the soul, acting through the body, perceives the ailing members, so the mind, in its activity, recognizes its own powers." II 29: "Just as fire by its power takes hold of its body, so the mind by its power shall take hold of the soul, being entirely mingled with it in the light of the Holy Trinity." ²)

Evagrius's psychology usually stops at this point. For him, the mind is truly the higher element in man. It is telling how rarely he introduces the actual supernatural factor of the divine Spirit <note>original Greek: πνεῦμα (*pneuma*)</note> into this consideration. He does so in detail once in the *Letter to Melania* 615, 189 a–b, and here the Word <note>original Greek: λόγος (*logos*)</note> also appears alongside the Spirit; furthermore, the distinction between mind and soul is maintained. Thus, a complicated system arises: "Just as the body indicates the soul within it through its actions, and the soul itself proclaims the mind as its head through its movements; so also the mind, being the body of both the Spirit and the Word... indicates them." Likewise, it says in 617, 190 a: the body does not know its own nature; the soul knows the nature of the body, but not its own. If it were able to do so, "it would no longer be a soul but a mind; and the mind does not perceive its own nature except through the Word and the Spirit that belong to the soul." ³)

Evagrius's doctrine of the Fall operates with this terminology. I should first note that he likes to describe this process with the mysterious term *movement* <note>original Greek: κίνησις (*kinesis*)</note>. For him, the Fall is the *movement* through which the created world strives away from the unity and rest of the divine essence. This is again conceived entirely in the style of Origen, except that here the *movement* has become a specifically anthropological process rather than a general cosmological one. Thus, he says in I 49: "The Monad <note>the divine Oneness</note> does not move in itself, but it moves in the receptive part of the mind, which in its negligence ⁴) turns its face away from it." Therefore, I 51: *“Movement is the cause of evil.”* Or Evagrius asks: "Who has contemplated the first separation <note>original Greek: ἀφωρισμός</note> and who has known the first movement, and how the rational beings return through their labors to their inheritance?" VI 20 were the attributes and activities of God...

---

1) The continuation is characteristic: "and only the man of God knows the man of knowledge." <note>original Greek: ἄνθρωπος τοῦ θεοῦ τῆς γνώσεως</note> Apparently the "man of God of knowledge" is placed here in parallel with the mind. The "psychics" <note>those governed only by the soul, not the spirit</note> would then stand in opposition to them. It is noteworthy how Evagrius avoids the term Spirit <note>πνεῦμα</note> here.
2) Cf. V 44 f. (mind as the head of the soul); III 71 (distinction between the "living soul" and the mind, not spirit); IV 67, VI 55, 85 (see below); *Mirror of Monks* 107: "In a gentle soul resides a pure mind"; IV 22 ("the beast-like impulses of the soul").
3) Somewhat further up: "The Word and the Spirit—the marks <note>characters?</note> of the Father—understand all and reveal all, as they are not creations but the exact image and true radiance of the Father's essence."
4) Regarding the term negligence <note>original Greek: ἀμέλεια (*ameleia*)</note>, cf. II 31, III 28: "a sinful soul is a mind that has fallen away from the contemplation of the Holy Monad through its negligence."

enumerated before and after the movement <note>original Greek: κίνησις (*kinesis*)</note> (cf. VI 75). In VI 36, it is stated that it was Satan who began the movement. According to VI 75, free will <note>original Greek: τὸ αὐτεξούσιον (*to autexousion*)</note> is named as the author of the movement.

A detailed and coherent presentation of the nature and consequences of this movement—the Fall—is then found in the *Letter to Melania* (Frankenberg 613 ff.). Through the Fall—this is also a line of thought already familiar to us—the Mind <note>original Greek: *Nus*</note> has lost the unity of its essence. It has fallen from the essence of the divine Monad <note>The "Monad" refers to the ultimate, indivisible divine unity</note> and entered the world of "number" (see above): "numbers which entered into the Mind because of the movement" <note>original Greek: ἀριθμοὶ οἳ διὰ τὴν κίνησιν εἰς τὸν νοῦν ὑπεισῆλθον</note> (Frankenberg 617). More precisely, the fragmentation of the human being into Mind, soul, and body is a consequence of the movement (617. 190 b α). Even more characteristic is the sentence (Frankenberg 618): "it happens that because of its free will, having fallen from its first state, it was named 'soul' and, having slipped down again... it was called 'body'" ¹), and so one and the same being is now body, soul, and Mind "through the changes of its own choices" <note>original Greek: διὰ τὰς μεταβολὰς τῶν αὐτοῦ προαιρέσεων</note>. Evagrius thus teaches quite clearly a degradation of the Mind to the soul, and again from the soul to the bodily essence through the Fall ²). In a slightly different way and in strict adherence to Platonic psychology, this is expressed in VI 85 as follows: "If we possess desire and anger in common with the beasts, it is clear that these were not created with us at the beginning of creation, but they crept into the rational soul after the movement" ³).

We effortlessly recognize the world of thought and terminology of Origen here throughout. For Origen, too, the fall of creatures is a movement, even if the specific term seems to be missing: "for the Creator allowed voluntary and free movements to the minds he had established" <note>original Latin: *voluntarios enim et liberos motus a se conditis mentibus creator indulsit*</note> (II 9, 2 p. 165 25). He speaks of "the ambiguous and fragile movements of the soul itself" <note>original Latin: *animae ipsius ambigui fragilesque motus*</note> (I 8, 4. 102, 6). — With him, too, the catchphrase appears that man fell through his "negligence" <note>original Greek: ἀμέλεια (*ameleia*)</note> (see above) ⁴). I further recall that a pair of sayings by Evagrius, whose meaning rests on the terminological distinction between Mind <note>original Greek: *νοῦς*</note> and soul <note>original Greek: *ψυχή*</note>, has proven to be a literal quotation from Origen: "the soul that acts is a lyre... the pure Mind is a psaltery" <note>original Greek: κιθάρα ἐστὶν ψυχὴ πρακτική .... ψαλτήριόν ἐστι νοῦς καθαρός</note> (VI 46. 48 see above p. 291).

The theory of the inferiority of the human soul <note>original Greek: *ψυχή*</note>, upon which Evagrius's entire outlook rests, is further developed by Origen in detail in his chapter *On First Principles* <note>original Greek: *περὶ ἀρχῶν* (*Peri Archon*)</note> II 8. He demonstrates here how the soul, the "imaginative and impulsive essence" <note>original Greek: οὐσία φανταστικὴ καὶ ὁρμητική</note>, is common to both humans and animals, how the angels are never called "souls" in Scripture, and how the "soul of God" is only spoken of exceptionally and improperly, while it is with

1) Cf. Frankenberg 619 191 b α: "Before sin separated the minds from God... they were one in Him without change; but as their sin became known, they were separated from Him and became alienated from Him and from His taste and from His color, as each one acquired his own body."
2) In connection with this are the terms "density" or "thickness" <note>original Greek: παχύτης, παχύς</note>, which Evagrius likes to use in relation to the bodily essence of humans. Cf. IV 46 "the density of this world," II 68 "dense bodies," II 62 "then the density of the bodies shall also be removed from our midst." *Letter* in Migne 32. 260 A "denser teaching" (cf. 256 B). *Practicus* 29 "the Mind having become thickened." — That Evagrius is dependent on Origen's usage here is proven by the circumstance that *Centuries* IV 36, where the "intelligible fat" is interpreted as the "density" of our Mind, stems literally from Origen, *Selections on the Psalms* (Lommatzsch XII 51). Cf. the latter's speculation on the "garments of skins" (Koetschau *On First Principles* p. 159 note) and *Against Celsus* III 35.
3) We find slightly different phrasing for the degradation of the Mind in the *Letter* in Migne 32. 257 c: "since our Mind, having become thickened, is bound to the dust and mingled with the clay." 260 A, 263 A "the Mind bound to the flesh." — *Practicus* 70 = *Centuries* VII 26: "the passions binding it [the Mind] through thoughts to things and to sensible objects." Cf. VII 52. 56, IV 62. 70, V 57.

It highlights how these ideas and specific terminologies, such as "negligence" and "density," are directly inherited from Origen's psychological and cosmological framework.</summary>

<page-num>301</page-num>
<header>III. Evagrius’s Overall Outlook in Relation to that of Origen.</header>

...that Christ's <term>soul <note>Greek: ψυχή (*psyche*)</note></term> has a special nature. He appeals to Paul's keywords of the "soulish man" <note>Greek: ψυχικὸς ἄνθρωπος (*psychikos anthropos*)</note> and the "soulish body" <note>Greek: ψυχικὸν σῶμα (*psychikon soma*)</note>. From 1 Corinthians 14:15, he concludes "that [Paul] joins and associates the mind <note>Latin: *mentem*</note> more than the soul with the Holy Spirit." When (Luke 19:10) speaks of the salvation of the soul by Jesus, he objects: "the soul that is saved no longer remains a soul" <note>original Greek: οὐκέτι μένει ψυχή ἡ σωθεῖσα ἡ ψυχή</note>. Only the higher part of a human's soulful being is saved. He points out that according to Scripture, God is fire and his angels are flames of fire, and that where the text speaks of falling away from the Godhead, it speaks of the preservation of love. And so, from here, he gains the turn of phrase that leads directly into his theory on the nature of the Fall: "we must ask whether perhaps the name for the soul [which in Greek is called *psyche*] was derived from its 'cooling down' <note>Latin: *a refrigerescendo*</note> from a more divine and better state, and transferred because it seems to have cooled from that natural and divine heat, and is thus placed in its current state and name" (p. 157, 14). "From all this, it seems shown that the mind, declining from its state and dignity, was made into or named a soul." Corresponding to this is a quotation which Methodius has preserved for us in *On the Resurrection* from Origen (Commentary on Genesis): he taught that Adam and Eve were "naked minds <note>original: γυμνοὺς νόας (*gymnous noas*)</note> before the garments of skin <note>A reference to the physical bodies given to Adam and Eve after the Fall in Genesis 3:21</note>, entirely incorruptible and immune to death, flux, eating, drinking, and sleep" (Koetschau 161, note).

Even clearer is the summary of Origenist teaching in Koetschau 161: 5: "the <term>Mind <note>Greek: νοῦς (*nous*); Latin: *mens*</note></term>, in falling, became the soul," and in the Anathemata <note>Formal condemnations or excommunications</note> of the 5th Ecumenical Synod (Koetschau 160: 1): "rational beings who had cooled from divine love <note>The Greek word for soul, *psyche*, was often linked by these thinkers to the word *psycho*, meaning 'to cool'</note> and were thereafter named souls, for the sake of punishment, were clothed in thicker bodies like our own and named humans." If one compares this with the description of the Fall in Evagrius’s *Letter to Melania*, one sees that the latter follows the view of his master almost word for word. However, a terminological difference between Origen and Evagrius must be emphasized here. To characterize the higher essence in man, Origen likes to use the biblical and specifically supernatural concept of <term>Spirit <note>Greek: πνεῦμα (*pneuma*)</note></term>, while Evagrius—as far as I can see—remains essentially focused on the opposites of "Mind" <note>*nous*</note> and "soul" <note>*psyche*</note>. That is, Evagrius prefers philosophical language and anthropological terms at this point, while Origen shows himself more strongly influenced by biblical (Pauline) or popular usage and the supernatural view. This will become particularly clear in what follows during the description of the return of the human being to divine unity. I note here Origen's sentence from the Anathemata (Koetschau 161: 2): "By the falling away and the cooling from living in the spirit, that which is now called the soul came to be." But Origen nonetheless employs different perspectives side-by-side;¹ in *On First Principles* (II. 10, 7), during an exegesis of Luke 12:42-46, he even places three views side-by-side as equally valid: the supernatural (the opposition between soul and divine spirit), the anthropological (the opposition of the higher and lower parts of the human essence), and the mythological (the natural essence of the human and his angel). Evagrius essentially borrowed the anthropological line of thought from his teacher.

2) Cf. above p. 289 and, for example, the immediate continuation of the sentence just quoted 161: 3: "(the soul) being also capable of the return to that which it was in the beginning... so that this whole being becomes Mind <note>*nous*</note>."

# Book III. Studies on Evagrius.

§ 5. Following the doctrine of the Fall, we find in Evagrius—as in Origen—the view of the human soul’s return to its original state of being. We find the clearest and most detailed testimony once again in the **Letter to Melania 617.** <note>Evagrius wrote this letter to Melania the Elder, a prominent desert mother and intellectual peer.</note> 190 a α: "And just as it shall be <note>original: καὶ ὥσπερ ἔσται</note> that these names and numbers shall be taken away from the midst of the body, the soul, and the mind during the ascent into the state of the mind, so it shall be that names and numbers <note>original: ὀνόματα καὶ ἀριθμοὶ</note> shall be taken away from the Father, His Son, and the Spirit, and from His rational creation, which is His body" (1 Corinthians 15:28). Evagrius thus hopes for a time when the reunification of the Trinity with the creature that fell away from it will take place. This will happen when the unity of the now-divided human being is restored by the lower components of its essence—the *soul* and the *body*—being taken up (*ἀνάγεσθαι*) <note>meaning to be raised up or sublimated</note> into the *essence of the <term>Nus</term>* <note>The "Nus" or Mind is the highest part of the human spirit in this system.</note>. Of this time it is said: "names and numbers are taken away, which entered into the mind because of the movement" <note>original: αἴρονται δὲ ὀνόματα καὶ ἀριθμοί, οἳ διὰ τὴν κίνησιν ὑπεισῆλθον εἰς τὸν νοῦν. In this theology, "movement" refers to the initial turning away from God that caused the Fall.</note>. Just as the sea receives the rivers into itself, so the individual beings will flow into the Holy Trinity and exist with it in unbreakable unity (*ἕνωσις*) and intermingling (*σύμμιξις*) (619. 191 a α).

In similar mysterious turns of phrase, Origen speaks of overcoming the fragmentation of the human being and its union with God (*On First Principles* I 84): *the sons of God, or those who, mortifying their members which are upon the earth and transcending not only their corporeal nature but even the uncertain and fragile movements of the soul itself, have joined themselves to the Lord, having been made entirely spirit.* Very clearly, too, speaks the passage in *On Prayer* 9, 2: "And the soul, being lifted up and following the spirit, and being separated from the body, and not only following the spirit but also coming to be in it... how does it not, by laying aside its being as a 'soul,' become spiritual?" A third passage I quote because it shows once again the role played in Origen's thought by the idea of the abolition of all "number" in the hereafter (Anathema XIV of the 5th Synod): <note>The 5th Ecumenical Council in 553 AD condemned several of these Origenist ideas as heretical.</note> "that there shall be a single unity <note>original: ἑνὰς μία</note> of all rational beings, their substances and numbers being taken away along with their bodies; and when the knowledge concerning rational beings is followed by the destruction of worlds, the laying aside of bodies, and the removal of names, there shall be an identity of knowledge just as there is of substances; and that in the storied <term>restoration</term> <note>original: ἀποκατάστασις (*apokatastasis*), the belief that all creation will eventually return to God.</note> they shall be alone and naked."

We have just seen in several examples how Origen, in these contexts, as already explained above, likes to let the term <term>spirit</term> <note>original: πνεῦμα (*pneuma*)</note> take the place of the <term>Nus</term>. However, in this context he can also speak of the <term>Nus</term> (II 8, 3 p. 158 23): *the mind, declining from its state and dignity, was made into or named a soul; if it is repaired and corrected, it returns to being a mind.*

---

1) Frankenberg 618: "It shall be that his choices and movements will produce differences. And he shall stand in his first creation."
2) Compare the Anathemas in Koetschau I 159 4: "that incorporeal and immaterial minds have come to be apart from all number and name, so that there is a unity of all these."
3) Compare the Letter in Migne 32. 260 B: "and number is destroyed by the arrival of the Monad," and the obscure hints in *Centuries* I 7, 8; VII 7, which become understandable in this context.
4) III 4, 3 p. 268: "the soul, before it turns itself to the spirit and becomes one with it... seems to be in a state that is neither good nor bad, but similar, if I may say so, to an animal state. It is better, however, if possible, that by clinging to the spirit it becomes spiritual." — It is interesting to see how Origen's Christology develops from here. Jesus had a soul which never separated itself from its connection to its higher essence: "that soul... from the beginning of creation and thereafter inseparably... clinging as it were to the wisdom and Word of God... and the whole receiving the Whole and passing into its light and splendor, it became primarily one spirit with Him."
5) Compare also *Commentary on John* XXX 218 (on the difference between <term>soul</term> <note>original: ψυχή (*psyche*)</note> and <term>spirit</term> <note>original: πνεῦμα (*pneuma*)</note>).

It highlights the technical distinctions between soul, spirit, and mind in the process of returning to God.</summary>
