### III. Evagrius's Overall Vision in Relation to that of Origen.

(161 7) The **mind** <note>original Greek: νοῦς (Nus)</note>, that is, the mind <note>original Latin: mens</note>, having fallen, became a **soul**, and conversely, the soul, instructed in virtues, shall become a mind again. According to Origen's *Selections on Jeremiah* (ed. Lomm. XIV 437), this ultimate goal of human life is already achieved in this world through the anchoretic—contemplative life. He who leads his existence in such a life can truly say: "I sat alone," <note>original Greek: κατὰ μόνας ἐκαθήμην</note> that is, he sits alone by not being troubled by the multitude of passions, but having withdrawn entirely into the mind and the "one" <note>the state of unity</note> that is within him.

Origen allows this entire development downwards and upwards (touching upon Platonic and Stoic lines of thought) to take place over infinitely many periods of time or worlds, so that each time the state of the spirit world in an **Aeon** <note>An "aeon" is a vast age or cycle of time in this cosmological system.</note> presents itself to him as the consequence and fruit of the deeds and labors of the spirits. This dangerous view—which undermines the specific significance of the redemption accomplished in Jesus and fails to do justice to the powerful earnestness of early Christian <term>eschatology</term> <note>theology concerned with the final events of history and the ultimate destiny of humanity</note>—seems to have been generally avoided by Evagrius. Possibly, however, we do find here and there a few hints pointing toward this doctrine. Specifically, Evagrius likes to speak of the **knowledge of the aeons**, which becomes manifest to the <term>Gnostic</term> <note>In Evagrius’s writing, a "Gnostic" is a Christian who has attained "gnosis" or deep spiritual knowledge, rather than a member of a heretical sect.</note>. This catchphrase recurs particularly in his letters: "The fullness of Christ is the spiritual knowledge of the aeons, both those that have been and those that are to come, along with true faith in the Holy Trinity" <note>original: πλήρωμα δὲ Χριστοῦ ἐστιν πνευματικὴ γνῶσις τῶν αἰώνων τῶν τε γεγονότων καὶ τῶν μελλόντων μετὰ ἀληθινῆς τῆς ἁγίας Τριάδος πίστεως</note> (Frankenberg 611. Letter 61), — "knowledge of the contemplation of the aeons (Frankenberg: worlds) both those that have been and those that are to come; those that have been through faith, and those to come through purity of heart" (Frankenberg 575. Letter 14). *Praktikos* 69: "A rational nature put to death by malice is raised by Christ through the contemplation of all the aeons." <note>original: φύσιν μὲν λογικὴν ὑπὸ κακίας θανατωθεῖσαν ἐγείρει Χριστὸς διὰ τῆς θεωρίας πάντων τῶν αἰώνων</note> In *Centuries* I 70, the "understanding of the aeons" <note>original: σύνεσις τῶν αἰώνων</note> stands as the "fourth" (see below) knowledge behind the knowledge of the Holy Trinity (1), of the incorporeal beings (2), and of corporeal things (3). Might Evagrius not have been thinking here in all these instances of the mysterious doctrine of the successive cycles of the world? Naturally, in this context, in closer connection with Greek terminology, the word **worlds** <note>original: κόσμοι (kosmoi)</note> could also have been used. The Syrian texts offer no possibility of distinction here. The latter term is confirmed by *Mirror for Monks* 135: "Contemplations of the worlds broaden the heart." <note>original: κόσμων θεωρίαι πλατύνουσι τὴν καρδίαν</note>

**§ 6.** Finally, it may be pointed out that, in connection with this conception of the height and purity of all spiritual essences and especially of the human essence, Evagrius shows an optimistic monistic basic mood which he shares with Origen and the Alexandrians, as well as with Eastern theologians in general. Sin and all evil are, after all, only an **accident** <note>In philosophy, an "accident" is a property that is not essential to the nature of a thing; thus, sin is not part of the human "essence."</note> in the great events of the world, arising from the freedom of the will; the goodness of "nature" remains untouched despite everything; evil is destined to disappear. "It is a cloud, it will pass." <note>original Latin: Nubila est, transibit.</note> This view finds particularly strong and powerful expression in Evagrius. He has treated it most coherently in the related (identical) passages *Centuries* I 39. 40. *Praktikos* 65. *Ber.* 18. *Fr.* 579; 43 *Fr.* 595; 59 *Fr.* 609.

***

1) Cf. Origen *Selecta in Psalmos* Lomm. XIII 43 and 44: "The inheritance of rational nature is the contemplation of the aeons that have been and those that shall be; the inheritance of Christ is the knowledge of God." <note>original: κληρονομία φύσεως λογικῆς ἐστιν ἡ θεωρία τῶν γεγονότων καὶ τῶν γενησομένων αἰώνων, κληρονομία δὲ Χριστοῦ ἡ γνῶσις τοῦ θεοῦ.</note>
2) Cf. also Letter 56 Frankenberg 605. 183 a β "the aeons both past and future."
3) A literal parallel in *Centuries* VII 24. Here, therefore, "aeons" is certainly to be translated instead of "worlds," contrary to Frankenberg.
4) Cf. *Centuries* VII 52, where there is talk of the spiritual contemplation which draws the human soul to itself "by the sweetness of the worlds (above: Frankenberg: aeons?)."
5) Cf. e.g., Origen at the place cited above: "because it seems to have cooled from that natural and divine color." <note>original Latin: quod ex colore illo naturali et divino refrixisse videatur.</note>

presented. While only two forces work against the good in us—the forces of the demons and the **choice** <note>original Greek: προαίρεσις (proairesis)</note> of our own will—three fundamental forces oppose evil: the assistance of the angels, the **choice** of our will toward the good, and the **goodness of our nature**. **No evil thought proceeds from nature, for we were not made evil from the beginning, since the Lord sowed good seed in his own field... for there was a time when evil was not, and there will be a time when it shall not be**¹) · **for the seeds of virtue cannot be erased**. Even in Hades, the rich man took pity on his brothers: **to show mercy happens to be the most beautiful seed of virtue**. Quite analogously, it is stated in *Centuries* I 41 (cf. II 8; I 59): **If death is second to life and sickness second to health, it is clear that evil is also second to virtue. For evil is the death and sickness of the soul; but virtue is older even than the intermediate state** <note>original Greek: μεσότης (mesotēs). This is a technical term used here to describe the current empirical or fallen state of human existence, situated between our original creation and our final restoration.</note> (a paraphrase for the empirical human being). — There are three types of human life: the natural, that which is above nature (the monastic life), and that which is against nature. The first two are according to God's will; the third stems from the **negligence** <note>original Greek: ἀμέλεια (ameleia)</note> of the human will (I 21)²). A perfected soul is therefore one **whose passionate power acts according to nature**³).

# II.

**§ 7.** If Evagrius is original in anything compared to Origen, it is on the ground of practical piety. At the very least, the shift toward the subjective plays a completely different role than it does with his master. To him, speculations about the world-whole, about the Godhead, the relationship of the three persons in the Trinity, and the two natures in Christ are relatively indifferent. He uses the entire worldview again and again to demonstrate his favorite ideas: the gradual elevation of the human soul. The old "Gnostic" favorite idea of the human soul's ascent to its heavenly home is also his. However, in his work, everything appears already spiritualized; the various levels of heaven are transformed into different stages of progressing knowledge, and only now and then does the original spatial conception of <term>Gnosis</term> <note>From the Greek word for "knowledge," referring here to the mystical insight into divine mysteries.</note> glimmer through, for instance, when he speaks of **places of knowledge** <note>original Greek: τόποι τῆς γνώσεως (topoi tēs gnōseōs)</note>. Furthermore, his theoretical view was everywhere tailored to the practical; I recall the strong emphasis on the practical-pedagogical importance of the angelic powers for the soul rising toward its heavenly home.

Above all, his view of the Fall and his resulting doctrine of the essence of fallen man stand in immediate connection with the goals and tasks that he sets for practical piety.

---

1) Origen, *Selections on the Psalms* (ed. Lomm. XIII 139): **Therefore, evil being in the middle, it exists neither in the beginning nor in the end.**
2) Evagrius emphasizes very strongly that the human free will, and not perhaps the natural determination of the body, bears the blame for sin: III 53. 54. 59. IV 60. 62. This point of view, moreover, is entirely compatible with the strong emphasis—also maintained by Evagrius—on the inferiority of the body within the human being. The seat and origin of sin is precisely not the body, but the free will. One must not look for any polemic against Origen here. Cf. also the characteristic passage: **The things commonly considered good and evil** (following the correction against Frankenberg) **are found partly within the soul and partly outside of it. But things that are truly evil cannot be found outside of it.**
3) Cf. *The Practicus* 58: **A rational soul acts according to nature when its desiring part** <note>original Greek: ἐπιθυμητικόν (epithymētikon)</note> **longs for virtue, and its spirited part** <note>original Greek: θυμικόν (thymikon)</note> **works for its sake.** *The Practicus* 14 regarding natural anger (against the demons); *Centuries* III 59 on the good and bad use of the **spirited** and **desiring** parts. Cf. the reflection on **wrath** <note>original Greek: ὀργή (orgē)</note> in Diadochos.

<page-num>305</page-num>
<header>III. Evagrius’ General Outlook in Relation to that of Origen.</header>
<sig>20</sig>
<meta>Bousset, Monasticism.</meta>

Through the Fall, as stated above, humanity lost the unity of its essence. Our original nature, which was **pure Mind** <note>original Greek: γυμνὸς νοῦς (gymnos nous), literally "naked mind"</note>, has deteriorated and become coarsened; the human being has become **soul** <note>original Greek: ψυχὴ (psychē)</note> and **body** <note>original Greek: σῶμα (soma)</note>, and the original clarity of our essence has been clouded. From this arises a two-fold task of the Christian life: the human being must overcome the lower nature and lead it back to its original unity—this happens through **ascetic practice** <note>original Greek: πρακτική (praktikē), the "practical life" of discipline</note>; but above all, one must return from the state of **ignorance** <note>original Greek: ἀγνωσία (agnosia)</note> to that of **spiritual knowledge** <note>original: Gnosis</note>—this happens through **contemplation** <note>original Greek: θεωρητική (theōrētikē), the "contemplative life"</note>. —

**Ascetic practice** and **contemplation** comprise the new fundamental tasks of the Christian life. Evagrius, following Platonic psychology, can also express this somewhat differently at times (*Praktikos* 6): **Reading, vigil, and prayer stabilize the wandering mind** <note>the contemplative life</note>. **Hunger, toil, and withdrawal wither inflamed desire; while psalmody, long-suffering, and mercy calm boiling anger** <note>the practical life</note>¹). Here, too, he seems to follow older authorities. At the very least, he himself quotes a very similar-sounding saying by Serapion of Thmuis: **The fallen mind is perfectly purified by spiritual knowledge; love heals the inflamed parts of anger; and self-control halts the influx of evil desires.**

But usually, Evagrius rests upon the two great requirements of **ascetic practice** and **contemplation**. It is almost superfluous to go into details here. I will cite a series of passages from the *Centuries* in which Frankenberg, in his translation, does not seem to have correctly rendered Evagrius’ terminology. VII 16: **The practical man** <note>original Greek: ἄνθρωπος πρακτικός (anthrōpos praktikos)</note>²) (Frankenberg: "worker") **is the one who uses the things given by God justly**³). In VII 41 and 42, a definition of the **practical man** (Frankenberg: "worker") stands alongside a definition of the **contemplative man** <note>original Greek: θεωρητικός (theōrētikos)</note>.

Incidentally, the terms **contemplation** <note>original Greek: θεωρία (theōria)</note> and **contemplative** are very frequently replaced by the others: **knowledge** <note>original: Gnosis</note> and **knower** <note>original Greek: γνωστικός (gnostikos)</note>. In VII 35 f., the **knower** and the **practical man** (Frankenberg: "worker") are contrasted (in the same way as the practical and contemplative were just now). Likewise, it says in *Gnostikos* 104: **Those in the practical life and those in the life of knowledge both understand the inner meanings of things, but only those in the life of knowledge see the questions of spiritual knowledge.** V 65: **A practical man** (Frankenberg: "worker") **is one who acts** (Frankenberg: "works") **with discernment, but a knower is a helper of wisdom.** VI 15: **The feet of Christ are practice and contemplation.** *Gnostikos* 132: **If ascetic practice coexists with knowledge, it teaches humility to those who possess it.**

---

1) Compare the similar phrasing in *Centuries* II 28, II 57, III 35, *Praktikos* 63, and II 26–62.
2) In the Syriac, the term **laboring man** <note>original Syriac: ܓܒܪܐ ܦܠܚܐ (gabra palkha)</note> appears throughout here. A related phrase is found in VII 49: **the man who acts** <note>original Syriac: ܓܒܪܐ ܥܒܘܕܐ (gabra aboda)</note>. Frankenberg translates this as "man the maker" <note>original Greek: ἀνὴρ ποιητής (anēr poiētēs)</note>; I would suggest **laborious** <note>original Greek: πονικός (ponikos)</note>.
3) I would also suspect **practical mind** <note>original Greek: νοῦς πρακτικός (nous praktikis)</note> in VII 11, 17, and **practical soul** <note>original Greek: ψυχὴ πρακτική (psychē praktikē)</note> in II 6. In I 11, there is mention of **spiritual bodies** (those of the perfected Gnostics) and **practical bodies** (Frankenberg: "workers"?). The correctness of this translation is proven by comparing Origen (*Lomm.* IX 392): **Judgment is the transition for the righteous from the practical body to the angelic** <note>that is, spiritual</note> **body.**
4) Here Frankenberg also translates the Syriac **worker and knower** with **practical and gnastic**.
5) Thus, although Frankenberg translates the Syriac **labor/service** with doubt.
6) Frankenberg’s translation from the Syriac: **the work of labor/service**.

IV 63 A spiritual ephod <note>original Greek: ἐφὼδ πνευματικόν (ephod pneumatikon). An ephod was a priestly garment in the Old Testament; here it symbolizes a spiritual covering or dignity.</note> is spiritual knowledge, which encourages those in the practical life (Frankenberg: "laborers")¹).

But I will break off here for now and refer in advance to the passages to be discussed below, where we will encounter the more precise Evagrian division into *practice* <note>original: πρακτική (praktikē)</note>, *physics* <note>original: φυσική (physikē), meaning the contemplation of the natural world</note>, and *theology* <note>original: θεολογία (theologia), the highest stage of contemplating God</note>, just as the equating of *contemplation* <note>original: θεωρία (theōria)</note> and *knowledge* <note>original: γνῶσις (gnosis)</note> still requires a more detailed explanation. But let it be pointed out now with all emphasis that Evagrius borrowed these two great slogans from Origen. I quote only a few passages from the *Selections on the Psalms* <note>original Latin title: Selecta in Psalmos</note>, which could be multiplied at will: Lomm. XII 6: The knowledge of God is divided into practice and contemplation . . . before contemplation comes practice. XII 41: the practical and contemplative life. XII 67: a person's feet are prepared like those of a deer through practice, but they are raised up through contemplation (bronze is a symbol of practice). XII 81: through practice we find God, but through knowledge we are found by Him. XII 136: through practice the Lord rescues someone, through knowledge He nourishes them ²). XII 321: through practice [the mind] gores its enemies, but through knowledge it brings to naught those who rise up against it. XIII 122: for the knowledge of God alone is of such a nature as to release the weariness of practice. XIII 131: the contemplative ones are in the house of God, but the practical ones are in the courtyards of the house of our God³).

§ 8. We will linger a little longer on what Evagrius calls *practice* <note>original: πρακτική</note>. The explicit end goal of *practice* for Evagrius is **dispassion** <note>original: ἀπάθεια (apatheia), a state where the soul is no longer troubled by impulsive emotions or passions.</note>. *Mirror of Monks* 3: A practical soul is the throne of dispassion⁴). 120: The flesh of Christ is the practical virtues, and he who eats them will become dispassionate. *The Praktikos* 53: Dispassion is the flower of practice. *The Praktikos* 64: Dispassion of the rational soul is a wedding garment. It is thus openly stated that such a state of perfection is indeed an attainable goal for the monk and not just a boundless ideal⁵). The monk should remember how, being full of passions, he has passed over to dispassion by the mercy of Christ, and how he again left the world (*The Praktikos* 22). He should be thankful to the Creator <note>original: Demiurge</note> that he has acquired the soul's dispassion in this body (*The Praktikos* 34). The monk is the "new man" in whom, through dispassion, there is neither male nor female (*The Praktikos* 63) ⁶). In *dispassion*, he experiences the resurrection even in this life: the small resurrection of the soul is the transition from dispassion into the state of dispassion <note>original: Cent. V. 22</note>. The life of such a perfected person stands beyond all toil and labor ⁷): the perfect man does not [need to] practice self-restraint, and the dispassionate man does not [merely] endure (*The Praktikos* 40) ⁸).

***

1) Origen Lomm. XIII 122: knowledge nourishes the soul by teaching it the principles <note>original: λόγους (logous)</note> of the practical life.
2) Cf. Evagrius *Praktikos* II 56: and we shall call dispassion the health of the soul, and knowledge its food.
3) XI 392 (see above) XII 49. 71. 108. 326. 341. XIII 23. 62. 75. 98 (laborers of virtue) 130.
4) Note how in Evagrius’s terminology it is specifically the "soul" <note>original: ψυχή (psychē)</note> (not the Mind or *Nus*) that is brought into connection with dispassion. This is understandable after all that has been said. I 81: the glory and light of the Mind is spiritual knowledge, but the glory and light of the soul is dispassion.
5) Here begins the well-known polemic of Jerome against Evagrius. *Letter to Ctesiphon*: Evagrius, who writes to virgins, writes to monks, writes to her whose name [Melania] testifies by its "blackness" to the darkness of her perfidy. *Letter to Melania*: he published a book and maxims "on dispassion" <note>original: περὶ ἀπαθείας</note>, which we can call "impassibility" . . . when the mind is never moved by any vice of disturbance and, to put it simply, becomes either a stone or a God. <note>Jerome is criticizing the idea that a human can become totally immune to emotion, suggesting it makes one inhuman.</note>
6) The second main sin (besides sexual immorality) from which dispassion frees us is anger. *Gnostikos* 107 f. 112. 147. (129, 130). Therefore *Mirror of Monks* 99 says: from gentleness, knowledge is born.
7) See above, Origen Lomm. XIII 122: for the knowledge of God alone is of such a nature as to release the weariness of practice.
8) Cf. also *Praktikos* II 56. 58. 60 (perfect and imperfect dispassion). *Gnostikos* 140. *Mirror of Monks* 6. 66. 68. 105 and elsewhere. V 38 (dispassion-truth) V 64, an unblemished mirror—the dispassionate soul V 86, VI 35, VII 2. 3.

<summary>This page analyzes the concept of "practice" (praktike) in Evagrius's thought, illustrating his debt to Origen and identifying "dispassion" (apatheia) as the practical life's ultimate, attainable goal. It also highlights the historical controversy surrounding these ideas, particularly Jerome's harsh critique of Evagrius and his patron Melania.</summary>

<page-num>307</page-num>
<header>III. Evagrius’s General Outlook in Relation to that of Origen.</header>

And here again, the influence of Origen shines through. Compare the following from the *Selections on the Psalms* <note>original Latin title: Selecta in Psalmos</note>, edited by Lommatzsch, volume XI, page 380: "The blessedness of the soul is dispassion <note>original Greek: ἀπάθεια (apatheia), a state of being free from emotional disturbance or 'passions'</note> together with the true knowledge of all that exists." And volume XIII, page 152: "The blessedness of the righteous is the soul’s dispassion together with the knowledge of God." It is highly characteristic of the language of monastic mysticism that this virtue of dispassion is either equated with love <note>original: ἀγάπη (agape), specifically spiritual or perfect love</note> or regarded as its preliminary stage. For the monastic mystic—as is generally the case in the language of Christian piety (a study of Clement of Alexandria's usage is recommended here)—love is not primarily "neighborly love" in a broad sense, but rather **love for God**. The mystic's heart is so filled with this love that, by comparison, love for one's neighbor plays no role at all; indeed, it is almost felt to be a hindrance to the love of God. Dispassion shares an inner kinship only with this love for God. At the same time, this spiritual love forms the transition from the *practical life* <note>original: πρακτική (praktikē), or ascetic discipline</note> to *spiritual knowledge* <note>original: γνῶσις (gnosis)</note> or *contemplation* <note>original: θεωρητική (theōretikē)</note>. Here I have gathered a series of sentences from Evagrius on this point:

*The Practical Life* <note>original title: Praktikon</note>, chapter 35: "The goal of the practical life is love (and the goal of knowledge is theology)."
*Mirror for Monks*, 67: "Dispassion leads the way before love, and love leads before knowledge."
Introduction to the *Praktikon*: "Dispassion, whose offspring is love; and love is the door to natural knowledge."
*Praktikon*, 53: "Love is the offspring of dispassion (and dispassion is the flower of the practical life)."
*Centuries*, I 86: "The surpassing state of the rational soul, in which it is impossible to love anything of this world more than the knowledge of God."
*Praktikon*, 24: "Self-control <note>original: ἐγκράτεια (enkrateia)</note> cuts away the passions of the body, but spiritual love cuts away those of the soul."¹)

The mysticism passed down by Evagrius can also express this in many other ways. Above all, the concept of purity <note>original: καθαρότης (katharotes)</note> or the pure mind <note>original: καθαρὸς νοῦς (katharos nous)</note> plays a leading role.

Only those who have purified their spirit through the practical life to reach dispassion can and may turn toward spiritual knowledge. *Centuries*, IV 70: "[There are those] who, through the purity of the soul and even without this body, are able to look upon the contemplation of all that exists." IV 90: "Even the impure can acquire education <note>original: παιδεία (paideia), referring here to secular or profane learning</note>, but contemplation belongs only to the pure." VI 34: "Through the service <note>possibly 'labor' or 'work'</note> of the commandments, God clothes us in the seal of His purity." VII 45: "The pure mind is the altar of God, which is not moved or disturbed by the memory of the world's structure" (compare VI 48: "A pure mind is one moved by spiritual knowledge"). V 52: "To see bodies we need a pure mind, but to see incorporeal things we need an abundance of purity; how much more so if we should attempt to see the Holy Trinity." V 66: "It is impossible for the mind to participate in spiritual knowledge before the passionate part of the soul is healed."²) Only the pure soul is a mirror, unstained by worldly things, which is capable of receiving the rays of divine knowledge. Evagrius also likes to describe this state of the mind <note>original: Nus</note> in dispassion with the keyword "nakedness" <note>original: γυμνότης (gymnotēs)</note>, meaning freedom from the lower powers of the soul and body. III 69: "Primary contemplation requires a naked mind" (see III 6). *Letter* 58: "The essential knowledge is revealed to a mind naked of passions." III 70: "It is the mark of a naked mind to ask: what is the nature of God?" ³).

---

1) *Centuries*, III 58 (spiritual love) IV 25. 50.
2) Compare the *Epistle* in Migne, volume 32, 257 C, where it says of the mind: "so that, having grown little by little, it may be strong enough to approach the Godhead in nakedness." — The slogans of "stripping" <note>original: γυμνωθῆναι (gymnōthēnai)</note> and "unfolding" <note>original: ἐξαπλωθῆναι (exaplōthēnai)</note> of the mind can be traced back to philosophical mysticism.
3) Compare also III 5, V 39. 57. 90, VI 67, VII 6. In Frankenberg's *Letters*, pages 559, 156 b a, 595, 615, 189 α β. Regarding the purifying power of knowledge itself, see V 76 and others.

It highlights the distinction between simple neighborly love and the intense, singular focus on the divine required by monastic mysticism.</summary>

<header>Book III. Studies on Evagrius.</header>

To describe the blessed state of the <term>pure mind</term> <note>original Greek: καθαρὸς νοῦς (katharos nous)</note>, Evagrius frequently uses the terms **state** <note>original Greek: κατάστασις (katastasis)</note> (of the soul or the mind), **peace**, **calm**, and **stillness**... In his *Centuries* V 39, he writes: "Peace is the state <note>original: κατάστασις (katastasis)</note> of dispassion belonging to the rational nature." In *The Practical Life* II 57: "There are two peaceful states of the soul." (Also in *The Practical Life* 52: "a peaceful state.") In *Centuries* VII 3: "Dispassion is a state of calm <note>original: γαλήνη (galene)</note> of the rational soul, consisting of humility and temperance." In III 17, there is mention of three different conditions of this **state**; we will discuss the higher levels of the **state**—which the "Gnostic" <note>In this context, a "Gnostic" is not a member of a heretical sect, but a Christian who has reached the stage of advanced spiritual knowledge</note> experiences in ecstasy—further below. Of the lowest level of the **state**, it is said here: "Those established in the ways of virtue are in the state of purity and are called third in order." Concepts like *calm*, *stillness*, and *tranquility*, which otherwise play a major role in monastic mysticism, seem to appear less frequently in Evagrius. In IV 44: "The Sabbath is the stillness (or perhaps calm?) of the rational soul." In Frankenberg’s edition of the *Letters* (555. 159 a b): "calm... peaceful... gentle... still." In *On the Foundations of the Monastic Life* <note>original Latin title: Rerum Monachalium Rationes</note> chapter 3: "Do you wish to take up the solitary life... and run toward the trophies of stillness <note>original: ἡσυχία (hesychia)</note>?" *Centuries* I 65: "The contemplation of the Holy Trinity is ineffable peace and stillness."

### § 9.
On the path of **dispassion** <note>original Greek: ἀπάθεια (apatheia), a state of being free from the disturbance of the "passions" or disordered desires</note>, the **purity of the soul**, **spiritual love**, and the **state of the soul**, the pious person now rises into the world of **contemplation** <note>original: θεωρία (theoria)</note> or **Knowledge** <note>original: γνῶσις (gnosis)</note>.

It is first important to note that Evagrius sharply and definitely distinguishes this **knowledge** or **contemplation** from all worldly science. Although these overlap in part regarding their content (see the notes below regarding **natural contemplation**), they differ essentially in their form and the manner in which they are acquired. This is already half-clarified by the sentence quoted above from IV 90: "For even the impure can acquire education, but contemplation is only for the pure." **Purity** is the only path by which **contemplation** and **knowledge** are acquired. Likewise, it is stated in IV 6: "Of knowledge, one part is known to the pure, and the other to the impure; the knowledge known to the pure is called spiritual, while the knowledge occurring to the others is called common to nature" <note>original: κοινὴν τῆς φύσεως (koinen tes physeos)</note> (compare V 90 and the commentary on it). Another interesting conceptual distinction is found in VI 2: "The contemplation of this world is twofold: one part is practical, the other spiritual. And while even ungodly men approach the first, only the holy draw near to the second." It is put slightly differently in *The Gnostic* 107: "The knowledge that comes to us from outside" <note>this refers to knowledge derived from material things</note>...

---

1) Frankenberg has rightly recognized the Greek term in the Syrian *tuqana* in numerous passages of the *Centuries*. Here and there, however, the term **disposition** <note>original: ἕξις (hexis)</note> also comes into consideration.

2) Thus Frankenberg translates: "calm state."

3) Compare IV 56: "an abundant state of the rational soul"; V 53, VI 21: "virtue is the state of the rational soul."

4) Double translation according to Frankenberg.

5) The "common knowledge of nature" is roughly equivalent to **scientific knowledge** or **education** <note>original: ἐπιστήμη (episteme) or παιδεία (paideia)</note>.

6) Evagrius himself gives the source of this sentence in *The Gnostic* 147, where he quotes a saying of Basil: "The knowledge that happens to us from men is made better by the study and exercise of prayer, but that which arises from the grace of God is made better by righteousness, the absence of anger, and mercy." Compare also *Centuries* V 79. Particularly instructive here is the explanation in the commentary on *Centuries* I 24 (also I 53, II 16), which seems to reflect Evagrius's own view. Here, a sharp distinction is made between "natural knowledge," which is perfected through speculation and Scripture (!), and that "sublime knowledge," which approaches perfection through asceticism and free will. This would again be the difference between **scientific knowledge** and **spiritual knowledge**. Regarding the placement of Scriptural study on the side of natural knowledge, compare Macarius, *Homily* 15, 20, and Diadochos of Photiki (edited by Weis-Liebersdorf, page 94, line 18).

<page-num>309</page-num>
# III. Evagrius’s General Outlook in Relation to that of Origen.

[Practical knowledge] demonstrates its own matter to us through reason, but that [knowledge] which arises in us by the grace of God presents things accurately to the intellect itself. Opposed to the former type is **error** <note>original: πλάνη (plane)</note>; opposed to the latter are **spiritedness** <note>original: θυμός (thymos)</note> and **anger** <note>original: ὀργή (orge)</note>. It thus takes place by way of the **purity of heart** <note>original: καθαρότης τῆς καρδίας (katharotes tes kardias)</note>. If I understand this saying correctly, Evagrius is describing here the difference between what we call discursive knowledge (through reason) and intuitive knowledge (by the intellect itself).

— In another place, he speaks of those who are able to know "through the purity of the soul and even without this body" (*Centuries* IV, 70). We will return to these definitions during the discussion of the higher forms of Evagrian <term>Gnosis</term> <note>In this context, Gnosis refers to deep, experiential spiritual knowledge rather than the Gnostic heresy</note>. That the higher knowledge, which stands in contrast to profane knowledge, stems from the grace of God (see above, *The Gnostic* 107), Evagrius also emphasizes in V 79: "While perceiving the contemplation of natures belongs to the mind, perceiving the Holy Trinity is not within its power alone, but is a gift of overflowing grace."¹) The polemic against worldly wisdom in VI 22 is particularly sharp: "If sensory words are useful even in the age to come, then the wise of this world shall also inherit the kingdom of heaven. But if purity of mind is deemed worthy of the vision (contemplation) of the age to come, it is clear that the wise of this world will be far from the knowledge of God."²)

**§ 10.** Natural (philosophical) knowledge is thus contrasted with the higher knowledge gained through the path of *dispassion*, *love*, and *purity*, which is granted through divine grace. And here we encounter a terminology that thoroughly dominates Evagrius’s presentation. He recognizes three stages of the pious life: *practice*, *natural contemplation*, and *theology*. He returns to this classification in repeatedly used phrases. *The Practical Life* 1: "Christianity is the doctrine of our Savior Jesus Christ, consisting of practice <note>original: πρακτική (praktike)</note>, natural contemplation <note>original: φυσική (physike)</note>, and theology <note>original: θεολογία (theologia)</note>" (cf. *The Gnostic* 114, 117). Immediately before this in the Prologue, we read the sentence: "**dispassion**³) gives birth to love, and love is the door to natural knowledge, which is succeeded by theology and **ultimate blessedness**" (this sentence is taken literally from Palladius, the student of Evagrius, in the *Lausiac History* chapter 40). In chapter 3 of the great letter (found in Migne’s collection, volume 32) that has been mistakenly included among the letters of Basil [of Caesarea], we find the sentence: "For he named his entire mystical visitation 'flesh and blood,' and revealed the teaching composed of practice, natural contemplation, and theology, through which the soul is nourished and prepared for the contemplation of beings for a time."⁴)

The following passage from the *Mirror for Monks* (120/1) agrees with this quite precisely:

-> *The flesh of Christ is the practical virtues,* <-
-> *and he who eats them shall become dispassionate.* <-
-> *The blood of Christ is the contemplation of created things,* <-
-> *and he who drinks it shall be made wise by it.* <-
-> *The breast of the Lord is the knowledge of God.* <-

***

1) Cf. VI 17: "Holy power is a constitution arising from the contemplation of beings and from the help of the grace of God." V 12: "If the mind has stripped off the passions and by the grace of the Lord is able to see beings..." V 81 (see above), III 5, III 82.
2) Cf. *The Practical Life* 71: "One will set aside passions through virtue, but bare words (profane knowledge) through spiritual contemplation."
3) Previously enumerated are: faith, fear, self-control, patience, hope, from which dispassion <note>original: ἀπάθεια (apatheia)</note> is born. — Evagrius seems here to follow Clement of Alexandria, *Miscellanies* II 31, 1, where the following are listed in order (also as the outline of *Miscellanies* II): faith, fear, hope, repentance, self-control, patience, love (= love for God) (!), knowledge.
4) Cf. the end of the letter, where in Sirach 11:3 the ant is interpreted as the **practical path**, the bee as **natural contemplation**, in which the discourse concerning the Holy Trinity is also blended. — See also here the phrase **ultimate blessedness** <note>original: ἐσχάτη μακαριότης (he eschate makariotes)</note> in Migne 32, 256 C, 257 A, 257 B. Cf. also *Centuries* VII 49.

-> "But he who reclines upon Him shall be a **theologian**." <note>original: ὁ δὲ ἀναπεσὼν ἐπ’ αὐτὸ θ ε ο λ ό γ ο ς ἔσται. This refers to the Apostle John reclining on Jesus at the Last Supper, seen as a model for the highest contemplative state.</note> <-
-> "The **gnostic** and the **practitioner** have met one another," <note>original: γνωστικὸς καὶ πρακτικὸς ὑπήντησαν ἀλλήλοις.</note> <-
-> "and in the midst of both stood the Lord." <note>original: μέσος δὲ ἀμφοτέρων εἱστήκει κύριος.</note> <-

Finally, as a characteristic point, we must mention a sentence from *The Practitioner* (56): "The end of **practice** <note>original: πρακτική (praktike)</note> is love; the end of **knowledge** <note>original: γνῶσις (gnosis)</note> is **theology** <note>original: θεολογία (theologia)</note>; and the beginnings of both are faith and **natural contemplation** <note>original: φυσικὴ θεωρία (physike theoria)</note>."¹)

And here we can once again make the important observation that even this classification—which is of fundamental importance for Evagrius’s way of thinking—was borrowed from Origen. I will quote once more his sentence from the *Selections on the Psalms* (Lommatzsch XIII, 121): "And through **practice** one acquires Him [Christ] as master of the house; through **natural contemplation**, as king; and again through **theology**, as God." From the way these terms are introduced, it can further be concluded that this classification was a given and established one for Origen, which he assumes to be well-known.²) It would not surprise me if this classification eventually proves to be even older than Origen.

A certain difficulty in this schema—which Evagrius borrowed from Origen and placed at the center of his presentation—is the inclusion of **natural contemplation** in the path of salvation specifically intended for the pious. In terms of content, it is essentially identical to what we characterized above as **science/wisdom** (*episteme/sophia*), **common knowledge**, or **knowledge entering from without**. But in terms of form, it is certainly different from these; it is also a holy knowledge resting on divine grace. For the pious person, it followed the stages of **dispassion** <note>original: ἀπάθεια (apatheia), the state of being free from the disturbance of passions like anger or lust</note> and **love**; it belongs only to the **pure** and the **impassible** (*Centuries* IV, 6). — This inclusion of natural contemplation corresponds exactly to the general worldview of Origen and Evagrius. If the "fall" of the creature consists in sinking down from unity with God and the blessedness of divine vision—thereby entangling the human spirit (and spirits in general) in the lower spheres of the world and corporeality—then it follows that the human spirit has the task of gradually rising again from these lower spheres to the knowledge of the **Holy Monad** <note>The "Unity" of God</note> or **Trinity**, turning back from **ignorance** to **knowledge**. Thus, "natural contemplation" (seen *sub specie aeternitatis* <note>Latin: "under the aspect of eternity"</note>) belongs within the process of salvation for the pious. It is characterized as follows: "**Natural knowledge** is the true understanding of those things which have come into being for the sake of the knowledge of the Holy Trinity" (*Centuries* I, 88). "**Contemplation** is [the knowledge] of everything that has been and shall be; a spiritual knowledge which enlarges the mind and makes it approach the perfection of its own image, according to how it was created" (*Centuries* III, 42). "The life of man is the Holy Trinity; and the goal of God's mercy is the **contemplation of beings**" (*Centuries* I, 73).

§ 11. Evagrius’s schema branches out even further; he distinguishes within natural contemplation between the **contemplation of bodies** and that of **incorporeals** (either the *logoi* <note>In this context, the underlying "reasons" or "divine blueprints" of things</note>, taken in the Stoic sense, of these...

---

1) This schema corresponds to the sentence regarding the triple temptation of the demons (*Centuries* I, 105): "Some of the demons oppose the **observance of the commandments** (practice), others the **knowledge of natures** (natural), and others the **discourses concerning God** (theology?); because the knowledge of our salvation also consists in these three." IV, 40: "The contemplation of spiritual observance (= practice?), the understanding in natures (natural), the discourses concerning the Godhead (theology)." *The Gnostic* 151: "The goal of **practice** is to purify the mind... of **natural philosophy**, to reveal the truth hidden in things. But for someone to withdraw the mind from all earthly things and lead it back to the essential knowledge is a gift of the **vision of God**."
2) Cf. above for other similar schemas found in Origen.

From countless passages, I will cite only a few. *Centuries* I, 74: "The light of the mind is distinguished in three ways: into the knowledge of the holy and adorable Trinity; into the nature of both the incorporeal and the corporeal" (here the inner nature of man is reckoned as part of the spiritual world); "and into the understanding of the natures of created things." <note>original: τὸ τοῦ νοὸς φῶς διακρίνεται τρισσῶς εἰς τὴν γνῶσιν τῆς ἁγίας καὶ προσκυνητῆς Τριάδος καὶ εἰς τὴν φύσιν τήν τε ἀσωμάτων καὶ ἐνσωμάτων ... καὶ εἰς τὴν σύνεσιν τῶν φύσεων τῶν κτισμάτων.</note> II, 63: "Of types of knowledge, some are **immaterial**, others are **material**;¹) but that of the Holy Trinity surpasses them all." <note>original: τῶν γνώσεων αἱ μέν εἰσιν ἄϋλοι, αἱ δὲ ἔνυλοι ... ἡ δὲ τῆς ἁγίας Τριάδος πάσας ὑπερβάλλει.</note>²) Thus, if **practice** <note>original: πρακτική (praktike)</note> is again included in the schema, a fourfold structure results. II, 4: "And the first is, *according to the fathers*, the transition from vice to virtue (= practice); the second is the transition from **apathy** <note>original: ἀπάθεια (apatheia), a state of freedom from disruptive passions</note> to **second natural contemplation**; the third is the ascent from this to the knowledge of rational natures (= knowledge of the incorporeal); and the fourth is the transition from all these to the Holy Trinity." <note>original: καὶ ἡ μὲν πρώτη ἐστὶ κατὰ τοὺς πατέρας ἡ ἐκ τῆς κακίας εἰς τὴν ἀρετὴν μετάστασις ... ἡ δὲ δευτέρα ἡ ἐκ τῆς ἀπαθείας εἰς τὴν φυσικὴν θεωρίαν τὴν δευτέραν ... ἡ δὲ τρίτη ἡ ἐκ ταύτης εἰς τὴν τῶν λογικῶν φύσεων γνῶσιν ἀναγωγή ... ἡ δὲ τετάρτη ἡ ἐκ τούτων πάντων εἰς τὴν ἁγίαν Τριάδα μετάστασις.</note> III, 61: "Virtue demonstrates to the mind the **second natural contemplation**, and this restores it to its **first** state. Its first state, in turn, leads it forward to the knowledge of the Holy **Monad** <note>original: Μονάς (Monas), referring to the oneness of God</note>."³)

Again, we find all the elements of this detailed schema together in Origen. In the appeal to the "fathers" emphasized above, Evagrius will have primarily had Origen in mind. I cite only a few decisive passages (see above), which could surely be multiplied, from *Selections on the Psalms* (Lommatzsch XII, 362): "The wings of the holy dove are the contemplation of bodies and incorporeal things, through which the mind, being raised up, comes to rest in the knowledge of the Holy Trinity." <note>original: πτέρυγές εἰσι τῆς ἁγίας περιστερᾶς ἡ θεωρία σωμάτων καὶ ἀσωμάτων δι' ἧς ὑψωθεὶς ὁ νοῦς καταπαύει εἰς γνῶσιν τῆς ἁγίας Τριάδος.</note>⁴) Lommatzsch XIII, 64: "The gate of knowledge, which is the contemplation of created bodies and incorporeal things." <note>original: πύλη τῆς γνώσεως, ἥτις ἐστὶν ἡ θεωρία τῶν γεγονότων σωμάτων καὶ ἀσωμάτων.</note>

Even clearer is Evagrius’s dependence on Origen on a point already mentioned above. In his work, the terms **accounts of providence and judgment** <note>original: λόγοι προνοίας καὶ κρίσεως (logoi pronoias kai kriseos)</note> frequently appear quite unorganically within the ladder of knowledge. Thus we obtain a five-part series: *Centuries* I, 27: "As the fathers say, there are five primary contemplations... the first is of the adorable Trinity; the second and third are of the incorporeal and corporeal; and the fourth and fifth are of the judgment and providence of God." <note>original: καθὼς λέγουσιν οἱ πατέρες πέντε θεωρίαι ἀρχικαί ... ἡ μὲν πρώτη τῆς προσκυνητῆς Τριάδος, ἡ δευτέρα δὲ καὶ τρίτη τῶν ἀσωμάτων καὶ σωμάτων, ἡ τετάρτη δὲ καὶ πέμπτη τῆς κρίσεως καὶ προνοίας τοῦ θεοῦ.</note> Or in reverse order, *Mirror for Monks* 135:

-> Contemplations of the worlds broaden the heart, <-
-> but accounts of providence and judgment exalt it. <-
<note>original: κόσμων θεωρίαι πλατύνουσιν καρδίαν, λόγοι δὲ προνοίας καὶ κρίσεως ὑψοῦσιν αὐτήν.</note>

***

1) The concept **immaterial** (ἄϋλος/ἄνυλος) and its opposite, like **incorporeal** (ἀσώματος), is very familiar to Evagrius. IV, 81: "material, immaterial contemplation"; IV, 86; VII, 56. *The Practitioner* 23: "material... immaterial war." *On the Causes of Monastic Life* ch. 2: "immaterial, carefree"; ch. 3: "immaterial, you shall be apathes <note>passionless</note>"; ch. 5: "do not dwell *with material men* and those distracted by circumstances... but dwell only *with immaterial brothers* of the same mind as you." *Epistle* in Migne 32, ch. 7, 257 B: "calling the resurrection the transition from material knowledge to immaterial contemplation."

2) Compare *Centuries* I, 70; 71; 78; 88; 89 (**natural knowledge** — **essential knowledge**). II, 2 (**second natural contemplation** distinguished from the knowledge of rational natures). II, 3 (the knowledge of the Monad, spiritual knowledge, older than all natural contemplation). II, 5 (sensible things, intelligible things, Holy Trinity). III, 8; 10; 24; 26 (knowledge regarding the nature of rational beings — knowledge regarding the *second* nature). III, 33; IV, 10 (heresies are distinguished according to whether they are directed against the *first* or the *second* contemplation or against that of the Holy Trinity). IV, 19 (number of the second natural contemplation). V, 40.

3) I, 70: 1. Knowledge of the Holy Trinity. 2. Knowledge of the incorporeal. 3. Contemplation of the corporeal. 4. Understanding of the ages (see above, p. 303). 5. Health of the soul. III, 17.

4) Compare XII, 405 where the wings (Psalm 67:13) are interpreted as **practice** and **contemplation**; others as "knowledge of bodies and incorporeal things." Origen thus already had predecessors in this terminology.

->The knowledge of incorporeal beings lifts up the mind,<-
->and presents it to the Holy Trinity.¹)<-
<note>original Greek: γνῶσις ἀσωμάτων ἐπαίρει τὸν νοῦν, καὶ τῇ ἁγίᾳ Τριάδι παρίστησιν αὐτόν. This summarizes the goal of Evagrius's system: moving from the spiritual understanding of angels/souls to the direct presence of God.</note>

As an immediate source, Evagrius cites the Alexandrian and Origenist Didymus <note>Didymus the Blind (c. 313–398), a prominent Christian scholar in Alexandria and a teacher of Evagrius</note> in *Gnostikos* 150: "Always exercise within yourself the reasons concerning providence and judgment, says the great and gnostic teacher Didymus." <note>original Greek: τοὺς περὶ προνοίας καὶ κρίσεως κατὰ σεαυτοῦ ἀεὶ γύμναζε λόγους, φησὶν ὁ μέγας καὶ γνωστικὸς διδάσκαλος Δίδυμος. "Providence" and "judgment" refer to God's ongoing care and his initial ordering of the universe.</note> But according to the evidence provided above, Evagrius will also be directly dependent on Origen at this point, in whose system the <term>reasons of judgment and providence</term> <note>original: λόγοι κρίσεως καὶ προνοίας (logoi kriseōs kai pronoias); the divine principles or "blueprints" behind how God manages the world and justice</note> already played a role. It is Origen he likely has primarily in mind when appealing to the "fathers" (I 27, cf. V 24).

§ 12. The highest level of <term>contemplation</term> <note>original: θεωρία (theoria)</note> or <term>knowledge</term> <note>original: γνῶσις (gnosis)</note> is then for Evagrius <term>theology</term> <note>original: θεολογία (theologia); for the desert fathers, this specifically meant the direct knowledge of the Trinity, not just academic study</note> or the knowledge (contemplation) of the **Holy Trinity** (the **Monad**), which he also likes to designate as <term>essential knowledge</term>²). <note>original: γνῶσις οὐσιώδης (gnosis ousiōdes); knowledge that concerns the very essence or "being" of God</note> Before we turn to the discussion of what "theology" means for him and how he describes this highest <term>state of the mind</term> <note>original: κατάστασις τοῦ νοός (katastasis tou noos)</note>, let us first discuss the nature of Evagrian "Gnosis" or contemplation in general. In the previous discussion of "natural contemplation," only individual points could be brought forward and the main discussion had to be postponed, because it is only in the description of the highest states of blessed knowing that it becomes quite clear what "knowledge" and "contemplation" mean for him.

I would first like to point out once again that, as has already been shown in numerous cases, the concepts of "knowledge" and "contemplation" constantly alternate in his work³). This itself is important. The concept of *Gnosis* is still completely familiar and intimate to Evagrius, as is also the case with Origen. Indeed, one must actually go back as far as Clement of Alexandria to find such an emphasis and central significance placed on Gnosis again. It is even more significant that the even stronger terminological concept of the <term>Gnostic</term> <note>original: γνωστικός (gnostikos); the spiritually advanced person who has attained deep knowledge</note> is so familiar to Evagrius. Here too he stands close to Clement, while in Origen, as far as I can see, the word already begins to recede. I will highlight a few particularly significant passages. Especially *Praktikos* II, 98. Here Evagrius speaks of an island located near Alexandria on the northern edge of "the lake called Maria" (Mareotis). "A most esteemed monk of the camp of the Gnostics dwells near it." <note>original Greek: προσοικεῖ δὲ αὐτῇ μοναχὸς τῆς παρεμβολῆς τῶν Γνωστικῶν ὁ δοκιμώτατος.</note> I also recall the beautiful passage already cited from the *Mirror of Monks* (120 ff.): "A Gnostic and a practitioner met one another, and in the middle of both stood the Lord." <note>original Greek: γνωστικός καὶ πρακτικός ὑπήντησαν ἀλλήλοις, μέσος δὲ ἀμφοτέρων εἱστήκει κύριος.</note> For him, the Gnostic is still the one initiated into the mysteries, who stands in contrast to the uninitiated. *Gnostikos* 128: "Do not reveal the things of the Gnostics to infants <note>the spiritually immature</note>, nor place such books in their hands." 105: "The Gnostic is like salt to the impure, but like light to the pure" ⁴).

### III. Evagrius’s General Outlook in Relation to that of Origen.

It is even more important to note that the term <term>contemplation</term> <note>original Greek: θεωρία (theoria); in this context, it refers to a direct spiritual "seeing" or vision of divine realities</note> is very often understood by Evagrius in the sense of actual "seeing," and has not become philosophically faded or abstract. Thus, the terms for <term>knowing</term> <note>γινώσκειν (ginōskein)</note>, <term>knowledge</term> <note>γνῶσις (gnōsis)</note>, and "contemplation" — or the "knower" <note>γνωστικός (gnōstikos)</note> and the "contemplative" <note>θεωρητικός (theōrētikos)</note> — alternate with terms for <term>seeing</term> <note>ὁρᾶν (horan)</note>, <term>sight</term> <note>ὄψις (opsis)</note>, <term>beholding</term> <note>θεᾶσθαι (theasthai)</note>, and being <term>visionary</term> <note>ὁρατικός (horatikos)</note>. This emerges with sufficient clarity even through the medium of the Syriac translation. Especially important here, of course, are the few passages preserved for us in Greek. I note a series of the more significant ones:

**VI 83**: "The mind is said to behold what it knows, and it does not behold what it does not know." <note>original Greek: ταῦτα λέγεται ὁ νοῦς θεᾶσθαι ἃ γινώσκει καὶ ταῦτα οὐ θεᾶται ἃ οὐ γινώσκει.</note> *Mirror of Monks* **136**: "Purifying himself, he shall see <term>noetic natures</term> <note>spiritual or intellectual realities</note>, and the monk shall recognize the reasons of the incorporeal beings through practice." <note>original Greek: καθαίρων ἑαυτὸν ὄψεται φύσεις νοεράς, λόγους δὲ ἀσωμάτων ἐπιγνώσεται μοναχὸς πρᾶξις.</note> **III 6**: "The <term>naked mind</term> <note>a mind stripped of all worldly images and concepts</note> is that which was perfected in its own vision and was deemed worthy to participate in the contemplation of the Holy Trinity." <note>original Greek: νοῦς γυμνός ἐστὶν ὃς ἐτελειώθη ἐν τῇ αὐτοῦ ὁράσει καὶ ἠξιώθη τῆς ἁγίας Τριάδος θεωρίᾳ κοινωνεῖν.</note> Particularly significant are the sentences where this "vision" of the Knower is placed in contrast to ordinary knowledge. **IV 90**: "The knowledge of Christ does not require a soul skilled in inquiry, but rather one that is visionary." <note>original Greek: ἡ τοῦ Χριστοῦ γνῶσις οὐ ψυχῆς τὴν ζήτησιν δεινῆς χρείαν ἔχει ἀλλ᾿ ὁρατικῆς¹</note> (followed by the sentence on the difference between education and contemplation; see above, p. 308). **Letter 62** (Frankenberg edition, 611): "The kingdom of God does not need the rational part of the soul, but rather for the soul to be visionary; for while the rational part is found even in defiled souls, the visionary part belongs only to the pure." *Gnostikos* **104**: "The practitioners and the knowers understand the <term>reasons</term> <note>λόγοι (logoi); the inner blueprints or divine logic</note> of things²: but the knowers see the inquiries of knowledge." Thus, for Evagrius, the "visionary" <note>ὁρατικός (horatikos)</note> seems to stand alongside the "knower" <note>γνωστικός (gnōstikos)</note>. **II 36**: "Every visionary of intelligible things." **Letter 41** (Frankenberg, 595): "The state of the practitioner is not the same as that of the visionary."³ *Gnostikos* **151**: "For the mind to withdraw from all earthly things and lead back to the essential knowledge of all is a gift of the vision of God."

On this occasion, it may be pointed out that Evagrius seems to make a distinction between <term>knowledge</term> <note>γνῶσις (gnōsis)</note> and <term>wisdom</term> <note>σοφία (sophia)</note>. *Mirror of Monks* **71**: "Knowledge turns away from blasphemous clamor, but wisdom flees deceitful words." **68**: "To knowledge, wisdom is added" (cf. 28). Explicitly, Diadochos of Photike (chapter 9) distinguishes the two concepts: "For while knowledge joins [the person] to God through experience, without moving the soul toward words... wisdom... reveals the very energies of knowledge." (Gregory of Nazianzus, cited in Evagrius’s *Gnostikos* 146, presents the same distinction regarding the terms <term>prudence</term> <note>φρόνησις (phronēsis)</note> and wisdom: "The work of prudence... is to contemplate the noetic and holy powers apart from words. For these are revealed by wisdom.") Thus, Knowledge is wordless, intuitive seeing; Wisdom is the proclamation or expression of that knowledge. This corresponds to Evagrius’s feeling (see above) that the opposite of Knowledge is "clamor," while the activity of Wisdom is the removal of "deceitful words." This distinction between Knowledge and Wisdom can perhaps be traced back to Clement of Alexandria (*Stromata* VII 55,4): "We say that knowledge differs from wisdom which is produced by instruction. For insofar as something is knowledge, it is certainly also wisdom; but where there is wisdom, there is not necessarily knowledge. For the name of wisdom only appears in the [gap in text] of spoken discourse." Clement seems to know a "wisdom" (of a worldly kind?) that is not based on spiritual knowledge. But the concept of wisdom (as knowledge presented in speech) emerges clearly. Did Paul perhaps know such a distinction between knowledge and wisdom (1 Corinthians 12:8; cf. also 1 Corinthians 2:6, "But we speak wisdom")? — Incidentally, it should also be noted that Evagrius makes a conscious distinction between wisdom and prudence. *Praktikos* **45**: "Rest is joined to wisdom, but labor to prudence." (cf. **VI 87**: "The mind, according to the word of Solomon, rests in the heart; prudence [rests] in the brain.") ... "[Prudence] preparing the way for wisdom." *Mirror of Monks* **123**: "Wisdom recognizes the phantoms of demons, but prudence tracks their wickedness" (cf. 131). According to *Praktikos* **61**, prudence is practical ethical understanding; <term>insight</term> <note>σύνεσις (synesis)</note> is goal-setting cleverness; and wisdom is "the contemplation of the reasons of bodies and incorporeals." Here too, Clement of Alexandria [is a predecessor].

***

1) "Visionary" <note>ὁρατική (horatikē)</note> is unmistakable in the Syriac. — Cf. also VII 10, "the visionary mind." V 10, "If the mind strips off the passions and by the grace of the Lord is visionary of all things." VII 51.

2) Regarding this formula originating from Stoic usage, which we have encountered several times, cf. I 23, V 54, VI 35, VII 5 ("reasons of the worlds"). VI 54 ("reasons, names, things").

3) [Syriac characters]? In another place, Frankenberg translates the Syriac term as <term>beholder</term> <note>ἐπόπτης (epoptēs), a term for someone initiated into the highest mysteries</note>; "the spiritual mind is the beholder of the Holy Trinity" (III 30; cf. V 40). But "beholder" would be just as characteristic as "visionary."

One should consider *Stromata* II 24, 1: "Since even **Xenocrates** <note>A Greek philosopher and head of Plato's Academy from 339 to 314 BCE</note> in his work *On Prudence* says that wisdom is the science of first causes and of intelligible substance, considering prudence to be twofold: one being practical and the other theoretical, which indeed is human wisdom. Therefore, wisdom is a form of prudence, but not every kind of prudence is wisdom." <note>original Greek: ἐπεὶ καὶ **Ξ ε ν ο κ ρ ά τ η ς** ἐν τῷ περὶ φρονήσεως τὴν σοφίαν ἐπιστήμην τῶν πρώτων αἰτίων καὶ τῆς νοητῆς οὐσίας εἶναί φησι, τὴν φρόνησιν ἡγούμενος διττήν, τὴν μὲν πρακτικὴν τὴν δὲ θεωρητικήν, ἣν δὴ σοφίαν ὑπάρχειν ἀνθρωπίνην. διὸ ἡ μὲν σοφία φρόνησις, οὐ μὴν πᾶσα φρόνησις σοφία.</note> Thus, <term>wisdom</term> <note>sophia</note> = theoretical insight, while <term>prudence</term> <note>phronesis</note> refers to understanding in general, especially practical understanding.

Evagrius thought about and psychologized the nature of this spiritual (ecstatic) vision in a remarkable and characteristic way. Thus, the idea of intuition and intuitive recognition developed for him. In repeatedly cycled phrases, he seeks to approach the mystery of this intuitive vision. In **IV 77**, it is said that what is perceptible to the senses lies outside the <term>Mind</term> <note>Nus; the highest part of the soul</note>, while the ability to see lies within it. In contrast, however, stands the way in which the Divine Trinity knows: "For knowledge is essential." <note>original Greek: γνῶσις γὰρ οὐσιώδης ἐστίν</note> This means that for the Godhead and its knowing, the opposition between the inner and outer world (subject and object) does not exist. This **essential knowledge** <note>ousiōdēs gnōsis</note> (see above) is now also the goal of the mystic. He is, of course, bound to this opposition of inside and outside, subject and object, and can basically only view the earthly world in this way. But it is also his ideal to grasp the truth "through the purity of the soul without this body." <note>original Greek: διὰ τὴν τῆς ψυχῆς καθαρότητα ἄνευ τούτου τοῦ σώματος</note> He can also recognize the Godhead through the path of reflection and deduction by ascending from these lower worlds; but when he rises beyond this to the direct vision of the **Holy Trinity**, this opposition of inside and outside ceases. Intuitive vision begins.

**V 60**: "One is the power of the mind when it looks into natures, and another is its power when it peers into its own contemplation. ^1) But its power is one and equal in itself when it peers into the Holy Trinity." <note>original Greek: ἄλλη ἐστὶ ἡ τοῦ νοὸς δύναμις ὅταν βλέψει εἰς τὰς φύσεις, ἄλλη δὲ ἡ δύναμις αὐτοῦ ὅταν εἰς τὴν θεωρίαν αὐτοῦ διακύψῃ. μία δέ ἐστιν ἡ δύναμις αὐτοῦ καὶ ἴση καθ᾽ αὑτὴν ὅταν εἰς τὴν ἁγίαν Τριάδα διακύψῃ.</note> **V 61**: "When we look at material things, we remember the contemplation ^2) of them, and when we receive the contemplation, we return again to the memory of the material things; but this does not happen to us [also] in the contemplation of the Holy Trinity." <note>original Greek: ὅταν βλέπωμεν εἰς τὰς ὕλας, τὴν θεωρίαν αὐτῶν μνημονεύομεν καὶ ὅταν τὴν θεωρίαν δεξώμεθα, αὖθις πρὸς τὴν τῶν ὑλῶν μνήμην ἀνερχόμεθα· ἀλλ᾽ οὐχ οὕτως συμβαίνει ἡμῖν [καὶ] ἐν τῇ τῆς ἁγίας Τριάδος θεωρίᾳ.</note> **IV 87**: "All contemplation is known in its underlying subject; but it is not so in the Holy Trinity." <note>original Greek: πᾶσα θεωρία ἐν τῷ ὑποκειμένῳ γινώσκεται· ἀλλ᾽ οὐχ οὕτως ἐν τῇ ἁγίᾳ Τριάδι.</note>

**V 62**: "The Holy Trinity is not a matter of compositions, or of qualities, or of deficiency, or of excess; for its substance is entirely of a single form and equal throughout." ^2) <note>original Greek: ἡ ἁγία Τριάς οὐκ ἔστι πρᾶγμα τῶν συνθέσεων ἢ τῶν ποιοτήτων ἢ τοῦ ὑστερήματος ἢ τῆς περισσείας· οὐσία γὰρ μονοειδής ἐστι πάντα καὶ διαπαντὸς ἴση.</note>

Evagrius can also express this in the following way:
**V 63**: "In the contemplation of beings, there are ascents and descents according to diligence and negligence; but it is not so in the contemplation of the Holy Trinity; for it is a vision equal in itself, in which there is no ascent and descent." <note>original Greek: ἐν τῇ τῶν ὄντων θεωρίᾳ ἀναβάσεις καὶ καταβάσεις εἰσὶ κατὰ τὴν σπουδὴν καὶ τὴν ἀμέλειαν· ἀλλ᾽ οὐχ οὕτως ἐν τῇ τῆς ἁγίας Τριάδος θεωρίᾳ· ἐστὶ γὰρ ὄψις ἴση καθ᾽ αὑτὴν, ἐν ᾗ οὐκ ἔστιν ἀνάβασις καὶ κατάβασις.</note> In **II 71**, the observation is even expanded: "The contemplation of incorporeal beings is not subject to being raised up or brought down." <note>original Greek: ἡ τῶν ἀσωμάτων θεωρία οὐκ ἀνάγεται καὶ κατάγεται.</note>

An even more strongly developed theory regarding the different kinds of **Knowledge** <note>Gnosis</note> ^3) is offered in **VII 23**: "The mind at one time moves from **thought** to **thought**, at another from **contemplation** to **contemplation**, and again from **thought** to **contemplation** and from **contemplation** to **thought**; and there are times when it changes from a **state beyond forms** to a **thought** or to a **contemplation**, and from these it ascends again to the state beyond forms. This happens at the time of prayer." <note>original Greek: ὁ νοῦς τότε μὲν ἀπὸ ν ό η μ α τ ο ς πρὸς ν ό η μ α μετάγει, τότε δὲ ἀπὸ θ ε ω ρ ί α ς πρὸς θ ε ω ρ ί α ν καὶ αὖθις ἀπὸ ν ο ή μ α τ ο ς πρὸς θ ε ω ρ ί α ν καὶ ἀπὸ θ ε ω ρ ί α ς πρὸς ν ό η μ α· ἔστι δὲ ὅτε ἀπὸ κ α τ α σ τ ά σ ε ω ς τ ῆ ς ὑ π ὲ ρ τ ὰ ε ἴ δ η πρὸς ν ό η μ α ἢ πρὸς θ ε ω ρ ί α ν μεταβάλλεται καὶ ἀπὸ τούτων πάλιν πρὸς τὴν ὑπὲρ τὰ εἴδη κατάστασιν ἐπαναβαίνει. τούτου δὲ προσευχῆς καιρῷ.</note>

---

1) <term>Contemplation</term> <note>theoria</note> is here the grasping of the inner spiritual essence of things, in contrast to external sensory comprehension. This opposition disappears at the highest stage of Knowledge. Compare **V 58**: "Sense perception distinguishes sensory things, but the mind distinguishes the contemplation of them." <note>original Greek: ἡ μὲν αἴσθησις τὰ αἰσθητὰ διακρίνει, ὁ δὲ νοῦς τὴν θεωρίαν αὐτῶν.</note>

2) Compare the enigmatic hints in **I 15, 16, IV 87**: the reason that beholds God is freed from the images of matter. **V 12**: "If the mind strips off the passions by the grace of the Lord, it is capable of seeing beings; then it will also despise all sensory things, because its spiritual part is being built up... and from there it will draw its intellect away from the vision of all manifest things." <note>original Greek: εἰ ὁ νοῦς ἐκδύεται τὰ πάθη χάριτι κυρίου ὁρατικός ἐστι τῶν ὄντων, τότε καὶ πάντων τῶν αἰσθητῶν καταφρονήσει, διότι τὸ πνευματικὸν αὐτοῦ οἰκοδομεῖται . . . καὶ ἐκεῖσε ἀπὸ πάντων φανερῶν ὁράσεως τὴν διάνοιαν αὐτοῦ ἑλκύσει.</note> The commentary on **I 20** is particularly clear here.

3) The 3 (or 4) stages are also clearly recognizable: **V 57**: "Just as we now see natures through sensory things and, being **purified**, we see the **contemplation** above, so being **more** purified we peer into the contemplation of incorporeal beings, and being purified threefold we shall be deemed worthy even of the vision of the Holy Trinity." <note>original Greek: ὥσπερ καὶ νῦν διὰ τῶν αἰσθητῶν τὰς φύσεις ὁρῶμεν καὶ κ ε κ α θ α ρ ι σ μ έ ν ο ι τὴν ἄνω θ ε ω ρ ί α ν ὁρῶμεν, οὕτως μ ᾶ λ λ ο ν κεκαθαρισμένοι διακύπτομεν εἰς τὴν τῶν ἀσωμάτων θεωρίαν, τρισσῶς δὲ κεκαθαρισμένοι ἐπαξιωθησόμεθα καὶ τῆς ἁγίας τριάδος ὄψεως.</note>

It details how the mind ascends from sensory perception to a "state beyond forms" where it achieves a direct, non-dualistic vision of the Holy Trinity.</summary>

...occurs ¹). Here, Evagrius clearly distinguishes three stages of knowledge: <term>concept</term> <note>original Greek: νόημα (nóēma)</note>, <term>contemplation</term> <note>original Greek: θεωρία (theōría)</note>, and a <term>state beyond forms</term> <note>original Greek: κατάστασις ὑπὲρ τὰ εἴδη (katástasis hypèr tà eídē)</note>. We will perhaps not go wrong if we relate the term <term>thought</term> <note>original Syriac: ܚܘܫܒα (hushaba), which Wilhelm Frankenberg renders as the Greek νόημα (nóēma)</note> to the concept obtained through discursive, step-by-step thinking. Then <term>contemplation</term>, the second stage, is clearly distinguished from it. The commentary by Mar Babai <note>A 6th-7th century East Syrian church father who wrote an extensive commentary on Evagrius's "Gnostic Chapters"</note> explains (Frankenberg 445, 216 a): “At another time it [the soul] hastens from one ‘contemplation’ to another, that is, from one spiritual vision to another; it contemplates the mysterious teaching which represents every individual nature with its movements and changes in time; it recognizes what is happening in its own mysterious depths; whether the thought stirring within it originates from angels... or whether they are evil memories of demonic thoughts... when it reads the Scripture, it also receives the deeper meaning of the words” ²). Regarding the sentence that the intellect turns “from contemplation to a concept,” the commentary notes: “This also often happens in many ways, that the intellect, after the spiritual vision (contemplation), turns to the understanding (concept) of the vision. This is what happened to Daniel: he had seen the deeper meaning in the revelation, but because he did not understand what he had seen, someone was commissioned to explain it to him.”

We find ourselves here, then, with "contemplation"—if Mar Babai has correctly understood the master—in the world of spiritual vision that reaches for the deeper reasons in nature and Scripture. It is characteristic that the commentary explains the spiritual processes it mentions using visionary experiences (cf. also the discussions on the vision of Peter in Acts 10) ³).

Beyond this lies only the <term>state of the mind beyond forms</term> ⁴), which one experiences during times of prayer. Regarding this, the commentary remarks (216 b): it may well be in blessed rest, if in prayer that ineffable light does not rise over it, stilling all restless movements within it and making the senses fall silent. This “state” is further described by him as a condition that knows no images or mental representations (beyond forms) ⁵), as a “silent rest in prayer,” as “that state which brings all unrest, all sensory perceptions, and thoughts to silence within it, so that it floats above the earthly in the ineffable.”

---

1) 1 = intelligence/understanding, 2 = meaning of the sense. <note>original Latin: 1 = intelligentia, 2 = significatio sensus</note>
2) Cf. also the remarks of the commentary on I 24 regarding a very obscure word of Evagrius (Frankenberg 69): “Thus, natural knowledge [concept] in us is one thing... and that which is developed from speculations on Scripture and on things [contemplation] is another; these three kinds are intended to lead upward to the perfection of that [knowledge] whose beauty is given to us by way of hint in our natural knowledge. The latter is alone ineffable light.” Cent. II 16 (“the knowledge of all existing things is such that it leads the soul participating in it up to the knowledge of the Holy Trinity”) <note>original Greek: οὕτως ἐστὶν ἡ πάντων τῶν ὄντων γνῶσις ὥστε τὴν ψυχὴν τὴν κοινωνοῦσαν αὐτῆς ἀναγαγεῖν πρὸς τὴν γνῶσιν τῆς ἁγίας Τριάδος</note>, the commentary notes: Our knowledge [concept] given to us in creation is able to nourish and promote the soul... through the insights [contemplations] from the realm of Scripture and nature, so that it comes to the knowledge of the Trinity.

It [the soul] turns, after the disappearance of that light (in the "state beyond forms"), to the understanding of the visible, to the study of Scripture (allegory), to meditating on the teaching of the Fathers, to divine service, or it turns to spiritual vision; it immerses itself in the future, remains in silent prayer under mortifications, and contemplates spiritually <note>original Greek: πνευματικῶς (pneumatikōs)</note> everything that evokes mental representations in the intellect from without or from within.

It draws heavily on Mar Babai's commentary to explain how the mind transitions between these visionary and intellectual states.</summary>

§ 13. However, with these latter explanations, we have actually already jumped ahead in our presentation and arrived at the highest level of Evagrian <term>knowledge</term> <note>original Greek: γνῶσις (gnosis)</note>. Let us step back once more: there was a gradual ascent of the soul <margin>1)</margin>, which is initiated through <term>the active life</term> <note>original Greek: πρακτική (praktike), the first stage of spiritual discipline focusing on virtue</note> and the <term>contemplation of bodily and bodiless things</term> <note>original Greek: θεωρία σωμάτων καὶ ἀσωμάτων (theoria somaton kai asomaton)</note>. In his work, as in all of Gnosticism, the song of the soul's ascent to its heavenly home still resounds, though for the most part, actual spatial ideas are set aside and everything is turned toward the spiritual-psychological. But every now and then, the idea of space still clearly emerges. For instance, in this characteristic sentence: "The soul... which by the grace of God has been set on a good path and is separated from the body, will be in those **places of knowledge** where the wings of <term>freedom from passions</term> <note>original Greek: ἀπάθεια (apatheia), a state of spiritual calm where one is no longer controlled by emotional impulses</note> <margin>2)</margin> will make it arrive" (compare II 54: "**Knowledge does not run in the places of ignorance**" <margin>3)</margin>). Thus, for Evagrius, the highest level of that ascent is <term>theology</term> <note>original Greek: θεολογία (theologia)</note> and the <term>ultimate blessedness</term> <note>original Greek: ἐσχάτη μακαριότης (eschate makariotes)</note> associated with it, which is the <term>essential knowledge of the Holy Trinity</term> <note>original Greek: γνῶσις οὐσιώδης τῆς ἁγίας Τριάδος (gnosis ousiodes tes hagias Triados)</note>.

We have already seen that the term **theology** was also borrowed by Evagrius from Origen. It has already been pointed out that in the language of mysticism—this emerges particularly clearly in Diadochos of Photike—**theology** is something quite different from what we are inclined to understand by the term today. In this context, **theology** is *the praise of God*, *the hymn to God*, which the mystic or the human soul that has reached the highest level of perfection strikes up. This concept of **theology** can also be traced back in the Christian sphere at least as far as Origen. In his *Selections on the Psalms* (Lommatzsch XIII 63), he remarks on Psalm 118:14 ("The Lord is my strength and my song"): "This word is also a **hymn**, in which **theology** consists." XII 120: "He also brings glory to the Lord who **speaks of God** <note>original Greek: θεολογῶν (theologon)</note> in the word of wisdom." And regarding the concept of **hymning**, one should again compare XIII 106: "But while **singing psalms** is fitting for humans, **hymning** is fitting for angels or those who possess an **angelic life**" <margin>4)</margin>.

Even when Evagrius speaks of the **ultimate blessedness** that follows **theology**, it is reminiscent of Origen. I refer to Lommatzsch XI 380: "**Blessedness of the soul is freedom from passions combined with true knowledge of things that exist.**" XIII 152: "**The blessedness of the righteous is freedom from passions of the soul combined with knowledge of God**" <margin>5)</margin>.

***

...God having color or shape. For these things imprint the mind through concepts, as we have said. — See *Gnostic Chapters* VII 21.

<margin>1)</margin> I would like to point out a particularly beautiful parallel here in Cassian, *Conference* I 8, which shows how firmly fixed the forms of mystical language were in Evagrius’s time: "He placed the **highest good** not in the **active life** <note>original Latin: *actuali*, corresponding to the Greek *praktike*</note>, however praiseworthy that work might be... but in his own **contemplation** <note>original Latin: *contemplatione*, corresponding to the Greek *theoria*</note>, which is truly simple and one (Origen, *On First Principles* I 4, 6): declaring that few things are necessary for **perfect blessedness** <note>original Latin: *perfectam beatitudinem*, corresponding to the Greek *eschate teleia makariotes*</note>, i.e., that **contemplation** <note>original Latin: *theoria*</note> which is first preserved in the consideration of the few **saints** <note>original Latin: *sanctorum*, here used for the Greek *hagion* or *aggelon*, meaning angels</note>, from whose contemplation he descends..., it will also reach that which is called **the One** (the ascent through the angelic world to the Monad), i.e., the **intuition of God alone**, with His help (emphasizing divine grace, as in Evagrius), so that, having wonderfully surpassed even the actions and **ministries** <note>original Latin: *ministeria*, for the Greek *leitourgias*</note> of the saints, he may now feed on the **beauty and knowledge of God alone**" (The concept of divine **beauty** <note>original Greek: κάλλος (kallos)</note> is relatively rare in Evagrius, but plays a large role, for example, in the mysticism of Basil the Great).

<margin>2)</margin> Regarding the image of the **wings of knowledge**, see the parallel in Origen already mentioned above on p. 311 (Lommatzsch XII 362).

<margin>3)</margin> Compare the image of the **door of knowledge** in the Preface to the *Praktikos* and in the *Letter* (Migne 32 c. 5): "**the door of knowledge must be heard.**" Also, the description of Evagrius by Rufinus, *History of the Monks*, ch. 27: "But God had bestowed such a gift of knowledge and wisdom upon him that you would believe almost none of all the fathers had so penetrated the **halls of all knowledge**."

<margin>4)</margin> Compare XIII 159: "**A hymn is an expression of awe combined with a song of praise upon the contemplation of things that have happened and are happening.**"

<margin>5)</margin> Quite correspondingly, it says in Evagrius, *Praktikos* 2: "**The kingdom of heaven is freedom from passions of the soul combined with true knowledge of things that exist.**"

The text draws heavy parallels between Evagrius and Origen, emphasizing that true blessedness is the combination of freedom from passions (apatheia) and divine knowledge.</summary>
