<page-num>317</page-num>
<header>III. Evagrius’s General Outlook in Relation to that of Origen.</header>

Evagrius never tires of praising this highest state, which the human soul experiences in the "ultimate blessedness" <note>original: ἐσχάτη μακαριότης (eschatē makariotēs)</note> of **theology**<sup>1</sup>), in the third "condition beyond forms" <note>original: κατάστασις ὑπὲρ τὰ εἴδη (katastasis hyper ta eidē)</note>, describing it in words of ecstatic enthusiasm. Here, in fact, the state of **contemplation** <note>original: θεωρία (theōria)</note> described above truly begins—a state in which all opposites of "inside" and "outside" vanish, and in which the pious person completely forgets the lower components of their soul, "as knowledge seizes them on high and separates them from the things of the senses" (Praktikos 38).

Of particular interest here is the confession<sup>2</sup>) found in section II 34: "Just as the magnet stone, through a natural power . . . draws iron to itself, so too does holy knowledge draw the pure mind <note>original: νοῦς (nous), the highest faculty of the human soul</note>." This sentence is found almost word-for-word in one of the Hermetic tracts (IV 11), suggesting hidden connections that link the individual branches of Hellenistic mysticism together.

§ 14. A characteristic thought of Evagrian mysticism must be highlighted at this point. Again and again, Evagrius returns to the idea that the soul, at this height of <term>Gnosis</term> <note>spiritual knowledge</note>, is able to behold its own "light-glory"—a radiance that is transfigured by the Godhead and incorporated into it. This is considered the perfect, blessed state of the mystic. Fortunately, his explanations on this point have been preserved for us in a Greek text. They read as follows in *Praktikos* 70:

> When the mind <note>original: νοῦς (nous)</note>, having stripped off the "old man," puts on the one created by grace, then it will also see its own condition <note>see above</note> at the time of prayer as resembling sapphire or a heavenly color; this is what the Scripture calls the **place of God**<sup>3</sup>) seen by the elders on Mount Sinai. 71. The mind could not see the "place of God" within itself unless it has become higher than all things found in material objects; but it will not become higher unless it has stripped off the passions that bind it through thoughts to sensible objects. It will set aside the passions through the virtues, and "bare thoughts" through spiritual contemplation. This happens, in turn, when that light appears to it, which at the time of prayer imprints the "place of God."

This confession is found almost word-for-word in *Centuries* VII 25. 26, meaning that Frankenberg's translation should likely be corrected in part according to the Greek wording of the *Praktikos*. In general, numerous parallels to these explanations are found precisely in the supplement to the *Centuries* (VII); see VII 2. 4. 21<sup>4</sup>). 28. 50. 52, and also Letter 39. 593. Elsewhere, brief remarks referring to these experiences are scattered throughout Evagrius's work. *Praktikos* 36: "A mind that has begun to see its own radiance is a proof of [the soul's] health." *Centuries* II 15: "When the rational nature receives its own contemplation, then the power of the mind will be perfect." On this, the commentary notes: "When spiritual prayer has scrubbed our rational knowledge clean of all 'rust' so that it beholds itself in the glow of pure beauty, then the mind <note>original: Nus</note> is also capable..."

1) In this context, I refer once more to the sentences in which **theology** <note>the direct knowledge of God</note> remains reserved as a **mystery** <note>original: μυστήριον (mystērion)</note> for the chosen circle of Gnostics. Especially *Gnostikos* 128 (see above, p. 312). Somewhat softened in 115: "It is necessary to converse with children and the young about the active life . . . and to explain a little about theology and the study of nature, because without these no one sees the Lord." See also ibid. 114. 116. 127. *Centuries* VI 65.
2) Compare *Praktikos* 38: "knowledge seizing him on high and separating him from the things of the senses."
3) Compare Origen, *Selecta in Psalmos* (Lommatzsch XII 96): "The one who has been perfected stands firm and is called the holy **place of God**."
4) VII 21 is again particularly characteristic: "(1) The mind <note>original: ὁ νοῦς</note> that exists in the observance of God’s commandments dwells in the understanding of the things of this world. (2) But being in knowledge, it dwells in contemplation. (3) And being in prayer, it exists in the formless <note>see above</note> light, which is called the **place of God**." — II 62: "When the minds of the saints receive the..."

It highlights the connection between Evagrian thought and broader Hellenistic and Hermetic traditions regarding the soul's ascent.</summary>

.... to contemplate itself as if in a mirror during prayer, when the inexpressible light rises over it¹).

The character of prayer (see already above) in this ecstatic experience is particularly emphasized. VII 21: "being in prayer, he exists in the formless light <note>original: ἐν τῷ ἀνειδέῳ φωτὶ (en tō aneideō phōti); see page 317, note 5</note>; it is named the 'place of God'." VII 29: "prayer is a state <note>original: κατάστασις (katastasis); see page 315</note> that destroys all thoughts on earth." VII 30: "prayer is a state of the mind <note>the highest faculty of the soul; original: νοὸς (noos)</note> alone under the light of the Holy Trinity through ecstasy²)..." VII 7: "the pure mind is fiery, which at the time of prayer does not bring forward sensory things." Letter (Frankenberg edition 585. 171): "the mind, bright in its vision and held in the meditation of God." VII 57: "he who is built upon himself by himself is satisfied with this strange food, the beauty of that same face³)."

§ 15. Finally, it is a peculiarity of Evagrian mysticism that its lofty spirituality ultimately takes on a sensory coloring again. The mystic rises from the somatic <note>bodily</note> to the incorporeal world and beyond to the **Holy Trinity** <note>original: ἁγία Τριάς (hagia Trias)</note> into even more spiritual and refined worlds. But in the end, he still wants to feel the highest Godhead in a tangibly sensory way.

This is clearly the meaning of the statements found here and there that speak of a **perception** <note>or sensation; original: αἴσθησις (aisthēsis)</note> of the <term>Nus</term> <note>The Intellect or Mind; the part of the human person capable of knowing God</note>: I 33: "The mind needs spiritual sensation." I 37: "Spiritual sensation is the <term>apatheia</term> <note>a state of holy "passionlessness" or detachment from worldly impulses</note> of the rational nature." II 10: "The sensation of knowledge." VII 44: "The kingdom of heaven is the knowledge of high and intelligible heavenly contemplation, occurring through the mind as a sensory organ and the taste of incorruptible sensation." And so it is even said in II 35: "And the mind has acquired five spiritual sense organs" (compare VII 20). One should feel, see, hear, taste, and smell the Godhead (the stench of the demons plays a large role in this mysticism; see V 78). In this context, the terms **fullness** <note>original: πληροφορία (plerophoria)</note> and **to fulfill** <note>original: πληροφορεῖν (plerophorein)</note> are also relevant. In Evagrius, they seem to still be rare in this sense. But when he says in I 54: "[The <term>Gnostic</term> <note>one who possesses spiritual knowledge</note>] will rest when perfect fullness leads those capable of it to the knowledge of the Holy Trinity," this **perfect fullness** is nothing other than this sensory fulfillment with the Godhead—the mystic filling himself with its essential substance. Again, these explanations can be traced back to <term>Origen</term> <note>A 3rd-century scholar whose complex theological systems deeply influenced later monks like Evagrius</note>. Thus we find in *On First Principles* <note>original Latin: "peri archon"</note> I 1, 7 the sentence: "But of these senses, which we spoke of above, because the sense of the mind <note>original: αἴσθησις τοῦ νοός (aisthēsis tou noos)</note> is much better, it is clear to all." II 9, 4: "He [God] who through his grace infuses himself into our senses." *Commentary on John* X 279: "so that the ascent from the sensory things to the so-called **divine senses**⁴) might be shown... for the understanding of intelligible things."

<page-num>319</page-num>
<header>III. Evagrius' Overall Vision in Relation to That of Origen.</header>

This emphasis on the sensory character of the mystical experience emerges particularly clearly in the mystics dependent on Evagrius, such as in the *Homilies of Macarius* and in the works of Diadochus of Photike. It is only from this later perspective that one learns to understand the full significance of the few suggestive remarks made by Evagrius (and Origen).

Thus, Macarius speaks almost exactly like Evagrius (Homily 4, 7) of the **five rational senses** <note>original: πέντε λογικαὶ αἰσθήσεις (pente logikai aisthēseis)</note>, and of a **perception of immortal life** <note>original: αἰσθάνεσθαι ἀθανάτου ζωῆς (aisthanesthai athanatou zōēs)</note> (IV 10, cf. 24, 6). Macarius raises the question of whether Adam **had perception and communion of the Spirit** <note>original: αἴσθησιν εἶχε καὶ κοινωνίαν τοῦ πνεύματος (aisthēsin eiche kai koinōnian tou pneumatos)</note>. Or, as stated in IV 12, **and with perception he shall see heavenly goods and inexpressible delight and infinite wealth of the Godhead** <note>original: καὶ αἰσθήσει ὄψεται ἀγαθὰ ἐπουράνια καὶ τρυφὴν ἀνέκφραστον καὶ πλοῦτον ἄπειρον θεότητος (kai aisthēsei opsetai agatha epourania kai tryphēn anekphraston kai plouton apeiron theotētos)</note>. Even more forcefully in IV 11: **and they may perceive His sweetness and the goodness of the ineffable light; they may enjoy it through actual experience** <note>original: καὶ αἴσθωνται αὐτοῦ τῆς γλυκύτητος καὶ τῆς χρηστότητος τοῦ φωτὸς τοῦ ἀρρήτου ἀπολαύσεως αὐτῇ πείρᾳ ἀπολαύσωσιν (kai aisthōntai autou tēs glykytētos kai tēs chrēstotētos tou phōtos tou arrētou apolauseōs autē peira apolausōsin)</note>. Perception <note>Greek: aisthēsis</note> is, at the same time, a **taste** <note>original: γεῦσις (geusis); see above Evagrius Centuries VII 44</note>. 19, 7: **having partaken of the taste of God and becoming a sharer of the Holy Spirit** <note>original: μεταλαβὼν γεύσεως θεοῦ καὶ πνεύματος ἁγίου μέτοχος γενόμενος</note>. 26, 17: No one can grasp God **except those who have tasted of Him** <note>original: εἰ μὴ οἱ γευσάμενοι ἐξ αὐτοῦ</note>. Simultaneously, perception and **assurance** <note>or "full conviction"; original: πληροφορία (plērophoria)</note> appear as synonyms. 10, 2: **in perfection with all perception and assurance** <note>original: ἐν τελειότητι μετὰ πάσης αἰσθήσεως καὶ πληροφορίας</note> (10, 3. 4 in all assurance), and likewise "taste" and "assurance" are found side-by-side in 15, 20: **but this taste is effective in assurance of the power of the Spirit** <note>original: ἔστιν δὲ ἡ γεῦσις αὕτη ἐνεργητικὴ ἐν πληροφορίᾳ δυνάμεως πνεύματος</note>, as well as in 17, 9: "taste, power, assurance," and 1, 12: "experience (see above 4, 12), assurance."

Diadochus of Photike speaks so often of **perception** <note>Greek: aisthēsis</note> that it is hardly worth enumerating the passages. I refer (though insufficiently) to the word index in the Weis-Liebersdorf edition and note only the pairing of perception and assurance on pages 46, 50, 84, 128 (taste, perception, assurance), 130, and 140. Furthermore, one should look in the Weis-Liebersdorf index for the words "taste" (to taste 50), "sweetness" (also 70, 74, 128), "sweetener," "experience" <note>original: πεῖρα (peira)</note> (also 34, 36, 38, 116, 13, 140; note "experience" and "perception" side-by-side on page 12), "to assure," and also "energy" <note>original: ἐνέργεια (energeia)</note>.

§ 16. With this shift, where Evagrian mysticism moves toward a "sensory realism," it is understandable that he also assumes an effect extending even into the body resulting from that elevation of the soul through <term>praktikē</term> <note>ascetic practice or moral action</note> and <term>theōrētikē</term> <note>spiritual contemplation</note>. With Origen, he shares thoughts (which follow Pauline theology) that the pious will receive a finer corporeality in the hereafter; that the **thickness** <note>original: παχύτης (pachytēs)</note> or earthly weight of this **body** <note>original: σῶμα (sōma)</note> will disappear, and a **finer kind** <note>original: λεπτότερον γένος (leptoteron genos)</note> of body shall arise¹), through which the previously discussed ultimate hope of the return of the <term>Nus</term> <note>the Intellect or highest part of the soul</note> to the unity of its and the divine essence, and its complete liberation from the psycho-somatic state, is achieved (often...

---

1) On the concept of "being filled" <note>original: πληροῦσθαι (plērousthai)</note> 9, 7: **receives the fullness of the adoption of the Spirit... of that spoken in mystery** (14, 2 **is assured** <note>original: πληροφορεῖται (plērophoreitai)</note>).
2) 17, 12: those are rebuked who speak of <term>apatheia</term> <note>freedom from passions</note> and perfection, **not having energy and assurance**.
3) e.g., II 77: **The final judgment of the righteous Judge will not produce an alteration of bodies** (cf. III, 25) **but will remove their thickness from their midst.** Cf. VI 58, IV 24, III 40: **The last trumpet is the command of the righteous Judge, who clothes the rational beings in their bodies according to the state of their conduct** (cf. also III 25). The commentary finds here a polemic against the teachings of Origen with their endless renewals and transformations of the body; in my opinion, this is an error. For even Origen, when developing his idea of the **spiritual body** <note>original: σῶμα πνευματικόν (sōma pneumatikon)</note> following Paul, can make the state reached at the judgment appear almost final. And even if the idea of continuous transformation recedes and only appears hidden in Evagrius, he must have also harbored this thought if he speaks of the final return of the Nus to the unity of its essence. III 47, with its emphasis on **one renewal** <note>original: μία ἀνακαίνωσις (mia anakainōsis)</note> and the specific rejection of **another renewal** <note>original: ἑτέρα ἀνακαίνωσις (hetera anakainōsis)</note>, is certainly anti-Origenist. Could a later revision of the Evagrian sayings <note>original: Logia</note> perhaps be present here?

...can be well combined with (hidden) thoughts of further development in the afterlife. Now, however, Evagrius teaches—as indeed all mysticism has since Paul in 2 Corinthians 3:18, who in turn incorporates influences of the mystery-cult piety—that this finer body is granted to the Gnostic <note>Evagrius uses "Gnostic" to mean one who has attained deep spiritual knowledge through asceticism.</note> already in this world, and it is characteristic that in this connection we again encounter the old Pauline watchword of the **spiritual body** <note>original: σῶμα πνευματικόν (sōma pneumatikon)</note>. The new "pneumatic" (spiritual) physicality already presented itself to the monk-mystics in a quite plastic and realistically tangible way. Has not the monk, through **ascetic practice** <note>original: πρακτική (praktikē)</note>, already achieved a piece of the **density** <note>original: παχύτης (pachytēs)</note> of the new physicality? If he has entered into **passionlessness** <note>original: ἀπάθεια (apatheia)</note> and **spiritual love** <note>original: ἀγάπη πνευματική (agapē pneumatikē)</note>, if he has succeeded in completely repressing the stirrings of **desire** <note>original: ἐπιθυμία (epithymia)</note>, in finally overcoming sexual lust, in entering the state of **freedom from anger** <note>original: ἀοργησία (aorgēsia)</note>, and in elevating his **intellect** <note>original: νοῦς (nous)</note> in **essential knowledge** <note>original: γνῶσις οὐσιώδης (gnōsis ousiōdēs)</note> above the entire world of interiority—does he not then already possess that **spiritual body**, that weightless physicality of the superterrestrial, heavenly beings?

Evagrius affirms this. Right at the beginning of the *Centuries* (I 11) we read the sentence: "All those who have already now acquired **spiritual bodies** <note>original: σώματα πνευματικά (sōmata pneumatika)</note> rule in the present age <note>original: ἐν τοῖς ἐνεστῶσιν [instead of Frankenberg's 'past'] αἰῶσιν (en tois enestōsin ... aiōsin)</note>; as many of them, however, as are still enclosed by bodies that toil <note>original: ἐν σώμασιν πρακτικοῖς [instead of Frankenberg's 'laborers'], see above</note>, will rule in the future age!" The Gnostic of Evagrius—we may also say the "Pneumatic" (Spirit-filled person)¹)—is in possession of the **spiritual body**; he is a ruler, a **god** <note>original: θεός (theos)</note> here on earth. Evagrius speaks just as decisively in II 72: "If the knowledge of spiritual beings is prior and more honorable than the knowledge of corporeal things, then clearly their bodies are also **fine** <note>original: λεπτά (lepta)</note>²) and luminous compared to those others." Evagrius also describes a present experience in II 90: "Those who have seen the light of the **two spiritual lamps** <note>original: δύο πνευματικῶν λαμπάδων (dyo pneumatikōn lampadōn)</note>³) will themselves be deemed worthy to see that first light of **blessedness** <note>original: μακαριότητος (makariotētos)</note>⁴), which we see by the grace of our Lord Jesus Christ, having been deemed worthy of the renewal of our bodies." The same likely applies to III 20 (despite the different interpretation of the commentary): "The transformation of 'practical' bodies is a renewal from the fleshly into the spiritual according to the measure of their state."

### § 17. This new somatic state of the Gnostic or Pneumatic means for Evagrius, expressed in other words, an elevation into the state of angelic beings. 

When Evagrius describes the nature of the angelic powers (III 5)—"the intellects of the heavenly powers are pure, full of true knowledge, and their bodies are radiating light"—he simultaneously sketches the ideal of the Gnostic that is attainable even in this life, at least temporarily. It is part of this same idea when Evagrius, like all the mysticism of his time, likes to speak of how knowledge (*gnosis*) and also **ascetic practice** <note>original: πρακτική (praktikē)</note> (the "working of the commandments") are the spiritual food of the Gnostic, and that by this path he partakes in the **bread of angels** <note>original: ἄρτος τῶν ἀγγέλων (artos tōn angelōn)</note>⁵). V 35: "If the food of rational nature is the knowledge of beings, and we must eat this in the sweat of our brow..."

1) The term "Pneumatic" <note>meaning a person led by the Spirit</note> is relatively rare in Evagrius. As far as I can see, II 72 stands almost alone. More frequent are phrases such as **spiritual intellect** (II 27), **spiritual knowledge** (I 72, II 3, 8, 14, 20, IV 6), **spiritual body** (I 90, IV 24, etc.; IV 82: **soulish body**), **spiritual contemplation** (II 13, VI 2, *Praktikos* 21, 48), **spiritual teaching** (VI 60), **spiritual vision** (II 62), **spiritual love** (*Tractatus* 24, 58), and **spiritual word** (V 28). Once even **spiritual desires** (I 85).

5) Compare I 23 and the parallels from Origen cited above on page 288.

...we have been commanded, it is clear that we ate this [bread] in the performance of the commandments of God. <note>original: παρηγγέλμεθα, δῆλον ὅτι ἐν τῇ τῶν ἐντολῶν θεοῦ ἐργασίᾳ τοῦτον φάγομεν.</note> *Praktikos* II, 56: "And we shall say that **passionlessness** <note>original: ἀπάθεια (apatheia); a state of being undisturbed by emotions or worldly desires.</note> is the health of the soul, but knowledge is its food, which alone is accustomed to join us to the holy powers." <note>original: καὶ τὴν μὲν ἀπάθεια ὑγείαν ἐροῦμεν εἶναι ψυχῆς, τροφὴν δὲ τὴν γνῶσιν, ἥτις μόνη συνάπτει ἡμᾶς ταῖς ἁγίαις δυνάμεσιν εἴωθεν.</note> But of course, a distance remains here between the **Gnostic** <note>In this context, "Gnostic" refers to a Christian who has attained high spiritual knowledge, not necessarily a member of the early "Gnostic" sects.</note> here on earth and the angelic powers; he must eat his bread "in the sweat of his brow" (see above) or, more clearly (*Chapters on Prayer* III, 4): "It is the part of angels to be nourished at all times by the contemplation of beings, but for humans [to be nourished] at the appropriate time." <note>original: τῶν μὲν ἀγγέλων ἐστὶ τὸ παντὶ χρόνῳ τρέφεσθαι ταῖς τῶν ὄντων θεωρίαις, τῶν δὲ ἀνθρώπων ἐπὶ τοῦ καιροῦ.</note>

Despite all this, Evagrius decisively declares that this blessed, angel-like state is reachable for the Gnostic and mystic for a shorter or longer time. We already saw this above where it concerned the **practice** <note>original: πρᾶξις (praxis); the active life of virtue and asceticism.</note> of passionlessness. For him, passionlessness is truly an achievable state. He rises to even greater certainty and enthusiasm when he visualizes the ideal of the "Theoretician" (the one dedicated to contemplation). Then we hear words such as those stating that those who possess **spiritual bodies** <note>original: σώματα πνευματικά (sōmata pneumatika)</note> are already kings in this life. Then it is said: "The inheritance of the saints is the end of labor and torment" <note>original: πέρας ἐργασίας τε καὶ βασανισμοῦ ἡ τῶν ἁγίων κληρονομία</note> (I, 18). "The perfect man does not [need to] practice self-control, and the passionless man does not [simply] endure" <note>original: ὁ τέλειος οὐκ ἐγκρατεύεται καὶ ὁ ἀπαθὴς οὐκ ὑπομένει</note> (*Praktikos* 40). Or even: "Infinite is the **fullness** <note>original: πλήρωμα (pleroma); a term for the divine totality.</note> of the first created beings; but vanity is circumscribed by a limit" <note>original: ἀπέραντόν ἐστι τὸ πλήρωμα τῶν πρώτων γεγονότων· πέρατι δὲ περιγέγραπται ἡ ματαιότης</note> (I, 54; cf. 55). This Gnostic, in the perfection of his virtues, stands beyond the law: "He no longer remembers the law" <note>original: οὐκ ἔτι μέμνηται νόμου</note> (*Praktikos* 42). He also enters into the dignified status of the holy angels in that he now, like them, takes over the education of those not yet perfected and those in need of support: "Not only do the holy angels labor with us for salvation, but also the saints who are our companions" <note>original: οὐ μόνον οἱ ἅγιοι ἄγγελοι πονοῦνται μεθ' ἡμῶν εἰς τὴν σωτηρίαν, ἀλλὰ καὶ οἱ ἅγιοι οἱ ἑταῖροι ἡμῶν</note> (VI, 88; cf. 90; III, 7). He is the "God-man" of whom it is said: "And only the man of God can know the man of knowledge" <note>original: καὶ μόνος ἄνθρωπος τοῦ θεοῦ τὸν τῆς γνώσεως ἄνθρωπον γινώσκειν δύναται</note> (II, 56). Here, at the height of Evagrian mysticism, we also find the great slogan of the **deification** of the mystic: "In the **Monad** <note>original: Μονάδα; the ultimate unity or the Divine Oneness.</note> there are neither those who rule nor those under rule, but all are gods" <note>original: ἐν τῇ Μονάδι οὐκ εἰσὶν οἱ ἄρχουσιν οὐδὲ οἱ ὑπ' ἀρχάς, ἀλλὰ πάντες θεοί εἰσιν</note> (IV, 51). "When the **intellect** <note>original: νοῦς (nous)</note> is deemed worthy to be in the Holy Trinity, then by grace it is also called God" <note>original: ὅταν ὁ νοῦς τοῦ ἐν τῇ ἁγίᾳ Τριάδι εἶναι καταξιωθῇ, τότε χάριτι καὶ θεὸς προσαγορεύεται</note> (V, 81). "They lead [the soul] up to the perfect mingling with God" <note>original: πρὸς τὴν τελείαν τοῦ θεοῦ σύμμιξιν ἀναβιβάζουσιν</note> (VII, 43). "The intellect is incorporeal when it is assimilated to God" <note>original: ἀσώματός ἐστιν ὁ νοῦς ὅταν ἀφομοίωται τῷ θεῷ</note>.

# IV. Relationships of Origen's (Evagrius's) worldview to the contemporary historical milieu.

In order to better maintain clarity in this difficult subject matter, I have so far restricted the presentation to the comparison between Origen and Evagrius and to the proof of the latter's absolute dependence on the former. However, it will still be worthwhile to take a brief look around and again examine the worldview and outlook of both regarding their further ancestry and origin.

<meta>This page transitions from the practical ascetic life (praxis) to the philosophical foundations of Evagrius’s thought. It explores how the concepts of the "Monad" and "Number" in the writings of Origen and Evagrius were influenced by Neopythagorean philosophy, particularly the distinction between divine unity and worldly multiplicity.</meta>

<page-num>322</page-num>
<header>Book III. Evagrius Studies.</header>

I begin with the Origenist-Evagrian presentation of the **Monad** <note>original: Monas; a term for a single, indivisible unit, used here to describe the essence of the Godhead as absolute unity.</note> as the essence of the Godhead (see § 1). Determining the origin of these ideas is not difficult; one will immediately point to **Neopythagoreanism** <note>A school of philosophy that revived the teachings of Pythagoras, focusing on the mystical and religious significance of numbers and the soul.</note>. Justinian says in his synodal letter against Origen (Koetschau, *On First Principles* p. 21, note): "For Pythagoras indeed said that the Monad is the principle of all things" <note>original: ὁ γάρ τοι Πυθαγόρας ἀρχὴν τῶν πάντων ἔφησεν εἶναι τὴν Μονάδα</note>. However, some more precise points of comparison should be recalled here. The characteristic feature of the Origen-Evagrius view is not just the understanding of God as the Monad, but primarily the contrast in which this divine Monad is placed against **Number** <note>In this philosophical context, "Number" represents plurality, division, and the created world, as opposed to the singular unity of God.</note> and the entire world of numbers. The Monad itself is not a number, a "one in number" <note>original: ἓν ἀριθμῷ; meaning a single unit within a mathematical sequence</note>, but is beyond all number and infinitely superior to it. This emerges even more distinctly in the explanations of Evagrius than in those of Origen, at least as far as I can oversee them. This, however, is specifically Neopythagorean, in contrast to the older Pythagorean, much simpler conception of number as the essence of all things. This is highlighted with particular precision in the presentation by **Sextus Empiricus** <note>A Greek physician and philosopher (c. 160–210 AD) who recorded various philosophical systems.</note> (X 276, see 282): "Therefore, the principles of all things emerged according to the highest level: both the first Monad and the **indefinite Dyad** <note>original: ahoristos Dyas; a principle representing duality, matter, or the potential for division.</note>. From these, they say, arise the 'one' in numbers and the subsequent 'two' [dyad]. From the first Monad comes the 'one,' and from the Monad and the indefinite Dyad come the 'two'" <note>original: ἀνέκυψαν ἄρα ἀρχαὶ πάντων κατὰ τὸ ἀνωτάτω ἥ τε πρώτη Μονὰς καὶ ἡ ἀόριστος Δυάς. ἐξ ὧν γίνεσθαί φασι τὸ ἓν τοῖς ἀριθμοῖς ἓν καὶ τὴν ἐπὶ τούτοις πάλιν δυάδα. ἀπὸ μὲν τῆς πρώτης Μονάδος τὸ ἕν, ἀπὸ δὲ τῆς Μονάδος καὶ τῆς ἀορίστου Δυάδος τὰ δύο</note>.

This contrast between Old and New Pythagoreanism is also very clearly expressed in the testimony of **Moderatus** <note>A Neopythagorean philosopher from the 1st century AD.</note> (in Stobaeus, *Eclogae* I 20): "Among the numbers, the more recent [philosophers] introduced the Monad and the Dyad as principles, while the [old] Pythagoreans [introduced] all the terms of the series in succession" <note>original: τῶν ἀριθμῶν εἰσηγήσαντο τὰς ἀρχὰς οἱ μὲν νεώτεροι τὴν Μονάδα καὶ τὴν Δυάδα, οἱ δὲ Πυθαγόρειοι πάσας παρὰ τὸ ἑξῆς τὰς τῶν ὅρων ἐκθέσεις</note>.

Furthermore, we saw above (§ 1) how Evagrius, in particular, contrasts the divine **Henad** <note>original: Henas; a 'Unity' or 'Unit' similar to the Monad.</note> and Monad (note the recurrence of these terms in both) with the "one in number" <note>original: ἓν τῷ ἀριθμῷ</note>. This terminology is also Neopythagorean and is linked to the substantive distinction just mentioned. This is clearest in the passage preserved by Justin (*Cohortatio* c. 19): "For the Monad is among the intelligible things, but the 'one' is among the numbers" <note>original: τὴν μὲν γὰρ Μονάδα ἐν τοῖς νοητοῖς, τὸ δὲ ἓν ἐν τοῖς ἀριθμοῖς</note>. Conversely, it is emphasized in **Theon of Smyrna** <note>A philosopher and mathematician who wrote about the mathematical aspects of Plato's works.</note> (*Mathematics* 4 [20₁₉ ed. Hiller]): "Archytas and Philolaus call the 'one' and the 'monad' indifferently, and the 'monad' the 'one'" <note>original: 'Ἀρχύτας καί Φιλόλαος ἀδιαφόρως τὸ ἓν καὶ μονάδα καλοῦσι καὶ τὴν μονάδα ἕν¹)</note>. It was emphasized above how Evagrius likes to speak of the world split by number and our split existence in this world. For this, I would like to draw upon a sentence from (the Neopythagorean or Platonist) **Numenius of Apamea** <note>A 2nd-century philosopher whose work bridged Platonism and Oriental mysticism.</note>. For him, the deity (Zeller III 2, 237) is likewise primarily the Monad. Alongside this highest deity, he famously assumes a second and third god (the **Demiurge** <note>original: demiourgos; the creator-god who fashions the physical world.</note> and the **Cosmos** <note>original: kosmos; the universe as an ordered system.</note>), and defines their essence: "The second and third god, however, is one. But by associating with matter, which is a **dyad** <note>A pair or duality; the opposite of the Monad.</note>, he indeed unifies it, but is split by it" <note>original: θεὸς μέντοι ὁ δεύτερος καὶ τρίτος ἐστὶν εἷς. συμφερόμενος δὲ τῇ ὕλῃ δυάδι οὔσῃ ἑνοῖ μὲν αὐτὴν, σχίζεται δὲ ὑπ' αὐτῆς</note>.

If Origen and with him Evagrius regard the world-miracle essentially as a falling away from the divine Monad, and the world-play as a return to it—as a dissolution of all number—then this overall view has grown essentially on Neopythagorean soil, although specifically the speculations about the **indefinite Dyad** <note>original: ahoristos Dyas</note> seem to be missing in both. If Origen—

---

1) Cf. also **Syrianus** <note>A Neoplatonist philosopher of the 5th century AD.</note> on Aristotle’s *Metaphysics* (Scholia 917 b, Mullach 116 a, citing Moderatus and Nicomachus): "that the 'one' and the 'monad,' being kindred, differ from each other" <note>original: ὅτι τὸ ἓν καὶ ἡ μονὰς συγγενῆ ἐόντα διαφέρει ἀλλήλων</note>. A slightly different conception seems to exist in **Eudorus** <note>An influential Academic philosopher of the 1st century BC.</note> (Age of Augustus, according to Simplicius, *Physics* 181): "The 'One' that is the principle of all things is one thing, and the 'One' that is opposed to the Dyad, which they also call the Monad, is another" <note>original: ἄλλο μέν ἐστιν Ἕν ἡ ἀρχὴ τῶν πάντων, ἀλλὸ δὲ Ἕν τὸ τῇ Δυάδι ἀντικείμενον, ὃ καὶ Μονάδα καλοῦσιν</note>. According to Theon of Smyrna (see above), most Pythagoreans place a second Monad before the Monad; cf. the material in Zeller I 362₃. 364₁, 349₁. Kroll, *The Teachings of Hermes Trismegistus*, 15.

It cites several ancient philosophers like Sextus Empiricus and Numenius to demonstrate that Evagrius’s focus on the soul's return from multiplicity to unity mirrors these earlier philosophical traditions.</summary>

<meta>This page continues the investigation into the philosophical roots of the Origenist-Evagrian worldview, specifically moving from the definition of the "Monad" to how the "fall" from this unity into the physical world was understood by contemporary thinkers like Numenius and the early Alexandrian teachers.</meta>

### IV. Relationships of Origen’s (and Evagrius’s) Worldview to the Historical Context of the Time. 323

(And somewhat hidden, yet also in Evagrius), Origen so energetically places the fall of spirits from the **Monad** <note>original: Monas; the ultimate, indivisible divine unity</note> of the incorporeal divine essence at the center of his system and seeks to understand the origin of the entire physical world from this point. In a similar vein, we hear from **Numenius** <note>A 2nd-century philosopher who bridged Pythagoreanism and Platonism</note> (according to Iamblichus, in Stobaeus I 910): "some of the younger ones... assert that all incarnations of the whole are evil, especially those following Cronius, Numenius, and Harpocration" <note>original: τινὲς δὲ τῶν νεωτέρων ... τὰς ἐνσωματώσεις τῶν ὅλων κακάς τε εἶναι πόσας διασχυρίζονται καὶ διαφερόντως οἱ περὶ Κρόνιόν τε καὶ Νουμήνιον καὶ Ἁρποκρατίωνα</note>.

It should also be pointed out that such speculations about the Monad were clearly widespread in the Catechetical School of Alexandria even before Origen. I refer here to a characteristic sentence in the *Excerpts from Theodotus* 10, 55: "the first-created beings, even if different in number and limited and circumscribed in each case, yet the likeness of things creates unity, equality, and similarity" <note>original: οἱ πρωτόκτιστοι εἰ καὶ ἀριθμῷ διάφοροι καὶ ὃ καθ’ ἕκαστον περιώρισται καὶ περιγέγραπται, ἀλλ’ ἡ ὁμοιότης τῶν πραγμάτων ἑνότητα καὶ ἰσότητα καὶ ὁμοιότητα ποιεῖ</note> (compare *Excerpts* 11, 2). Here too, we clearly see the opposition of the world of **unity and equality** <note>original: ἑνότης καὶ ἰσότης</note> against a world split apart by **number** <note>representing plurality and division</note>. We find traces of this perspective in **Clement of Alexandria** as well. A peculiar speculation about the divine Monad—which one reaches through an analytical path by detaching oneself from the "depth, width, and length" of the physical world to press forward to the "remaining point" of the Monad—is found in *Stromata* V 71 2–3.

We are reminded even more of Evagrius and Origen when we read in *Stromata* IV 152 1: "the man who is divinized into **passionlessness** <term>apatheia: a state of being undisturbed by emotions or worldly desires</term> becomes immaculately monadic" <note>original: εἰς δὲ τὴν ἀπάθειαν θεούμενος ἄνθρωπος ἀχράντως μοναδικὸς γίνεται</note>. And in IV 157 1: "Therefore, to believe in Him and through Him is to become monadic, being united in Him without distraction; but to disbelieve is to be divided, to stand apart, and to be partitioned" <note>original: τὸ δὲ ἀπιστῆσαι διιστάσαι ἐστὶ καὶ διαστῆναι καὶ μερισθῆναι</note>. Furthermore, Clement himself points us directly to the source of these views in IV 151 3: "Mystically, therefore, among us it was said of the Pythagorean that a man also must become one, since the High Priest himself is one, God being one, according to the unchangeable habit of always moving toward good things."

Finally, I refer to the characteristic passage of the thirteenth **Hermetic Tractate** <note>A collection of mystical and philosophical texts attributed to Hermes Trismegistus</note>: "Life and light are united there, where the number of the **Unity** <note>original: Henados; the One</note> of the spirit naturally exists." With this, the "milieu" in which the speculations of Origen and Evagrius move is fairly well defined.

Much more could be said about the diversely graded and structured system of the spirit realm, the idea of a constant rising and falling of this spirit world, and the thought of the educational significance of the higher classes of angels for the lower ones. However, I have already presented most of this in my *Jewish-Christian School Tradition*. The closest parallels we have to note are in the *Excerpts from Theodotus* and the *Eclogues* of Clement of Alexandria. I refer to what I said on pages 157 ff. of *School Tradition* regarding this and quote only the two particularly striking passages: "For those who have transitioned from men into angels are apprenticed for a thousand years by the angels, being restored to perfection; then those who taught are transferred to archangelic authority, while those who learned in turn apprentice those who are again transitioning from men into angels. Then, in such stated periods, they are resto—" <note>the original text breaks off mid-word: ἀποκα- (apoka-), likely part of 'restored'</note>

***

Such a sentence could also be found in Origen or Evagrius.

3) Compare IV 73 3: "Love... restoring the **gnostic** <note>the spiritually 'knowing' person</note> to the unity of faith," and also VII 68 1, V 82 1.

...they are established in the appropriate angelic stationing of the body <note>original: τῇ οἰκείᾳ τοῦ σώματος ἀγγελοθεσίᾳ (tē oikeia tou sōmatos angelothesia); the term "angelothesia" refers to being ranked or placed among the angels</note>. **Excerpt 27:** But the naked soul ... becoming as it were a body of power, passes into spiritual things, having truly become rational and high-priestly, just like the archangels. They become high priests of the angels, and of these again, the first-created <note>original: πρωτόκτιστοι (protoktistoi); a term for the highest order of created beings, often identified with the highest angels</note>.

Here we have everything side by side: the various classes of spirits—here in a more definite form than in Origen—Evagrius, those of the first-created archangels, and angels; the ascent of the various classes over long periods of time; and the instruction that the lower receive from the higher. I further recall the significant passage in Clement’s *Miscellanies* <note>original: Stromat.</note> VII 9, 2–3: "all looking toward the first administrator of the whole, who governs the salvation of all by the Father’s will; with others set as leaders under others, until one reaches the Great High Priest. For from one origin above, acting according to the will, depend the first, second, and third ranks; then at the end of the visible world, the blessed angelic stationing <note>original: ἀγγελοθεσία (angelothesia)</note> at the summit, and indeed down to ourselves, some under others."

I then further investigated (*School Practice* 178 ff.) the origin of these strange fantasies and (following Collomp’s investigations) pointed out the striking parallels in Porphyry’s *Letter to Anebo* and Iamblichus’s *On the Mysteries*. The second book of *On the Mysteries* develops a detailed theology of the hierarchy of spirits: gods, archangels, angels, demons, heroes, rulers <note>original: ἄρχοντες (archontes)</note>, souls. Porphyry also already lists all the members of the spirit world (according to *On the Mysteries* II 3 p. 70 edited by Parthey). *On the Mysteries* I 5 p. 16 presents a simpler classification: gods, demons, heroes, souls. The question of the origin of the speculations in Iamblichus’s *On the Mysteries* (and Porphyry’s *Letter to Anebo*) led further to the speculations of the Hermetic circle of writings. *On the Mysteries* refers directly to Hermes and Hermetic revelations at the beginning of the first book (cf. also the important passages VIII 5, X 7). In *The Key*, Tractate X of the *Corpus Hermeticum*, we read the sentence: "But human souls have a beginning of immortality by changing into demons. Then in this way, they dance into the choir of the fixed stars. There are two choirs of gods: one of the wandering [planets], the other of the fixed [stars]. And this is the most perfect glory of the soul." We again have a sequence of stages: fixed stars, wandering stars, demons, souls. Regarding the nature of the connection between these levels of spirits, we read in chapter 14: "From one origin all things are suspended. And the origin is from the One and Only." Chapter 22: "There is a communion of souls, and those of the gods commune with those of humans, and those of humans with those of the irrational animals. The superior ones care for the inferior: gods for humans, humans for irrational animals..."

<page-num>325</page-num>
<header>IV. Relationships of the Worldview of Origen (Evagrius) to the Contemporary Historical Milieu. 325</header>

"...but God is the God of all" <note>original: ὁ δὲ θεὸς πάντων (ho de theos pantōn)</note>. In this context, I finally placed (in *School Practice* 181) the speech of Cleombrotus in Plutarch’s *On the Obsolescence of Oracles* <note>original: de defectu oraculorum</note> ch. 10, 415 B: "In this way, from men into heroes, and from heroes into demons <note>term: demons; in this Greek context, 'daimones' refers to intermediary spirits between gods and humans, not necessarily evil beings</note>, the better souls receive their transformation. And from demons, a few, after a long time and having been purified through virtue, share entirely in divinity"¹).

And these observations can be traced even further back. This doctrine of a hierarchically organized realm of spirits is certainly clearly expressed also in the Alexandrian Philo (main passages *On the Giants* <note>original: de gigant.</note> 12 ff.; *On Planting* <note>original: de plantat.</note> 18; *On Dreams* <note>original: de somn.</note> I 138 ff., cf. *School Practice* 18 ff.). Here too, the classes of "heroes, demons, and angels" <note>original: ἥρωες, δαίμονες ἄγγελοι</note> are named, even if not in a clearly defined sequence of stages, just as the entire worldview regarding the hierarchy of spirits and the ascent and descent of souls exists here only in more general and indistinct outlines. In particular, it should be emphasized that the striking idea of the sympathy of higher spiritual beings for the lower, and the friendly promotion of the latter by the former, is presented repeatedly in Philo. According to *On Dreams* § 147, for example, the higher souls descend: "because of love for humanity <note>original: φιλανθρωπία (philanthrōpia)</note> and mercy for our race, for the sake of help and alliance, so that they might revive the soul still being carried along as if in a river in the body by breathing salvation into it" (cf. *On the Giants* 12, *On Planting* 14, *On Dreams* I 140)²). And since long ago, the striking explanations in Plutarch’s *On the Sign of Socrates* <note>original: de genio Socratis</note> ch. 24 and in Maximus of Tyre, *Dissertation* XV 6, have been brought into relation with this (Richard Heinze, *Xenokrates* pp. 100–110). One is inclined to see Posidonius <note>term: Posidonius; a Stoic philosopher (c. 135–51 BC) who attempted to harmonize various fields of knowledge and influenced later views on the soul's journey</note> as the ultimate source here, as with all of Philo’s expositions on the hierarchy of spirits. In *School Practice* (pp. 18–20), I explained why I cannot absolutely agree with this for these views, as for some others. The numerous inconsistencies and variations in these fantasies make it hard to believe that we are seeing the work of a single man everywhere. We may judge that these are widespread popular views that begin to penetrate philosophy with Posidonius and continue to flow in again later, until they are finally built up into increasingly bold and fantastic systems by later writers. — At the end of this entire development stands someone like "Dionysius the Areopagite"³) with his system spanning both earthly and heavenly hierarchies.

And finally, a parallel between Evagrius (Origen) and Clement of Alexandria (or his sources) should be pointed out in this context. Attention was drawn above (§ 3 and § 17) to the idea that the perfected Gnostic <note>term: Gnostic; here Clement refers to the "true Gnostic" as the ideal Christian philosopher/intellectual</note> participates for his part in the angels' work of educating the lower-standing souls, and that he thereby enters the position of dignity of the spiritual powers guiding the great process of the ascent of souls. Likewise, it is stated in the *Excerpts* <note>original: ἐκλογαί (eklogai)</note> 37.2, that the Gnostic "practices angelic service while in the flesh" <note>original: ἐν σαρκὶ μελετήσαντος ἀγγελικὴν ὑπουργίαν (en sarki meletēsantos angelikēn hypourgian)</note>. In the Gnostics, God himself is alive and actively present: "Thus God does good through men... he gave birth to us through men and educated us through men..."

1) Cf. the striking passage in Evagrius V 11 about the ranks <note>original: βαθμοὶ (bathmoi)</note> of angels, men, and demons.
2) Still more parallels: *School Practice* 20.1.
3) This name already appears in the commentator on Evagrius II 17; cf. II 78, the explanation of the new angelic choirs we encounter in the Areopagite, but which on the other hand already appear in an older Jewish writing, the Slavonic Book of Enoch.

It highlights the idea of higher beings assisting lower ones out of "philanthropy," a theme that culminates in the rigid hierarchies of Pseudo-Dionysius.</summary>

...men (16). Knowledge <term>Gnosis: In this context, a deep spiritual or "true" knowledge of divine matters</term> is "truly divine wisdom... the pure light, which enlightens those among men who are pure." <note>original Greek: ἡ τῷ ὄνti θεία σοφία . . . τὸ φῶς τὸ εἰλικρινές, τὸ φωτίζον τοὺς καθαροὺς τῶν ἀνθρώπων</note>

The investigation has already clearly shown us the entire milieu to which the speculations of Evagrius and Origen belong. Behind Origen emerges the thought-world of the Alexandrian Catechetical School <note>A famous center of Christian scholarship in Egypt that sought to harmonize the Bible with Greek philosophy</note>, the *Extracts from Theodotus* <note>original: Excerpta ex Theodoto; a collection of Gnostic teachings</note>, the *Selections* <note>original: Eklogai</note> (perhaps by Pantaenus?), and Clement of Alexandria. Behind the Alexandrian Catechetical School lie Hermetic (Neopythagorean) speculations, which on the other hand make their way toward the Neoplatonists. If we travel back a bit further, we encounter the sources of Plutarch's mystical speculations and Philo of Alexandria <note>A Jewish philosopher who lived at the time of Jesus and used Greek philosophy to interpret the Hebrew Bible</note>; finally, the figure of the Stoic Posidonius becomes visible. However, one should see him not as the originator, but rather as the conveyor of these largely popular fantasies. The magical power with which this image of the great hierarchy of spirits—how heavenly powers ascend and descend and hand each other the golden buckets <note>A literary allusion to Goethe's *Faust*, describing the harmonious movement of the universe</note>—dominated minds is shown on the other hand by the figure of Dionysius the Areopagite.

The peculiar psychology which, as we saw, Evagrius shared with Origen, also requires a special investigation. It is upon this basis that their doctrine of the Fall of man and the return to the unity of the original being arises. In the end, it rests on Aristotelian psychology (*Mind* <term>Nus: The Greek term for the 'Intellect' or 'Mind', considered the highest, most divine part of the human spirit</term>, the highest component of psychology); only here and there did Platonic elements appear in the listing of the lower elements of the human soul (which supposedly arose through the Fall). In any case, however, the abrupt way in which the elements of human soul-life are torn apart and set against one another—how the *Mind* is viewed as an existence in itself, and its sinking and submerging into *Soul* <note>original: Psyche</note> and *Body* <note>original: Soma</note> is regarded as the Fall—is mythology and no longer philosophy.

<margin>
1) Regarding the following, see my review of Kroll’s *Teachings of Hermes Trismegistus* <note>original: Lehren des Hermes Trismegistos</note>, *Göttingische Gelehrte Anzeigen* 1914, p. 725 ff.
2) We find this grading of value between *Mind* and *Reason* <term>Logos: Often translated as 'Word' or 'Reason', here it refers to discursive, logical thought as opposed to the higher intuitive 'Mind' (Nus)</term> very frequently in Philo of Alexandria. In his work, we very often find the division of the human being into *Mind*, *Reason*, perception <note>original: αἴσθησις (aisthēsis)</note>, and body <note>original: σῶμα (sōma)</note>, and the requirement that the *Mind* free itself from all these lower elements of the human being. According to him, this is then the "stripping bare" <note>original: γυμνωθῆναι (gymnōthēnai)</note> and "unfolding" <note>original: ἐξαπλωθῆναι (exaplōthēnai)</note> of the *Mind*. Cf. among many passages *Allegorical Interpretation* <note>original: Leg. Alleg.</note> I 39; *That the Worse Attacks the Better* <note>original: quod det. pot.</note> 91 (129); *On Drunkenness* <note>original: de ebriet.</note> 70; *On Migration* <note>original: de migrat.</note> 2; *On Flight and Finding* <note>original: de fuga</note> 92, 219; *On the Confusion of Tongues* <note>original: de confus</note> 52; *On Abraham* <note>original: de Abrah.</note> 28; *Who is the Heir of Divine Things?* <note>original: q. rer. div. haer.</note> 69 ff., 81 ff., 109 ff., 118; *On the Cherubim* <note>original: de Cherub.</note> 116, etc. Kroll, *Teachings of Hermes Trismegistus* p. 262, cites only Marcus Aurelius <note>original: Mark. Aurel</note> V 27, VII 55, IX 8 for this sharp contrast between *Mind* and *Reason*. We are dealing here with a singularity in which Philo and the Hermetica appear linked. — I gave an explanation of this speculation from the mystery cults in *Göttingische Gelehrte Anzeigen* 1914, 744.
</margin>

We are therefore not surprised to find the best parallel to this psychological mythology in the Hermetic writings <note>Sacred texts attributed to the legendary figure Hermes Trismegistus, blending Greek and Egyptian wisdom</note> ¹). Here the conviction is expressed that the *Mind* is a supernatural essence, which for that reason does not even belong to all people. Here, in the final part of *The Key* <note>original: Kleis (Tractate X)</note>, we encounter the sentence that the *Mind* does not tolerate a sluggish soul <note>original: νωθρᾶ ψυχή (nōthra psychē)</note>, but rather leaves it: "Such a soul... does not possess Mind. Hence one should not even call such a person a human being." <note>original: ἡ τοιαύτη δὲ ψυχὴ . . . νοῦν οὐκ ἔχει. ὅθεν οὐδ’ ἄνθρωπον δεῖ λέγειν τὸν τοιοῦτον</note> Or XII 4: "But as many human souls as have not obtained Mind as a pilot, they suffer the same as the souls of irrational animals" <note>original: ὅσαι δὲ ψυχαὶ ἀνθρώπιναι οὐκ ἔτυχον κυβερνήτου τοῦ νοῦ, τὸ αὐτὸ πάσχουσι ταῖς τῶν ἀλόγων ζώων</note> (cf. the fragment in Stobaeus <note>original: Stobaios</note> I 800). The parallels in the Hermetica are partly not quite clear only because, strangely, *Reason* ²) also appears here as the lower element compared to the *Mind*, and it is then said that only the *Reason* belongs to all people, but not the *Mind*, which is granted only to the chosen in the sacrament of the Mixing Bowl <term>Krater: A symbolic vessel or "Mixing Bowl" mentioned in Hermetic texts where souls are dipped to receive Mind/Intellect</term>...

It specifically highlights the "mythological" view of the human Mind (Nus) as a separate, supernatural entity that "falls" into the lower states of soul and body.</summary>

# IV. Relationships of Origen’s (Evagrius’) Worldview to the historical milieu of the time. 327

[...] becomes a part (Book IV, chapter 3; compare Book I, chapters 19, 22, 23). Accordingly, in the intricate psychological system of nested layers presented in X 13, 16–18; XII 13–14, 18 (also XI 2–4), we find the sequence: **Mind, Reason, Soul, Spirit, Body** (see below). <note>original Greek: νοῦς, λόγος, ψυχή, πνεῦμα, σῶμα</note> Yet here too, we find a striking parallel in form to the schema in Evagrius (see above, § 4), though it is oriented quite differently in substance: **Reason, Spirit, Mind, Soul, Body.** <note>original: λόγος, πνεῦμα, νοῦς, ψυχή, σῶμα</note> The analogy on both sides emerges with particular clarity where it concerns the idea of man's return to the original unity of a single being (see above, § 5): *“For when the soul has run back into itself, the spirit is contracted into the blood, and the soul into the spirit”* (here the author refers to the lower, semi-physical element of the soul). *“But the Mind, having become pure of its garments”* (1) *“being divine by nature, and having taken hold of a fiery body”* (!) *“circles every place, leaving the soul behind for judgment and the justice it deserves”* (X 16). <note>original: ἀναδραμούσης γὰρ τῆς ψυχῆς εἰς ἑαυτὴν συστέλλεται τὸ πνεῦμα εἰς τὸ αἷμα, ἡ δὲ ψυχὴ εἰς τὸ πνεῦμα . . . ὁ δὲ νοῦς καθαρὸς γενόμενος τῶν ἐνδυμάτων θεῖον ὢν φύσει, σώματος πυρίνου λαβόμενος περιπολεῖ πάντα τόπον, καταλιπὼν τὴν ψυχὴν κρίσει καὶ τῇ κατ᾿ ἀξίαν δίκῃ</note> We also encounter the idea of the return to the Monad <term>Monad: A term for the ultimate "One" or divine unity</term> in this context: *“Life and light are united there, where the number of the Spirit's unity is naturally found.”* <note>original: ζωὴ δὲ καὶ φῶς ἡνωμέναι ἐκεῖ εἰσιν, ἔνθα ὁ τῆς ἑνάδος ἀριθμὸς πέφυκε τοῦ πνεύματος</note>

As a further parallel, we may add the remarkable speculations in Plutarch’s *Concerning the Face Which Appears in the Orb of the Moon* 943 A B (chapter 28), 944 (chapter 30, before the passage beginning “Those former ones happen to be”), which originally stood in a related context according to the sources (2). Here too, the Mind <note>original: νοῦς (Nus)</note> is fundamentally distinguished from the Soul <note>original: ψυχή (Psyche)</note>, while the Word <term>Logos: Here used as Reason or the mediating Principle</term> stands as a middle being between the two. The Soul originates from the moon, the Mind from the sun. Through the “first death,” the soul separates from the body; through the “second death,” the Mind separates from the “shadow” <note>original: εἴδωλον (eidolon)</note> of the soul—which gradually fades away on the moon—in order to ascend to the sun. Some souls descend from the moon back to earth without the Mind. This is no trivial or permissible matter, *“whenever they take hold of the body's passivity without the Mind.”* <note>original: ὅταν ἄνευ νοῦ τῷ παθητικῷ σώματος ἐπιλάβωνται</note> There are rational and irrational souls! (943 c). The first death makes two out of the three components of man; the second makes one out of the two (a return to the Monad! compare Philo, *Life of Moses* II 288).

If the idea of the fundamental separation of Mind and Soul <note>original: νοῦς and ψυχή</note> meets us here in even more colorful mythological dress, we find the same contrast in more refined philosophical language in Porphyry's writing *To Marcella*. This is hardly surprising for a follower of a philosophical system in which Mind and Soul simultaneously appear as entities within a world-encompassing system of emanation <term>Emanation: The Neoplatonic idea that all reality flows out from a single divine source</term>. I note the following sentences: *“Let the Mind follow God, being mirrored in the likeness of God; and let the soul follow the Mind, and let the soul* [the lower soul] *serve the soul* [the higher soul]*”* (chapter 15). <note>original: ἐπέσθω τοίνυν ὁ μὲν νοῦς τῷ θεῷ, ἐνοπτριζόμενος τῇ ὁμοιώσει θεοῦ· τῷ δὲ νῷ ἡ ψυχή, τῇ δὲ αὖ ψυχῇ ὑπηρετείτω ἡ ψυχή</note> *“The divine law is unknown to a soul* <note>The original text has a typo "υπουχῇ" for "ψυχῇ"</note> *made impure through folly and lack of restraint, but it shines forth through passionlessness* <term>Apatheia: A state of being free from emotional disturbances or "passions"</term> *and wisdom; Mind alone knows it... and finding it stamped within itself, it draws nourishment from it and lights up the soul, which is as if its body. For one must posit the rational soul as the body of the Mind, which the Mind nourishes with the thoughts within it, which it has stamped and engraved from the truth of the divine law.”* <note>original: ὁ δέ γε θεῖος (νόμος) ἀγνοεῖται μὲν ψυχῇ δι᾿ ἀφροσύνην... νοῦ γὰρ σῶμα ψυχὴν λογικὴν θετέον...</note> To be sure, Porphyry depicts the relationship between Mind and Soul only from its harmonious side, and he demands above all the struggle against man's physical nature (chapters 28–33). On the other hand, however, he emphasizes that the causes of evil should be ascribed not to the flesh, but to the soul (chapter 29).

### Book III. Evagrius Studies. 328

He assigns to philosophy the task of **expelling the passion of the soul.** <note>original Greek: τὸ τῆς ψυχῆς ἐκβάλλειν πάθος</note> He speaks of the liberation of the Mind <term>Mind: translation of the Greek 'Nus', referring to the highest, most divine part of the human intellect</term> as a **running back.** ¹) <note>original: ἀνατρέχειν</note> **"Having been sent out naked, he shall call upon the one who sent him while stripped bare. For God listens only to the one who is not burdened by foreign things."** <note>original: γυμνὸς δὲ ἀποσταλεὶς γυμνητεύων καλέσει τὸν πέμψαντα. μόνον γὰρ τοῦ μὴ τοῖς ἀλλοτρίοις πεφορτισμένου ἐπήκοος ὁ θεός.</note>

We shall broaden this overview further and include psychological speculations which, while differing greatly in terminology, possess the same fundamental character. Particularly interesting here is Clement of Alexandria and the sources he employs. As far as I can see, we do not find the opposition of Mind <note>Nus</note> and Soul <note>Psyche</note> in his work. He replaces the concept of Mind almost everywhere with the concept of **Spirit.** <note>original: πνεῦμα / pneuma</note> Nevertheless, the underlying idea is present here as well: *Miscellanies* <note>original: Stromat.</note> III 92₂: **"When, therefore, no one, having indulged either anger or desire... but having stripped off the mist from these... unites spirit and soul according to the obedience of the Word (!) ... then ... there is not among you male and female. For having departed from this form ... the soul is transformed into unity."** <note>original: ὅταν οὖν μήτε τις θυμῷ μήτε ἐπιθυμίᾳ χαρισάμενος . . . ἀλλ’ ἀποδυσάμενος τὴν ἐκ τούτων ἀχλὺν . . . πνεῦμα καὶ ψυχὴν ἑνώσῃ κατὰ τὴν τοῦ λόγου (!) ὑπακοήν . . . τότε . . . οὐκ ἔνι ἐν ὑμῖν οὐκ ἄρρεν καὶ θῆλυ. ἀποστᾶσα γὰρ τοῦδε τοῦ σχήματος . . . ψυχὴ μετατίθεται εἰς ἕνωσιν.</note> III 69₄: **"According to the likeness of the Savior, you have united knowledge, faith, and love... being one from that point in judgment and truly spiritual, refusing the reasonings of anger and desire... thus the two and the three (Matthew 18:20) are gathered together into the same Gnostic man."** <note>original: κατὰ τὴν πρὸς τὸν σωτῆρα ὁμοίωσιν ἕνωσας τὴν γνῶσιν, πίστιν, ἀγάπην . . . εἷς ὢν ἐνθένδε τὴν κρίσιν καὶ πνευματικὸς ὄντως ἀπαράδεκτος τῶν κατὰ τὸν θυμὸν καὶ τὴν ἐπιθυμίαν διαλογισμῶν . . . οὕτως οἱ δύο καὶ οἱ τρεῖς (Mtth 18₂₀) ἐπὶ τὸ αὐτὸ συνάγονται τὸν γνωστικὸν ἄνθρωπον.</note> V 80₉ (Parable of the Leaven): **"For either the threefold... soul is saved through the... spiritual power placed within it, or because the power of the Word given to us... invisibly draws everyone who accepts it... toward itself and leads his entire system into unity."** ²) <note>original: ἤτοι γὰρ ἡ τριμερὴς . . . σώζεται ψυχὴ διὰ τὴν ἐγκυβεῖσαν αὐτῇ . . . πνευματικὴν δύναμιν, ἢ ὅτι ἰσχὺς τοῦ λόγου ἡ δοθεῖσα ἡμῖν . . . πάντα τὸν καταδεξάμενον . . . ἀφανῶς πρὸς αὑτὴν ἕλκει καὶ τὸ πᾶν αὐτοῦ σύστημα εἰς ἑνότητα ἄγει</note>

Even more interesting is the terminology found in a series of related passages, again in Clement. VI 52: **"Whatever has become thickened from sin, this is cast away with the fleshy spirit that desires against the soul."** <note>original: ὃ δὲ ἂν παχυμερὲς ἐκ τῆς ἁμαρτίας πεπαχυμμένον τύχῃ, τοῦτο ἀπορίπτεται σὺν τῷ σαρκικῷ πνεύματι τῷ κατὰ τῆς ψυχῆς ἐπιθυμοῦντι.</note> VII 79₆: **"But he also rises up against the bodily soul,³) putting a bit in the mouth of the unruly, irrational spirit."** <note>original: ἀλλὰ καὶ τῆς σωματικῆς ψυχῆς³) κατεξανίσταται, στόμιον ἐμβαλὼν ἐφηνιάζονti τῷ ἀλόγῳ πνεύματι.</note> VI 136: **"Through the bodily spirit, therefore, man perceives, desires, feels pleasure, gets angry, is nourished, and grows."** Further up in 134₂, alongside the five sense organs, the faculty of voice, and the faculty of reproduction, an eighth component is listed as **"spiritual according to the creation"** <note>original: *κατὰ τὴν πλάσιν πνευματικόν*</note> and all of this is contrasted with **the governing part of the soul** <note>original: τὸ ἡγεμονικὸν τῆς ψυχῆς</note> and the characteristic quality of the **Holy Spirit** which comes through faith (compare 135₃).

What is striking here is that—contrary to all typical Christian usage—the Spirit <note>Pneuma</note>, or "bodily spirit," is persistently understood as the lower soul-substance (see above, how in 134₂ this and Christian terminology clash). At the same time, we see the origin of this terminology quite clearly here. What is being presented is nothing other than the **Stoic conception** of the *Pneuma* as a material soul-substance. <term>Stoic: A school of Greek philosophy that believed the soul was a physical "breath" or "spirit" (pneuma) pervading the body.</term> The Stoic psychology, however, is overlaid with an idealistic one, and so the Stoic Pneuma (= soul-substance) appears only as a lower element within the human soul, whose overcoming is the task of the Gnostic. Thus, Clement helps us understand a whole series of psychological speculations that are otherwise difficult to interpret. We now understand the complicated psychological schema in a series of Hermetic tracts (see above): **Mind, Reason, Soul, Spirit.** <note>original: νοῦς, λόγος, ψυχή, πνεῦμα</note>

Here, anger and desire naturally belong to the **spirit**. The fall of the evil spirits stems from the fact that they were dragged down by the uncontrolled **spirit**. ³)

Schmidt. # Book III. Studies on Evagrius. 330

...destiny) in our text, we can set that aside for now. What interests us here is the **counterfeit spirit**. <note>original Greek: ἀντίμιμον πνεῦμα / antimimon pneuma</note> In this Gnostic text—just as it sees the "Power" as the source of all goodness—it views this spirit as the cause of all malice and wickedness (Schmidt p. 183 9 f.). It originates from the Archons <term>Archons: "Rulers" or planetary deities who in Gnostic thought often hinder the soul</term> of the Great Fate, <note>original: Heimarmene</note> namely the planets (183 19). It carries out their commands and performs all their evil deeds (185 35). After a person's death, it plays the role of the pursuing, punishing demon (184 13 f. 20; 193 20). Therefore, for the believers, the "mystery of the dissolving of the seals" and all the bonds of the **counterfeit spirit** is an absolute necessity (185 30; 186 1, 32). The soul that has received this mystery dismisses its adversary after death and speaks to the Archons: "There you have your counterfeit spirit... I have become a stranger to you forever" (187 33 ff.). Light-wings grow upon her soul (187 10), and she ascends to the Virgin of Light (188 12 ff.). The sacrament has separated the **counterfeit spirit** and destiny from the "soul" and the "power" (193 32 ff.).¹)

Despite the colorful apparatus of new sacramental and mythological chains of thought—for example, the well-known theory of the "cloak of vices" originating from the planets is clearly presented here, which I have treated in detail elsewhere²)—we can easily recognize the foundation: the doctrine of the inferior, naturalistic spirit <note>original: Pneuma</note> confirmed by so many witnesses.

We have still not finished our overview of these connections. I would like to point out—even if Evagrius is no longer considered here—the fact that Origen, in his work *On First Principles* (III, 4), grapples with the theory that man has two essentially separate souls, one lower and one higher: *“which some are accustomed to assert: that there is one good and celestial soul in us, but another inferior and earthly; and that the one which is better is inserted from heaven.”* <note>original Latin: quod adstruere solent quidam, quia una sit bona in nobis anima et caelestis, alia vero inferior et terrena, et quod ea quidem quae melior est, caelitus inseratur</note> Origen takes a hesitant stance toward this view; without deciding in favor of it, he does not entirely reject it. We raise the question: from what milieu does this view treated by Origen originate? Koetschau (p. 265) has pointed here to a series of statements by Clement of Alexandria. If we look closely, these are the statements discussed above, which contrast the **soul** <note>original: ψυχή / psyche</note> with the lower **spirit**. Strictly speaking, however, those are not applicable here. Rather, a fragment preserved by Clement in the *Excerpts from Theodotus* (cf. *Schulbetrieb* 169) should be mentioned: Here we find the sentence, "The material [soul] was like flesh to the divine soul." ³) <note>original Greek: ἦν τῇ ψυχῇ <τῇ> θείᾳ οἷον σὰρξ ἡ ὑλική</note> The "bone" mentioned in Genesis 2:23 is interpreted as: "it hints at the divine soul hidden in the flesh," <note>original: τὴν θείαν ψυχὴν αἰνίσσεται τὴν ἐγκεκρυμμένην τῇ σαρκί</note> while the "flesh" of Genesis 2:23 is: "the material soul being the body of the divine soul." <note>original: τὴν ὑλικὴν ψυχὴν σῶμα οὖσαν τῆς θείας ψυχῆς</note> And in section 53, 1 it says: "this is called a weed [darnel] growing together with the soul." <note>original: τοῦτο ζιζάνιον ὀνομάζεται συμφυὲς τῇ ψυχῇ</note> Accordingly, in the *Prophetic Eclogues* (25, 2), the "wheat" is interpreted as the higher essence, and the "chaff" as "that which has grown around the soul." <note>original: τὸ περιπεφυκὸς τῇ ψυχῇ</note> The uniformity of the presentation in the *Excerpts* and the *Eclogues*, and their difference from the terminology of Clement explained above, makes it extremely probable that Clement is following a source here (which, however, is hardly Valen-

<meta>This page continues the investigation into the origins of the "dual soul" doctrine, tracing it through Hermetic sources, Numenius of Apameia, and the Gnostic teacher Isidorus. # IV. Relationships of Origen's (and Evagrius') Worldview to the Historical Milieu of the Time.

To this source used by Clement is added the Hermetic source *On the Mysteries* VIII, 6: "For man has two souls... and one is from the first intelligible <term>intelligible: referring to the realm of pure thought or spirit, accessible only to the mind</term> [realm]... but the other is given from the revolution of the heavenly [spheres], into which the god-beholding soul enters." <note>original Greek: δύο γὰρ ἔχει ψυχὰς . . . ὁ ἄνθρωπος. καὶ ἡ μέν ἐστι ἀπὸ τοῦ πρώτου νοητοῦ . . . ἡ δὲ ἐνδιδομένη ἐκ τῆς τῶν οὐρανίων περιφοράς εἰς ἣν ἐπεισέρπει ἡ θεοπτικὴ ψυχή</note> Above all, however, it should be pointed out that the assumption of two souls, according to Porphyry's report (Stobaeus I 836), was put forward by Numenius of Apameia: "Others, including Numenius, do not think there are three parts of one soul, or even two... but they believe we have two souls... one rational and the other irrational." <note>original Greek: ἄλλοι δὲ ὧν καὶ Νουμήνιος, οὐ τρία μέρη ψυχῆς μιᾶς ἢ δύο γε . . . ἀλλὰ δύο ψυχὰς ἔχειν ἡμᾶς οἴονται . . . τὴν μὲν λογικὴν τὴν δὲ ἄλογον</note> According to Iamblichus (ibid. I 894),³) these souls in Numenius are in constant struggle with one another. "Others stretch these into a state of conflict, just as Numenius does." <note>original Greek: οἱ δὲ εἰς μάχην ταῦτα κατατείνοντες ὥσπερ Νουμήνιος</note> Origen may have had Numenius—whom Porphyry (see below) counts among Origen's authorities—primarily in mind during his discussions, and probably also the Alexandrian catechist whom Clement quotes in the *Excerpts* and *Eclogues*. If we now add that Clement remarks concerning the Gnostic Isidorus: "For he too assumes two souls in us, just like the Pythagoreans" (Stromat. II 113, cf. V 88 1), <note>original Greek: δύο γὰρ δὴ ψυχὰς ὑποτίθεται καὶ οὗτος ἐν ἡμῖν καθάπερ οἱ Πυθαγόρειοι</note> then once again a characteristic and sharply defined milieu stands before our eyes: Hermetic speculations in *On the Mysteries*, Numenius of Apameia, Neopythagoreans, the older authority of Clement of Alexandria, and finally Origen—who, though he enters this path only hesitantly and with reservations, nevertheless considered this doctrine important enough to devote an entire section to it in his great presentation of Christian doctrine.

It is a vibrant picture of swirling speculations that presents itself to the eye here. In the end, it is the same spectacle everywhere. Popular, mythological, astrological, and sacramental views crowd around the old psychological frameworks: fantasies of several souls possessed by man, of Fate <note>original: Heimarmene</note> and the vices originating from the planets, of the soul's journeys to the sun and moon, of the eradication of the lower elements of human nature through sacramental fire, and of the "gathering of oneself" <note>original Greek: συλλέγειν ἑαυτόν / syllegein heauton</note> of the initiate into the unity of the divine being, experienced in the consecration. All of this appears trimmed with philosophical concepts which, however, cannot master the colorful original ideas, and thus a wondrous theosophical scholasticism arises. And the witnesses of this syncretism <term>syncretism: the blending of different beliefs and schools of thought</term> are always the same: Philo of Alexandria, the Hermetica, the *Chaldean Oracles*, the Neopythagoreans, semi-philosophers like Plutarch (or his sources), Numenius of Apameia, Cronius, and ultimately the Christian Alexandrians and the Neoplatonists. Origen’s great work carries forward a wealth of this material, and Evagrius appears as an offshoot of this tradition.

Porphyry, in his characterization of Origen found in Eusebius’ *Church History* VI 19, 2 ff., states: "He was always in the company of Plato and the writings of **N u m e n i u s** and **C r o n i u s**," <note>original Greek: συνῆν τε γὰρ ἀεὶ τῷ Πλάτωνι τοῖς τε Νουμηνίου καὶ Κρονίου</note>

---

1) This phrase is reminiscent of the doctrine of the planetary vices attached to the heavenly soul (see above p. 330); this is naturally closely related to the view of the double soul, but not identical with it, and can therefore remain outside the discussion here.
2) Cf. the almost literal contact with the sentence excerpted from Origen above.
3) "Others stretch these into a state of conflict, just as Numenius does." According to Stobaeus I 896, Numenius and Cronius (!) are said to have derived evil in the soul "from that which grows upon it from without." <note>original Greek: ἀπὸ τῶν ἔξοθεν προσφυομένων</note> Is this again an allusion to the doctrine of planetary vices? Note the very similar phrases in the doctrine of the Basilidian regarding the "appendages of the soul" <note>original Greek: προαρτήματα τῆς ψυχῆς</note> and Isidore’s (son of Basilides) work *On the Attached Soul* <note>original Greek: περὶ τῆς προσφυοῦς ψυχῆς</note> in Clement, *Stromata* II 112. Cf. *Gött. G. Anz.* 736. *Main Problems of Gnosis* 365 f.

### Book III. Evagrius Studies.

"He frequented the writings of Apollophanes, Longinus, Moderatus, Nicomachus, and the famous men among the Pythagoreans. He also used the books of Chaeremon the Stoic and Cornutus, from whom he learned the figurative <term>figurative: the Greek term 'metaleptikos' refers to a method of transposing or interpreting the hidden meanings within myths</term> method of interpreting the Greek mysteries and applied it to the Jewish scriptures." <note>original Greek: Ἀπολλοφάνους τε καὶ Λογγίνου καὶ Μοδεράτου Νικομάχου τε καὶ τῶν ἐν Πυθαγορείοις ἐλλογίμων ἀνδρῶν ὡμίλει συγγράμμασιν. ἐχρῆτο δὲ καὶ Χαιρήμωνος τοῦ Στωικοῦ Κορνούτου τε ταῖς βίβλοις, παρ' ὧν τὸν μεταληπτικὸν τῶν παρ' Ἕλλησιν μυστηρίων γνοὺς τρόπον ταῖς Ἰουδαϊκαῖς προσῆψεν γραφαῖς.</note> I believe that this characterization is generally correct. And my work, which has ultimately evolved from Evagrius into an investigation of Origen's worldview, aims to encourage further research in this direction. However, it is regrettable that our sources for most of the authorities mentioned are so extremely fragmentary.

I conclude this investigation with a contribution concerning the practical-mystical piety of Evagrius, which is independent of Origen in many points. We encountered in his work (specifically in his commentator) repeatedly the confession that the mystic beholds the mysterious divine light in prayer; indeed, even more specifically, that he is able to behold his own God-illuminated (and thus renewed) soul in this mysterious light. Evagrius himself provided us with the nearest source for this view when he quotes the sentence of Basil in *Gnosticus* 147: "It is possible for even those who are still subject to passions to receive the former [knowledge], but for the second, only those who have achieved passionlessness <term>passionlessness: 'apatheia,' a state of spiritual stillness where one is no longer controlled by emotional impulses</term> are receptive; these also behold, at the time of prayer, the mind's own radiance shining around them." <note>original Greek: τὴν μὲν προτέραν (γνῶσιν) δυνατὸν καὶ τοὺς ἐμπαθεῖς ὑποδέξασθαι, τῆς δὲ δευτέρας οἱ ἀπαθεῖς μόνοι εἰσὶ δεκτικοί, οἳ καὶ παρὰ τὸν καιρὸν τῆς προσευχῆς τὸ οἰκεῖον φέγγος τοῦ νοῦ περιλάμπον αὐτοὺς θεωροῦσιν</note>

That we are facing hidden, widespread connections here is shown by a glance at Tertullian's *On the Soul*, chapter 9. Tertullian reports here of a Montanist <term>Montanist: an early Christian movement known for its emphasis on prophecy and ecstatic experiences</term> prophetess: "There is today among us a sister who has been granted gifts of revelations, which she undergoes in the church during the Lord's services through ecstasy in the spirit; she converses with angels, sometimes even with the Lord, and sees and hears mysteries, discerns the hearts of some, and provides medicine for those who desire it." <note>original Latin: est hodie soror apud nos revelationum charismata sortita, quas in ecclesia inter dominica sollemnia per ecstasin in spiritu patitur; conversatur cum angelis, aliquando etiam cum domino, et videt et audit sacramenta et quorundam corda dinoscit et medicinas desiderantibus submittit.</note> Of this sister it is said: "Among other things, she said: 'A soul was shown to me in bodily form and it appeared as a spirit, but not of an empty or void quality; rather, it was of a nature that promised to be even touchable, soft and bright and of an airy color, and in form human in every respect.'" <note>original Latin: inter cetera, inquit, ostensa est mihi anima corporalis et spiritus videbatur, sed non inanis et vacuae qualitatis, immo quae etiam teneri repromitteret, tenera et lucida et aerii coloris et forma per omnia humana.</note> To be sure, there is no clear mention here of the vision of one's own soul, and Tertullian reports the whole story with the tendency to prove his thesis of the soul's physicality. Nevertheless, similar phenomena obviously underlie this as with Evagrius.

However, in my opinion, we can venture to go back much further. We find the first traces of this peculiar light-mysticism already in such an early witness as Philo of Alexandria.

I begin the proof with a general description of this light-mysticism, which in every word reminds us of what Evagrius says about the Gnostic's experience of light during prayer. *Questions on Genesis* IV, 1: "For indeed..."

---

"...but a certain unspeakable and indescribable, truly divine solitude... but it [the soul] is in peace, in favor, the calm ruling part <term>ruling part: 'hegemonikon,' the governing part of the soul in Stoic and early Christian thought</term>, graciously riding upon its essence." <note>original Greek: ἀλλά τις ἄφατος καὶ ἀδιήγητος ἀτεχνῶς ἐρημία θεσπέσιος ... αὐτὸ δὲ ἐν εἰρήνῃ, ἐν εὐμενείᾳ, τὸ ἤρεμον τὸ ἡγεμονικόν, ἵλεων ἐποχούμενον ἐπὶ τῇ οὐσίᾳ.</note> One does not reach Him in the way one perceives the physical world, but rather as one suddenly glimpses a ship alone on the sea from a high watchtower (seeing sharply with a single glance): "Thus, someone who has gone far away from sensible things <term>sensible things: things perceived by the senses rather than the mind</term> communes alone with the Good alone, where there is neither any man... nor any body, great or small." <note>original Greek: οὕτω δή τινα ἀπελθόντα πόρρω ἀπὸ τῶν αἰσθητῶν ὁμιλῆσαι τῷ ἀγαθῷ μόνῳ μόνον, ἔνθα μήτε τις ἄνθρωπος ... μηδὲ σῶμα μέγα μηδὲ σμικρόν.</note> Compare this with what was cited above concerning Evagrius' theory of intuitive vision.

1) Gregory relates in his eulogy on Basil: (Migne 46, 809 C) "When it was night, a flash of light came to him while he was praying in his house; that light was something immaterial, illuminating the dwelling by divine power, kindled by no material thing." <note>original Greek: νυκτὸς οὔσης γίνεται αὐτῷ φωτὸς ἔλλαμψις κατὰ τὸν οἶκον προσευχομένῳ· ἄϋλον δέ τι τὸ φῶς ἐκεῖνο, θείᾳ δυνάμει καταφωτίζον τὸ οἴκημα ὑπ' οὐδενὸς πράγματος ὑλικοῦ ἐξαπτόμενον.</note> Cf. K. Holl, *Amphilochius of Iconium* 206. For the later history of light-mysticism, cf. his *Enthusiasm and Penitential Power* 181 f. 211 f.
