### IV. Relationships of the Worldview of Origen (Evagrius) to the Contemporary Milieu.

[God] is incomprehensible not only to the human race but also to all the purer parts of the entire heaven; he caused a certain splendor <note>original: *splendorem* (Greek: φέγγος)</note> to flash forth <note>original: *coruscare* (Greek: περιλάμπειν)</note> from himself, which we rightly call a "form" <note>original Latin: *formam*; suggested Greek: τύπος or σχῆμα</note>, scattering incorporeal rays around the whole mind, and filled it <note>original Latin: *adimplevit*; suggested Greek: ἐπλήρωσεν or ἐπληροφόρησεν</note> with super-celestial light. Guided by this light, the intellect is carried by means of this "form" toward the prototype. *Questions on Exodus* II 51: "In this way, may you be initiated with a worthy initiation and be able to be consecrated to God, and in some sense be a golden <note>original Latin: *aurimatum*</note> (or perhaps spiritual? <note>original Greek: πνευματικόν</note>) temple of the Father. First, with open eyes, look upon him, never closing them, and depart as one who is vigilant, free from the deep sleep in which you were previously held captive. Then may he appear visible to you, he who makes the incorporeal rays rise for you, giving visions of nature that are unexpected and inexpressible."

> *On Drunkenness* 44: "For just as the sun, upon rising, hides the stars from our vision by pouring out its own light all at once, so it is when the intelligible <term>intelligible: *noetai* in Greek, referring to realities perceived by the intellect or spirit rather than the physical senses</term> rays of the 'light-bearing' God—pure, unmixed, and far-shining—flash into the eye of the soul: it can see nothing else. For the knowledge of Being <note>original: ἡ τοῦ ὄντος ἐπιστήμη</note>, having shone forth, illuminates everything with its light." <note>1)</note>

The sentence below, though heavily stamped with philosophical terminology, reminds one of the soul’s vision of itself: "Wisdom is not only an instrument for seeing, in the manner of light, but it also sees itself. This is the archetype of God, the splendor, the imitation, and the image-sun."

It is particularly significant that Philo, in his *Questions on Exodus*, attaches this mysticism to the exact same passage (Exodus 24:10 in the Septuagint) regarding the beholding of the "place of God" <note>original Greek: τόπος τοῦ θεοῦ</note> that we encountered so frequently in the writings of Evagrius. To be sure, exact parallels are missing here; the specific "light-mysticism" is not present in this exact spot. However, Philo already relates the entire passage to the ascent of the soul to God. Regarding Exodus 24:10 (*Questions on Exodus* II 37), he remarks: "All these things are fitting and worthy of a theologian, primarily so that no one, indulging in pride, might boast of seeing the invisible God. But that same 'place' alone is holy and divine, in which he is said to have appeared—not because he himself moved away or changed his location, but by sending powers that indicate his essence, so that, if it be permitted, one ought to call that place 'rationality' <note>original Latin: *rationalitatis*</note>. For he never gave cause for suspicion of movement, but of standing perpetually, since the form remains, and the nature of the Father is immutable, clearer and simpler than unity, which is the unique form of likeness."

Philo clearly relates all of this to the inner spiritual experience of the "chosen race" (*Questions on Exodus* 24:11), and regarding the sentence in 24:11 ("they beheld God"; Septuagint: "they were seen in the place of God"), he notes: "Attaining the face of the Father, they clearly stay nowhere in a mortal place... but they arrive at the holy and divine place, which is called by another name, the Word <note>original Latin: *Verbum*; Greek: *Logos*</note>. Existing in this [Word] through the Dispenser, they see the Principal, looking upon God in a holy and constant manner with the sharp eyes of the intellect. Such an appearance is the food of the soul, and true participation in life is the cause of immortality, which is why it is also said: 'they ate and drank.'" And finally, it says in II 40 regarding 24:12: "The holy soul is noted as being deified <note>original Latin: *deificari*</note> through this ascent, not into the air or the ether or the highest heaven of all, but above all heavens."

Thus, in Philo of Alexandria, we discover the first reachable echoes of Evagrian mysticism on the soil of monotheistic pie—

1) Compare, for example, *On Migration* 39: "through which the divine light also becomes the act of seeing, being indistinguishable from knowledge <note>original: ἐπιστήμη</note>, which opens the eye of the soul." *On Dreams* I 72: "But the most radiant and far-shining light of the invisible and greatest God. When this shines upon the mind, the secondary lights of words <note>original: λόγοι</note> set" (even the "second-degree" contemplation <note>original: θεωρία</note> is often, in Evagrius, a "contemplation of the inner meanings/words of Being"). I 115: "(the mind) when it is gifted and raised to the heights, is illuminated by the archetypal and incorporeal rays of the rational fountain of the perfect God; but when it descends, it is illuminated by their images, the immortal words <note>original: λόγοις</note>, which it is the custom to call angels."

### Book III. Evagrius Studies.

[...piety], then a look into the *mysticism of Plotinus*, the Neoplatonist, can make it clear to us what it means for the mystic to behold his own soul specifically in the radiant light of the deity. *Porphyry* tells us the following episode in the *Life of Plotinus*, chapter 10: An Egyptian priest asked *Plotinus* to come with him to the Temple of *Isis* so that he might see his own *guiding spirit* <note>original Greek: *δαιμόνιον* (daimonion)</note> appear there. When the *spirit* <note>original: *Dämon*</note> was called to appear through an incantation, a god appeared who did not belong to the race of spirits. At this, the *Egyptian* cried out: "Blessed are you, for you have a god as your *attendant spirit* <note>original Latin: *Genius*</note> and not one of a lower race."

At first glance, this looks very different from the experiences of the Christian *Gnostic* and *mystic*. But fundamentally, we have identical concepts. The idea of the *guiding spirit* <term>daimonion: in Greek thought, a personal spirit or divine voice that guides an individual; similar to the Roman *genius*</term> can, as Stoic speculations among others show us, very easily transition into the idea of one's own higher, hidden *Self*. Just as the pagan mystic there is meant to behold his *spirit*, so the mystic here desires to behold his own higher *Self*. If, on the ground of polytheistic mysticism, it is said that the *spirit* is identical with a higher deity, then on monotheistic ground, the mystic sees his soul irradiated by the light of the Holy *Trinity*. The Egyptian magician leads *Plotinus* to the sacred site of *Isis* as a pure place; the Christian experiences his divine light-glory "during the time of prayer" <note>original Greek: κατὰ καιρὸν προσευχῆς</note>.

Those more primitive, polytheistic, popular ideas do not only clarify for us the genesis of Evagrian light-mysticism; we also gain an insight into the immense process of spiritualization and purification that has taken place in Christian mysticism compared to that starting point.

But this spiritualization process had already occurred on the ground of Hellenistic mysticism as well. Only now, in this context, does a mysterious word of Hermetic mysticism become clear in its connections. We read in *Hermetica* XIII, 3 (The Mystery of Rebirth) the sentence: "What can I say, my child? ... I see <at some point> an unformed vision <note>original Greek: ἄπλαστον θέαν</note> produced within me by the mercy of God, and I have gone out from myself into an immortal body, and I am not now who I was before, but I have been born in the Intellect" <note>original Greek: ἐγεννήθην ἐν νῷ</note> ¹).

Here too, the initiate <note>original: *Myste*</note> speaks of the blessed vision of the new state of being that has come to him. Even if the weight here falls on the bodily side of the new existence (the "immortal body" <note>original Greek: ἀθάνατον σῶμα</note>; compare the statement of the initiate in the so-called Mithras Mystery that he ascends to see his heavenly body), the Hermetic mystic would hardly have thought of the body as anything other than superterrestrial light. One should remember the words in *Hermetica* X, 12: "Life and light are united where the number of unity is produced by the spirit," or X, 32: "Therefore I believe and bear witness: I go into life and light" ²).

Thus, the characteristic turn of Evagrian mysticism fits into the great context of Hellenistic mysticism. Again, from—

---

1) Regarding the connection of this imagination with the idea of rebirth (*Hermetica* XIII, 14: "essential birth" <note>original Greek: οὐσιώδης γένεσις</note>), I note that Philo also has the thought of rebirth within his mystical explanations based on Exodus 24:10ff. In *Questions on Exodus* II, 46 regarding Exodus 24:16: "Moreover, the calling upward of the prophet is a second birth (or regeneration) better than the first" <note>original Latin: *sursum autem vocatio prophetae secunda est nativitas (sive regeneratio) priore melior*</note>. Compare the following: "the unmixed and simple governing soul... changed from the begotten to the unbegotten, which has no mother, but only a father... the calling upward, or as we said, the divine birth" <note>original Latin: *incommixta simplexque anima principalis . . . mutata a genita ad ingenitam, cuius non est mater, sed pater solus . . . sursum vocatio, sive ut diximus divina nativitas*</note>.

2) Compare above also the parallel between *Evagrius* and Hermetic mysticism in the description of the magnet-like effect of the divine "vision"; see above, § 13.

The author of the homilies that circulate under the name of **Makarios** <note>Saint Makarios the Egyptian, a 4th-century desert monk</note> poses the question in Book VII, section 6: "whether someone sees the soul through revelation and divine light?" <note>original Greek: *εἰ βλέπει τις δι᾿ ἀποκαλύψεως καὶ φωτὸς θείου τὴν ψυχήν;*</note> and gives the answer: "those who have been enlightened see the image of the soul, but few Christians see this." <note>original Greek: *οἱ φωτισθέντες βλέπουσι τὴν εἰκόνα τῆς ψυχῆς ἀλλὰ ταύτην ὀλίγοι ὁρῶσι χριστιανοί.*</note> And **Diadochos of Photike** <note>a 5th-century bishop and spiritual writer</note> in chapter 40 agrees: "that when the mind begins to be frequently energized by the divine light, it becomes entirely transparent, so that there is no doubt it sees its own light abundantly." <note>original Greek: *ὅτι ὁ νοῦς ὅταν ἄρξηται πυκνῶς ὑπὸ τοῦ θείου φωτὸς ἐνεργεῖσθαι, διαφανής τις ὅλος γίνεται. ὥστε τὸ ἑαυτοῦ φῶς αὐτὸν πλουσίως ὁρᾶν, οὐ δεῖ ἀμφιβάλ- λειν.*</note> The **Messalians** <note>a radical ascetic group accused of heresy for claiming to physically "see" God</note> likely had similar, though crudely sensory, experiences in mind when they stated, according to **Theodoret** <note>Theodoret of Cyrus, a 5th-century church historian</note> in Book IV, chapter 10: "then the Holy Spirit visits sensibly and visibly, signifying its own presence." <note>original Greek: *ἐπιφοιτᾷ λοιπὸν τὸ ἅγιον πνεῦμα αἰσθητῶς καὶ ὁρατῶς τὴν οἰκείαν παρουσίαν σημαίνων.*</note>

## V. The Letter of Evagrius Handed Down under the Name of Basil.

The last letter of the collection of **Evagrian** <note>referring to Evagrius Ponticus, 345–399 AD</note> letters published by Frankenberg from the Syriac and retro-translated into Greek is found, as Frankenberg himself later saw and noted, as Number 8 in the letter collection of **Basil** <note>Basil the Great, Bishop of Caesarea (330–379 AD)</note> (Migne PG 32. 245–268 <note>referring to the *Patrologia Graeca*, a standard collection of the writings of the Greek Church Fathers</note>). Frankenberg assumes without further ado the authenticity of the Syrian tradition in favor of **Evagrios**. However, given the importance of this document—I know of no more important piece preserved for us in the Greek language by **Evagrios** than this—it will be worthwhile to investigate the critical question more closely and examine which tradition is correct. And there can indeed be no doubt that our letter belongs to **Evagrios** and not to **Basil**. Already the external milieu of the same does not fit well into the life of **Basil**. The author of the letter writes to a community whom he addresses in chapter 2 as "my divine and most beloved heads of all." <note>original Greek: *θεῖαί μου καὶ προσφιλέσταται πασῶν κεφαλαί*</note> He excuses himself for having run away from their community: "I confess that I have become a fugitive." <note>original Greek: *ἐγὼ δὲ τὸ μὲν φυγὰς γεγονέναι ὁμολογῶ.*</note> For a long time, he was so startled by his deed, as one is paralyzed by terror at unexpected noises, and therefore he persisted in his flight ("I went far away in flight") <note>original Greek: *ἐμάκρυνα φυγαδεύων*</note>. Afterward, however, the longing for the "divine teachings" <note>original Greek: *θεῖα δόγματα*</note> and the "philosophy concerning those things" <note>original Greek: *περὶ ἐκεῖνα φιλοσοφία*</note> seized him. And in **Gregorios** <note>Gregory of Nazianzus, one of the Cappadocian Fathers</note> ("the mouth of Christ") <note>original Greek: *τὸ τοῦ Χριστοῦ στόμα*</note> he has found an exquisite vessel and a deep well in this regard. Therefore, he asks for patience if he remains away for a while longer. It is not the stay in the cities, but the fellowship with **Gregory** that captivates him. He wishes "to gain a state of contemplation that is hard to lose." <note>original Greek: *ἕξιν δυσαπόβλητον θεωρημάτων λαμβάνειν.*</note>

According to the heading in the Greek tradition, the letter is supposedly addressed to the people of **Caesarea** and contains an **apology** <term>apologia: a formal written defense of one's opinions or conduct</term> of **Basil** "concerning his withdrawal." <note>original Greek: *περὶ ἀποχωρήσεως*</note> The **Maurists** <note>a congregation of French Benedictine monks known for their high standards of scholarship</note> (1) rightly remark that the content contradicts the heading; the letter could not have been written to the people of **Caesarea**, but was written to a monastic community. It also contains no defense of, for example, the author's flight into solitude from the city (**Caesarea**), but precisely the flight from **withdrawal** <term>anachoresis: the act of withdrawing from society to live as a hermit</term> into the city. How could the author write to a city population that he had fled: "not embracing the stay in the cities, for it has not escaped our notice that the evil one works deception on humans through such things." <note>original Greek: *οὐ τὴν ἐν ταῖς πόλεσι διατριβὴν ἀσπαζόμενοι οὐδὲ γὰρ λέληθεν ἡμᾶς ὁ πο- νηρὸς διὰ τῶν τοιούτων τὴν ἀπάτην τοῖς ἀνθρώποις ποιούμενος.*</note> — Finally, there is the relationship in which the author finds himself here with the aforementioned **Gregorios**...

### Book III. Evagrius Studies.

represents, throughout, that of a dependent scribe. If the *Gregory* mentioned here refers to *Gregory of Nazianzus* <note>a 4th-century Archbishop and theologian, one of the "Cappadocian Fathers"</note>, then the author could not, in turn, be *Basil*.

Can we, on the other hand, place the letter within the life of *Evagrius*? We know for a fact that he was closely connected with *Gregory of Nazianzus* in his youth, that Gregory made him a deacon (after *Basil's* death) and took him to Constantinople for the Great Synod. (*Lausiac History 38* <note>a collection of biographies of early Christian monks, written c. 419–420 by Palladius</note>). If this letter is indeed by *Evagrius*, it must have been written before that event, and we may assume with some probability that he was with *Gregory of Nazianzus* in Constantinople at the time. However, the letter seems to indicate that the author had run away from a monastic community and was therefore apologizing. Was *Evagrius* already a monk before his stay with *Gregory* and his time in Constantinople, only returning to monasticism after those dark experiences in Constantinople of which the *Lausiac History* tells us? The *Lausiac History* and the sources dependent on it know nothing of this. I believe, however, that this suspicion can now indeed be proven.

The commentator of *Evagrius*, *Mar Babai* <note>Babai the Great, a 6th-7th century monk of the Church of the East</note>, informs us—entirely dependent, by the way, on the *Lausiac History* in the introduction to his commentary (*Frankenberg* <note>refers to Wilhelm Frankenberg’s 1912 scholarly edition of Evagrius</note> p. 20/21)—about the life fortunes of his hero. He tells us here that Saint *Basil of Caesarea* <note>Basil the Great, known for his monastic rules</note> had made him a lector <note>an appointed reader in the church, a minor clerical rank</note> (following the *Lausiac History*). On this occasion, however, he thankfully mentions a letter that *Evagrius* wrote to *Basil* at that time and quotes a sentence from it. This information makes it possible for us to find the letter again in the collection published by *Frankenberg*, in which, unfortunately, the names of the addressees are missing throughout. It is found there under No. 22 (*Frankenberg* 581). And here, in a letter to *Basil*, we find the remarkable sentence that *Mar Babai* quotes in his introduction: "However, I glorify our Lord and the day of His resurrection, on which you gave me the holy habit <note>original Greek: *σχῆμα* (schema) — the distinctive garment of a monk</note> and joined me to the number of the monks." <note>original: *πλὴν δοξάζω τὸν κύριον ἡμῶν καὶ τὴν ἡμέραν τῆς ἀναστάσεως αὐτοῦ, ᾗ μοι τὸ ἅγιον σχῆμα δέδωκάς τε καὶ τῷ τῶν μονάχων ἀριθμῷ συνέμιξας.*</note> — According to this letter, *Basil* did in fact receive *Evagrius* into his monastic community. The note that *Mar Babai*¹)—following the *Lausiac History*—links to this, stating that he made him a lector, will be correct, but it contains only half the facts. The full truth—that *Evagrius* was already a runaway monk in Constantinople—will have been suppressed by the *Lausiac History* in his favor. Thus we perhaps also understand the remark in the *History* that he was made a deacon by *Gregory* after *Basil's* death. It is unlikely that *Gregory of Nazianzus* would have taken such a position toward a monk who had left *Basil's* monastic community during the latter's lifetime.

Now, the letter to *Basil* and the letter we are to treat confirm each other. There can hardly be any doubt about it. We obtain a new, important date for the life and development of *Evagrius*. *Basil* received him into his monastic community and made him a lector within it. After the death of *Basil*, however, *Evagrius* went off and away—we do not know exactly for what reasons. He came to *Gregory of Nazianzus*, who through his theological wisdom—

### V. The letter of Evagrius transmitted under the name of Basil. 337

completely captivated and imprisoned him. In this situation, he writes the extensive present letter to his old monastic community, asks for forgiveness for devoting himself for so long to the instruction and personal contact with Gregory, and at the same time presents a sample of his theological skill.

That the great letter was therefore written by Evagrius and strayed into the letter collection of Basil should by now be beyond doubt. However, it also emerges with desirable clarity from its content down to every detail. We turn now to this proof.

And here we encounter the sentences, already used many times above in the summary presentation, regarding the divine Monad <note>original: *Monas*; a term for the ultimate "One" or divine unity</note> and its opposition to all number. The deity is **simple and uncompounded** <note>original: *ἁπλοῦς καὶ ἀσύνθετος* (haplous kai asynthetos)</note>; they are therefore not **one in number** <note>original: *εἷς τῷ ἀριθμῷ* (heis tō arithmō)</note>. Neither the world, nor man consisting of body and soul, nor the angels—whose *hypostasis* <term>hypostasis: the individual reality or "personhood" of a being</term> is "**essence with sanctification**" <note>original: *οὐσία μεθ' ἁγιασμοῦ* (ousia meth' hagiasmou)</note>—are units by nature (essential unity), even though we apply the number one to them. Thus, we must completely exclude number altogether from "the blessed nature that is recognizable only by the intellect." Number belongs to the world of **quantities** <note>original: *τοῦ ποσοῦ* (tou posou)</note>. It designates the **material** <note>original: *ἔνυλον* (enylon)</note> and **definable** <note>original: *περιγραπτήν* (perigraptēn)</note> nature: **But the Monad and the Unity are indicative of the simple and incomprehensible essence.** <note>original: *ἡ δὲ Μονὰς καὶ Ἑνὰς τῆς ἁπλῆς καὶ ἀπεριλήπτου οὐσίας ἐστὶ σημαντική*</note>. Whoever turns the Son of God into a number (!) or a creature introduces, in secret, a **material and definable nature** <note>original: *ἔνυλον καὶ περιγραπτὴν φύσιν*</note>.

As far as I can see, such characteristic and deep-reaching explanations are hardly found in Basil (or the other Cappadocians <note>a group of influential 4th-century Greek theologians including Basil the Great, Gregory of Nazianzus, and Gregory of Nyssa</note>). On the other hand, we find none of the peculiarities of Cappadocian trinitarian theology in the letter: nothing of the fundamental distinction between *ousia* <term>ousia: "essence" or "substance," what God is</term> and *hypostasis* <term>hypostasis: "person," who the Father, Son, and Spirit are</term>, and nothing of the **properties** <note>original: *ἰδιότητες* (idiotetes)</note> and **dignities** <note>original: *ἀξιώματα* (axiomata)</note> of the Hypostases. However, that the line of thought sketched above fits entirely into the overall worldview of Evagrius has been sufficiently proven in the previous presentation (§ 1).

The following explanations (Chapter 3) seem equally un-Cappadocian to us. One can apply neither the attribute **like** nor **unlike** to the Son. For these terms belong to the world of **qualities**: **the divine is free from quality.** <note>original: *ποιότητος δὲ τὸ θεῖον ἐλεύθερον*</note>. Therefore: **confessing the identity of nature, we accept the "consubstantial" and flee from what is composite.** <note>original: *ταυτότητα δὲ τῆς φύσεως ὁμολογοῦντες καὶ τὸ ὁμοούσιον ἐκδεχόμεθα καὶ τὸ σύνθετον φεύγομεν*</note>. Again, we find no trace of the distinction between *ousia* and *hypostasis*. Accordingly, the "homousie" <note>the doctrine that the Son is of the same substance as the Father</note> is understood in the sense of **identity** <note>original: *ταυτότης* (tautotes)</note>. And the explanation that the deity stands beyond all quality corresponds entirely to its opposition to all number.

With Chapter 4, the letter writer turns to the biblical evidence of his opponents. In general, this biblical proof rests on the principle established at the end of Chapter 3 (252 c.): **being careful of the Holy Spirit so that... attending to the theology, we do not despise the economy.**<sup>1)</sup> <note>original: *ἀσφαλιζόμενος τοῦ Πν. ἁγ. ἵνα μὴ . . . τῇ θεολογίᾳ προσέχοντες τῆς οἰκονομίας καταφρονῶμεν*</note>. This means that one must distinguish exactly whether the statements of Scripture refer to the divine essence of the Logos or to his human appearance on earth. This is, admittedly, also the explicit principle of Basil.<sup>2)</sup>

Compare, for instance: Gregory of Nazianzus, Migne II 589 C (concerning the Evangelists): **some were more preoccupied with the fleshly aspect of Jesus, while others proceeded to the theology.** <note>original: *οἱ μὲν τῷ σαρκικῷ τοῦ Ἰησοῦ πλέον ἐνησχολήθησαν, οἱ δὲ τῇ θεολογίᾳ προσέβησαν*</note>. ### Book III. Evagrios Studies.

This principle is, of course, much older, and we can with equal right already attribute it to Origen. Furthermore, it is characteristic of the exegetical procedure of the letter that it does not pursue the principle one-sidedly, but seeks to address the errors of the opponents from various sides¹).

The author of the letter (c. 4 253 B) places the saying of John 6:57b (in contrast to 6:57a) within the realm of "theology" <term>theology: in this context, the study of the internal nature of God, distinct from His actions in history</term>. And he gives the following explanation for it: "For by 'flesh and blood' he named his entire mystical advent, and he revealed the teaching consisting of the practical, the natural, and the theological, by which the soul is nourished and prepared for the temporary contemplation of beings." <note>original: σάρκα γὰρ καὶ αἷμα πᾶσαν αὐτοῦ τὴν μυστικὴν ἐπιδημίαν ὠνόμασε, καὶ ἐκ τῆς πρακτικῆς καὶ φυσικῆς καὶ θεολογικῆς συνεστῶσαν διδασκαλίαν ἐδήλωσε δι’ ἧς τρέφεται ἡ ψυχὴ καὶ πρὸς τὴν τῶν ὄντων τέως θεωρίαν παρασκευάζεται</note>. It requires no further proof (see above, § 10) that this sentence is Evagrian.

In the treatment of the passage Mark 13:32 ²) regarding the ignorance of the Son, the author of the letter first (c. 6) follows the well-trodden path (see above). But then he continues: "And let these things be said more **thickly** <note>original: παχύτερον (pachyteron); meaning a literal or material interpretation</note> according to the first approach³). But now we must examine the meaning of the saying more loftily and knock on the door of knowledge" <note>original: καὶ ταῦτα μὲν κατὰ τὴν προτέραν ἐπιβολὴν εἰρήσθω παχύτερον. ἤδη δὲ ἐξεταστέον ὑψηλότερον τὴν διάνοιαν τοῦ ῥητοῦ καὶ κρουστέον τὴν θύραν τῆς γνώσεως</note> ⁴).

Now he begins (c. 7) the gnostic, allegorical interpretation of the saying in the situation described by Mark, where the disciples of Jesus, "having been purified by the Word, seek the end and desire to know the ultimate blessedness" <note>original: καθαρθέντες ἀπὸ τοῦ λόγου τὸ τέλος ἐπιζητοῦσι καὶ τὴν ἐσχάτη μακαριότητα (s. o. § 13) γνῶναι ποθοῦσιν</note>. There, the Lord emphasized the difficulty of reaching this *Gnosis* <term>Gnosis: higher spiritual knowledge or insight</term>. The "day" is "the entire accurate comprehension of the conceptions of God," and the "hour" is "the contemplation of the Enad and Monad <term>Enad and Monad: terms for the ultimate, indivisible unity of God</term>, the knowledge of which he assigned to the Father alone." In this context, we now encounter—at least applied to the earthly mode of existence of the Logos—a decidedly subordinationist <term>subordinationist: the belief that the Son is secondary or subordinate to the Father in nature</term> sentence: "Our Lord, according to the conception of the incarnation and the thicker (see above) teaching, is not the ultimate object of desire. Therefore, our Savior does not know the end and the ultimate blessedness." It is again immensely characteristic here how **Holl**, from his penetrating knowledge of Basil, judges our specific passage: he suggests that in one of his earliest writings, Basil actually **fell back** into the Origenist idea ⁵) that the knowledge mediated through the historical Christ was not yet the absolute one. What we actually have here is the doctrine of the "Origenist Evagrius." We hear him quite clearly also in the following sentence: "But neither do the angels know, he says; that is, neither the contemplation within them nor the reasons for their ministries are the ultimate object of desire. For even their knowledge is thick in comparison to that which is 'face to face.' But only the Father knows, he says, since he himself is the end and the ultimate blessedness" ⁶).

The following sentence is again Evagrian in every word: "For they say that the kingdom of Christ is **material knowledge**, but that of God the Father is **immaterial** <note>original: ἄϋλον (aylon)</note>¹) and, as one might say, the contemplation of the Godhead itself . . . for what does he say in the Gospel? 'And I will raise him up on the last day'; calling the 'resurrection' the transition from material knowledge to immaterial contemplation, and calling the 'last day' that knowledge after which there is no other; for at that time our mind <term>mind: original 'νοῦς' (nous); the highest faculty of the soul capable of knowing God</term> rises up and is stirred toward the blessed height, whenever it *contemplates* the *unity* and the *oneness* of the *Word* (257 B C)." <note>original: Χριστοῦ γὰρ βασιλείαν φασὶν εἶναι τὴν ἔνυλον γνῶσιν, τοῦ δὲ θεοῦ καὶ πατρὸς τὴν ἄϋλον . . . ἀνάστασιν λέγων τὴν ἀπὸ τῆς ἔνυλου γνώσεως ἐπὶ τὴν ἄϋλον θεωρίαν μετάβασιν . . . ὁπηνίκα ἂν θεωρήσῃ τὴν ἑνάδα καὶ μονάδα τοῦ Λόγου</note>

I cite as parallels *Tractate 69*: "Christ raises the rational nature, which was deadened by vice, through the contemplation of all the ages²) <note>original: διὰ τῆς θεωρίας πάντων τῶν αἰώνων</note>, but his Father raises the soul that has died the death of Christ through the knowledge of Himself." *Centuries VII 24*: "Christ raises the rational nature, which had died to righteousness, through the contemplation of all the ages (Frankenberg reads *worlds*)²), but the Father raises the soul that has died from death through the knowledge of Himself" (cf. V 19. 22).

When it then says in the following (260 B): "Do not think of 'times and seasons' as being perceptible to the senses, but rather as certain intervals of knowledge produced by the **intelligible sun**"³) <note>original: διαστήματά τινα γνώσεως ὑπὸ τοῦ νοητοῦ ἡλίου</note>, the style and thought of Evagrius are again unmistakable. Likewise in the remark on John 6:72: "and the number is lost in the arrival of the Oneness."

The conclusion of the refutation of the biblical objections of the opponents in chapters 8—9⁴) contains nothing especially worth considering. I only highlight the last sentence (261 B): "And again, all creatures either consist of opposites or are receptive to opposites; but the Son is **justice itself**⁵) <note>original: αὐτοδικαιοσύνη (autodikaiosunē)</note> and is immaterial"—and note the parallel *Centuries I 4*: "Everything that has come into being is either receptive to opposition or consists of opposites" (Frankenberg reads *is established*).

With chapter 10, Evagrius—here a student of the Cappadocians <note>The Cappadocian Fathers: Basil the Great, Gregory of Nazianzus, and Gregory of Nyssa</note>—turns to the defense of the "same essence" (*homousia*) of the Spirit. I note here once more the sentences mentioned above in which—likely following Origenist thoughts—it is rejected that the Spirit "possesses holiness as something acquired" (251 C), or that he is composite (like the angels) "out of essence and sanctification" (264 B); further, that the devil "fell away from the **Monad**" <note>original: τῆς Μονάδος (tēs Monados); refers to the primordial divine unity</note> (264 A); and finally, the opposition of the simplicity of the divine being against that which is "one in number" (264 A).

In chapter 11, the writer of the letter determines the various spheres of activity of the three persons of the Trinity: "We have found three 'creations' named in the Scripture: one and first, the leading forth from non-being into being; second, the alteration from the worse to the better; third, the resurrection of the dead; in these, the Holy Spirit works as a benefactor alongside the Father and the Son." Should this sentence not be based on the decidedly **subordinationist** <term>subordinationist: the heretical view that the Son and Spirit are inferior in nature to the Father</term> line of thought in Origen's *On First Principles* I 3, 6: "God the Father, holding all things together . . . imparting to each from his own that they exist; but the Son, being less than the Father, reaching only to rational beings . . . and still less the Holy Spirit, reaching only the holy ones"⁶). ### Book III. Evagrius Studies.

The thought is certainly bent thoroughly in favor of the dogma of **consubstantiality** <note>original: "homousie" (the doctrine that the Father and Son are of the same substance)</note> by emphasizing the Spirit’s cooperation in all three creations.

In passing, I also mention a remarkable sentence in chapter 11. To prove the divinity of the Holy Spirit, the letter's author begins with a definition: "For God is named either from his having **placed** all things or from his **beholding** all things" <note>original: "παρὰ γὰρ τὸ τεθεικέναι τὰ πάντα ἢ θεᾶσθαι τὰ πάντα ὁ θεὸς ὀνομάζεται" (para gar to tettheikenai ta panta e theasthai ta panta ho theos onomazetai)</note> (265 A). Where might he have gotten this sentence? This double etymology <term>etymology: the study of the origin and history of words</term> is, as far as I can see, less common among the Greeks than the widespread derivation of the word *God* <note>original: θεός (theos)</note> from *beholding* <note>original: θέα (thea)</note>¹), which itself stems from astral religion. I note the partial parallel in Plutarch’s *On Isis and Osiris* 60: "Just as for all the gods, from two letters, the name is common from that which is **beheld** and that which **runs**" <note>original: "ὥσπερ τοῖς θεοῖς πᾶσιν ἀπὸ δύο γραμμάτων τοῦ θεατοῦ καὶ τοῦ θέοντός ἐστιν ὄνομα καινόν" (hosper tois theois pasin apo dyo grammaton tou theatou kai tou theontos estin onoma kainon)</note> ²).

Regarding the sentence at 265 A: "If the sword of the Spirit is the word of God, the Holy Spirit is God," one might compare *Centuries* V, 28: "A spiritual sword is a spiritual word, which separates the soul from the body..."

With chapter 12, the letter hastens to its conclusion. We clearly recognize the pen of Evagrius when 265 C says: "And do not think, brothers, that the **kingdom of heaven** is anything other than the **true contemplation of beings**, which the divine scriptures also call 'blessedness'" <note>original: "καὶ μηδὲ ἀλλά τι, ἀδελφοί, τὴν βασιλείαν τῶν οὐρανῶν νομίσητε ἢ τὴν τῶν ὄντων ἀληθῆ κατανόησιν, ἣν καὶ μακαριότητα ὀνομάζουσιν αἱ θεῖαι γραφαί"</note> (compare *Tractates* 2 and 3³). At the end of the chapter, we find the comparison already extracted above (§ 10) of the ant and the bee (Proverbs 6:6) with the **practical way** <note>original: "πρακτικὴ ὁδός" (praktike hodos); the path of ascetic practice and virtue</note> and **natural contemplation** <note>original: "φυσικὴ θεωρία" (physike theoria); the spiritual knowledge of the created world</note>, "in which the word concerning the Holy Trinity is also mingled."

With all this, in my opinion, the proof is irreproachably established that the great missive, which has been preserved for us in Greek as the eighth letter of Basil, is to be attributed to Evagrius. This is, first of all, a highly valuable result for the assessment of the Basilian collection of letters. But it is even more valuable for Evagrian research. We thereby obtain a substantial document transmitted in Greek that allows us to look deeply into Evagrius’s terminology and literary character. Furthermore, we obtain a document that dates from his youth—from his pre-monastic, or more precisely, from the period between his first and second monastic phases and his pre-mystic early period in Constantinople. The Evagrius of this letter is interested in dogma in a completely different way than the later monk and theorist of prayer. Here he shows himself as a pupil and follower of the **Cappadocians** <note>The "Cappadocians" refers to the influential theologians Basil the Great, Gregory of Nazianzus, and Gregory of Nyssa</note>. Yet again, he proves to be a quite independent spirit compared to them, and already here we discover everywhere the reason for this independence: a much stronger and more immediate return to their common great teacher, **Origen**. Finally, a new, unknown piece of the early history of this interesting man has been revealed to us here in a surprising way.

I will add another small observation here. In both the collection of letters of Gregory of Nazianzus (No. 243) and that of Gregory of Nyssa (No. 26), a letter to a monk named Evagrius has been preserved. The same letter appears in the Syriac tradition as the property of Gregory the Wonderworker. Thus, the tradition leaves us a choice between three Gregories in determining the author of this letter, and researchers consequently waver in their judgment. I believe, however, that we...

# V. The Letter of Evagrius Transmitted under the Name of Basil.

We can also reach a definite conclusion here. For I believe I can demonstrate that the recipient of the letter, **Evagrius the Monk** <note>original: "Εὐάγριος μόναχος" (Euagrios monachos)</note>, is none other than our Evagrius. This Evagrius, in fact, posed the following question to the letter-writer (cf. the text in Migne <note>Migne refers to the *Patrologia Graeca*, a massive 19th-century collection of Greek Church Father writings</note> 46, 1101 A):

"In what way might the nature of the Father, Son, and Holy Spirit be—which one might more correctly call essence <term>essence: Greek *ousia*, the fundamental 'whatness' or being of God</term> rather than nature—whether it is simple or composite? For if it is simple, how will it admit the number of the three mentioned? For that which is **simple is uniform and beyond number** <note>original: "ἁπλοῦν μονοειδὲς καὶ ἀνάριθμον" (haploun monoeides kai anarithmon)</note>, but that which is subject to numbers must be divided, even if it is not [initially] subjected to them. And that which is divided is passible <term>passible: from the Greek *pathos*, meaning capable of being acted upon, changed, or suffering</term>; for division is a passion. If, therefore, the nature of the Better <note>original: "τοῦ κρείττονος" (tou kreittonos), a common philosophical way to refer to the Divine</note> is simple, the assignment of names is superfluous. But if the assignment of names is true . . . it seeks the uniform and simple."

Now the letter-writer strives—generally not very successfully or penetratingly—to dispel the questioner's doubts. His main thesis (1104 B) is: "For the assignment of names will not harm the indivisible union of the Better" <note>original: "τὴν γὰρ ἀμερῆ τοῦ κρείττονος ἕνωσιν οὐ καταβλάψει τῶν ὀνομάτων ἡ θέσις"</note>. In his view, these **names** <note>original: "ὀνόματα" (onomata)</note> are merely improper designations that do not strike the true essence of things: "since no sovereign name exists for things intelligible and incorporeal" <note>original: "ἐπειδὴ κύριον ὄνομα τῶν νοητῶν τε καὶ ἀσωμάτων οὐδέν"</note>. He argues that one also gives names to the human soul, yet it remains a unity; a spring divides into two streams and yet remains a unity, and so on.

As stated, the answer is very little characteristic. The phrasing of the question, however, is all the more characteristic. And I believe, after all that has been said previously, one recognizes Evagrius in the questioner. It is his style and his terminology present here. To be sure, he is still wrestling with his thoughts here; the problem is not yet solved for him. He has not yet reached the conclusion that the essence of the divine Monad <term>Monad: the ultimate, indivisible 'One' or unity</term> lies beyond all number, and that therefore the distinction between Father, Son, and Spirit cannot be understood under the category of number. But his thoughts are moving in this direction. I would like to place Evagrius's inquiry very early in his career (his first monastic period), and the respondent in this present letter would then be none other than **Gregory of Nazianzus** <note>One of the "Cappadocian Fathers," a famous 4th-century theologian and friend of Basil the Great</note> (see the introduction of the letter just discussed). That the characteristics of Gregory's theology are hardly found in the letter may be due to the unusual nature of the question.

One might only be concerned that Gregory, in his *Oration 31*—as I learn from Holl's *Amphilochius of Iconium*, p. 175—sets aside the images common among the "Old Nicenes" <note>Theologians who strictly followed the Creed of Nicaea (325 AD) but sometimes used older, less precise metaphors for the Trinity</note> . . . **fountain, river, sun, light** <note>original: "πηγή, ποταμός, ἥλιος, φῶς" (pege, potamos, helios, phos)</note>, which appear precisely at the end of the letter, as inappropriate. But Gregory admits here at the same time that he knows of no other suitable image (Holl 176). Thus, he may have made use of them again in another place. On the other hand, Holl (p. 176) emphasizes that Gregory liked to use a psychological schema for the representation of the Trinity. And the psychological schema (though not **intellect, word, spirit** <note>original: "νοῦς λόγος πνεῦμα" (nous logos pneuma)</note>, but rather **intellect, reflection, soul** <note>original: "νοῦς ἐνθύμησις ψυχή" (nous enthumesis psuche)</note>) plays the main role in the letter.

<summary>This page argues that a letter traditionally attributed to Basil the Great was actually a correspondence between a young Evagrius Ponticus and Gregory of Nazianzus. The author bases this on the philosophical style of the questions regarding how God can be both a "simple" unity and a Trinity of three persons.</summary>
<keywords>Evagrius Ponticus, Basil the Great, Gregory of Nazianzus, Trinity, Essence, Ousia, Simple Nature, Monad, Nicene Theology, Psychological Schema, Patristics</keywords>

## ERMAN-RANKE

# EGYPT

## AND EGYPTIAN LIFE IN ANTIQUITY

->*<-

->With a color frontispiece, 100 illustrations on 42 plates,<-
->as well as 276 line drawings, 2 maps, and script samples<-
->within the text. Base value 37.5; in elegant full cloth binding 45<-
<note>The "Base value" (Grundzahl) was a system used during the German hyperinflation of 1923 to set stable prices that were then multiplied by a daily exchange rate.</note>

. . . It is currently considered the preeminent book on Egypt, offering an extraordinary amount to both the layperson and the scholar. The great value of this exemplary publication lies precisely in the fact that everyone receives an absolutely clear picture; one can begin reading without any prior knowledge, while the scholar simultaneously gains a wealth of inspiration. This is achieved by documenting all the research results produced by German and foreign Egyptologists between the years 1886 and 1922 . . . If Erman’s merit lies in the fact that he was the first to write a readable book about Egypt—not merely building on the research of others, but often having to conduct it himself—then it is no less a merit of Ranke that he provided the content to bring this established work up to the level of modern research while fully preserving its original character and structure. . . . The 20 chapters provide information on all aspects of Egyptian culture: the history of the land and its people, their customs and traditions, family life, science, art, and craftsmanship. One is enthralled from the first word to the last. It often reads like a great epic dedicated to this great, culturally sophisticated people. The inclusion of Egyptian fairy tales, recorded almost verbatim, is also very valuable. An excellent subject index facilitates later reference. The scholar will find further material in the list of cited text passages. Here, and in the list of abbreviations (12 pages), one can truly appreciate the enormous amount of material that has been processed. This work is new proof of German thoroughness <note>original: "deutsche Gründlichkeit"</note>, but also demonstrates that German scholars understand how to write scientific books in a form that speaks to everyone. Special recognition is also deserved by the immensely active publisher, who has recently released many exemplary publications and has once again proven its capability with this one. Good paper, clear print, and excellent plates are the great advantages of this work—qualities that are particularly valued today and, unfortunately, often missed.

->*Dr. W. Schmidt in the Frankfurter Zeitung <note>A major German newspaper of the era</note> No. 8 from August 26, 1923.*<-

->*<-

->*The domestic price is determined by multiplying the base value listed under the title by the "key number" <term>key number: German *Schlüsselzahl*, a multiplier used during hyperinflation to calculate the actual price in Marks</term> set by the boards of the Exchange Association of German Booksellers and the German Publishers Association, which can be found in any bookstore. International prices are calculated based on the ratio of 1 base value = 1.25 Swiss Francs, according to the conversion table recommended by the Exchange Association of German Booksellers.*<-

# **A. DEISSMANN / LIGHT FROM THE EAST**

The New Testament and the newly discovered texts of the

> That this well-known work has been able to appear in a new, somewhat expanded edition is due not only to its again excellent production and its beautiful prose, but above all to its content, which will increasingly assert itself as an indispensable key to the New Testament alongside older and newer works. The biblical documents almost all bear the mark of their origin from the non-literary strata of popular life: many details of the language, the formal world, and the framing of the documents of early Christianity receive surprising illumination from the everyday world of Hellenistic popular life, as it reveals itself to us ever more clearly and movingly from thousands of shards, letter fragments, and monuments. These insights can be recorded as a lasting achievement of Deissmann’s work, which has succeeded in placing details and trifles into a larger context and making them fruitful for the understanding of early Christian documents.
